Title: $2 Million+ Drained From Polymarket Traders in New Supply Chain Attack
Context: According to the prediction market’s status page, the exchange was first switched to cancel-only mode, with relayer actions suspended
Full Text:
Polymarket halted trading on its international platform on October 29 after users reported unauthorized withdrawals.

According to the prediction market’s status page, the exchange was first switched to cancel-only mode, with relayer actions suspended.

“We’ve identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole,” the company said.

Trading resumed about an hour later, and Polymarket pledged to reimburse all affected traders. It has not named the vendor or disclosed losses.

Researchers have linked the theft to malicious code served from DebugBear, a UK-based website performance monitoring firm. Polymarket’s US platform was reportedly unaffected.

DebugBear confirmed being “impacted by an ongoing security incident” and urged users of its real user monitoring (RUM) product to pull its snippet from their websites. It also said it brought in specialist incident responders.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Hudson Rock obtained a copy of the malicious JavaScript from a DebugBear address used by Polymarket. The code hunted for a logged-in user’s trading tools and portfolio. Depending on the account type, it then tried either to sell positions and move the proceeds, or to send position tokens straight to an attacker-set address.

“The sample reads credential-related material, but our review did not identify a routine that sends the credential map, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to its reporting endpoint. Its central approach is to reuse authority already available in the authenticated application,” Hudson Rock said.

The firm also spotted a Polymarket production build, timestamped 17:59 UTC, with a change note about removing the DebugBear script.

Loss figures vary. A screenshot reviewed by Hudson Rock showed about $2.19 million at the script’s hard-coded fallback address, though the firm said this is not a verified tally.

Blockchain security firm GoPlus, which also attributed the attack to a supply chain compromise of DebugBear’s RUM script, puts losses at roughly $2.71 million. According to its on-chain analysis, the main attack path ran through 710 deposit wallets and 731 addresses, though the address count does not equal the number of victims.

Arkham data showed a suspected attacker wallet holding approximately $2.65 million. That is the same address hardcoded in the script as its fallback recipient.

Hudson Rock has not determined how the script was tampered with or how many users were hit. Its findings do not indicate that other DebugBear customers were targeted.

The attack came the same day Binance was hit by a roughly $6 billion hack that blockchain intelligence firms have attributed to North Korea. In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, with losses reported at around $3 million.

Title: Open-weight AI model GLM-5.3 cheated its way to correct answers
Context: 3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an LLM’s ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic...
Full Text:
Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security

October 30, 2026

Share

Open-weight AI model GLM-5.3 cheated its way to correct answers

Irregular evaluated Zhipu AI’s open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an LLM’s ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic constraints.

The model refused none of the tasks and completed three scenarios at least once each, carrying attacks through dependent stages to reach objectives in simulated networks. Irregular said this was the strongest result it had recorded for an open-weight model.

Offensive cyber capabilities

Researchers used the officially released checkpoint. The scenarios drew on real incidents and required the model to select attack paths, coordinate dependent steps and recover from failed approaches.

Across the three completed scenarios, GLM-5.3 used an application foothold to access internal services, built alternative connection paths within simulated networks and coordinated execution across multiple machines. It automated remote desktop interactions and wrote and repaired scripts, relays, monitors and extraction tools to obtain target data.

The results followed a progression the company had previously observed in closed frontier models, beginning with GPT-5.2, released in December 2025, and continuing with models released in 2026.

Memorized code and instruction adherence

Researchers also examined how GLM-5.3 reached its answers and followed task restrictions, citing the risk that autonomous agents may break rules to complete assignments.

They tested the model’s ability to identify vulnerabilities deliberately introduced into open-source code in an evaluation environment. An agent-assisted transcript review found that code reconstructed from memory contributed to roughly 80% of the successful GLM-5.3 runs examined. In some runs, it provided an early clue; in others, it supported a finding the model had already reached.

Using memorized code violated no instructions in those tests. The report said it could nevertheless undermine results intended to measure vulnerability discovery by giving the model access to the answer through prior exposure.

Irregular had observed this behavior in closed models as well. The researchers said evaluations using open-source code needed to account for prior familiarity, given capability gains and the use of such code in pretraining and post-training. Restricting internet access does not remove that familiarity.

Reward hacking and deployment risks

In separate instruction-adherence tests, GLM-5.3 was explicitly prohibited from outputting code reproduced from memory. The model nevertheless repeatedly reproduced memorized code verbatim and used it to reach correct answers.

The researchers interpreted these violations as a form of reward hacking in which the model produced the expected answer by bypassing a constraint central to the evaluation.

They warned that judging answers solely on correctness could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions. Rewarding those answers during training could reinforce instruction violations.

The report advised operators to monitor the model’s reasoning alongside its actions and outcomes, assessing compliance with instructions as well as answer accuracy.

“Organizations adopting these models should test how reliably they follow task restrictions before granting them broader access or autonomy. The more capable a model is in offensive cyber operations, the more caution any misaligned behavior it shows calls for,” the company concluded.

Title: Binance links $6.3 billion crypto theft to compromised DevOps laptop
Context: The crypto exchange said the access let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions after they accessed a service container, and it hasn't yet found evidence of a...

By

Sergiu Gatlan

October 30, 2026

05:18 AM

0

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has linked the theft of about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency to a DevOps engineer's compromised laptop.

The crypto exchange said the access let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions after they accessed a service container, and it hasn't yet found evidence of a leaked wallet private key.

"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual," Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said.

Binance also said it "uncovered additional points of breach" but was "still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."

The company confirmed the breach in a statement shared with BleepingComputer on Thursday and reassured customers that their funds were safe.

"Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company's funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete," it said.

Since the attack, Binance has suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks, revoked authorizations for the affected address, and is working with blockchain intelligence partners and law enforcement to trace and recover the stolen funds.

Crypto theft linked to North Korean hackers

Although the company didn't link the incident to a hacking group or threat actor, blockchain analysis firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38.

"On October 29, 2026, an attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC. That makes this the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the USD 1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025," TRM said.

Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis confirmed TRM Labs' findings, stating with "a high degree of confidence" that TraderTraitor is responsible for the Binance $6.4 billion hack.

While stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle, Ripple, and others have frozen roughly $2.7 billion since the incident, the attackers still have control of about $2.4 billion that can't be frozen.

"Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about USD 2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly USD 2.7 billion," TRM added.

"The attacker raced the freezes by selling USDT to market makers and borrowing ETH against USDT on Aave. It now holds more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about USD 2.4 billion in assets beyond any issuer's reach."

The TraderTraitor hackers were previously linked to many other major crypto theft incidents, including the theft of $1.5 billion in the February 2025 Bybit hack. At $6.36 billion, the Binance attack is now the largest recorded crypto heist.

Title: TeamViewer Flaw Could Let Malicious Hosts Take Over Support Technicians’ Machines
Context: A high-severity vulnerability in the popular remote-access tool TeamViewer could be exploited to take over a viewer’s (an IT support technician’s) system, cybersecurity firm...
Full Text:
A high-severity vulnerability in the popular remote-access tool TeamViewer could be exploited to take over a viewer’s (an IT support technician’s) system, cybersecurity firm Remedio warns.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111585 (CVSS score of 8.8), the flaw is described as an integer overflow affecting the remote-control screen processing component of TeamViewer clients across Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android.

Successful exploitation of the security defect could allow attackers to crash the viewer’s TeamViewer or execute arbitrary code on their system.

“Exploitation requires a user to establish a remote-control session to an attacker-controlled or compromised host,” TeamViewer notes in its advisory.

The issue, Remedio says, is rooted in how the host’s screen dimension is transmitted and used in the viewer: the host announces the geometry of the screen and the viewer uses the received dimensions to allocate an in-memory pixel buffer it then uses to decompress incoming screen updates.

This decode surface is only used if a hardware video decoder is not available for the session, but the host may refuse to negotiate the video codecs, thus forcing the viewer to that path.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A host can request a surface larger than what a screen can reach, and the path accepts it. An example would be 32768 by 32768 pixels at 32 bits per pixel, which overflows 32 bits, with every row past 31 being written out of bounds.

“The screen dimensions a host announces are used to size the drawing surface as-is, with no upper bound enforced on what arrives over the network,” Remedio explains.

The attacker-controlled host controls both the declared surface and the screen updates that can overflow the buffer, causing the viewer’s application to repeatedly crash.

“That means a malicious or compromised host can trigger the bug from inside an ordinary, established session, using only messages the protocol already supports,” Remedio explains.

In addition to triggering the denial-of-service (DoS) condition over a normal TeamViewer session, Remedio discovered that it could use CVE-2026-111585 to execute arbitrary code on the viewer’s system.

“The corrupted surface is a live object the viewer later calls through a pointer in its own first field, so overwriting that pointer redirects the call,” Remedio notes, explaining that it bypassed existing protections to route the call to WinExec and run the code in the viewer.

“The surface is reachable in the default configuration. An accepted session is all it takes, and that is the product’s normal mode of operation,” the company says.

Version 15.83 of TeamViewer’s clients (including Full Client, Host, Portable, and Remote Control App for Android) contains the necessary patches. TeamViewer also released security updates for multiple legacy versions.

The macOS and Linux updates also resolve CVE-2026-92372, an out-of-bounds write with similar consequences: an attacker could supply crafted screen-image data or convince a user to open a specially crafted TeamViewer session recording (.tvs) to execute arbitrary code.

“Missing destination bounds checking in the decoder allows crafted screen-image data to cause an out-of-bounds write to the image buffer. Exploitation requires user interaction,” TeamViewer notes.

On macOS, the updates also resolve CVE-2026-92374, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition with improper symbolic link handling flaw that could allow a low-privileged local attacker to install a malicious package and gain root privileges.

Additionally, TeamViewer patched six high-severity local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the TeamViewer Remote Management add-ons, urging users to update both the clients and the components to the latest versions.

TeamViewer says it is not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

Title: $6 Billion Binance Hack Bears Hallmarks of North Korea’s TraderTraitor
Context: The Binance wallet ended up delegated to a contract that only the attackers could command, which they used to empty it
Full Text:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hit by the biggest crypto heist ever recorded, and blockchain intelligence firms say North Korean state-sponsored hackers are the likely culprits.

Binance has put the damage at roughly $6.3 billion. TRM Labs, which followed each transfer on-chain, calculated about $6.36 billion siphoned from Binance wallets across ten blockchains on October 29. Most of the money left within roughly 20 minutes.

The haul dwarfs the $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025, which previously held the record. Binance has halted withdrawals and pledged to reimburse all losses using company funds and its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU).

The exchange’s early findings suggest the intrusion may have started with an employee’s laptop.

“Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak,” Binance stated.

TRM’s analysis shows the attackers spent at least a day and a half getting ready. The wallet used to run the operation was funded with a few small Tornado Cash withdrawals, and the malicious code was trialed on other wallets before going live.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Ethereum, the attackers leveraged EIP-7702, a mechanism through which a standard wallet can delegate its behavior to a smart contract by signing a permission. They sent a batch of 50 such permissions, all signed beforehand by a Binance hot wallet, so that one would match the wallet’s transaction count at execution time.

The Binance wallet ended up delegated to a contract that only the attackers could command, which they used to empty it.

According to TRM, the Ethereum activity initially looked like the result of phishing. That theory does not account for the other nine blockchains, where Binance wallets sent funds to the attackers through regular, validly signed transactions.

“These wallets use different chains, key types and signing schemes. All of them produced valid signatures for the attacker within about half an hour. In TRM’s assessment, the most likely explanation is that the attacker gained the ability to make Binance’s hot wallet signing system sign transactions of its choosing across chains,” TRM said.

Researchers point to North Korea

“TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence. We make this judgment with high confidence,” the blockchain intelligence firm said.

TRM found traits this attack shares with the Bybit heist and the KelpDAO hack from April 2026. These include a mixer-funded operator wallet, preparations made long before any money moved, and signatures collected ahead of time and then used all at once.

The laundering seen so far sets this operation apart. Instead of leaning on cross-chain bridges as in the Bybit case, the hackers have mainly relied on big trades with market makers and on lending platforms.

Chainalysis CEO Jonathan Levin said his company also believes TraderTraitor is the likely perpetrator, citing ties to an earlier hack. Chainalysis investigators found proceeds from last month’s Bitget exploit mixed with funds taken from Binance.

Blockchain sleuth ZachXBT also named the Lazarus Group as the probable attacker.

The FBI attributed the Bybit theft to TraderTraitor. Binance has not publicly identified the hackers, saying it is cooperating with law enforcement to determine who they are.

Billions frozen, billions still movable

Stablecoin issuers were quick to act. By 00:30 UTC on October 30, TRM tallied around $2.7 billion in frozen assets, including roughly 1.77 billion USDT locked by Tether and about 825 million USDC locked by Circle.

Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze smaller amounts, and Arbitrum’s Security Council used its emergency powers to move about $30 million out of an attacker wallet. Binance estimates the frozen total at roughly $3 billion.

To stay ahead of the issuers, the attackers sold USDT for ETH at more than 10% below market price. TRM says they still hold over 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about $2.4 billion in assets that no issuer can freeze.

As Russia's Cyberwar Evolves, Belarus Steps Forward

The "FrostyNeighbor" advanced persistent threat (APT) launched a destructive attack in Ukraine and is raising concerns about deeper alignment with Russian cyber objectives.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 30, 2026

Source: Oleksii Liskonih via Getty Images

Researchers have spotted the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor against a critical target in Ukraine, suggesting Belarus may be upping its support for Russian national objectives — carrying implications for much of Europe.

ESET this week published its APT Activity Report for Q2 and Q3 2026. The report highlights a range of state-sponsored activity across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, but one of the most significant assertions involves Belarus, an Eastern European country that has been close allies with Russia in the latter's invasion of Ukraine.

Historically, Belarusian cyber operations have been tracked separately from those attributed directly to Russian intelligence services, though researchers have long observed overlap in targeting and strategic interests. The Belarusan state-affiliated group FrostyNeighbor — also tracked as UNC1151 — has been known for disinformation and cyber espionage, the latter conducted through various means such as spear phishing and malware.

Related:Russia's Hybrid Cyber-Physical War in Europe Heats Up

While the Eastern European country has also set its sights on Ukrainian and Polish targets in phishing attacks to further its own and possibly Russia's goals, ESET identified a recent escalation in these activities. Mainly, ESET's report notes that its researchers "identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater."

Specifically, FrostyNeighbor deployed Chisel, UltraVNC, Cobalt Strike, and a VBScript wiper via Group Policy against a manufacturing company in Ukraine that ESET said "plays an important role in the country's transportation sector," which is notable because destructive operations up until this point have been explicitly Russia-aligned.

"While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia," the report read. "We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas."

FrostyNeighbor APT Attacks Its Neighbors

Damien Schaeffer, senior malware researcher at ESET, says that the strongest evidence for an increasing operational closeness with Russia is the number of attacks and the victimology that appears closer to and aligned with Russia's strategic priorities than Belarus's own, as well as a sophistication behind these attacks, "which seems relatively high to Belarus's potential interests alone." He says ESET first observed this trend of increasing aggressiveness at the beginning of 2024.

This comes as North Korea expands its own military cooperation with Russia in the latter's war on Ukraine, which ESET added could mean cyber activity will continue to align as well.

Russia's war on Ukraine stretches far beyond Ukraine, especially in the realm of cyber operations. Russia has grown bolder in cyberattacks particularly against European countries that support Ukraine militarily or politically, are on NATO's eastern flank, and support critical logistics hubs for aid flowing into Ukraine.

This, to varying degrees, has included Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Sweden, Czech Republic, and Germany, among others. In other words, if Russian allies are growing bolder in their cyberactivities explicitly supporting Russia, that carries consequences for all of Europe.

Continue to Treat Belarus as Its Own Entity

Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, tells Dark Reading that its evidence shows FrostyNeighbor as an actor executing sustained operations and evolving its techniques, though not necessarily an overall increase in operational scale nor shared operational command.

Recorded Future's recommendation is to explicitly track Belarus-linked clusters and correlate their infrastructure, tools, and targeting with Russian threat campaigns "while preserving attribution distinctions."

"Threat models should cover credential theft, persistent access, and the use of compromised accounts to reach additional people. Intelligence collection should include malicious login infrastructure, email exploitation, personal-account targeting, and abuse of trusted contacts, which are the access routes documented in these campaigns," Leslie says. "Defenders do not need proof of Russian tasking to prioritize an actor already targeting them."

While researchers differ on whether Belarusian activity represents deeper operational integration with Russia, they appear to agree that defenders should not dismiss Belarus-linked actors as secondary threats. As Leslie explains, CERT Polska in June 2026 identified UNC1151 as one of the most active APT groups it monitors, "observing new phishing domains almost daily in the preceding weeks."

Organizations in sectors tied to government, transportation, and defense that show support for Ukraine may increasingly encounter campaigns whose objectives align closely with Moscow's broader strategic interests.

Title: Fake IT help desk callers got by on little more than names and email addresses
Context: In another, the attacker launched two phishing waves, likely expecting that at least one target would be compromised,” she said
Full Text:
Mirko Zorz, Director of Content, Help Net Security

October 30, 2026

Share

Fake IT help desk callers got by on little more than names and email addresses

Attackers posing as IT help desk staff contacted employees by phone, email and Microsoft Teams in the third quarter of 2026 and talked them into opening remote access sessions, Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) found across several engagements. In one case, that access ended in ransomware.

They knew names and email addresses

“The attackers appeared to know employee names and email addresses, as they contacted users directly by email and Teams and used identities that mimicked legitimate company help desk personnel,” Aliza Johnson, a researcher at Cisco Talos, told Help Net Security.

“They likely had broad, generic knowledge of how IT support interactions typically work as they successfully guided victims into Teams sessions and remote access and showed familiarity with common enterprise platforms like Quick Assist; however, there is no clear evidence of deep company- or victim-specific profiling beyond basic identity and contact information,” she said.

The targets were not limited to senior or technical staff. “The contacted victims varied both across organizations and within the same organization, suggesting the actors were primarily seeking any susceptible user for initial access rather than targeting specific individuals for privileged or specialized access,” Johnson said. Protections built around administrators and executives would have missed many of the people these attackers reached.

“Some of these attacks appear opportunistic. In one case, the victim called a fake IT support number shown in a generic browser-based scam pop-up that did not appear to spoof the victim organization, and later granted the adversary remote access. In another, the attacker launched two phishing waves, likely expecting that at least one target would be compromised,” she said.

In the first of those cases, the victim dialed the number.

One Quick Assist session, then ransomware

In an engagement involving VYPR, a ransomware variant Talos considers new and still operationally immature, the actor used a voice phishing call to get a user to start a Microsoft Quick Assist session. Talos could not confirm what the caller said. RMM software already on the network then ran PowerShell commands that downloaded and installed a Microsoft Software Installer package from a remote IP address.

The VYPR operators built on older leaked Conti-derived source code with minimal changes. To knock out EDR tools, they loaded trusted but flawed drivers to gain kernel-level access, a technique called bring your own vulnerable driver, and dropped an unusually large number of them, possibly as backups. Data exfiltration ran over multiple days, which Talos does not commonly see in ransomware cases. The group had no data leak site until after the engagement ended.

A script went after Claude Code credentials

On a separate macOS endpoint, infected through a trojanized application, attackers scripted a search of the keychain, the Mac’s built-in password store, for credentials tied to Anthropic’s Claude Code assistant.

“We observed an attacker-controlled account executing the following command to target Anthropic Claude Code credentials, possibly for credential dumping. There was no indication of the actor using these credentials,” Johnson said. The command was /bin/sh -c security find-generic-password -a “[USER_NAME]” -w -s “Claude Code-credentials”. Its -w flag tells macOS to print the stored secret.

In another case, an insider hired under false credentials used privileged access to install GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code. Investigators found no evidence of malicious activity or data theft. The employee’s developer access, which included cloning repositories and connecting to databases, could have let them use those tools to automate malicious actions.

Logs, MFA and help desk checks

Talos IR recommends phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and hardware security keys in place of push and SMS prompts. It also recommends requiring help desk verification before employees can enroll new MFA methods themselves.

Among engagements where the entry point was known, phishing remained the top initial access method at 37 percent, down from over 50 percent last quarter. Exploitation of public-facing applications followed at 33 percent. Credential and secret management problems and weak authentication or MFA each turned up in 33 percent of engagements.

Insufficient logging led the list of weaknesses, appearing in over 40 percent of engagements, partly because attackers deleted logs and partly because customers had not retained or configured them. Talos recommends at least 90 days of centralized log retention, with logs forwarded off each device so they survive tampering and rebuilds.

Title: What exactly is ISOC? And what does it mean for you?
Context: The goal of identifying ISOC as a new category then, is instead to adapt and assess the ability of a vendor to integrate classic SIEM logic with an expanded threat detection...
Full Text:
Aimei Wei, CTO, Stellar Cyber Sponsored

October 30, 2026

Share

What exactly is ISOC? And what does it mean for you?

Gartner recently released a new category of assessing security tools: the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC). Even though SIEM isn’t going anywhere, a rapidly evolving threat landscape is forcing a shift in industry logic that is reflected in the emergence of this new category.

For years, SIEM has dominated as an all-encompassing category. But SIEMs are no longer sufficient to collect data, support investigations, and manage incidents; instead, the SIEM has separated into distinct architectural layers. SIEM platforms, which remain the security system of record for collecting, normalizing, searching, and analyzing event data, are now distinct from the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) solutions. ISOC is tasked with unifying detection, investigation, case management, and response across security domains and security/observability data pipelines.

As AI empowers attackers and more threat landscapes emerge, this stratification becomes essential. Data management, analytics, and operational response are now separate problems, and, as a result, demand separate solutions. This is where ISOC finds its space: to reduce costs, latency, and operational friction.

The goal of identifying ISOC as a new category then, is instead to adapt and assess the ability of a vendor to integrate classic SIEM logic with an expanded threat detection investigation and response (TDIR) capability. Reduced complexity is especially key for lean teams who prioritize efficiency and streamlined workflows, and the goal of ISOC is to reduce the friction that comes with conglomerating a wide variety of different security tools to contrive full visibility.

In short, ISOC addresses the pain point that every security team faces today. Instead of juggling an array of disjointed tools provided by different vendors, a single vendor streamlines the production of a providing a flexible and adaptable, yet holistic and transparent security solution. This gives a business the efficiency and flexibility to reduce costs, reduce deployment time, and allay growing SIEM complexities.

Common features of the ISOC, as Gartner writes, include native detection and response services, incident case management, and extended case management of data ingestion. ISOC should reduce the friction between security tools and the latency between data, context, decision, and action. Machine-speed responses are more essential than ever in an age where attackers are all armed with the most advanced AI tools.

Latency challenges in Native Detection and Response, Security Data Ownership, Incident Case Management, Cross-Domain Correlation, and Automation and Agentic Response, and Open Ingestion and Response Fabric are becoming issues that business can’t afford to ignore.

Detection and response must operate on the same underlying security data, not through loosely connected point products. Native controls reduce latency between signal, correlation, investigation, and action. ISOC starts with control of the data layer: ingesting, normalizing, enriching, retaining, and making telemetry available for detection and AI reasoning. If the platform does not control the data model, every downstream analytic or agent is working through integration boundaries.

Alerts, entities, evidence, timelines, and analyst actions are assembled into a persistent incident object. The case becomes the operational unit for investigation and response rather than individual alerts. Endpoint, network, identity, cloud, application, and third-party telemetry must be correlated against a common schema and context model. This is what allows weak individual signals to become a high-confidence attack story.

Automation should operate directly against normalized data and incident context, enabling AI agents and playbooks to investigate, enrich, recommend, and execute actions without repeatedly rebuilding context. ISOC must connect broadly to existing security infrastructure while minimizing translation and API friction.

The objective is a common data and control plane where third-party tools contribute signals and become response surfaces.

Looking ahead

As the SIEM market grows, the market share will be divided to include ISOC vendors, who will expand their offerings to include coverage in identity, cloud/Saas management, and email security.

The market is only reflecting the dynamics that security teams have been feeling for years, which has been exacerbated exponentially by the adoption of AI by threat agents. Simply agglomerating more tools is neither strategic, nor effective. And a single vendor approach is key to striking the right balance between efficacy and simplicity. Finding the right tool portfolio now means finding the right vendor.

The market confirms what Stellar Cyber postulated: modern operational needs demand integrated, unified capabilities. From setting an open integration standard to incorporating AI-native capabilities, ISOC environments are meant to simplify operations without compromising coverage or visibility.

Anticipating the limitations of fragmented security stacks leads to natively unified operational platforms. By normalizing raw data from any source through high-context schema technology, modern ISOC solutions deliver the precise, consolidated out-of-the-box outcomes now expected in the market.

An AI SOC that starts with somebody else’s alert is already too late.

Stellar Cyber collects and normalizes telemetry, detects suspicious activity, correlates evidence, builds cases, investigates incidents, triages findings, and drives response from the same security architecture. That gives people and AI access to the evidence behind the alert – not just the alert itself.

Title: Scammers rebuild fake shopping sites within hours of a takedown
Context: Attackers place phishing pages on compromised websites, exploiting the reputation attached to an established address
Full Text:
Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security

October 30, 2026

Share

Scammers rebuild fake shopping sites within hours of a takedown

One retail scam used more than 1,200 look-alike .shop domains sharing a single IP address. The sites reused HTML, JavaScript and payment-page designs intended to harvest card numbers, expiry dates and security codes, according Akamai’s Fraud and Abuse Report 2026.

A ticket scam used a similar setup. Several websites impersonating official ticketing and hospitality portals for a major sporting event were designed to route payment and personal information to the same collection system. Some checkout flows requested passport or identity-document details under the pretext of arranging ticket delivery or event access.

The addresses gave criminals multiple entrances to the same operation. If one domain was blocked or removed, another could continue directing information to the shared collection system. Stolen information could then support payment fraud, account takeover and identity abuse.

Following the offer

In one documented campaign, a paid social media advert directed consumers to a counterfeit app marketplace. Visitors then downloaded a malicious app that collected sensitive information and abused device permissions.

An example of a recruitment scam (Source: Akamai)

Recruitment scams exploited the expectation that applicants would submit personal details. Fake hiring content appeared across four major social platforms, directing people toward phishing forms designed to collect sensitive information.

Replacing websites within hours

Operators register look-alike addresses in bulk and leave them dormant for weeks or months. This can help a domain build a clean reputation before a scam launches.

Some sites vary their content according to the visitor. An automated security scanner may receive harmless material while an intended victim sees the fraudulent offer. Location and browser information can determine which page appears.

Attackers place phishing pages on compromised websites, exploiting the reputation attached to an established address. Reused phishing kits, hosting arrangements and payment infrastructure allow replacement sites to appear within hours of a website being removed.

Turning passwords into purchases

Credentials exposed through scams and data breaches can provide access to existing accounts.

Automated programs test credentials exposed in earlier breaches across other services. When someone has reused a password, attackers may gain access to saved payment methods, reward points or personal details. They can then change account details and recovery settings to make it harder for the owner to regain control.

In a 30-day sample spanning July and August 2026, Akamai classified 26.6% of recorded login attempts as high or critical risk. These attempts were flagged as potential threats requiring investigation.

Account verification requests accounted for 40% of the high- or critical-risk login traffic examined. Such requests can help attackers establish whether an email address belongs to an account before attempting credential stuffing.

Victims may discover the theft through a purchase notification, missing points or a password that stops working. Businesses handle disputed transactions, reimbursement requests and the work of restoring access.

Account opening abuse starts at registration

Criminals create accounts to collect welcome bonuses, exploit promotions, test stolen cards and reserve products for resale. 8.3% of account creation attempts were linked to suspected fraud in 2025.

Small transactions through fake accounts help criminals check if stolen cards work before attempting larger purchases. Businesses can incur processing fees, chargebacks and penalties. Fake accounts can be used to hoard limited stock, reducing availability for shoppers and supplying resellers.

Verification creates another opportunity. In SMS pumping schemes, automated requests trigger registration or password-reset messages to premium-rate international numbers, generating charges for the business sending them. Some operations involve rogue telecom carriers that share the resulting revenue with the fraudsters.

Title: In the year AI re-wrote the infosec rulebook, it’s comforting to know crypto exchanges still have bad security
Context: “Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service...
Full Text: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades. Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. It also promised to cover any losses. About an hour ago at the time of writing, Binance posted an update on the incident that explains what it thinks went wrong. “Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the post states. The company also hiked the amount it thinks is at risk to $6.3 billion and repeated its promise to cover any customer losses. The update also says Binance found no evidence of any wallet private key leak, suggesting that customers’ holdings remain secure. When they can use them again, as Binance is yet to resume trading. Binance hasn’t explained how attackers gained access to the engineer’s laptop. The scant details provided make it hard to rule out a successful phishing attack, or perhaps a supply chain attack on a package the developer used. Binance says it will spill once it knows exactly what happened. Cryptocurrency outfits have a long and inglorious history of falling victim to cyberattacks, perhaps starting with the 2011 raid on Mt Gox, to incidents allegedly perpetrated by nation-states, and, just last week, another situation possibly involving an AI-powered attacker. ®

Title: Hugging Face malware campaign returns to hijack GPUs for crypto mining
Context: Back within days of takedown Pluto found the campaign through a test account whose leftover backup files pointed to the attacker's main accounts
Full Text:
By

Ax Sharma

October 29, 2026

06:09 PM

0

A cryptomining and backdoor campaign that abuses Hugging Face model repositories came back within days of being taken down.

Its most popular malicious model was downloaded more than 28,000 times.

Separately, researchers flagged a fake Solana starter kit on GitHub, live since late 2025, that is positioned to trick AI coding agents into installing a remote access trojan.

Code runs before the model loads

Researchers at Pluto Security found 31 malicious repositories across seven Hugging Face accounts, published in two waves since September.

The models pose as small Qwen2 test checkpoints. They target GPU hosts running self-hosted inference servers such as Xinference and GPUStack.

With linked models included, the repositories have more than 32,000 downloads. Pluto notes that this counts downloads, not confirmed infections.

Instead of using poisoned weights or pickle exploits, the campaign abuses a Hugging Face option, trust_remote_code, that lets a model ship its own Python code. When a user enables it, that code runs on their machine as soon as the model loads.

The most downloaded model, MENXIANGYU/qwen2-tiny, contained no actual model at all. Its code quietly installs a cryptocurrency miner disguised as a Linux system process, restarts it if killed, and removes competing miners from the machine.

Some versions also open a reverse shell, giving the attacker direct access to the infected server.

Back within days of takedown

Pluto found the campaign through a test account whose leftover backup files pointed to the attacker's main accounts. It reported the first wave to Hugging Face and China's ModelScope, and both removed the accounts.

A second wave of 19 repositories appeared under new accounts within days.

Hours after Pluto reported it, the operator published another model with a script that can break out of a container and take over the server underneath.

Pluto says the second-wave repositories were still live eight days after it reported them. Downloads of the flagship model climbed from 7,354 at the time of the report to 28,412 by October 28.

As of writing, Hugging Face has disabled access to that model. A near-identical copy uploaded on October 25 by a newer account, htt0118, is still live, and BleepingComputer confirmed it contains the same miner and reverse shell:

Clean scans, real payouts

Hugging Face scans uploads with antivirus and partner tools from Protect AI and JFrog. Pluto says these look for known malware and unsafe model formats, rather than what a model's Python code actually does.

"The second-wave flagship scanned clean while it collected 28,412 downloads," the researchers said, adding that JFrog reported the payload file was "not a machine-learning model."

According to Pluto, the operator's main wallet has received roughly $5,000 in Pearl (PRL) cryptocurrency. It was still active on mining pools after the repositories behind it were removed.

While the researchers watched, nine machines that appear to belong to a shared research GPU cluster started mining for the operator at once.

They dropped off about six minutes later, which Pluto says fits an admin killing the jobs.

Pluto attributes the campaign to a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking operator. It cites Simplified Chinese code comments, command-and-control servers on Alibaba Cloud, and activity times that fall late at night in China.

Anyone who loaded these models with trust_remote_code enabled should treat the machine as compromised, check it against the indicators in Pluto's report, and rotate any credentials it could reach. Killing the miner alone doesn't remove the backdoors.

Fake Solana kit targets AI coding agents

In a separate report, Air Security describes a GitHub repository, SolanaUpdateTools/solana-starter-kit, that it says ranks as the top result when AI coding agents search for a Solana starter kit.

An agent that picks the repository and follows its README could run the attacker's command without the developer ever seeing it.

The repository was created in November 2025 and has 286 stars. Its README promises a full Solana app template, but none of that code exists, and the README is the only file in the repository:

The README's only "installation" step tells users to paste a PowerShell one-liner into a command prompt. The Windows-only command assembles a URL on developer-update[.]app from fragments, then fetches and runs a script from it in memory.

BleepingComputer obtained the archived payload from the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine and confirmed Air's findings.

The payload installs NetSupport Manager, a legitimate remote-access tool, configured to connect to maxwintodaybtc[.]com and give the attacker hidden control of the machine at every login.

The script then displays a fake error saying "developer functionality is temporarily paused due to load" and to "try again in 72 hours," which an agent could easily relay as a routine server hiccup.

Air linked the setup to a known NetSupport RAT operator tracked by eSentire, and to an earlier campaign that lured crypto traders with fake TradingView "AI signal" tools.

The payload URL returned a 404 when Air checked. At the time of writing, the GitHub repository was still live.

Title: Japan Airlines suffers third-party data breach exposing passenger info
Context: Amadeus published a statement on its website on October 1, 2026, announcing it had discovered a vulnerability in its travel booking display environment that could expose...
Full Text:
By

Bill Toulas

October 29, 2026

06:08 PM

0

Japan Airlines (JAL) has announced that a data breach at Amadeus’s Passenger Service System exposed the data of about 92,000 customers.

JAL Group, which operates the airlines JAL and Japan Transocean Air, uses the system to handle passenger reservations, ticketing, and check-in.

According to its announcement, Amadeus notified the airline on October 23, 2026, that unauthorized access to its systems occurred between August 10, 2023, and September 23, 2026.

As a result of this lengthy breach, the threat actor accessed reservation codes (PNRs), names, flight dates, routes, and travel classes for approximately 90,000 customers.

An additional 2,000 customers had the above data types exposed, plus their email addresses, phone numbers, passport numbers, nationalities, frequent flyer numbers, and flight, ticket, and seat numbers.

JAL says credit card numbers and passwords were not compromised, and assured that it currently has no evidence of customer information being misused.

The company said Amadeus has now implemented the necessary security measures and flight operations are unaffected.

Broader impact

Amadeus is an IT firm that provides solutions for travel agencies, airlines, airports, and hotels.

It is a major tech supplier to global aviation, used by over four hundred airlines, 210 airport operators, 34 cruise and ferry lines, and 2 million hotels.

Amadeus published a statement on its website on October 1, 2026, announcing it had discovered a vulnerability in its travel booking display environment that could expose travelers’ data.

At the time, the company said ransomware actors had not exploited the flaw and assured that no payment or other financial data had been exposed.

As JAL has confirmed now, the vulnerability appears to have been maliciously exploited.

It appears they were not the only victim of the campaign.

All Nippon Airways (ANA) has also announced a customer data breach earlier today tied to Amadeus, according to local media.

The airline has also suspended certain related services on its website and mobile app since October 21, although that action appears linked to the PHP2Shell threat rather than the Amadeus incident.

Other airlines that have confirmed impact from the Amadeus flaw are Asiana Airlines and Korean Air, both major South Korean carriers.

BleepingComputer has asked Amadeus for more information about the scope of the impact, specifically whether more airlines and other countries/markets were affected, but the company has not provided more information as of publication.

Title: Polymarket halts trading after crypto-draining script breach, $2.5M traced
Context: Hudson Rock's researchers also discovered Polymarket production build metadata containing the commit message, "chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337),"...
Full Text:
By

Lawrence Abrams

October 29, 2026

05:47 PM

0

Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading on Thursday after hackers compromised a third-party service to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript, with approximately $2.5 million in assets traced to a suspected attacker wallet.

The company confirmed the security incident, saying it had identified and fixed the issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com, and referred the breach to law enforcement.

"One of our third party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement," Polymarket said.

"Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading and are working to bring the platform back online."

Polymarket initially placed its exchange into cancel-only mode at 2:05 p.m. ET and paused relayer actions while investigating the incident. At 2:37 p.m., the company announced that the issue had been fixed and that trading was temporarily halted out of an abundance of caution.

Trading resumed approximately one hour after the initial suspension, with the incident marked resolved at 3:05 p.m. ET.

"Trading is now fully back online," the company announced on X. "We'll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders."

Polymarket has not disclosed how many users were affected, how much cryptocurrency was stolen, or how the reimbursement process will work.

Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified a suspected attacker-controlled wallet (0x3F99139F1C5854bb628c2e576Aaf638e99dFfc18) embedded in the malicious JavaScript.

BleepingComputer's examination of the wallet's blockchain activity found that it transferred approximately 28.6 million POL, valued at roughly $2.57 million, to three additional wallets.

Blockchain records also show that the wallet conducted numerous transactions involving Polymarket's prediction-market token contract between 1:50 p.m. and 1:56 p.m. ET, shortly before the exchange suspended trading.

Hudson Rock reported that the wallet held approximately $2.19 million in cryptocurrency at the time of its investigation.

Malicious JavaScript used to drain wallets

Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified malicious JavaScript distributed through cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js that was designed to steal cryptocurrency and prediction-market holdings from Polymarket users.

The script was hosted on infrastructure belonging to DebugBear, a website performance-monitoring service that helps organizations track website loading speeds and user experience.

DebugBear's Real User Monitoring (RUM) service uses JavaScript embedded in websites to collect performance metrics from visitors' browsers.

DebugBear has since confirmed that it is investigating an ongoing security incident and warned customers to remove its monitoring JavaScript from their websites.

"We're impacted by an ongoing security incident," DebugBear said in a post on X.

"If you use our RUM product, please remove the embed code from your website."

At the time of writing, DebugBear's website was inaccessible, displaying a Cloudflare error. It is unclear whether the website outage is related to containment efforts or another consequence of the incident.

Hudson Rock's researchers also discovered Polymarket production build metadata containing the commit message, "chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337)," indicating that the platform had removed the DebugBear monitoring integration.

The build was timestamped October 29 at 1:59 p.m. ET, shortly before Polymarket publicly announced the incident.

BleepingComputer analyzed a copy of the malicious JavaScript file (VirusTotal), finding that it was designed to hijack authenticated Polymarket trading sessions, liquidate users' prediction-market positions, and transfer cryptocurrency and other assets to an attacker-controlled wallet.

The malware checks whether a visitor is logged into Polymarket and attempts to use their existing trading session and the platform's trading functionality to carry out unauthorized transactions.

It then checks the user's cryptocurrency balances and prediction-market positions to determine the value of their holdings.

Depending on how the user authenticated to Polymarket, the malware attempts to steal their assets in different ways.

For some users, it tries to automatically sell their prediction-market positions. For others, the malware attempts to transfer their prediction-market tokens directly to an attacker-controlled wallet.

The malware also attempts to convert users' cryptocurrency holdings into assets that can be transferred to an attacker-controlled wallet, using Polymarket's existing transaction functionality.

BleepingComputer found that the malicious script communicated with data.debugbear.com to receive instructions and send data about targeted accounts, wallet addresses, balances, and transaction results.

The use of DebugBear's infrastructure to both distribute the malicious script and serve as a command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration server raises questions about the how much access the attackers had to the company's systems.

BleepingComputer has contacted Polymarket and DebugBear with questions about the incident and will update this article if we receive a response.

Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Obvious phishing emails with numerous red flags are somehow getting past some of the industry-leading secure email gateway (SEG) products.

Nate Nelson,Contributing Writer

October 29, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: beast01 via Getty Images

Attackers are managing to sneak low-grade phishing emails through brand name email security products, as evidenced by a recent Anthropic impersonation campaign.

The campaign, described in a new blog post by Cofense, won't impress anybody. Since September, an unidentified threat actor has been sending out emails around the world, pretending to grant early access to Anthropic's cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Their goal: stealing Google and Microsoft account credentials.

To avoid being relegated to spam folders, the attacker has been using novice tactics: shortening their malicious URLs, adding CAPTCHAs to their phishing flow, and leveraging legitimate video conferencing tools. The only remarkable thing about the campaign, really, is that it actually seems to be working.

Fake Emails Steal Google, Microsoft Credentials

Even as far as phishing campaigns go, this one's pretty lazy.

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

Attackers are appealing to targets with VIP invites to a "private preview" of Anthropic's supposed "new social media AI tool." Emails emphasize that this special early look is "private, invitation-only."

Right off the bat, there are ample reasons to be suspicious. The email titles have a grammatical error. The email sender's name includes a typo — "Austin from nthropic" — and their domain belongs to GoTo Webinar, not Anthropic. Visually, the messages are barebones, possessing no visual elements that even attempt to impersonate Anthropic branding.

If for some reason someone actually clicks on the fake registration link — a link that doesn't point to an Anthropic or even a conferencing app domain — they'll end up on a fake Zoom meeting page. If, further, the victim doesn't catch that a GoTo Webinar invite led to a Zoom call, they might choose to sign into Zoom via Google or Microsoft Single-Sign On (SSO). If they choose Google, they won't even be prompted for a password, thus making half of this malicious campaign completely useless, even to the attacker running it.

Inconsistent brand impersonations and missing or broken data theft flows are endemic to AI-generated campaigns; Cofense couldn't confirm if AI was used here. "However, due to the multiple variations of Zoom pages, it's likely generative AI was used," Cofense researcher Jacob Malimban says.

He points to one bit of additional evidence: Beginning Oct. 28, the threat actor began spoofing Anthropic's website instead of Zoom's. The similar but slightly off format of the Anthropic spoofing page, he says, also suggests AI generation.

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

How Weak TTPs Beat Email Security Solutions

The overall package is so maladroit that one can only wonder how such an email bypassed any spam filter in the first place. In fact, Cofense found these emails getting through market-leading email security products like the Proofpoint Secure Email Gateway (SEG) and Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Cofense pointed to a few little details that might help explain why.

First, the emails are sent from a legitimate email address, customercare@gotowebinar[.]com — a shared sender address that any GoTo Webinar user might use to distribute webinar information. The legitimacy and ubiquity of this shared address shields the sender from scrutiny.

Second, the malicious registration link in the emails was run through a URL shortener, Zapier, eliminating a security product's ability to interpret red flags in the domain itself.

Lastly, the phishing flow incorporates two separate CAPTCHAs. The first — a Cloudflare CAPTCHA, presented before the fake Zoom or Anthropic page — is meant to stop an automated scanner in its tracks.

The second CAPTCHA — placed between the fake Zoom or Anthropic page and the fake SSO page — is a malicious twist on the form, designed to block VPN services, Tor browsers, and other tools defenders might use. "Some phish kits used that specific type of CAPTCHA before. It appears to have been actively developed by threat actors to detect the tools of both automated and human activity, as well as see if the IP address was proxied," Malimban explains.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

None of these tactics will knock anyone's socks off but, in the gestalt, they seem to do the trick.

Takeaways for Cybersecurity Awareness Month

To Keeper Security chief information security officer (CISO) Shane Barney, it's no surprise that threat actors are successfully bypassing perimeter email defenses, even with cookie cutter tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

"The reality of modern cybersecurity is that Secure Email Gateways (SEGs) will always have blind spots," he says.

Barney adds that organizations should assume phishing emails will end up in employees' email inboxes, and therefore security teams need to build defenses that focus on identity.

"If an employee is tricked by a fake Anthropic lure and their Microsoft or Google credentials are compromised, strict least-privilege access policies, phishing-resistant multifactor authentication and privileged access management are what prevent the attacker from moving laterally, elevating privileges and accessing sensitive data," he advises. Lastly, he adds, "Utilizing a centralized password manager that validates domain URLs before autofilling credentials provides a critical last line of defense against the lookalike domains used in this attack, neutralizing the threat at the point of interaction."

In the spirit of Cybersecurity Awareness Month 2026, and its emphasis on avoiding and reporting phishing scams, Malimban adds, "We hope that employees are trained using Secure Behavior Management to recognize and report phishing. To defend against suspicious account access, organizations should have robust account monitoring, like with CISA's free tool (Logging Made Easy). All in all, having multiple controls and defense in depth is necessary to defend against modern attacks."

Context: fun, is web-only, so any mobile apps impersonating it, including the one previously available on the App Store, are malicious
Full Text:
By

Bill Toulas

October 29, 2026

03:23 PM

0

A fake cryptocurrency trading app called Padre Terminal, previously available on the Apple App Store for iOS devices, has been linked to the theft of approximately $23,000 from 27 Solana wallets.

Blockchain investigator Iris confirmed that one victim was compromised through the malicious App Store app, but has not determined how the other affected wallets were compromised.

The researcher says the app drains wallets after unsuspecting users import their private keys into it.

Padre was a cryptocurrency trading platform, mainly used to buy and sell meme coins on Solana. It was later renamed Terminal by pump.fun, a platform focused on creating, buying, and selling cryptocurrency “meme coins” on the Solana blockchain.

Iris says the legitimate Padre trading service, now Terminal by pump.fun, is web-only, so any mobile apps impersonating it, including the one previously available on the App Store, are malicious.

At the time of BleepingComputer's initial investigation, we found two Padre apps on the App Store (ID 6802739263 and ID 6717572591). The former was the Iris-confirmed drainer app, while the latter is likely pump.fun's official app, live since October 2024.

The malicious Padre Terminal app has since been removed from the App Store, with its listing now returning a 404 error.

Iris told BleepingComputer it suspects the trading interface of the fake app is served remotely, but has not directly observed the wallet-draining screen.

According to Iris, the operation has drained 27 Solana wallets since October 25, 2026, stealing approximately $23,000 in cryptocurrency. The stolen cryptocurrency was traced to the Solana address 3LAgKYoNenWrGWT3U4XWhpgVJWyYkP9wKpiPk8TJT1LN.

Iris says the attacker converted all remaining USDC (4,070 tokens) into SOL on October 29, eliminating the possibility of Circle freezing those funds.

The attacker then transferred 192 SOL to a new wallet (H84yazsUVCF8eJ6brh27rURMHjdKEVv2BuLS4iuUUQbu). According to Iris, the two wallets held a combined 229.66 SOL, with no funds cashed out at the time of the researcher's update.

The drainer remained active after the app's removal, with the latest reported theft occurring at 17:06 UTC on October 29.

More suspicious apps on the App Store

Iris identified at least five suspected crypto-brand impersonators on the App Store, including Padre Terminal, Axiom Pro: Focus, GMGN AI, HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools, and Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs.

Their listings feature seemingly harmless descriptions, but user reviews below sometimes reveal their true nature, with many exposing them for wallet theft and scams.

The Axiom Pro: Focus app, for example, had approximately 25 user reviews alleging wallet theft since February. One reviewer claimed the app had presented itself as a meme coin trading platform before changing into a focus application.

A review of the GMGN AI app alleged that $2,000 had been stolen, while a review associated with HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools reported the theft of $2,020.

Another app, Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs, presented itself as a notes application but had a review explicitly accusing it of stealing cryptocurrency.

Iris also found a script on the fake Axiom website containing backend addresses associated with Axiom, Aster, and GMGN impersonators, suggesting a common operator. However, Padre Terminal was not linked to that cluster.

Also, a script on the GMGN website blocks visitors from several CIS countries, potentially indicating that the attackers are attempting to avoid targeting users in those regions.

Iris has not independently confirmed cryptocurrency theft for the four suspicious apps.

BleepingComputer has contacted Apple about the Padre drainer and the other four suspicious apps available on the App Store, but we have not heard back as of publication.

In March 2024, a fake Leather cryptocurrency wallet app appeared on the Apple App Store, and multiple users reported losing their assets after connecting their wallets to it.

Apple eventually removed the app two weeks later and blocked the publisher from its developer program.

Users are recommended to follow links to the App Store from the projects' official websites and avoid installing apps with only a handful of downloads and reviews, or those published by entities with names that appear completely unrelated to the project.

Full Text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

“The darkest period of my life, so far, arrived the summer I was pregnant with my eldest son. The future was growing in me with all of its terrifying unpredictability, and I found myself anxious, unable to work and woefully at sea.” — Lauren Groff

I doubt Lauren had this maniacal infosec news cycle in mind when she wrote about the terrifyingly unpredictable future, but honestly, she’s got our current careers down cold. Let he who is not woefully at sea cast the first water balloon? I’ll work on it. Here we are with PHP taking up every available ounce of oxygen, Node.js adding its own spice to the sauce... and here’s me, staring my screen blankly, waiting for an original thought to leak out and onto this page. Not to worry, none have. There is simply nothing novel to say because the entire internet has it covered. In triplicate. With graphs and compelling statistics and AI-generated evil bad guy images galore.

These vulnerabilities are serious, and the remediations matter. Teams need to know what they run, find the affected systems, and get them patched and determine ways to secure systems that can’t be patched. I’m simply not going to add another dramatic headline to the stack or pretend there’s a clever new angle hiding in the margins. The thing I keep looping on is that the work underneath the headlines is familiar and it’s the real story. To defend your environment, you need a team that knows that environment, has enough time and expertise to investigate the telemetry, that can tell an anomaly from the usual benign noise, and take action. Yes, the right tools help, and without them you can’t do it — but the people doing the work are still what make those tools useful.

Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. This is the entire ballgame. Read it again: Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. Because a good response starts way before the headline. Know what you own, who owns it, what version is running, whether it can be reached from the internet, what identities can do what task on the device, etc. When a fix is available, make sure it actually reaches the system you meant to fix. If a system cannot be updated yet, give that exception an owner and a deadline. Reduce its exposure, add monitoring, and keep checking until the fix is in place. “We’ll get to it” is not a plan.

So, there may be nothing new to say about PHP this week, but the work is still worth talking about: Know your environment, take care of your team members, and keep paying attention when the weird thing stops being weird and starts becoming evidence. When the next headline arrives, help your teammate do the same.

“The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.” — Ursula K. Le Guin

The one big thing

Cisco Talos has recently discovered "NIK C2," a new command-and-control framework that integrates AI directly into its attack chain. This Go-based Windows implant allows adversaries to dump credentials, stream keystrokes, and deploy screen-locking ransomware. It also uses an integrated OpenAI model to analyze harvested data on the fly. By hijacking the victim's own API keys to fund these requests, NIK C2 collapses data collection and exploitation into a single, continuous session.

Why do I care?

By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, NIK C2 turns a compromised host into an active operational asset rather than a passive foothold. Because it processes data and generates context-aware payloads locally, it erases the offline processing delays that historically gave defenders a critical detection window. Furthermore, by piggybacking on the victim's OpenAI account, threat actors completely mask their infrastructure, leaving no attributable trace and complicating incident response.

So now what?

Defenders must embrace continuous behavioral vigilance. Ensure endpoint solutions monitor for unusual local proxy routing, unexpected PowerShell executions, and unauthorized access to browser databases or crypto wallets. Update your defenses using the ClamAV signature and indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided in the full blog.

Title: When Risk Becomes Personal: What Security Leaders Can Learn From a Cancer Diagnosis
Context: (Etay Maor) AI Has Changed Attack Speed, Not Security Fundamentals As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation, so-called virtual patching still comes down to...
Full Text:
Risk management leaders educate people on measuring exposure, testing assumptions and advising on how best to prepare for incidents they hope won’t occur. They know that the absence of a security alert does not stand for safety; that resilience depends on preparedness, and that a plan is only as good as the people who can execute it.

But when the risk is personal, those ideas take on a heavier meaning.

Receiving a Cancer Diagnosis

I was diagnosed after a routine physical that included a PSA blood test. I had not noticed any symptoms and had no known family history. That raised a few eyebrows and ultimately, a stage-three prostate cancer diagnosis.

My experience is not a case for making a personal health choice or offering clinical advice. That’s far from my wheelhouse. However, it is a helpful framework for a profession that often talks about preparedness, leadership and resilience, but sometimes forgets to consider the people expected to deliver all three.

Risk Appetite Changes When the Asset is You

In professional life, leaders can be admirably objective. They can challenge a security control, decide whether a certain risk falls within an agreed tolerance, and explain to a board why a difficult trade-off is necessary. They are typically analyzing a faceless enterprise.

Risk management is more than recommending a set of analytical frameworks. It is also decision making under duress, usually done with incomplete information and nervous tempers. Leaders who never acknowledge that human aspect may be poorer prepared, not richer, when pressure mounts on their own lives or teams.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The parallel with cyber governance should be handled carefully, but it is useful. A security leader should not accept at face value a supplier assurance statement, a default technology configuration, or management recommendations without formal review.

Similarly, a patient should not be made to feel that asking questions is somehow confrontational. In both situations, agency derives from available information, psychological safety, feeling able to say: help me understand the options, the assumptions, and the consequences of the mitigation plan.

Resilience is Preparation, Not Performance

Before my radiotherapy, I prepared deliberately, focusing on fitness, diet, rest, meditation and mental conditioning. I had to reevaluate my relationship with alcohol and caffeine. I sought to make a game out of it, imagining my 37-week treatment as a daily tournament: one demanding day at a time, with the aim of arriving at my best condition possible for each “game.” Doing this gave structure to an experience where I would otherwise feel a loss of control.

The more general leadership lesson here is that resilience grows under certain conditions: clear routines, manageable goals, supportive relationships, and the right to rest. And to change course when the original plan has ceased to be appropriate.

At times I felt like I had overdone it; my body forced me to listen. That matters. Cyber teams are told to endure while normalizing exhaustion: pulling all-nighters for incident response, always on call, the idea that commitment is measured by availability.

But a security function cannot be resilient if its people have little opportunity to recover. Personal resilience is not an individual productivity program. It is an ability reinforced by support, boundaries, and a culture that sees recovery as part of a sustained performance.

Transparency Can Be a Control, Not a Liability

Cancer can carry stigma, especially in senior environments where strength is too often interpreted as invulnerability. I decided to go public with my diagnosis to raise awareness because I did not want to hide what was happening. Not surprisingly, the response was mixed. Some people just plain didn’t know what to say, while others were supportive.

That is a familiar dynamic for security leaders. We want people to disclose incidents early, raise concerns and ask for help. But organizations can unintentionally discourage the openness they say they value. If the culture demands polished certainty from leaders, it becomes harder for anyone to share a vulnerability or need.

Everyone should have the right to control what they disclose and when, and with whom. Leaders who embody the notion that humanity and accountability are not in opposition can help lead by example. They can model a better kind of strength: the ability to hold space for others without pretending to be invincible.

This is not only a show of goodwill to the employers. It is a resilience issue. Workplace support for people undergoing cancer treatment can come in many forms, from time off and flexible hours to adjusted responsibilities, regular check-ins, occupational health support or employee assistance.

A More Human Model of Risk Leadership

Of course, personal health and cybersecurity are not interchangeable. A PSA result is not a vulnerability scan, and treatment is not incident response. The analogy breaks down when trying to make illness sound like a management problem to be solved through willpower.

But risk leaders can still take away something important. The habits that help organizations confront uncertainty, things like curiosity, preparation, trusted expertise, purposeful communication and adaptive recovery, matter in human life too. So does acknowledging what those habits cannot control.

For a profession built around anticipating harm, the challenge is not to become more alarmed. It is to become more attuned to the weak signals we ignore, to the people we expect will cope in silence and to the difference between seeming okay and actually being supported.

We need to let go of stigmas or assumptions and begin an honest dialogue around prostate health for men. The responsible version of that message is just as blunt: talk to a clinician about your personal risk and what PSA testing can reveal.

Cybersecurity leaders often ask organizations if they are prepared for disruption. A more personal question may be just as important: are we creating an environment where people can freely discuss risk, ask for help if they need it and recover without having to compromise their dignity?

Disclaimer: This is a personal account of my experiences and not meant as medical advice. Concerned readers should consult with qualified healthcare professionals.

Title: Chrome extensions with 13.4 million installs caught hijacking searches
Context: Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access
