Title: Zero Standing Privilege: Give the Next CVE Nothing to Inherit
Context: On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites
Full Text:
Zero Standing Privilege: Give the Next CVE Nothing to Inherit

Delinea Blog > The next CVE is already being found; make sure it finds nothing standing

The next CVE is already being found; make sure it finds nothing standing

Why new CVEs outpace patching, how a foothold inherits standing privilege, and how just-in-time access and secrets management limit what one exploit can reach. Includes five questions to test your environment.

On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites.

The PHP maintainers shipped fixes four days later, on October 21. Any vulnerable server that an attacker exploited before the server was patched could have given up the database passwords, API keys and cloud tokens the server held.

New vulnerabilities now arrive faster than organizations can patch them. Zero standing privilege limits what each exploit can reach

On October 23, Delinea published “PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks,” which covers which secrets to rotate first and how to prepare for the attacks that follow.

This blog covers the pattern behind PHP2Shell. New exploits now arrive faster than patching programs can absorb them, so organizations need a defense that does not depend on knowing which flaw comes next. Zero standing privilege (ZSP) gives an attacker nothing standing to inheritno matter which system the attacker breaks into first.

PHP2Shell was one of three vulnerabilities in the news during the week of October 19. On October 21, CISA added Plex2Shell, a chain of four vulnerabilities that gives attackers code execution on Plex Media Server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Plex had fixed the flaws in early August, yet the Shadowserver Foundation counted more than 36,000 exposed servers still unpatched in early September. Researchers also published a working proof-of-concept exploit for a critical, unauthenticated flaw in Fortinet FortiSIEM about a week after Fortinet shipped the fix.

More exploits are likely to follow before the month ends. The pattern matters more than any single bug. New exploits arrive at a rising pace; defenders get less time to respond to each one, and some systems go months without a patch.

Vulnerabilities now arrive continuously

The 2026 data show the same acceleration. CISA added 247 vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog between January 1 and October 1, more than the 245 it added in all of 2025. Since June 10, CISA has given federal agencies three days to remediate most new KEV entries, down from 21 days for most 2025 entries. Even under the longer deadlines, organizations took a median of 43 days to fully remediate KEV vulnerabilities in 2025, according to the Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group recorded an average of 11 zero-days a month from January through August, up from 8 a month in 2025. The October Microsoft Patch Tuesday release fixed more than 1,400 CVEs, the largest release since the program began. Only a fraction of those CVEs will be exploited, but an attacker needs only one.

AI now speeds up both the discovery of flaws and the development of exploits. In June, Microsoft Vice President of Engineering Tom Gallagher said AI-assisted vulnerability discovery was enabling bug hunting “at a speed and scale previously unseen.” Amazon Threat Intelligence wrote that AI-assisted analysis “makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit.”

The pace of new vulnerabilities is likely to keep climbing. No patching program, however well run, closes the gap between disclosure and deployment to zero. Patching remains essential, and organizations should fix KEV entries first. A strategy that depends on patching faster than attackers can find and weaponize flaws will lose over a long enough timeline.

A foothold inherits whatever privilege is standing

Each of the three exploits gives an attacker the same thing: code running on a system the organization trusts. Security teams call that position a foothold. What happens next depends less on the vulnerability than on what the compromised system can reach. Field Effect made the same point about Plex2Shell, noting that further impact “depends on the permissions assigned to the [Plex Media Server] service account and the resources accessible from the host.”

A web server running PHP often holds database credentials, API keys and cloud tokens in its configuration or environment. A SIEM collects logs from across the environment and often stores the credentials it uses to access monitored systems, making an unauthenticated SIEM flaw a high-value target. Management consoles and orchestrators often hold administrative rights over the systems they manage.

Standing privilege is access that an identity holds at all times, whether or not anyone is using it. The vulnerability gets the attacker in the door. Standing privilege decides how far the attacker gets.

An AI agent ran the full attack chain in July

A July incident at Hugging Face showed what happens when exploitation no longer needs a human at the keyboard. An AI agent running in an internal evaluation at a frontier AI lab escaped its sandbox and ran a four-and-a-half-day campaign, roughly two and a half days of which it spent inside Hugging Face production infrastructure. Hugging Face reconstructed the campaign from roughly 17,600 recovered agent actions.

The agent got in through two flaws in a dataset-processing pipeline. One flaw handed the agent the secrets and tokens stored in the environment of a production pod. Nearly every escalation after that ran on standing credentials: a shared broker credential bound to cluster-admin, a VPN key built for automation and tokens for source control. The agent went from code execution in a single pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under 13 hours. None of the escalations Hugging Face describes involved a human login, so stronger authentication for people would not have stopped them.

Hugging Face named “short-lived credentials” among its defensive priorities. After the incident, Hugging Face rotated credentials across its infrastructure and rebuilt the broker with a separate credential for each cluster.

Machine-speed attackers are likely to chain together the weaknesses that PHP2Shell, Plex2Shell and the FortiSIEM flaw expose: find a foothold, harvest what is standing and move. The foothold is the part defenders can’t always prevent. The standing privilege is the part defenders can remove.

ZSP works whichever CVE lands next

ZSP means no identity, whether AI agent, human or machine s, holds privilege it isn’t actively using. Just-in-time (JIT) access puts ZSP into practice. An identity requests access for a specific task, and an access platform grants that access for a limited time and revokes the access when the time ends. ZSP doesn’t depend on knowing which vulnerability attackers will exploit next, which is why ZSP fits an era in which new vulnerabilities arrive continuously.

The graphic below compares the same foothold in three scenarios: with standing privilege, with JIT Admin and JIT Access added, and with short-lived secrets added.

The model is illustrative, and the entry point is identical in each scenario.

Layer 1: JIT Admin removes standing root from hosts

An exploit usually runs with the permissions of the process it compromises. Researchers ran the Plex2Shell exploit, for example, as the Plex Media Server service account. The attacker’s next move is to escalate to root, the account with full control of a Linux or Unix server, or to local administrator on a Windows server. Standing root and local administrator rights turn one compromised server into many, because an attacker with those rights can read the SSH keys, service-account passwords and other credentials stored on the server.

JIT Admin replaces standing admin rights with elevation on demand. An administrator requests privilege for a task, the system checks the request against policy and grants the privilege for a limited time and records the elevation. Delinea Privilege Control for Servers (PCS) replaces standing root and local administrator rights with just-in-time elevation for specific commands.

PCS also enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA) at server login and again at privilege elevation. On a host that PCS protects, an exploit finds no standing admin rights to inherit, and PCS records each failed escalation attempt.

Layer 2: JIT Access limits spread across infrastructure

Once an attacker holds a foothold, the attacker’s next move is lateral movement: using credentials found on the first system to reach other servers, databases and clusters. In the Hugging Face incident, one shared broker credential gave the agent cluster-admin on two Kubernetes clusters within one second.

Delinea Runtime Authorization grants access to servers, Kubernetes clusters and databases per identity, per resource and for a limited time, so an attacker with a stolen credential reaches one resource for a limited time. The Runtime Authorization proxy injects credentials into each connection, so the client does not hold the credential and a compromised host has no stored credential to steal. Network access alone no longer grants access to a resource. A compromised application host or management server does not inherit access to every resource the host can reach on the network, and Runtime Authorization logs each connection it brokers.

Layer 3: Delinea Secret Server shrinks what an attacker can steal

PCS and Runtime Authorization limit where an attacker can go. Delinea Secret Server limits what the attacker finds on arrival. Secret Server brings privileged-account vaulting and workload secrets management together, so workloads (the applications and services that run without a person at the keyboard) retrieve credentials at runtime instead of carrying static values in environment variables and config files.

Secret Server rotates service-account and database passwords, API keys and other secrets on a schedule or after each use. Secret Server also issues dynamic credentials. Secret Server creates each dynamic credential on demand for a single workload, and the credential expires after a set time.

Secret Server doesn’t make a compromised host blind. An attacker with code execution can still read whatever credentials are present on the host at that moment, which is why the earlier Delinea blog—PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks—advises treating each secret a compromised server could read as stolen. What Secret Server changes is the value and lifespan of what the attacker reads.

Continuous CVE discovery demands continuous identity discovery

Vulnerability management identifies which systems are exposed. Identity security identifies what an attacker can reach from a compromised system. Security teams cannot reduce standing privilege they haven’t found. Machine and service identities are often the hardest to find. Hugging Face wrote that it had “wrongly provisioned” its broker with one credential shared across clusters and bound to cluster-admin. An inventory of privileged machine identities is the kind of check that surfaces a credential like that before an attacker does.

Delinea Continuous Identity Discovery uses AI to find human, machine and AI identities across the environment and flag the identities that hold standing privilege.

ZSP doesn’t patch a vulnerability. The flaw is still there, the exploited process still runs and an attacker with code execution can still do whatever that process is permitted to do. Patching, configuration hardening, network restrictions and detection all remain necessary. After the incident, Hugging Face closed both code-execution paths, blocked pod access to cloud metadata and added detection, in addition to rotating credentials.

ZSP does a different job. ZSP shrinks what the exploited process is permitted to do and how long the process holds that permission, so the window between disclosure and patch carries less risk.

Five security questions to ask about your environment

If an attacker compromised one of your internet-facing or management systems today, such as a web server, a SIEM or an orchestrator, what admin rights and credentials could the attacker reach from that system?

How many human, machine and AI identities hold standing privileged access, and when did your team last inventory those identities?

Does any single credential grant admin rights across more than one system, cluster or environment?

How long would a stolen service-account password, API key or token stay valid?

When the next exploited CVE lands on a product you run, how quickly can you tell which privileged identities and secrets the affected system holds or can reach?

Each question your team cannot answer points to standing privilege that an attacker could inherit.

Plan for the exploit that arrives before the patch

Prevention will sometimes fail, and sometimes the patch will arrive after the exploit. The organizations that fare best are likely to be the ones that removed standing privilege, not the ones that patched fastest every time.

Privilege Control for Servers keeps a foothold from escalating to root on hosts. Runtime Authorization limits how far the attacker can move across infrastructure. Secret Server shortens the life of each credential the attacker steals. Together, the three products apply ZSP across human, machine and AI identities, which helps one compromised system stay one compromised system.

Full Text:
BAE Systems has restored the federal judiciary’s Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) and says no data was taken in the cybersecurity incident that knocked it offline for more than two weeks.

“BAE Systems, Inc., working closely with the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts (AOUSC), has resumed operations of the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) system. No other systems were affected. No data was extracted. There was no breach of any PII,” a BAE Systems, Inc. spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

The BNC, which BAE operates under contract with the judiciary, is the channel through which all federal bankruptcy courts in the US send their notices. Notices stopped flowing through the center around October 9.

When the incident first came to light, neither BAE nor the judiciary addressed whether any data had been compromised. BAE’s new statement still leaves out what caused the incident and whether it was a cyberattack.

On October 27, the Administrative Office of the US Courts confirmed that, according to BAE, the problems had been fixed and the BNC was available again.

Bankruptcy court notices show the center came back on October 26 and began clearing the delayed notices, oldest first.

In response to the outage, the Judicial Conference declared a “Bankruptcy Rules emergency” on October 22. The declaration lets bankruptcy judges push back deadlines, pause time periods and issue related orders to deal with the fallout.

Title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
Context: The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age
Full Text: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither. BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet. "The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all." 'Circumvention inevitable' Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented. It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks. Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout, committing to implementing more robust measures that promote the ban’s aims. It said it has identified some mitigations that could be taken to counter circumvention, such as making it easier for users to report suspected underage social media users, and “using age inference models.” The regulator said it will closely monitor circumvention for the first 12 months after the ban is enforced to understand possible methods to prevent children from finding ways around the age checks. In May, nearly a year after the OSA’s age verification requirements kicked in, researchers found that the existing age checks proved largely ineffective at keeping under-18s away from adult content online. Some reported beating age checks with just a drawn-on moustache. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said recently that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children’s ability to access potentially harmful online content. Commenting on today’s announcement, Ofcom chief exec Dame Melanie Dawes said that when the social media ban takes effect, it will take a whole-of-society approach to ensure the ban is upheld. ?This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right," she said. "It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply. "We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play." The UK government is expected to outline the first set of regulations related to the under-16 social media ban by the end of the year, and Ofcom is in the process of developing draft guidance for platforms. ®

By

Sergiu Gatlan

October 29, 2026

08:00 AM

1

Microsoft released the KB5127936 preview cumulative update for Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 26H2, with 41 changes, including File Explorer and Cloud rebuild improvements.

KB5127936 is a preview update that adds new features and fixes at the end of each month, letting IT admins and users test them before they roll out to the entire user base during next month's Patch Tuesday.

However, unlike regular Patch Tuesday cumulative updates, monthly preview updates are optional and don't include security patches.

The October 2026 preview update makes the File Explorer context menu faster and easier to customize, letting users choose which app extensions and commands appear and how they're organized.

After you install KB5127936, Cloud rebuild can also reinstall Windows without USB media or a custom image, using an image and drivers downloaded directly from Windows Update, even when Windows won't start.

Microsoft also updated XBOX mode to include a refreshed Gaming Task View with quick access to key system actions like Power Options and Exit to Desktop while gaming via a new navigation bar.

​You can install the KB5127936 preview update by downloading it from the Microsoft Update Catalog or by opening Settings, going to Windows Update, and selecting "Check for Updates."

Because this is an optional update, you will need to click the "Download and install" link unless you have "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" enabled (which prompts the OS to install it automatically).

Windows 11 KB5127936 highlights

Once installed, this optional non-security update will upgrade Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2 devices to builds 26200.9818 and 26300.9818, respectively.

The October 2026 preview update adds further changes and improvements, some of the more important ones highlighted below:

New! This update improves the Privacy & security page in Windows Settings by grouping related Camera, Microphone, and Location privacy controls and elevating usage information from linked pages onto the main page.

New! This update enables Windows recovery (WinRE) to automatically reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles already saved in Windows, including supported certificate-based networks. Devices can now get online automatically during recovery scenarios such as quick machine recovery or cloud rebuild, without preconfiguring Wi-Fi credentials in WinRE. This capability is on by default, and IT admins can disable it. Microsoft disclosed this feature last month, and it is now beginning to roll out.

New! This update introduces a Restore Summary that appears after you restore a backup profile to a new device. The summary clearly shows what was restored, including Windows settings and the list of Microsoft Store apps. This improves transparency during device transitions, helps you validate your restore results, and lets you continue setup on your new device with confidence.

New! This update improves the adaptive hibernate policy to provide faster Modern Standby instant-on resumes while helping preserve battery life when the charge is low. Noticeable changes include less hibernation when the battery is above 80% and earlier hibernation below 10%.

This month, Microsoft also reminded users that updated Secure Boot certificates are rolling out to replace the original 2011 certificates, which will expire in late June 2027.

Microsoft first announced plans to refresh expiring Secure Boot certificates on eligible Windows 11 systems in January, after warning users and IT admins in November 2025 to update them before they expire.

The company also warned customers they may need to reboot one more time after installing the October 2026 optional update and updates rolling out over the next several months.

"With recent and upcoming Windows updates over the next few months, a limited number of consumer and business devices might experience one additional restart during installation," Microsoft noted in a message center update. "This one‑time restart occurs after a Secure Boot certificate update is applied as part of the Secure Boot update process."

Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked

Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

Title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
Context: A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain...
Full Text: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register. Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register. Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register. A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.” Which repos were affected? As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects. The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular. Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K). “These projects are used by thousands of organizations," Babo said. The researchers disclosed their findings to all of the projects’ maintainers, and most of the repositories were closed or fixed, but they can’t confirm that all of them were. This campaign follows several earlier supply chain attacks against open source security and dev tools as attackers increasingly look for new methods to steal credentials and other secrets. “There is no way to stop the attackers from attempting,” Nakibly said. “The only way is to make sure that the workflow code is resilient, and not vulnerable to such attacks." The researchers recommend applying least-privilege access to CI/CD workflows, and separating as much as possible workflows triggered by external events from jobs with elevated permissions. “Developers should treat external content as untrusted, and also limit the secrets and environment variables that are available to the workflow,” Babo said. ®

Online Scam Volumes Double to Overtake Phishing

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

Detections of online scams doubled between July 2025 and June 2026, as cybercriminals focused on more direct ways to generate revenue from victims, according to Akamai.

The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time.

It recorded around 6.4 million online scams in the period April-June 2026, versus 3.2 million in July-September 2025.

This category typically includes fake stores, investment scams, tech support scams and payment fraud, it said.

“The fight against fraud is no longer just an isolated financial function; it is a critical, cross-functional cybersecurity imperative,” said Patrick Sullivan, CTO, security strategy at Akamai. “As autonomous AI agents and synthetic identities redefine how customers interact with brands, threat actors are exploiting these same vectors to conduct business logic abuse and zero-click data exfiltration.”

Read more on digital scams: Social Media Platforms Earn Billions from Scam Ads.

However, phishing – which Akamai defines as attempts to steal credentials, authentication info and data via brand impersonation – also rose during the period.

Phishing detections increased by 61%, driven by reusable phishing kits, industrialized infrastructure, and AI.

The latter has helped to decrease the average phishing attack lifespan by more than 50%, dropping from 48 days (Q4 2025) to 22 days (Q2 2026), the report claimed.

“Adversaries leverage AI to generate dynamic templates, produce multilingual lures at scale, and deploy condition-aware evasion – drastically lowering costs while bypassing legacy defenses,” it explained.

“Conversely, security teams use AI to compress investigation and reduce workflows from days to less than an hour through automated indicator analysis, infrastructure clustering, and evidence collection, disrupting attacks before victims are impacted.”

Over 80% of scam victims in the US reported suicidal thoughts following the crime, according to new data from the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) published on October 28.

A large part of this is down to the self-blame and social stigma attached to scams, the ITRC claimed. It also blamed “institutional ghosting" for the mental anguish that victims often feel.

“When general consumer scam victims overcame their shame to seek help, institutions frequently compounded the injury,” it explained. “Nearly nine in 10 general consumer scam victims asked an organization for help and were never contacted, and 67.2% reported that the organizations they contacted ‘made me feel it was my own fault.’”

A lack of support can also leave victims exposed to recovery scams.

“Abandoned by legitimate institutions and desperate to undo the damage, 78.9% of general consumer scam victims (and 90.9% of those experiencing suicidal ideation) paid a fee to a third party who promised to recover their stolen money, fix their credit or catch the scammer – compared to just 6.5% of scam victims who connected with the ITRC,” the report said.

Title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
Context: In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at...
Full Text:
In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.

It was September 25, 2026, and Alex, a professional online poker player, was using his Claude AI agent to review some play statistics. (Alex only agreed to speak with WIRED under a pseudonym to avoid any risk of reprisals from threat actors.) After Alex’s SQL database crashed and needed to be reset, the Claude agent noticed something suspicious: A program called MeshAgent was operating in the background, where it seemed to be capable of capturing Alex’s screen and even controlling his entire machine.

Thanks to the Claude agent’s report, Alex could see the program had been installed on April 24, and not by Alex himself. Alex says the agent identified 11 time-stamped events when the program had been capturing his screen based on graphic errors it caused during screen sharing instances. During all 11, Alex had been playing a session on ACR, also called Americas Cardroom, a major worldwide online poker operator.

He checked his hand histories and quickly found the most troubling info yet: The same opponent, playing under the handle OxOO, was at his table for 10 of those 11 sessions.

The handle was familiar. Alex and several friends in the high-stakes community had shared suspicions about this player’s behavior in the past. Alex checked the player’s win rate stats via a public tracking site; they were astronomically higher than the best players in the world, a statistical impossibility given the sample of hands played. In Alex’s view, it was glaringly obvious that this player was cheating.

An investigation by Alex and other members of the high-stakes community in subsequent days confirmed his fears—and then some. Alex was one of hundreds of players allegedly targeted with this type of malware by the same reported threat actor across a period of multiple years. Alex, who was the first to discover MeshAgent on his computer, claims he was “only” ripped off for around $30,000, a relatively moderate sum for the level he plays at; many of his peers weren’t so lucky.

With millions of dollars allegedly stolen across the biggest sites on the internet, the poker world is searching for answers about how the scheme was allowed to continue so long, whether major sites took the risk seriously after it was reported, and whether online poker itself has been irreversibly compromised.

Poker has never been short on cheating controversies; online poker especially so. The “superuser” method, in which a cheater gains unauthorized access to their opponents’ cards and can therefore act with perfect information against them, was one of the first to show up online.

Two major sites in online poker’s early days, Absolute Poker and Ultimate Bet, served as cautionary tales in the mid-2000s. In separate instances, superuser cheaters were able to gain insider access to the websites and bilk players for millions of dollars. (Much of the loot was refunded to players following an investigation.) Those high-profile incidents led to tightened security measures from many top poker sites.

Another minor superuser incident took place in 2013, when a Finnish high-stakes player said his laptop had been stolen from his hotel room during a European Poker Tour tournament in Barcelona. When the laptop was recovered, it had been infected with malware that allowed a hacker to view his screen remotely. And maybe the most famous superuser scandal of all took place on the live felt: In a story that made it all the way to SportsCenter, a player named Mike Postle was accused of stealing over $250,000 from livestreamed games at Stones Gambling Hall in 2018 and 2019 with the aid of what observers believed to be an alleged accomplice with access to live card data who fed information to Postle’s phone. (Postle denied the accusations, alleging it was “fake news.”)

Outside one relatively small (and quickly remedied) incident in 2023, though, the online poker world had gone years without a confirmed superuser incident—until now. And some of what’s known about this latest attempt signals a savvier threat actor than in previous scandals, plus a degree of patience not typically seen in attacks like these.

“Traditionally, when you see these types of financially motivated threat actors, they will get access to a system and then as soon as they’re on it, they’ll do a scope of what they have access to and then they’ll hit everyone all at once and dump all the wallets,” says WolfSec, a cybersecurity professional who consults with many high-stakes poker players on security measures. He was first to break the news of the MeshAgent scam on September 29, on his X account. (WolfSec agreed to speak to WIRED under the condition his real name not be used out of fears of reprisals from hackers; WIRED independently confirmed his credentials as a cybersecurity expert.)

But this hacker didn’t do any of that, despite many of these players having large cryptocurrency holdings and other investments accessible on their machines. The attacker seemed instead to be performing advanced reconnaissance. In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at the time, no other action was taken once the players wiped the malware from their computers.

It appears, though, that the hacker was simply biding his time and improving his methods in preparation for an eventual strike.

Instead of targeting individual players directly, this more recent attack involved third-party software programs called IntuitiveTables and Jurojin. These programs allow professionals to play dozens of online poker hands at once. Using these popular “multi-table” tools, players can switch between live games with a keystroke, place bets or make plays with hot keys, and other actions that make it easier to play at several virtual tables at the same time. The hacker compromised both applications, WolfSec says, pushing malicious software to over a thousand estimated users.

In the case of Jurojin, the attacker gained access to the developer’s own system for software updates and was able to deliver the remote-access agent to existing users through normal, automatic updates.

The developer of Intuitive Tables was running Jurojin on their test computer, and that machine got the remote-access agent as part of Jurojin’s compromised software update. Using the agent, the attacker added malicious code to the Intuitive Tables application before the developer signed the security certificate for an updated build of the app. That version carrying the malicious code was posted to the Intuitive Tables website as a public download, and everyone who installed that version of the app unknowingly also installed a backdoor on their computer.

In both instances, the malicious code was delivered through a standard update channel or an official release, so neither the users nor their antivirus apps detected anything amiss.

The modified version of Intuitive Tables behaved exactly like the clean version, with one exception: It also checked players’ files for their usernames.

“If you were on a hard-coded list that was stored on the attacker’s infrastructure, which [the malware] reached out to and downloaded and compared your username to, then it acted as a malicious program and downloaded additional malicious files,” WolfSec says. “If you weren’t on that list, then it became the normal program and didn’t do anything malicious at all.”

The list appears to have been populated primarily with regular high-stakes players across several sites. All of the players on the list appear to have had the MeshAgent program installed covertly on their machines. The hacker was ready to pounce.

In early 2025, a couple of new players began frequenting high-stakes games—one on ACR (using the handle “JackKlompus”) and another major global site called CoinPoker (handle: “Europe”). Strangely, despite not being familiar to other regulars in these games, the players refused to identify themselves in table chats, a common request that’s typically granted by new players in high-stakes poker. The new opponents were also winning with improbable frequency. (Later, once the pros started sharing information about their games, it was pieced together that these players were the same person.)

Mike, a professional poker player who spoke to WIRED using a pseudonym due to fear of reprisals from hackers, played on both sites at the time and was at tables with the player using these handles. Mike says at first he wondered if the mystery player’s success was somehow explainable. Maybe they were doing something new that Mike and his fellow pros just hadn’t figured out.

“You could kind of excuse it” at first, Mike says. “Maybe this guy is really, really good or something.”

As the number of winning hands grew, though, Mike and several high-stakes friends became more suspicious. They initially suspected that the player was using real-time assistance via game-theory-based engines that outperform the best human players. Real-time assistance is banned across major sites, but is difficult to police perfectly and is something pros are regularly watching out for. Mike mostly stopped playing at tables with the mystery player, as a precaution.

Like WolfSec, Mike reflects on a relative level of skill and discipline employed by this player during those 2025 sessions, especially compared to other known cheaters in poker history. The account generally used standard bet sizes and played normal hand ranges. Its session-by-session play never raised too many eyebrows; only the account’s win rate over time drew scrutiny.

But in June 2026, Mike played a two-hour heads-up (one-on-one) session on a different site, ClubWPT Gold, which he’d later determine—following reviews with the website’s security team—came against the same player from the 2025 sessions. The player used a different handle to evade detection, so Mike didn’t see a reason to be extra cautious. The opponent simply steamrolled Mike, making every correct decision even in seemingly impossible spots—almost like he could see Mike’s cards. “It was very blatant,” Mike says.

Immediately after the session, Mike messaged several friends in the high-stakes world to say he thought he’d been cheated.

Turns out he was right. When word of the hack broke publicly on WolfSec’s X account, ClubWPT Gold investigated. The site banned the account Mike had played against and refunded him for his losses, says Randy Lundy, head of customer operations for ClubWPT Gold.

This alleged cheater’s presence in online circles was an open secret across the community by this point. In fact, Mario Mosböck, a poker ambassador for CoinPoker who was authorized to speak about the company’s response to the hack, says the site began investigating this player as early as 2025, banning them and refunding over $100,000 in allegedly stolen funds to affected players. (Mosböck says the return of funds was delayed several months because the alleged cheater appealed the confiscation to regulators.) The player’s simple win rate and play style statistics appeared to be evidence of malfeasance, even if the site couldn’t definitively determine how the cheating was happening.

How, then, was the same alleged cheater allowed to keep ripping off players like Alex and Mike on multiple other supposedly reputable sites more than a year later?

“They confirmed multiple times that they looked at my report, but for whatever reason they didn't act on it,” says Patrick Howard, a professional poker player and founder of the coaching company Mobius Poker.

The “they” he’s referring to is GGPoker, arguably the most well-known site in the world for non-US players. Howard says he submitted a report to the site in early September 2026, weeks before the MeshAgent hack became public, highlighting the alleged cheater’s unusual play and urging the site to investigate.

“I found multiple three- to four-standard-deviation outliers,” Howard says, and that was across a limited hand history sample sent to him by friends and clients. He sent his findings to the GGPoker team but received no response. He got a reply only after WolfSec’s public reveal of the hack on X, with the site telling him there “wasn’t conclusive evidence” to act at the time of his complaint.

Various online poker sites handled the incident differently. Players have largely praised CoinPoker for proactively banning the player based on win rate and play tendencies alone, which are accepted as definitive indicators of cheating at stakes this high and with samples this large; while ClubWPT Gold only seems to have been impacted later in the scheme, that site also appears to have acted decisively upon discovering it.

But the hacker remained active on GGPoker and ACR until late September, allegedly stealing between $1.5 million and $4 million, based on the estimates of the sources WIRED spoke to for this story.

“Players are frustrated, because they had been reporting this for a year,” says John Andress, head of game integrity for A5 Labs, a cybersecurity platform that provides anti-cheating services to ClubWPT Gold and other brands. “A few of the platforms just completely ignored them.”

This was despite signs that many feel were all too obvious.

CoinPoker says the player’s alleged true identity was known early in this process, after the company conducted a webcam security interview with them in February 2025. The name the player gave matched the handle the player later used on GGPoker, which requires players to use their real name as their handle instead of a pseudonym for certain high-stakes games. (WIRED is not naming the player because they have not been charged with any crime. The player did not respond to multiple requests for comment on this story). The CoinPoker spokesman says their team reached out to ACR with their findings as well and received no response. (Requests for comment from WIRED to ACR and GGPoker received no reply.)

To its credit, GGPoker acknowledged the incident and announced several fixes in an October 15 blog post, including banning third-party tools and adding win-rate anomaly detection. The site also says it traced the accused attacker’s funds to a Coinbase account and has asked the crypto company to restrict the account and preserve its records; it says it also provided the wallet addresses to industry watchdogs and law enforcement.

But ACR is going the opposite direction: On October 18, it emailed players claiming its security team found no compromised game outcomes or wrongdoing and will not issue any refunds—despite, in the same email, announcing a new feature to stop remote-viewing tools from capturing the images of the cards in players’ hands.

Other entities have taken concrete action: Both Jurojin and IntuitiveTables (via its Discord channel) released tools to help users detect whether the MeshAgent hack had affected their machines. AceGuardian, a research group that’s part of A5 Labs, put out an open-source “superuser detection” tool designed for use on any poker site. WolfSec says he submitted a complaint to the the Internet Crime Complaint Center, the cybercrime arm of the FBI, and has been working with players on improving machine security. The FBI, when reached for comment by WIRED, would not confirm receipt nor any details of this complaint.

But these efforts will be so successful only if the sites treat these incidents with more scrutiny and don’t just spring into action in the aftermath of major attacks.

“Ultimately, the sites have to ban the players,” Howard says. “I think they dropped the ball here.”

ICO Reprimands Staffordshire Police After Domestic Abuse Breach

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

A UK police force committed a serious breach of data protection law after sharing the home address of a domestic abuse victim with their abuser, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has revealed.

The privacy regulator issued a reprimand to Staffordshire Police on October 28, following the incident in March 2024.

The force had served the abuser, “P,” a Domestic Violence Protection Notice (DVPN) on their release from prison in order to protect the abuse victim, or “data subject.”

However, it erroneously included that person’s home address, which was not previously known to P.

“As a consequence of the investigation into the relevant incident the commission has become aware of allegations that P subjected the data subject to both physical and emotional abuse over a period of several years, resulting in the data subject having to relocate their home address on numerous occasions in order to escape the alleged abuse,” the reprimand noted.

“In this context, the data subject’s current address was highly sensitive information and should have been handled as such.”

Read more on police privacy breaches: Police Scotland Fined After Sharing Victim’s Phone Data.

Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to prevent the disclosure, “including poor completion rates for mandatory training in both data protection and issuing DVPNs.”

It argued that Staffordshire Police had since made improvements to reduce the risk of a similar event taking place in the future. These included increased training completion rates, new leadership roles for domestic abuse cases, new internal procedures and new technology to improve services for victims.

ICO head of investigations, Sally-Anne Poole, said the case is a reminder of the importance of getting the basics right.

“Every organization must be doing everything necessary to protect the personal information in their care, especially where there is a known risk to someone's safety,” she added. “Whether in policing, health or local government, we urge organizations to take responsibility for training their staff and putting appropriate systems in place to avoid these incidents and the harm they can cause.”

Advice for Handling Sensitive Information

The ICO warned back in 2023 that organizations handling the personally identifiable information (PII) of domestic abuse victims could put lives at risk if breaches occur.

It said at the time that it had issued reprimands to seven organizations in the previous 14 months after sensitive PII was breached, including one police force.

The latest revelations will do little to allay concerns that the regulator’s public sector approach – which favors warnings, reprimands and enforcement notices over fines – is not having the desired effect.

After this latest incident the ICO advised organizations handling sensitive PII to:

Ensure staff know how to handle the PII of people experiencing domestic abuse with extra care

Review default templates and processes to ensure PII is only included where legally necessary

Regularly check contact information to avoid disclosing information to an old address, email or phone number

Always double check before any PII is transferred, altered or disclosed

Ensure training is thorough, relevant and tailored to the tasks staff actually carry out

Title: NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework
Context: NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.”

NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session.

In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically.

In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies.

NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows.

Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline.

NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool

The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module.

Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2.

The observed NIK C2 implant samples in the wild contains an embedded build path (/opt/nik_panel/data/build_52b79724a1fc4b8f/main.go), which identifies the project as "nik_panel" and indicates that the implant was cross compiled for Windows from a Linux development environment. Furthermore, the embedded eight-byte hex token matching the build identifier highlights that the threat actor's infrastructure actively tracking and versioning the implants.

Figure 1. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture.

NIK C2 implant evolution timeline

Talos observed that the NIK C2 implant development trajectory spans at least three distinct versions. All binaries observed in the wild were compiled with Go 1.23.4 (which was released in December 2024), placing the entire sample set compiled no earlier than late 2024. The actor has Zeroed PE TimeDateStamp fields and near-epoch filesystem timestamps (manifesting as Nov 29, 1979) are applied consistently across all samples.

We developed a timeline based on the initial sighting dates of NIK C2 implant variants in OSINT.

Figure 2. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline.

The pace of capability addition across the three versions indicates a technically proficient team with prior malware operations experience is actively expanding NIK C2 towards a full-service adversarial framework.

Active NIK C2 server seen in the wild

During our research, we observed that a threat actor hosted the NIK C2 framework on a server at IP address “87.120.196[.]120”, resolving the domain “total-sitevv[.]lol”. The C2 server hosted an SSL/TLS certificate (serial number 7d16381a9de823943b5a0987dbd0f26edf22052b and jarm:"28d28d28d00000000042d42d0000001f361a1bf80ed39a1e352adeb016a07b" ) with the Common Name (CN) set to nik-panel. This CN value matches strings embedded within the implant binary. Observing the NIK C2 infrastructure active in the wild allowed us to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is not merely a proof of concept, but a fully functional, AI-integrated C2 framework.

Figure 3. NIK C2 was observed in the wild during the research period.

NIK C2 implant integrates OpenAI’s API

AI integration is one of the most architecturally distinct features of NIK C2 implant. It constructs a fully formed HTTP request to OpenAI’s production inference endpoint, transmits it from the victim machine IP address, parses the JSON response, and returns the AI-generated text to the actor’s panel. The entire operation from receiving the actor prompt to returning the large language model (LLM) reply is executed synchronously with a 60-second timeout.

The implant begins by extracting three fields from the command payload received from the C2. The first field, identified by the key prompt, is the text the actor wants to send to the AI model. If the prompt string has zero length, the handler immediately constructs an error response and returns without making any outbound network call. The second field, identified by the key api_key is the OpenAI API key to use for authentication. The third field, identified by the key model, specifies which OpenAI model to use.

Figure 4. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

After extracting the three parameters, the implant checks whether the actor supplied an API key. If not, it calls the operating system's environment variable reader with the string OPENAI_API_KEY and uses the victim’s API key. This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications. If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference. OpenAI's billing system will charge the victim's payment method, and OpenAI's access logs will show the victim's API key as the one that made the requests, allowing no trace attributable to the threat actor.

If the actor does not specify a model name, the implant falls back to a five-character default string stored in the binary data section. Decoding the five-character value showed gpt-4 confirming that GPT4 is the default when no model is specified. The actor can override this by passing any valid OpenAI model identifier in the command payload, allowing selection of newer models as they become available without requiring a binary update.

The implant builds the OpenAI API request body by constructing a map with four fields. The first field uses the key model and contains the resolved model name. The second field uses key messages and contains a two-element array of message maps. The third field uses the key temperature and contains a floating-point value read from a constant in the binary data section. The fourth field uses the key max_tokens and contains an integer value also read from binary.

The message array is constructed in the order that the OpenAI Chat Completions API expects. The system message is first followed by the user message. The system message map has the role system and a content string that is exactly 68 bytes long hardcoded in the binary. This 68-byte string is the implant's behavioral instruction to the AI. It defines the model's operational role and response style for the duration of the session. The user message map has the role user and contains the actor's prompt text verbiage. The complete map structure is then serialized to JSON. The JSON message is sent to the URL https:// api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions, the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint, through an HTTP POST request.

Figure 5. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

When the HTTP response arrives with a 200 status code, the handler uses Golang's JSON decoder to parse the response body directly into a generic map structure without defining a typed schema. It then navigates the decoded map by string key lookups in the sequence that the OpenAI Chat Completions API response structure defines. The outermost map is queried for the key choices which in a successful response contains an array. The implant checks that this array is non-empty, then accesses its element keys message and content. The string value at key content is the AI model-generated text response.

After successfully extracting the AI-generated content, the handler assembles a result map with four entries. The key status is set to a constant string that reads as generated. The key code is set to the AI model's response text, so that the actor receives the full content of the model’s replies. The key model is set to the resolved model name that was used for the request, confirming which model produced the output. The key usage is set to the raw usage object from the OpenAI response, which contains the prompt token count, completion token count, and total token count. This usage data allows the actor to track how many tokens are consumed per request. The completed result map is ultimately transmitted to the C2 server over WebSocket or through the HTTP fallback C2 address.

Figure 6. AI model response is encapsulated in JSON message and will be sent to C2.

Dual execution modes of NIK C2 implant

Upon execution, the implant inspects its command-line arguments to determine its execution path. The argument watchdog activates supervisory monitoring to relaunch the core process if terminated, the copywatchdog tracks file copy operations, and the absence of either defaults execution to primary agent mode.

In primary mode, it uses a named mutex to enforce single-instance execution, logs a message reading [NIK] Starting, generates a 32-byte cryptographic session key if uninitialized, decodes its obfuscated C2 address, and sets its masquerade name to “svchost.exe” or “simvol.exe”.

After initial setup, the binary records its process ID (PID) in the victim's temporary application folder and executes its persistence and evasion routines. These routines include copying to %appdata%/Roaming/Microsoft/Network with modified access controls, configuring Windows autostart registry entries, and masquerading its process. Finally, it starts the local proxy server, initiates the WebSocket communication loop in a separate goroutine, and enters a continuous heartbeat polling loop on the main thread.

Implant’s C2 command surface overview

The implant command dispatcher module facilitates over 52 commands that are directed by the C2 panel. The dispatcher module uses byte-level string matching to map the associated modules that are launched as concurrent goroutines, allowing multiple operations to run in parallel.

Implant deploys screen-locking ransomware

The ransomware module of the implant operates as a multi-stage attack controller that the actor runs in sequence to prepare, deploy, and retract a screen-locking ransomware payload.

At first, it executes PowerShell to execute a raw disk copy command that reads directly from the physical drive device path (“\\.\PhysicalDrive0”) and writes the first sector, which is Master Boot Record (MBR), to a file named “mbr_backup.bin” in the Windows temporary directory.

Figure 7. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s boot ransomware handler function.

Next, the module constructs a complete self-contained HTML lock screen code entirely at runtime from a hardcoded format string, parameterized with actor supplied Bitcoin and USDT wallet addresses, prices, contact email, timer duration, and custom text from the C2 command message, allowing the actor to fully customize the ransom demands.

Figure 8. Screenlocker HTML code is hardcoded in NIK C2 implant binary.

After generating the HTML code, the binary writes it to the file “lock_screen.html” in the system temporary directory. It then generates a Windows batch script that calls mshta.exe with the path to the HTML file, followed by an infinite loop construct with a five-second timeout between iterations, ensuring that if the user somehow closes the window it reopens within five seconds. This batch file is written to the temp directory as “lock_start.bat”.

The implant then runs a reg add command that writes a registry Run key named “SystemLock” under the current user's autostart path, pointing to a cmd /c invocation of the batch file, so the lock screen is executed on every user's logon. Additionally, a background goroutine is spawned that continuously monitors and relaunches the lock screen process. Finally, the module sends a confirmation response to C2 with the path of the deployed HTML file and the timer value.

The design of this ransomware module is notable for several reasons. It does not encrypt any files, which means it leaves no forensic trail of file modification timestamps or encryption markers. It relies entirely on a screen lock, which is considerably faster to deploy than a file encryption ransomware. The persistence via registry Run key and a self-healing loop ensures the screen lock survives user attempts to dismiss it and survives a system restart.

Figure 9. Desktop lockscreen page of the ransomware deployed by the NIK C2 implant.

Implant’s bootkit preparation feature

The bootkit preparation module of the implant is designed to survey the victim machine's boot firmware environment and then stage a bootkit payload file.

It executes bcdedit /enum, the Windows Boot Configuration Data editor, with the output flag that enumerates all boot entries while hiding the console window. The implant reads the full output and searches for three specific substrings in sequence including EFI, Windows Boot Manager, and Windows Legacy OS Loader. If any of these are found, the boot type is classified as UEFI. The binary also searches for ntldr, the legacy Windows NT loader used by BIOS-mode systems as a fallback. Based on which string was matched, the boot type is recorded as either "UEFI" or "BIOS" as a string of the appropriate length. Separately, the binary runs a PowerShell command invoking Confirm-SecureBootUEFI, which is a built-in PowerShell command that returns to the current Secure Boot state. The output is searched for the string True to detect an enabled Secure Boot and for False to detect an explicitly disabled Secure Boot. If neither is present, the value is recorded as unknown. The result is sent back to the C2, a map containing the boot type classification and the Secure Boot status string.

Then the implant writes a 16-byte placeholder file named “bootkit.bin” to the system temporary directory. The bytes written spell out "NIK_BOOTKIT_PREP" in ASCII, which serves as a staging marker rather than an actual bootkit binary. This placeholder confirms that the target path is writable by the current process, establishes the file location that subsequent operations will reference, and can be overwritten by the actual bootkit binary delivered through the implant's file-upload or file-write command handlers. The path to the staged file is returned to the C2 in response.

Implant’s theft functionality

When the actor issues the theft category commands from the C2, the implant executes the associated goroutines to collect the targeted data into a result map space in the victim machine memory:

WiFi password theft (wifi_steal)

The implant executes netsh commands directly via Go’s exec.Command function by passing arguments as discrete tokens rather than through a shell string. Harvested results are formatted under specific labels: plaintext Wi-Fi passwords appear under Key Content:, saved network names are cataloged under WiFi Profiles: (with missing entries flagged using the per-entry format [%s] not found), and execution failures or absent interfaces return standardized error strings such as [WiFi] no wireless adapter or access denied and No WiFi profiles found.

netsh wlan show profiles netsh wlan show profile name="" key=clear

The implant stages targeted browser database files into an archive alongside the Local State file, which contains the AES master key protected by Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI). The implant imports and executes the CryptUnprotectData Windows API to unwrap the AES key and decrypt the databases locally. Otherwise, it exfiltrates the raw encrypted databases to the C2 server for offline extraction.

Seed phrase, private key file, and system reconnaissance

The implant performs two regular expression patterns to search on the entire filesystem of the victim machine. These two regular expressions are designed to scan file names for sensitive cryptographic assets and credentials, functioning as case-insensitive patterns ?i. The first expression targets cryptocurrency recovery materials and wallet backups by matching keywords like "seed," "mnemonic," or "wallet" paired with common plain-text and data file extensions (.txt, .md, .csv, .dat), while the second seeks out asymmetric private keys and general secrets using terms like "private," "privkey," or "secret" paired with both text files and standard cryptographic key containers (.key, .pem). Because both patterns use unanchored, greedy matching (.*) without start (^) or end ($) boundary anchors, they capture any file where these sensitive terms precede the target extensions. The implant also performs victim machine reconnaissance by executing the following commands and uses chcp 65001 prefix to force the output in UTF-8 format.
