Title: Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a Major Leak of DHS Employee Records
Context: Emma Best, cofounder of DDoSecrets, says this is not the first time a social media platform has wrongly labeled the organization's website malicious or tried to restrict access...
Full Text:
Bluesky is blocking users from opening links to a newly leaked archive of records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors, and labels the pages “malicious.”

The files include people’s email addresses and phone numbers, “shared without their authorization,” Bluesky tells WIRED, in violation of its community guidelines. The company says it chose to block the links, rather than remove individual posts, “to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary.”

The DHS records, published Wednesday by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, list employees’ and contractors’ names, contact information, and membership in internal groups, tied in some cases to surveillance and undercover operations. A WIRED investigation found that the files lay out in detail how DHS is organized, from senior leadership to individual immigration agents, and in some cases appear to show who has access to certain technologies.

Users who try to open the archive through Bluesky’s website or app land on a page labeled “Blocked Link,” which says the URL has been identified as “malicious” and blocked for their safety. Bluesky did not respond to questions about whether the block was imposed automatically or whether any government agency had asked the company to restrict access to the data.

The DDoSecrets homepage loads normally from Bluesky. At least one third-party app, Klearsky, opens links to the DHS archive with no warning.

Bluesky promotes a decentralized approach to content moderation that lets users pick independent services that label or filter posts. Its current community guidelines bar sharing “home addresses, personal contact info, financial or medical data, or identification documents.” (A preview of the DHS leak analyzed by WIRED apparently contained work-related contact information one expert described as details that would be printed “on a business card.”) The same guidelines explicitly protect “factual reporting” on matters of public interest that are “related to government transparency and public officials.”

Bluesky started in 2019 as a Twitter research project, later became independent, and opened to the public in February 2024. By August of this year, it counted 45 million registered accounts, and an estimated 10.4 million people used its mobile app in June. Toni Schneider, the founding CEO of Automattic, has run the company since cofounder Jay Graber stepped down in March. Because the network runs on an open protocol, outside developers can build their own Bluesky apps and decide which of the company’s moderation labels to apply.

Emma Best, cofounder of DDoSecrets, says this is not the first time a social media platform has wrongly labeled the organization's website malicious or tried to restrict access to its publications. Twitter suspended DDoSecrets’ account in 2020, prior to the Elon Musk acquisition and X rebrand, and blocked links to its website after the group published BlueLeaks, a 269-gigabyte trove of internal records from hundreds of police agencies and fusion centers. Best says tech platforms often give in to government pressure but insists they cannot prevent the information from spreading. “They can’t stop the signal,” they say.

A group calling itself the Department of Peace gave the archive, dubbed “Icepick,” to DDoSecrets and journalist maia arson crimew. crimew also built a website for searching the records, and Bluesky blocks that site in its website and app as well.

At least one of Bluesky’s competitors has taken a different tack. Title: Prediction Markets Emerge as a New Vertical for Traffer Teams
Context: Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since the spring of 2026, Insikt Group has observed multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have quickly adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance. This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.

Artificial intelligence (AI) further accelerates this opportunism by reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events. Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement.

The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities. Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.

Key Findings

AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team supply affiliates with simulated prediction-market websites, administrative panels, payment infrastructure, and promotional support. Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.

AtlasCore’s Telegram posts recorded approximately $10.97 million in claimed deposits across its scam offerings between May 2 and September 18, 2026, with the deposits predominantly associated with prediction markets. PolyFucked separately advertises approximately $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures rely on threat actor reporting and remain unverified.

Magnetic Team advertises more than 3,000 simulated traders across more than 5,000 markets to fabricate convincing trading activity. Its code exposes configurable withdrawal-blocking pretexts, forced-loss controls, and pools of up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. AtlasCore similarly exposes settings to force wins or losses and impose individualized withdrawal restrictions.

All three traffer teams advertise or provide AI-assisted victim support. AtlasCore and PolyFucked also supply guidance for AI-generated promotional content, including synthetic influencers and branding, respectively. Magnetic Team’s source code contains indicators of likely AI-assisted development, suggesting AI use may extend to building and maintaining the underlying fraud platforms, although that assessment remains unconfirmed.

Insikt Group identified over 100 unique domains and subdomains associated with AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team, including administrative infrastructure and scam websites likely operated by the teams or their affiliates.

Threat Analysis

AtlasCore

In August 2026, Insikt Group identified a post on a low-tier cybercriminal forum seeking affiliates to join the traffer team “AtlasCore”. The thread was first created on May 15, 2026, by the user “AtlasCore”. The affiliate program was also advertised on a top-tier cybercriminal forum by the user “AtlasCorp” on May 28, 2026. The program includes an offering for prediction markets, as well as more typical traffer scams such as cryptocurrency exchanges and casinos.

Title: CCoP 2026: Strengthening Cyber Resilience Across Singapore’s Critical Infrastructure  by Yusri Mohamed Yusop
Context: The attack path extends beyond the CII environment An attacker may first compromise a user account, remote-access system, engineering workstation or management server before...
Full Text:
Singapore’s Cybersecurity Code of Practice for Critical Information Infrastructure 2026 marks an important shift in how CII owners must think about security.

The focus is no longer limited to protecting the designated CII environment itself. CCoP 2026 places greater emphasis on Board and senior-management accountability, visibility into systems connected to CII, continuous monitoring, behavioural baselining, threat hunting and evidence that security controls are working as intended.

For security leaders, the challenge is clear: attackers do not respect organisational or network boundaries.

The attack path extends beyond the CII environment

An attacker may first compromise a user account, remote-access system, engineering workstation or management server before moving toward the systems that deliver essential services.

CCoP 2026 reflects this reality by extending security requirements beyond the designated CII itself. The Code distinguishes between enterprise systems, CII interconnected systems, and the CII systems that deliver essential services, with new Section 12 requirements focused specifically on systems that connect to or communicate with CII.

This means CII organisations need more than a static view of what should exist. They need to understand what is communicating, how identities and systems are behaving, and whether suspicious activity is progressing toward critical infrastructure.

Where Vectra AI can support CCoP readiness

Vectra AI supports CII organisations in the areas where visibility, detection, investigation, and response are most important.

“CCoP 2026 reflects today’s evolving threats to critical infrastructure. Vectra AI supports 31 of the 38 clauses relevant to its capabilities within the Code’s 53 clauses, helping organisations detect threats earlier and respond before critical operations are disrupted.”

— Hock Leng, Vice President of Sales, APJ, Vectra AI

See what is communicating with CII

Based on our clause-by-clause assessment of CCoP 2026, Vectra AI directly or supportively aligns with 31 of the Code’s 53 clauses. That alignment is strongest across visibility, monitoring and detection, threat hunting, incident response, OT monitoring and interconnected-system security. Alignment does not mean Vectra AI alone satisfies each clause, but that its capabilities can directly support or strengthen the required control.

Detect abnormal behaviour earlier

Section 6.2 requires CIIOs to establish normal operational and network activity, monitor deviations, correlate cybersecurity events, and trigger alerts for investigation. The Code also recognises that attackers may use less-monitored areas as stepping stones toward CII.

This aligns closely with Vectra AI’s core capabilities. The platform analyses activity across network, identity and cloud environments to identify abnormal behaviour, correlate related events, and prioritise the entities that present the greatest risk.

Instead of presenting analysts with disconnected alerts, Vectra AI helps show how an attack is progressing and what requires immediate attention.

Support threat hunting, investigation and response

CCoP also places greater emphasis on proactive threat hunting and incident readiness.

Vectra AI provides enriched metadata, behavioural context, and investigation workflows that help analysts search for hidden activity, reconstruct attack paths, and determine whether a cybersecurity incident is underway.

When response is required, integrations can support native actions such as isolating a host, restricting a compromised account, or blocking malicious traffic. These capabilities strengthen the technical execution of incident response, while the CIIO retains ownership of its response plan, regulatory reporting, forensics, and recovery processes.

Supporting OT and interconnected environments

Many CII environments include OT, legacy systems, and devices that cannot support endpoint agents.

Vectra AI can passively monitor visible traffic in these environments without requiring agents on sensitive systems. This is particularly relevant to the requirement in Section 10.2 to monitor OT-to-enterprise data flows for anomalies, as well as Section 12.7 requirements to investigate suspicious activity across interconnected systems.

Additional controls are still required for areas such as endpoint logs, virtualisation infrastructure, patching and formal reporting to CSA, but Vectra AI can provide an important layer of behavioural visibility across the communication paths attackers may use.

Start with the visibility gap

For CII organisations preparing for CCoP 2026, a practical starting point is to ask:

Do we know every system that communicates with the CII?

Can we detect when a valid identity or trusted system begins behaving abnormally?

Can we show what the security team saw, investigated, and did in response?

Vectra AI does not replace the governance, certification, IAM, patching, backup or regulatory-reporting controls required by CCoP. Its role is to help CII organisations see attacker behaviour earlier, investigate faster and produce stronger operational evidence that their detection and response controls are working.

Title: Inside KeyDrift: Analyzing historical UAT-11473 activity on Cisco SD-WAN
Context: Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems.

UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as “KeyDrift” consisting of multiple components geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts.

Observed targeting spans across space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research.

Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473’s operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” covert access network.

KeyDrift is a custom malware framework that is designed to operate in Cisco SD-WAN controller environments. Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records.

The framework's primary component is PolyFlame, a memory-resident module deployed through modified runit service paths. PolyFlame is injected into legitimate running vdaemon processes, and it can also masquerade as a packed “aaamgrd” loader variant. Once resident, PolyFlame interposes socket, DTLS, and runtime-linker behavior through functions such as recvfrom, sendto, getpeername, dlopen, dlsym, mprotect, and “/proc/%d/maps” parsing. This gives KeyDrift access to SD-WAN control-plane traffic from inside legitimate controller daemon execution rather than through a conventional endpoint beacon.

LittleFilch, another component of the KeyDrift framework, provides the collection and exfiltration capability identified in the framework. The module hooks “SSL_read” inside vdaemon, inspects decrypted control-plane buffers, extracts keying material for a list of predefined edge nodes, and stages the data locally in encrypted format for exfiltration.

Talos assesses with high confidence that KeyDrift's intended operational purpose is Cisco SD-WAN control-plane collection: persistent controller residence, in-band traffic access, key-material extraction from decrypted control messages, and encrypted staging or exfiltration of the recovered material. Observed variations of the KeyDrift modules and deployment mechanisms suggest active development of the framework’s capabilities.

KeyDrift analysis

KeyDrift uses Cisco SD-WAN runit service paths as its primary execution anchor. In the PolyFlame sshd deployment, the actor modifies the service run script, remounts /rootfs.rw executable, launches a malicious script “conf_sshd” in the background, and then starts the legitimate sshd service. The loader script enumerates running vdaemon PIDs, records them in “/tmp/system-vdaemon”, and invokes the injector component “rsshd” to inject PolyFlame (“libdssl.so”) into each process.

Recovered conf_sshd logic uses the same control flow across reviewed samples:

Figure 1. conf_sshd control flow logic.

Runit launchers

The observed sshd runit launcher preserves normal Cisco SD-WAN sshd startup logic while adding two malicious lines before service execution, which remount “/rootfs.rw” executable and background execution of conf_sshd, which then drives rsshd injection into vdaemon.

Figure 2. conf_sshd execution logic.

The recovered aaamgr runit launcher from an affected vBond appliance uses a parallel service-wrapper pattern, but it executes the packed aaamgrd PolyFlame loader directly. The deletion of the writable-overlay PAM configurations for sshd and login before remounting “/rootfs.rw” executable if part of the legitimate script, along with the invocation of the aaamgrd daemon via Python:

Figure 3. aamgrd daemon launch.

PolyFlame

PolyFlame is the primary operational module in the KeyDrift framework. PolyFlame operates at the socket and DTLS control-plane layer. PolyFlame serves two primary purposes:

Command execution via a TinyShell-styled backdoor

Intermediate C2 that can forward commands to and from the C2 to other peers

PolyFlame is primarily injected into the vdaemon process, providing operational obfuscation and access to all in-process state: DTLS session keys, vEdge topology, OMP routes, and policy tables. No hardcoded IPv4 addresses, binding ports, callback domains, URLs, host headers, or polling interval were recovered from the analyzed PolyFlame samples. PolyFlame is designed for in-band control or tasking over Cisco SD-WAN control-plane traffic rather than a conventional fixed external beacon.

This implant is meant to serve as a hook of the recvfrom() API call. The original recvfrom is replaced by a malicious subroutine in the vdaemon process. When recvfrom is called in the vdaemon process, the malicious subroutine will first execute the real/legitimate recvfrom() API to obtain the C2 IP address info for communicating with it in the future.

PolyFlame’s time check

The recvd data from the C2 consists of the MD5 value of a specific DATE. PolyFlame will calculate the local time on the device in format “%Y-%m-%d" and calculate its MD5 hash. If the MD5 calculated by the device does not match with the one sent by the C2, the implant will stop further execution. Otherwise, the implant then uses an “administrative code” from the C2 and performs an action.

PolyFlame’s tasking

PolyFlame contains an administrative mode that processes the admin code sent by the C2, that defines operations — it's one of the first flags checked in the backdoor:

Code = 1: Generate random bytes and send to C2. This is likely a check-in beacon or heartbeat for the C2.

Code = 2: Set implant type to backdoor (TinyShell) or intermediate C2.

Code = 3: Set up the command handler for the intermediate C2.

Any other code value: Check the implant type flag currently set. Based on the implant type flag, either send the accompanying data to TinyShell or the intermediate C2 component for processing.

PolyFlame’s command execution

PolyFlame contains a backdoor that matches the capabilities of TinyShell: file read, file write, and arbitrary command execution, but not interactive shell. This backdoor component’s implementation is quite similar to TinyShell, but the command codes differ. PolyFlame handles the following command codes:

Code = 0x100: Execute command using “/bin/sh -c <command>”

Code = 0x200: Write file to disk.

Code = 0x300: Read file from disk and send to the C2.

PolyFlame as an intermediate C2 component

The intermediate C2 component is a one-to-many handler (somewhat like a one-to-many multiplexer) — meaning the implant can connect to only one C2 but can connect to many peers who can be served by the intermediate C2 component. Similar to the TinyShell-backdoor component, the intermediate C2 component also accepts and processes specific command codes from the C2:

Code = 0x403: Create a thread to connect to the specified peer IP. Make a new connection and keep socket alive until specified.

Code = 0x404: Send data recvd from the C2 to a connected peer.

Code = 0x405: Remove a peer from the list of active connections.

Code = 0x407: Send a response recvd from a peer, back to the C2.

Code = 0x408: Set a specific value in memory.

PolyFlame variant: aaamgrd

Talos has observed a distinct PolyFlame variant that masquerades as the aaamgr service. The legitimate Cisco aaamgr component is a Python package; it does not normally appear as a compiled ELF runit service. This PolyFlame variant is executed by a malicious runit service under “/etc/sv/aaamgr/” with aaamgrd and a modified run launcher.

aaamgrd is a statically linked ELF64 executable with no section headers, a single RWE loader segment, and an RC4-encrypted embedded ELF payload. The loader uses direct syscalls including ptrace, fork, wait4, kill, tgkill, mmap, and mprotect. It performs an anti-debug check by deobfuscating /proc/%d/status and TracerPid: and exits if a tracer is present.

The observed staging sequence was:

Figure 4. PolyFlame staging sequence.

Note that in addition to the implant execution staging, there are also indications of timestomping.

LittleFilch: libcommon.so TLS interception module

LittleFilch is a control-session interception module positioned to collect data-plane keying material from control sessions visible to the injected vSmart process.

LittleFilch installs an SSL_read hook inside vdaemon. The hook calls the original SSL_read, then processes returned buffers only when the returned size is greater than 0x18F, the first decrypted byte is 0x07, and three marker patterns are checked for presence. These marker bytes are followed by the actual artifacts that LittleFilch aims to record:

LittleFilch records the extracted keying material and RSA-encrypts it before writing the output to “/var/tmp/vdaemon.bin”. It can then send the encrypted content over UDP in a DTLS 1.2 application-data style record.

Figure 5. Keying material recording format used by LittleFilch.

LittleFilch expects its configuration file — located at “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” — to contain two host port lines: one local bind IP/port and one remote destination IP/port. It deletes “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” after reading it. Talos has not been able to recover the “vdaemon.conf” file.

Bill Toulas

U.S. law enforcement has seized the primary domain of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service advertised on cybercrime forums for facilitating illegal activities.

The service also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, and promised to shield customers from legal complaints and requests from law enforcement and other authorities.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) confirmed that Virtualine marketed services that permitted “illegal/black hat activities” ranging from phishing, spamming, and carding to port scanning.

The FBI seized the primary domain of the service, virtualine[.net], following an investigation that involved Germany’s Polizei Hessen, the Netherlands’ Politie Midden-Nederland, the U.K.’s National Crime Agency, as well as private partners OverRIPE and Lumen.

Although Virtualine drew an apparent line at child content, authorities say that the operator knowingly hosted an online forum promoting child abuse material and ignored repeated notices from law enforcement, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and a victim’s attorney.

Authorities allege that after legal pressure against the forum increased, Virtualine worked with the administrators to set up a new site.

"Virtualine hosts this new website to this day, and it has already received at least one abuse complaint about sexually explicit images of children found on that website," the DoJ said.

The administrator of the Virtualine rejected the allegation in an open letter to authorities published on a new website, virtualine[.]org, captured by cybersecurity company Silent Push.

The operator said that while claims about the service's illegal activities and customers "deserve a fair investigation," they regarded "sexual exploitation of children as a crime against humanity."

Cybercrime ecosystem

Virtualine also accepted direct Bitcoin payments from customers, helping cybercriminals launder proceeds stolen elsewhere.

Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, which provided intelligence support to law enforcement, linked Virtualine’s payment addresses directly to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, scams, and phishing platforms.

“Virtualine accepted direct bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without flagging their funds through hosted exchange compliance programs,” Chainalysis notes.

“Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin,” the blockchain company added.

In a report published today, blockchain intelligence firm TRM said ransomware groups were responsible for 5% of Virtualine’s financial flows, while a Russian drug marketplace made up approximately 44%.

"A large sextortion scheme and a mixer were also major sources of funds," the company said.

TRM says that Virtualine also received payments from the StealC infostealer this year, with transactions indicating a constant financial relationship.

A press release from the Dutch police notes that dozens of physical servers were seized in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline.

Politie also said its investigators recovered data from more than 3,000 Virtualine customers, and follow-up action against them is underway.

According to the authorities in the Netherlands, the illegal platform was facilitating cybercrime operations since at least 2022, including ransomware, botnets, infostealers, phishing, and distribution of child abuse material.

Although the bulletproof hosting provider remains partially online, researchers observed that its network prefixes currently have very low routing visibility, suggesting that much of its infrastructure may no longer be reachable.

Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The Cat Has Left the Bag

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

As the official advisory puts it:

During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode.IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle): for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field, and it advances the destination pointer by the cumulative rather than the per-fragment length, so an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path restricts the message length.

The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.

Yet Another Forever Day

CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail, stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.

Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include:

PKFail, a supply-chain failure resulting from non-production test platform keys, public for more than a decade before they were discovered, used in hundreds of device models;

BootHole;

Bootkit; and

BlackLotus.

Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.

There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.

“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars.

“Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”

CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).

In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code, however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation … for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well.

Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2.

While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them.

Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond.

Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting.

Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts.

This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

Title: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents
Context: In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs
Full Text:
An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates.

The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace.

DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”

An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says.

The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces. The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles.

The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group.

The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED.

“DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.”

The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS.

According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors.

Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).”

The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media.

Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment

Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer.

“If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.”

More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal, the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona.

Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025.

Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members.

Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.”

More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department.

The Trump administration has prosecuted protesters for posting information about individual ICE officers and warned others for doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities. More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats.

Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119, a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them.

“This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize."

Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool.

“The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.”

Updated 10/28/2026 at 8:02 pm ET: Added comment from DHS.

Title: Oracle celebrates end of Cybersecurity Awareness Month with quadruple trouble
Context: The first issue is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), which gives attackers a foothold in the PeopleSoft application
Full Text: Attackers are probing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution (RCE), despite Oracle issuing a patch earlier this month. Meanwhile, new analysis indicates that an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day exploited by ShinyHunters as early as May involves three distinct vulnerabilities that can be combined to achieve RCE. Patching alone may not remove attackers from already compromised systems, particularly if they've installed web shells. First up: CVE-2026-101767, a critical, unauthenticated SQL injection bug in Oracle EBS that can lead to RCE. “Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27,” Defused Cyber said in an X post. Horizon3 researchers found and disclosed the bug to Oracle, and the vendor patched the issue in its October release. “An attacker can send a crafted request to the vulnerable servlet to execute SQL with the privileges of the APPS database user,” Horizon3 explained at the time. “The attack chain also enables operating system command execution with the privileges of the EBS application account.” This means an unauthorized user can modify application data accessible to APPS, and execute commands. “Depending on the deployment, affected data may include financial, payroll, HR, and procurement records,” the bug hunters said. The Register reached out to Oracle with multiple questions for this story - including whether it has documented any successful exploitation of CVE-2026-101767 - and did not receive an immediate response. Moving on to the PeopleSoft-ShinyHunters fiasco: TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) found and reported the PeopleSoft issues on June 10, and Oracle issued a patch under one vulnerability identifier: CVE-2026-35273. In early June, ShinyHunters told The Reg that the group hacked more than 100 organizations via an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day, CVE-2026-35273. Google’s consulting and incident response biz, Mandiant, later confirmed the data theft and extortion crew exploited CVE-2026-35273 as a zero-day, mostly against schools and the education sector. By late September, however, Mandiant said ShinyHunters massively expanded its targeting, “deploying web shells on dozens of systems globally, spanning higher education, technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and government.” According to ZDI bug hunter Bobby Gould, there are actually three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components, and each should receive its own CVE identifier rather than being grouped under CVE-2026-35273. Gould, along with TrendAI researchers Minh Giang and Lucas Miller, originally found and reported three distinct bugs to Oracle in June. “We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue,” he said in a Tuesday blog. The first issue is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), which gives attackers a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. In June, Oracle introduced a “validateClient” method to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. The SSRF bug, however, allows crims to make requests that satisfy the validation requirement to access endpoints vulnerable to RCE, Gould wrote. “While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB,” he said, referring to PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB). “Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.” The second bug is an external control of file path vulnerability in PSEMHUB’s ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler. This message handler is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem - but it doesn’t properly validate requests, which allows an attacker to write a web shell into a file path and achieve RCE. The third vulnerability, also in PSEMHUB, is a deserialization of untrusted data flaw. An attacker can use a file-write vulnerability to plant a malicious XML file inside a PeopleSoft directory that stores environment configuration data, then wait for PSEMHUB to initialize, such as after a service or system restart. This triggers deserialization of the malicious XML file, potentially allowing the attacker to achieve RCE. “Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft,” Gould warned.®

GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The supply chain attack campaign's shift toward developer endpoints and cloud access signals what could be next for the cybercrime outfit.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 28, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: GrafikLab via Getty Images

A new wave of GhostAction attacks has largely failed, but this supply chain campaign operator is well-positioned to cause more chaos down the line.

GhostAction, an ongoing campaign in which attackers target GitHub by compromising developer accounts and injecting GitHub Actions workflow files into repositories.

Workflows tell GitHub Actions what code to execute when events occur (such as when a commit is pushed or a pull request is opened); these malicious workflows rely on GitHub's high trust in these files (by design), seizing repository secrets, package publishing tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, credentials embedded in source code, and much more.

The idea is that an initial compromise could be leveraged into more compromises and access points across repositories, CI/CD systems, and cloud environments, not unlike many supply chain worms observed in the wild lately, albeit functioning differently.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations. What has changed is an apparent escalation of the technique beginning this month. During an earlier Oct. 8-12 wave, attackers pushed the security-audit.yml workflow into roughly 30,000 repositories, using compromised accounts to distribute credential-stealing code at scale. But GitGuardian on Oct. 27 published research highlighting further escalation. GitGuardian's Gaetan Ferry wrote that between Oct. 13 and 21, GhostAction's operator "pushed 72,000 commits to 23,000 public repositories," noting that 8,000 of them were new targets.

Various Payloads Targeting Compromised Developers

During this latest wave of the campaign, GitGuardian observed that once a developer account is compromised, the operator would deploy different payloads depending on which runner the repositories were hosted on. Runners are the systems that execute GitHub Actions workflows. Many organizations use GitHub-hosted runners, while others configure self-hosted runners that run inside their own environments.

These payloads include one called "seven workflows," which searches GitHub runner repositories and wikis for credentials including AI-provider API keys; the "Security-audit.yml" file seen in earlier GhostAction attacks that searches GitHub-hosted source code and Git history for credentials; self-hosted runner payloads targeting self-hosted CI runners; a payload targeting GitHub runners and AWS-requesting GitHub OIDC tokens (in order to assume AWS roles and achieve cloud account access); and the font stealer payload, which is the most notable workflow payload seen in recent attacks, due to its provenance.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

The font stealer family installs a Node.js credential stealer on local developer machines, disguised as a VS Code task. The technique appears to be copied from PolinRider, a campaign that hides obfuscated loaders in developer repositories to steal credentials and has been associated with North Korea. The attacker also added PolinRider loaders between Oct. 22 and 26 to repositories already impacted by GhostAction. Ferry says that out of the five payloads, only the PolinRider-styled local stealer had a chance to successfully run, but GitGuardian has no evidence that any run actually occurred.

GitGuardian could not assess whether there was overlap between GhostAction and PolinRider, but hypothesized that GhostAction's operator possibly copied a public PolinRider launcher in order to target an overlapping set of victims.

Jenn Gile, cofounder of OpenSourceMalware (which previously covered the GhostAction attacks this month and detected signs of the PolinRider copycat a few weeks ago), tells Dark Reading that the PolinRider clone illustrates some of the inner workings of the GhostAction group.

"What we're seeing looks like imitation, not evolution. The fake-font technique in GhostAction is a copy of what DPRK's PolinRider campaign has been using nearly all of 2026," she says in an email. "The multiple payloads are real, but they're variations on a theme (five workflow versions over about ten days in one repo we examined), not a new capability. Historically, we might have called this evolution because it took real skill to figure out. But this looks a lot like an LLM helping the threat actor test different variants."

Related:Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

All of that said, GitHub identified and prevented execution of the malicious workflows, GitGuardian noted. However, importantly, the attackers still demonstrated persistent access to nearly 1,800 compromised accounts, many of which had already been used in earlier GhostAction activity; "1,382 of the 1,792 compromised accounts had already been used on Oct. 8, so the same stolen tokens keep working," according to Ferry.

A "Failed" Wave of Attacks, but Still Plenty to Worry About Long Term

Ferry tells Dark Reading that the campaign has been "highly ineffective on the malicious workflows side." But even if there's no sign this wave succeeded, the nature of the payloads (such as the one aimed at gaining cloud access) also shows where the attackers may intend to pivot next, toward internal networks where there are fewer platform-level protections that could thwart their efforts.

"We expect new waves to appear in the near future, with revised payloads," he explains. "This 'fail early and adapt fast' strategy has already been observed for this threat actor."

Given that targeted accounts or repositories remain compromised, repo owners should look for and delete the files that GitGuardian lists in the IoC section of the blog, on every branch. And, if signs of compromise are detected, users should revoke the account's tokens across the board and rotate every credential committed in the affected repository or its history, as well as every Actions secret and wiki credential.

Introduction

During the 2025 peak holiday shopping season, the National Retail Federation predicted that retail sales would surpass $1 trillion USD for the first time, with Salesforce later reporting that online sales equated to $1.3 trillion globally. This included $294 billion in the United States and $262 billion influenced by AI and agents. Cybercriminals are highly aware that the holiday season is generally the most profitable for retailers, and look to capitalize on it for their own financial gain.

This blog explores the main cyber threats that retail organizations need to be aware of and prepared to defend against as we approach peak shopping season in 2026. We highlight notable security events that occurred in prior years during this time period. We also examine relevant threats from both an enterprise and guest point of view and provide examples of the evolving trend of autonomous attacks that could impact retailers.

Background

Since 2020, there have been several notable security events disclosed toward the end of peak shopping season. This includes the SolarWinds software supply chain compromise in December 2020 and the exploitation of a Log4j zero-day vulnerability in December 2021. Both events posed complexities for retail security teams as they occurred during a period where code freezes were likely in place. This limited the ability for organizations to make changes to critical technology systems to prevent any operational disruption to core technology infrastructure.

In addition to these broader threat landscape events, retailers typically face an increase in many types of financially-motivated attacks during this time period. This includes tactics and techniques designed to target both enterprises and guests alike.

Based on years of previous activity against Fortune 100 retailers from cyber threats during peak shopping season, these are the types of attacks that retailers should be primarily focused on detecting and responding to this time of year.

Enterprise-Focused Threats

Ransomware

Ransomware continues to pose a major risk for retail organizations heading into peak shopping season due to potential for operational disruption that could negatively impact the guest experience (in-store and online) and supply chain requirements (inventory).

As of Sept. 30, 2026, ransomware operators have claimed 565 retail organizations as victims this year, with the median company revenue hovering around $22 million. The top three ransomware operators that claimed retail victims are TGR-CRI-1173 (aka The Gentlemen), Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Howling Scorpius (aka Akira).

One example of a ransomware incident that impacted a retailer during peak shopping season occurred in December 2023, when Ambitious Scorpius (aka ALPHV) stole millions of customer records from a victim and caused significant operational disruption in terms of delayed order fulfillment, canceled e-commerce orders and slowed inventory replenishment.

To mitigate ransomware risks that jeopardize uptime, retailers need to deploy automated containment mechanisms alongside robust network segmentation strategies. Security teams should:

Leverage advanced endpoint protection featuring real-time behavioral analysis to rapidly isolate compromised assets

Enforce zero trust access across the enterprise to limit lateral movement

Utilize inline sandboxing capabilities to inspect suspicious binaries and stop zero-day exploits before execution

Data Theft and Extortion

Data theft and extortion attacks continue to rise in volume as cybercriminals like Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters) and Hazy Scorpius (aka CL0P) forgo ransomware to accelerate their attack lifecycles without compromising their actions on objectives.

The 2026 Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report found that extortion incidents without the use of encryption (78%) in 2025 dropped below the 90% range for the first time in several years. Consumers put a lot of trust in retailers safeguarding their personal data, and such extortion incidents this time of year severely damage it.

One notable example occurred in December 2021, when Bling Libra stole hundreds of gigabytes of data from a victim. This included customer email addresses, hashed passwords, customer payment invoices and internal employee files containing salaries and tax IDs.

To mitigate data theft and extortion risks threatening customer personal information and transactional records, organizations must deploy comprehensive enterprise data loss prevention (DLP) controls across their enterprise environments to identify and restrict illicit data exfiltration. Security teams should combine DLP capabilities with continuous attack surface management (ASM) to identify and remediate publicly accessible systems, while implementing zero trust access to strictly limit access privileges based on the principle of least privilege.

Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)

DDoS also poses a major risk for retailers during peak shopping season because these attacks severely impact the operational uptime for e-commerce platforms if successful.

During the December 2025 holiday rush, the pro-Russian hacktivist group Noname057(16) used the DDoSia botnet to launch coordinated TCP SYN and HTTP GET request floods targeting the victim's web-facing portals and API endpoints. This DDoS attack knocked its central systems offline, paralyzed package tracking tools, disrupted e-commerce merchant payment services and delayed parcel processing across their retail distribution networks.

To mitigate DDoS risks threatening e-commerce and payment processing platforms, organizations must combine inline application-layer protections. Security teams should:

Deploy dynamic rate-limiting controls to protect against web site request floods

Implement automated mitigation to filter malicious connections

Utilize distributed edge networks to absorb large-scale traffic spikes before impacting critical systems

Digital Skimming

Although carding shops are not as prevalent as they were in prior years, digital skimming continues to be a popular technique used by cybercriminals to steal and monetize payment card information.

One example of a digital skimming incident that impacted retailers during peak shopping season occurred in October 2024, when unspecified threat actors exploited the CosmicSting vulnerability (CVE-2024-34102) to execute remote code on unpatched servers. This led to the installation of persistent backdoors and the injection of payment skimming scripts into checkout flows, affecting roughly 5% of all online stores running on prominent e-commerce platforms worldwide leading into Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

To mitigate digital skimming risks threatening payment processing workflows, organizations must implement web application and API protection (WAAP) solutions to monitor web traffic, intercept remote code execution attempts and prevent unauthorized client-side script manipulation. Security teams should:

Leverage cloud security posture management (CSPM) alongside application security posture management (ASPM) to continuously identify server vulnerabilities

Remediate unpatched flaws

Correct security configuration drift prior to holiday code freezes

Guest-Focused Threats

Account Takeover

Credential stuffing attacks are a major concern for retailers during peak shopping season as they directly impact the trust of their customers if an account is compromised. This is even more damaging if the customer has payment card information saved in their account.

One key example occurred in December 2022, when unspecified threat actors used automated scripts targeting the victim’s mobile app and web login APIs. They used large databases of stolen credentials to conduct the attack, which ultimately led to the compromise of thousands of loyalty accounts. The actors were able to drain stored gift card balances, steal mobile payment funds and collect rewards points before advertising access to the compromised accounts on dark web forums.

To mitigate account takeover risks threatening mobile applications and authentication APIs, organizations must implement WAAP solutions with advanced bot mitigation capabilities to effectively distinguish credential stuffing campaigns from legitimate customer access without friction. Security teams should complement this by deploying advanced security to identify and block traffic attempting to communicate with malicious command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used to orchestrate automated login attempts.

Gift Card Fraud

Retail customers typically increase their purchase of gift cards during holiday periods. Cybercriminals are aware of this trend and typically ramp up their targeting of this form of digital currency during peak shopping season.

Unit 42 reported on the credit card fraud-based Jingle Thief campaign in October 2025. We continue to track this activity as CL‑CRI‑1032 (aka Storm-0539).

These threat actors send phishing and smishing messages to socially engineer employees at targeted retailers to obtain credentials for initial access. From there, they typically exploit cloud-based infrastructure, gain unauthorized access to sensitive data and issue unauthorized gift cards to monetize them at scale for financial gain.

AI-Powered Attacks

Back in May 2026, we predicted that threat actors would weaponize frontier AI models within 3–5 months. That prediction has already come true. Unit 42 recently disclosed an incident where a human attacker used frontier AI models to autonomously conduct various aspects of their intrusion to condense the timespan of their attack to under 10 hours. This typically would’ve taken multiple human operators at least two weeks to accomplish.

Since our report, several other security vendors have disclosed similar findings that directly relate to the types of threat that retailers are likely to face this peak shopping season. This includes Anthropic's reporting on Bling Libra using Claude to accelerate reconnaissance and exfiltration activities. Gambit Security has reported on an attacker using multiple open source harnesses to steal more than 600,000 payment card records from retailers using JavaScript-based web skimmers. NorForge also published their own findings related to Gambit Security's report on the usage of the Cairn autonomous penetration testing agent by a threat actor to infiltrate retail e-commerce sites, POS infrastructure, and web applications across the globe.

To defend against autonomous AI threats capable of compressing intrusion timelines to less than 10 hours, retailers must unify endpoint, network, cloud and identity data into an automated security operations infrastructure. Integrating centralized visibility with machine-learning triage and real-time automation orchestration enables security teams to:

Swiftly isolate affected systems

Invalidate compromised accounts

Drastically reduce mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR) from hours to minutes.

Conclusion

Peak shopping season is the most critical time of the year for retailers to ensure consistent operational uptime and maintenance of customer trust. The types of enterprise and guest-facing threats listed in this blog pose a clear and present risk to disrupting the core tenants of the retail shopping experience.

The ability for cyber defenders at retailers to reduce their MTTD and MTTR from hours to minutes is even more critical given the adoption of frontier AI models by financially-motivated actors.

To achieve this level of operational resilience, retail security teams can leverage the Palo Alto Networks security platform for an integrated, AI-driven security architecture that unifies enterprise-wide telemetry into automated response. Integrating Cortex XSIAM and XDR for real-time threat containment alongside Zero Trust network defense allows organizations to stop complex intrusions before they disrupt peak holiday operations. Furthermore, deploying Cortex Cloud will safeguard e-commerce platforms, protecting critical transaction paths from high-impact threat vectors.

Title: Managed for Malice: How Attackers Turn MDM into Remote Access
Context: Background Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks
Full Text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Lindsey Welch, Anton Ovrutsky, and Harlan Carvey for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks. In these cases, legitimate management tools are being weaponized for malicious purposes, as opposed to threat actors taking advantage of inherent weaknesses in the applications themselves, such as vulnerabilities.

MDM platforms are legitimate tools that organizations use to manage employee laptops, phones, and other devices. These tools help IT teams to enroll and configure company devices remotely, enforce security policies, and deploy approved applications. However, these applications' centralized control and trusted level of access can create an entry point for threat actors if the tools are misused.

These incidents often begin with social engineering—users falling subject to business-themed lures that arrive through messaging applications and email. While not a definitive list of MDMs that could be used in such attacks, we have seen threat actors recently using well-known applications from Hexnode and Rippling.

Once registered with the MDM application, the attacker gains a trusted and privileged management path on the system. In both cases described here, Huntress observed the threat actors installing unauthorized RMM (remote monitoring and management) tools in order to further their attacks.

Mystery of the reappearing ScreenConnect

Imagine receiving an alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation. Naturally, given the severity of such an alert, you prioritize it and remove the ScreenConnect agent immediately. However, several hours later, you receive another alert—same unauthorized installation. Something's clearly going on behind the scenes.

A recurring ScreenConnect installation is the first clue that this is more than an isolated, rogue RMM deployment. If both installations connected to the same destination relay, this would suggest the same threat actor was involved both times.

So how are they managing to get back in after being removed once?

We observed this activity in a recent incident, where two Huntress alerts for unauthorized ScreenConnect activity on the same device, separated by several hours, connected to the same relay.

As it happened, a threat actor had previously managed to install an MDM client from Hexnode on the system that ScreenConnect kept appearing on. Removing the RMM did little to deter them. They simply staged and installed the RMM software again.

The attack began with a phishing email. The target received several emails with proposal-related subjects like "ATTN: Official Invitation to Submit Proposal" and "Review Required" that mentioned an organization that the target likely had a business relationship with.

Clicking a link contained within the email downloaded a file from https://webdocusign.viewportal[.]es/Windows/download/index.php

which was saved to the Microsoft Edge temporary downloads folder as eD0cuSign_Installer.msi.

While the file had been named to mimic a DocuSign installer, it actually contained an installation package for a Hexnode MDM, a legitimate device management application. The package included Hexnode Gateway, the Hexnode agent, and supporting PostgreSQL components, all of which were installed on the system.

Figure 1: Execution of the Hexnode MSI, designed to resemble a (fake) DocuSign installer.

The threat actor followed up by installing ScreenConnect shortly thereafter and connecting to the attacker-controlled relay, relay.bobdthjau[.]com:8041. This resulted in a Huntress alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation, and the MSP removed the RMM from the compromised computer shortly thereafter.

However, several hours later another instance of ScreenConnect was installed and reconnected to the relay. This triggered another alert, which led Huntress to isolate the endpoint, and a thorough remediation began.

Enrollment from a link

Not all incidents involve phishing techniques that trick a user into running an MSI installer. In another instance, a receptionist opened an email titled "Re: Tax Planning and Preparation Inquiry." The email included a link to what appeared to be a Microsoft Teams meeting invitation.

Clicking the link brought the target to a page titled "Calendar." While the site was taken down shortly after the attempt, it likely impersonated a Teams scheduling calendar. This page redirected to a .php file that appears to have helped facilitate enrollment into an attacker-controlled Rippling MDM tenant. All three links resided on the following domain (see the IoCs section for full URLs):

https://teams-microsoftcom5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592.kiratham[.]com

About a minute after clicking the link, a Rippling enrollment registry key appeared on the compromised system, which is consistent with registration in the MDM platform. An installation MSI for the Rippling agent was subsequently downloaded to C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\mdm\{GUID}.msi. The agent was then installed with SYSTEM-level permissions as C:\Rippling\daemon.exe.

Further investigation by Huntress determined that this activity originated from the online Rippling management agent, suggesting that the threat actor had previously created an account to carry out the attack.

Approximately 35 minutes after installation, the attackers used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM, connecting back to an attacker-controlled domain relay.pronconetydesire[.]online:8041, triggering a Huntress alert for a malicious ScreenConnect instance.

Tradecraft patterns & motivations

These instances, and the abuse of MDM applications in general, highlights a frustrating situation for security practitioners. The challenge is that more tools designed to help organizations manage endpoints are becoming mechanisms to compromise them. Similar to the illegitimate use of RMMs, this further complicates what we can safely consider trusted software, because reputation alone is just not sufficient to determine intent. Neither Hexnode nor Rippling are at fault here—users are simply being socially engineered into installing their software.

So where does this leave us? MDM enrollment should be treated as security-sensitive activity as opposed to a routine administrative task. An unexpected enrollment can establish persistence, provide a privileged deployment path, and allow an attacker to introduce additional tooling without relying on conspicuous payloads like known malware.

These incidents also demonstrate how detection cannot treat RMM installation as an isolated event. While the RMM client, and its subsequent activity, may have been the most visible part of the intrusion, removing it does not remove the unauthorized management architecture that delivered it.

The sequence of events observed makes for a stronger signal—social engineering -> a new MDM enrollment -> RMM installation -> outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay. Because the chain can vary, correlation across identity, MDM, endpoint, and network telemetry is our best hope in providing the resiliency needed to defend against these attacks.

Mitigation Guidance

Organizations can reduce the risk faced by these techniques by controlling both the enrollment path and the applications that MDM platforms are allowed to deploy.

Maintain an inventory of authorized MDM products, tenants, agents, and RMM instances. Treat any unexpected enrollment, management agent, or RMM instance as a security event.

Train users to verify unexpected meeting, document-signing, and proposal-review requests. Email and web controls should also scrutinize business-themed lures.

If a compromise is suspected, isolate the endpoint, remove the endpoint from the unauthorized MDM tenant, disable attacker-created accounts, revoke active sessions or tokens, reset affected credentials, and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed.
