Title: The CISO’s evolving role: Protecting and defending in the agentic era
Context: And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale
Full Text:
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months.

A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report, the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed.

At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish.

For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter.

Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report

For builders: Build securely in the agentic era

Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you.

Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off.

Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. If you give it access to information or systems, it will act on that access, and that can quickly become a problem.

Your CISO wants you to build. They also need to know what’s being built, so they can help you do it safely. The best thing you can do for your security leader is to have the identity and data conversation early, before you build, not after.

For CISOs: Protect the enterprise as agent adoption grows

Your first job is to put guardrails in place so people can innovate carefully, without slowing them down. Good guardrails help teams move faster because they know where the lines are.

Start with observability, and make it deep. You need to know which agents exist, who owns them, what they can reach, and what they’re doing. You can’t protect what you can’t see. Deep observability also means knowing when an agent’s behavior changes, so your team can step in before a small issue becomes a big one.

Then hold people’s feet to the fire on identity and data. These are the two areas where I wouldn’t give any ground. Every agent needs a governed identity with only the access it needs, and the data it can reach needs to be classified and protected. When those two are in place, most other decisions get easier. Here’s how we’re approaching agent governance.

For CISOs: Defending differently

Your second job is to defend differently than you have historically done.

Attackers are using AI to move faster, and our latest Microsoft Digital Defense Report shows how much that is compressing the time defenders have to respond. But defending differently isn’t simply about adopting faster tools. It’s about changing how security teams turn information into action. The more integrated your environment is, the faster you’ll be able to see an attack and respond to it. An attack rarely shows up in just one place. Signals across identity, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments need to come together with threat intelligence and organizational context so defenders can understand what’s happening and respond before an incident escalates. When your tools work together, your team sees the full picture instead of pieces of it. It also requires a security approach built to continuously assess risk, make decisions, and act at the speed threats are developing.

You also need the right threat intelligence and the right partner. Threat intelligence helps organizations understand how threats are changing, which ones matter to their environment, and where to focus their defenses. Working with partners that have visibility across industries and organizations can provide broader context than an individual organization may have on its own. And you’re not going to operate at this speed without agents helping you. The same capabilities that make attacks faster can make defense faster, with agents working alongside your analysts to investigate and respond. That’s why we’re bringing integrated security operations and agentic defense together.

Two jobs, one goal

The pace of change over the last year has been significant, and it is likely to continue. None of this means slowing down. The CISOs I talk with want their companies to innovate. They need to protect the enterprise as it uses AI and the increasing speed of AI-enabled threats.

Prepare for an agent-driven workplace

Explore Work Trend Index insights on the changing role of agents at work and the trends shaping how organizations operate.

Explore the Work Trend Index

If you’re building with AI, bring your security team in early and have the identity and data conversation. If you’re a CISO, focus on those two jobs and make sure you have the right partners for both.

Title: Serial ransomware crook gets 70 months behind bars for Nefilim, Hive roles
Context: One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto...
Full Text: Ukrainian ransomware crook Artem Stryzhak has been sentenced to 70 months in the slammer by a New York federal court for his role as an affiliate of the Nefilim and Hive ransomware gangs. Prosecutors believe the cybercriminal began working with Nefilim in or around June 2021, while living in Barcelona, Spain. The Nefilim ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was known for targeting wealthy companies, with its operators encouraging affiliates to pursue businesses capable of paying substantial ransom demands. One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto ransomware attack. Court documents [PDF] state that Stryzhak agreed with alleged Nefilim boss Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who remains at large, to pay the ransomware crew a 20 percent cut of the ransom proceeds he collected. Tymoshchuk told Stryzhak that his preference was for attacks to target companies based in the US, Canada, and Australia that turn over more than $100 million annually. This guidance was soon tweaked to encourage targeting companies in the same regions with more than $200 million in annual revenue. Prosecutors claim that around the time Stryzhak joined forces with Nefilim, he also signed up to the Hive ransomware operation as "one of its earliest affiliates," and used its platform to attack approximately seven victims. Hive's operators claimed they targeted circa 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023. According to separate court documents [PDF], Hive's victims included a law firm and an Ohio hospital, which paid approximately $1.7 million in Bitcoin after the gang initially demanded $2 million during the COVID-19 pandemic. Before its infrastructure was seized in an international law enforcement operation in January 2023, Hive was known for attacking healthcare facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as being one of the ransomware groups that battered Costa Rica in 2022. Brett Leatherman, assistant director at the FBI’s cyber branch, described Stryzhak as a “prolific cybercriminal” who played a role in groups that were responsible for more than $100 million in victim damages. “Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners,” he said. “Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.” Stryzhak was arrested by Spanish police in June 2024 before being extradited to the US in April 2025. In announcing Stryzhak's sentencing, the Justice Department took the opportunity to remind the public that rewards totaling up to $11 million are available for qualifying information about alleged Nefilim operator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk and other key ransomware suspects. ®

Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

A virtual desktop service provider in Japan has told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by hackers.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service is delivered via a network of tens of thousands of servers operated by the firm and is popular with foreign-exchange traders.

However, the firm was forced to suspend the service on October 21 after discovering the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments.”

A security alert claimed that some information may have been accessed and that as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions.

An extortion email sent on October 21 demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen ($50.7m).

Read more on ransomware attacks in Japan: Japanese Railway Operators Hit with Weekend Cyber Attacks

Having refused to pay the ransom, GMO Internet was notified by its attackers that they would deploy ransomware on October 27 as 12pm. As a result, it advised its customers to perform a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power.

In the meantime, GMO Internet has been asking for customers to ship their PCs so that its security team can investigate.

“As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed,” it explained.

“However, the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

“This demonstrates how a vulnerability in a remote access service can have consequences far beyond the compromised system,” said Suzu Labs chief security evangelist, Phillip Wylie.ㅤ

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization.”

Wylie added: "The biggest takeaway is that preventing the initial compromise is important, but limiting what attackers can do once they gain access is equally critical.”

The breach is the latest in a string of security incidents impacting Japanese firms this year. Organizations as diverse as Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (eight million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million) have suffered major data breaches.

AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Artificial intelligence (AI) is everywhere in healthcare, from doctors’ intake forms to cancer screenings. But in some cases, life-and-death uses are outpacing cybersecurity.

Arielle Waldman,Features Writer,Dark Reading

October 28, 2026

6 Min Read

Source: iStock/Getty Images Plus via Getty Images

Patients walk into a doctor's office and are swiftly asked permission for artificial intelligence (AI) scribes to document notes full of sensitive health information. That intake conversation is just one entry point as AI is now embedded throughout the patient lifecycle, accessing more data than most organizations can secure.

This raises significant concerns for a sector that historically struggles to secure legacy equipment and highly sought-after data, even before AI was added to the mix. Advancements could save invaluable time during patient care, but security will present hurdles in the form of supply chain risks that stem from AI vendor compromise, data leakage through prompts, and AI-generated social engineering campaigns.

A recent Proofpoint report, "2026 Study on Cybersecurity in Healthcare" warned that "AI adoption is accelerating faster than governance." Forty-five percent of organizations confirmed they had embedded AI into their systems but 60% lacked the necessary controls to govern that sensitive data.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

Healthcare organizations are rapidly deploying AI to record intake conversations, and customer conversations increasingly revolve around how physicians are using AI for clinical decisions, and more importantly, how they are protecting those tools, explains Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint. Some Proofpoint customers use the OpenEvidence open-source AI tool for research and diagnoses because it can integrate with Epic Systems, a widely used platform for Electronic Health Records (EHR).

"The challenge is making sure physicians aren't putting sensitive information into that tool, so it does get challenging," Biddle tells Dark Reading. Even seemingly generic details, like a patient's eye color, combined with a specific injury like a left tibia fracture could qualify as Protected Health Information (PHI).

That makes data sensitivity a major concern when feeding information into AI tools. Therefore, organizations should focus on securing the underlying data rather than the tool itself, advises Biddle.

What Do CISOs Want to Know about AI in Healthcare?

AI's use is spreading fast and that complicates how organizations think about risk. Tony Sabaj, head of Americas channel SEs at Check Point, says AI's pattern-recognition capability is already improving clinical care, catching early signs in cancer screenings, triaging critical patients, and reviewing electrocardiograms to "generate reports faster and with more accuracy."

Beyond the clinic, health insurers are using AI for claims processing and fraud detection, and like other industries, healthcare is building digital twins to model operational scenarios at scale.

Related:Is Your Organization Ready for 2027's AI Accountability Era?

Some of AI’s most visible momentum is in reducing administrative burdens including documentation that converts clinician-patient conversations into draft notes, scheduling, intake, coding, and patient communications, says Cindi Carter, global chief information security officer (CISO) at Check Point. But she warned it's also being used behind the scenes to support operational planning, research, and cybersecurity.

Organizations often sort AI tools into "medical" or "administrative" buckets. The first consists of diagnostic AI or treatment recommendation systems, while the latter includes intake forms or scheduling. Carter is concerned that these labels may undermine the downstream risks administrative tools can still pose because a "documentation tool can still influence what becomes part of the medical record" and lead to clinical consequences.

In pharmaceutical and precision medicine, AI investment is outpacing security investment, Sabaj says. And as AI reaches further into healthcare, organizations need to ensure existing regulatory frameworks keep pace. Guardrails often center on protecting data leakage, but safeguards should also ensure that if AI is taking any kind of medical action, it's limited to known parameters, he recommends.

Related:How the CISO-CMO Alliance Builds Trust Before Crisis Strikes

"We continue to see breaches of medical information and AI has the potential to exacerbate this issue," Sabaj tells Dark Reading. To get ahead of the threat, some hospitals are building their own AI tools, using open weight models and training large language models on proprietary data rather than relying on public platforms to handle sensitive PHI.

Carter's concerns extend beyond confidentiality. Despite progress, AI is known to hallucinate. What if AI produced an inaccurate summary, omits an important detail, or acts on manipulated information? The organization can lose confidence in the information supporting care without a record ever being stolen, she adds.

The CISO question then becomes broader, shifting from "What data left?" to "What can this system see, what can it change, and can we reconstruct what happened?" she says.

"In healthcare, we are protecting sensitive information and the integrity of decisions that depend on it," she explains.

Leading Causes of Major Healthcare Breaches

In the relatively short time span since rapid AI adoption took off, Phil Englert, VP of medical device security at Health-ISAC, has already observed changes that will affect how much sensitive data floods systems. As AI becomes increasingly integrated, when a cyber incident occurs, organizations frequently lose patient identifiers, medical records, insurance details, and other clinical or financial data— all considered PHI.

Englert cited recent Health and Human Services data that shows hacking and other IT-related incidents continue to be the leading causes of major healthcare breaches. Denver Health Medical Plan reported a breach Oct. 1 that affected 238,083 individuals, triggered by an exposed vendor access key through AI platform SquareML.

This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that an organization's security posture is often only as strong as that of its partners."

While organizations need to secure AI within their own environments, they also need to protect themselves against it as threat actors use it to craft more convincing and effective social engineering attacks, warns Englert. Healthcare organizations are seeing increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, deepfakes, voice impersonation attacks, and QR-code phishing— any method to exploit human trust in a sector driven by speed and precision.

While healthcare organizations can't seem to shake the ransomware threat, which "remains one of the most damaging facing the sector," AI-enabled attacks are a top cybersecurity concern for 2026, he adds.

"Cyber Safety is Patient Safety"

Implementing effective guardrails has proved significantly challenging. Carter offers five recommendations informed by the governance and lifecycle risk themes in the Joint Commissions and the Coalition for AI Health guidance: Visibility, boundaries around data and actions, evidence from vendors, validation and meaningful human oversight, and continuous monitoring.

Organizations should maintain AI inventory and give staff a straightforward way to disclose unsanctioned uses as shadow AI risks pummel the sector. Limiting what data AI can handle e is also essential; Carter recommends that access to information should not automatically confer authority to update records, send communications, or initiate transactions.

"AI compresses the time between a mistake and material loss," Carter warns. That should be reflected in organizations' safeguards.

Implementation also depends on organizational maturity. While talking with security officers across the industry, Proofpoint’s Biddle observed varying levels of AI adoption. Some are quite far in the process, while others are still cautious and taking it slow, she adds. She points out healthcare does tend to lag behind other industries when it comes to technology.

Many organizations lack resources but continually face disruptive attacks that severely affect patient care. "It doesn't seem to be getting any better, unfortunately, "Biddle says .

Getting better requires money, but when CISOs stand in front of the board and request investments to shore up defenses, they are often hit with: “Why do you need to spend this amount?” says Biddle. It's difficult, because they are competing with budget dollars for life-saving devices, she says.

"But I would say: Leverage the impact of cyber safety," Biddle adds. "Cyber safety is patient safety."

Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang's systems

Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang's systems

A Ukrainian man has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison for his role in a series of ransomware attacks.

36-year-old Artem Stryzhak became an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group around June 2021, receiving an 80% cut of the ransoms he managed to extort in attacks against hospitals, government organisations, law firms, and businesses around the world.

The rest of the ransom would go to Nefilim's administrators - including fellow Ukrainian Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who was charged last year in relation to attacks against hundreds of corporate victims using the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware, as well as Nefilim.

At the time of writing, Tymoshchuk is not in US custody and a US $11 million bounty has been offered by the US State Department for information leading to his arrest.

Nefilim was not the only ransomware gang that Stryzhak worked closely with. He was also an early affiliate of the Hive ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation which targeted businesses and, in particular, organisations working in healthcare.

The FBI later warned that Hive had extorted US $100 million from businesses and organisations globally in a period of just 18 months.

According to the US Department of Justice, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators were behind Hive ransomware attacks against a number of victims, including law firms, a dentist's office, and a healthcare provider, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector.

In January 2023, it was revealed that a multinational law enforcement operation had secretly penetrated the Hive ransomware operation in late July 2022, capturing decryption keys and quietly passing them to victims so they did not have to pay a ransom.

The DOJ said that the operation saved corporate victims of Hive over US $130 million in ransom payments.

At the time I speculated that the take-down of Hive may lead to the identification and possible apprehension of some of those involved in Hive ransomware attacks. In June 2024, Stryzhak was arrested in Barcelona, and subsequently extradited to the United States where he pleaded guilty.

The infiltration into Hive's infrastructure took place in 2022. Stryzhak was arrested in 2024, and sentenced in 2026. If there's a lesson for ransomware affiliates who think they got away with it, it's that law enforcement is prepared to be patient, and the evidence does not go away.

That's something that Volodymyr Tymoshchuk may also want to consider.

Graham Cluley is an award-winning security blogger, researcher and public speaker. He has been working in the computer security industry since the early 1990s.

Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots

The threat actor lurked behind bots posing as agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others to find exposed data.

Elizabeth Montalbano,Contributing Writer

October 28, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: NicoElNino via Adobe Stock Photo

A threat actor lurked behind more than 30 different AI bots to find and steal exposed credentials, continuously scanning for sensitive data without success. The findings highlight a growing problem for organizations: distinguishing between which AI agents belong in their networks and which may be malicious.

A scanner impersonating 32 bots — including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Meta, and others — hunted for exposed credentials to various organizations, according to a report published today by CQ Prime Research, part of Cequence Security. The scanner requested files from affected organizations — which spanned retail, financial services, telecommunications, energy, and software — that hold passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

The scanner has been running since late September and was still active as of late October, according to the researchers. They identified the activity on Oct. 21, discovering that on a single day this month, 48% of Cequence-protected organizations received the malicious AI bot traffic.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The findings highlight a growing challenge for security teams at a pivotal time, as businesses must figure out which AI agents to trust and permit access to their services.

"Attackers can test every one of those allow and deny decisions, and Cequence is seeing them probe which agents a business trusts, then impersonate the agents they expect to get through," Will Glazier, director of CQ Prime threat research and data science, wrote in the report.

Malicious Scanner Gives Itself Away

The scanner operates by firing off a burst of 50 to 190 requests in about 8 seconds and then moving on, working through targets one at a time, around the clock. Fortunately for the organizations affected, nearly all of the requests were blocked or failed, according to the report.

"It sends random nonsense paths first to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique," Glazier wrote.

CQ Prime Research identified the traffic as malicious through some telling behaviors that undermined the scanner's attempt to blend in with other traffic. The scanner rotates through about 32 bot identities evenly, which real bots do not do, according to the report; one machine claimed to be an agent from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Perplexity, all within seconds.

The attacker also used the contact address of Anthropic's crawler for all of its fake Claude identities, even when posing as different Claude agents, which shows the text was copied and not unique to each agent, according to CQ Prime Research.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

The scanner also makes requests for configuration files, cloud credential files, and private SSH keys, from a list of about 90 paths, while never identifying itself or providing a contact address. Legitimate Internet-scanning services would never need these files and always identify themselves.

"The requests gave it away," observes Collin Hogue-Spears, senior director of solutions management at security firm Black Duck, which means "what Cequence documented is the test, not a breach."

Financial Accounts at Risk

However, what happens when AI agents scanning a network get through? This is what organizations are facing, particularly banks and financial institutions, with growing concern among experts that rogue agents are already logging into customer accounts at these organizations without them knowing. The result of such activity could cause global economic fallout.

For now, CQ Prime Research found that at financial services firms, AI agents acting for customers represented fewer than 1 in 4,000 requests. "The agents banks worry about most log in with a customer's own credentials through an ordinary browser and don't announce themselves," Glazier wrote in the report.

At this point, financial institutions should be starting to take action to identify which AI agents are legit and which aren't. But acting now already could mean they're playing catch-up to the activity of threat actors, observes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability

"Banks are currently scrambling to figure out which AI bots belong on their networks, but cybercriminals have already moved on to the next phase," he says. "They are no longer trying to break into these systems. Instead, they are simply logging in disguised as trusted AI agents."

Defending Against AI Agent Impersonation

To mitigate the growing threat from AI bots and agents, security leaders must treat AI agents, API keys, and service accounts with the same operational rigor as human administrators, Barney suggests. "That requires eliminating implicit trust across every access path," he says.

Indeed, organizations should not trust a bot's claimed identity on its own, according to CQ Prime Research, and they should verify agents through signed requests, published address ranges, or direct integrations.

They also should monitor for behavior that does not match the claimed identity, "such as an AI assistant requesting configuration or credential files," Glazier wrote.

Organizations also should stop leaving static credentials in vulnerable files where scraping bots can easily find them to eliminate obvious security gaps. Instead, Barney says, "Security teams must move away from long-lived local credentials in favor of centralized, zero-knowledge secrets vaults."

AI Is Turning CISOs Into Business-Risk Translators, Says Nvidia’s Head of Cyber

Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

In the AI era, cybersecurity leaders must explain how AI-related risks connects to business goals and help executives understand who is responsible for accepting those risks, according to Nvidia’s head of cybersecurity policy, Mark Weatherford.

Speaking at ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Weatherford argued that the broad adoption of AI in the workplace, including in cybersecurity workflows, has transformed the CISO role from a security gatekeeper to a business-risk translator.

As organizations weigh AI adoption, CISOs must help executives understand the tradeoffs and clarify who owns the risk, he said.

Weatherford recalled a board meeting where a CISO struggled to explain the relationship between security and the business. Ultimately, the board challenged the CISO on their understanding of the company’s business model. This event, he said, had a negative impact on the perception the board had of the CISO’s credibility and ability to protect the business.

Weatherford said the exchange taught him that CISOs need to understand how their organizations generate revenue, not only how to protect them.

He added that business perspective is especially important as organizations weigh the potential benefits and risks of AI.

For instance, boards may worry that moving too slowly will cost them competitive advantage, Weatherford said, while moving too quickly can mean deploying tools without appropriate controls or an understanding of the risks.

While he argued that CISO rarely owns the business risk from deploying things like AI, he emphasized that modern CISOs must interpret that risk and make sure leaders understand who owns it.

Balancing AI Innovation With Cybersecurity Risks

Weatherford described two main challenges CISOs face with AI.

First and the “pace of technological change” makes their work more challenging.

Second, CISOs need to focus both on “security for AI and AI for security,” protecting the AI systems their organizations deploy while also considering how AI can support security operations.

Combined, these challenges mean traditional cybersecurity approaches may no longer be sufficient, he argued.

“If you’re not doing pentesting 24/7, 365, you’re probably behind the curve,” he said.

Weatherford also cautioned against investments driven by “fear of missing out.”

Leaders, he said, should do business due diligence before spending heavily on AI. CISOs can contribute by preparing concrete proposals for reducing risk. He recommended putting together a short plan that describes the proposed work and the resources it would require.

Vendor evaluation is another area where CISOs need to apply judgment. Weatherford said he looks for AI-native products that address security problems, rather than older products with AI added on.

He urged CISOs to consider supply-chain dependencies, too. Multiple vendors may depend on the same suppliers, creating single points of failure that can affect more than one product or service. Some dependencies may sit several tiers down the supply chain, beyond the suppliers an organization knows it relies on directly.

Weatherford’s advice for keeping pace with these changes was to stay curious and keep learning and even relearn things as technologies evolve.

For instance, he encouraged CISOs to “learn one new thing every week,” suggesting focusing on one AI topic at a time, such as model context protocol (MCP), prompt injections or sandboxing.

Finally, Weatherford recommended CISOs to join and create formal and informal peer communities. He mentioned that he created a CISO Exchange Network in which he invited CISOs from Nvidia’s major partners, customers and suppliers, where they share experience, concerns and tips.

Energy Giant Engie Notifies Customers of Supply Chain Breach

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

One of the world’s largest natural gas suppliers has notified an undisclosed number of customers that their personal data may have been compromised in a recent breach.

French multinational Engie employs over 90,000 people across 30 countries, supplying gas, nuclear power, and renewables. Its revenue in 2025 was almost €72bn ($80bn).

According to screenshots of the customer notification posted to X, the compromised data could include: full name, postal and email address, telephone number, unique IDs for energy supply (PCE/PDL), customer ID, and contract number.

The firm confirmed that no banking data was involved in the breach.

Engie urged customers to be on the lookout for potential fraud and phishing stemming from the incident.

“A malicious person could use the information mentioned above to impersonate you or use your personal details to contact another organization in your name, obtain additional information, or attempt to make a payment,” it warned. “Fraudulent emails may appear to come from trusted sources, such as organisations you know, in order to deceive you.”

According to a statement from the firm sent to Infosecurity, its own IT systems weren’t compromised. Engie blamed a third-party marketing platform used by its partners which was then compromised by threat actors.

“Engie recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers in France,” it explained.

“As soon as this activity was detected, the relevant access was disabled. At the same time, Engie launched an in-depth technical investigation to understand the circumstances of the incident, accurately assess its scope by identifying customers potentially affected, and ensure that the situation was fully secured. Enhanced monitoring measures were also put in place.”

No Group Has Claimed Responsibility

At the time of writing, no extortion group had admitted responsibility for the breach, which Engie said is now contained.

However, in October last year, extortion group Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters listed the firm on its leak site, after compromising over 100 Salesforce instances and claiming to have extracted more than one billion records.

In that incident, Engie’s US retail energy business Engie Resources was the victim, with the group claiming to have obtained 3GB of data.

According to claims data from insurer Resilience shared with Infosecurity, no UK or European energy and utilities clients have reported ransomware since July 2025.

European claims with a recorded cost involved only fraud or exposed customer data. That contrasts with the US where ransomware comprises around 70% of incurred losses across claims on record in the sector, Resilience said.

Title: LABScon26 Replay | Keynote: A Sober Analysis of AI Impact
Context: He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security
Full Text:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, delivered in his inimitable comedic style, Harvard University professor James Mickens questions whether the scale of current AI investment is justified. Starting from US tech capex of roughly 1.4% of GDP in the second quarter of 2025, he argues that computers are already good enough, and notes that the world has so many CPUs and GPUs that they are put to work solving cryptocurrency puzzles to make imaginary money. More seriously, the AI models that investment is building, he says, grow increasingly opaque as their parameter counts rise.

Mickens then cites research and incident reports on model behaviour, including models acting to prevent another model being shut down and recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and other labs. On economics, he rejects the assumptions that AI will create more jobs than it destroys and that universal basic income will follow widespread automation.

He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security. Mickens own contribution is Guillotine, a hypervisor design that runs a model’s CPU code on isolated cores unable to read or write the hardware state of the cores running the hypervisor. Arguing that hardware-based mechanisms for isolating misaligned frontier models will be an important direction for research over the next five years, he invites those interested in this approach to collaborate.

This keynote speaks to security practitioners and researchers interested in AI risk, the economics behind current AI investment, or hardware-level containment of frontier models

About the Author

James Mickens is a Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard University. His research focuses on the performance, security, and privacy of large-scale online services; a current focus is the interpretability and sandboxing of potentially misaligned frontier models. Prior to becoming a professor at Harvard, Dr. Mickens spent seven years at Microsoft Research, working in the Distributed Systems group.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

Title: 123 Reg discloses 'AI cyberattack' on customer data, suspects China nexus
Context: 123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus...
Full Text: UK domain registrar 123 Reg (no relation – Ed) says it was the victim of an “AI-driven cyberattack” that exposed customer data. Customers began receiving their notification emails this week, informing them that their contact information, "related customer relationship data," company VAT numbers, and "product information from an application programming interface (API)" were compromised. A company spokesperson elaborated, saying this means that names, phone numbers, countries, language and currency preferences, account creation dates, the products on the account, and marketing preferences were affected. 123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus attacker. "Our investigation identified IP addresses that we assessed to be the core attacker infrastructure, which were hosted in China and Singapore, indicating a strong Chinese nexus," the spokesperson said. "Our investigation further identified AI cyberattack 'skills' hosted on Chinese infrastructure, including copies of skills open sourced by Anthropic and several other AI exploitation frameworks and scripts." They went on to say that many of the artefacts left behind led 123 Reg to suspect that a Chinese state-sponsored group, known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations, could be behind the break-in. There is also a suspicion that the same group that hit a number of South Korea’s financial institutions using open-source Chinese AI tool ARTEX, was behind the attack on 123 Reg too. "The TA's mirror of 'anthropic_skills,' and the account naming conventions found on the Chinese servers are consistent with preparation of this class of AI-augmented operation," the spokesperson told us. "In addition, on October 7, 2026, CrowdStrike published CSA-261162, describing an unknown, likely Chinese-speaking actor that targeted several South Korean financial organizations starting in late September 2026, which is the same period during which we were attacked. "That actor used ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us." The GoDaddy-owned registrar reported the attack to law enforcement agencies, brought in outside cybersecurity support, and notified the FTC, as well as the data protection authorities in the UK and EU. The company spokesperson added that it worked with Singapore-based ISPs to shut down the attacker's servers in the region, which helped disrupt the attack, in addition to "other actions by us and industry partners." 123 Reg's email to customers stated the attacker's activity "was limited to reading" customer data, although the spokesperson told us "it's possible they created copies of the information," and that this is what prompted the notification. The registrar urged customers to stay alert to the potential misuse of their data, and to treat communications appearing to come from the company with caution. "If you receive a message or call and aren't sure it's from 123 Reg, go directly to our website and log in," the email said. "We will never contact you to request your password, payment details, or verification codes by email, text, or phone. "We also strongly recommend turning on two-step verification (2SV), which helps keep your account protected even if someone tricks you into sharing your password. You can find instructions for setting up 2SV in your 123 Reg account. "We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." ®

Title: Lessons from Cybersecurity Black Week
Context: In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection
Full Text:
Lessons from cybersecurity Black Week

Lessons from Cybersecurity Black Week

A critical PHP flaw, leaked Linux kernel reports, a poisoned LiteLLM release, and more, all in seven days. Which threats called for immediate action, and which generated more noise than real danger?

The week leading up to October 25, 2026, was every cyber defender’s nightmare: a barrage of critical vulnerabilities in PHP and the Linux kernel, a compromised LiteLLM release, a maximum-severity flaw in GitLab, a Node.js Brotli flaw, and a certificate authority incident affecting TLS trust.

A few years ago, a backlog like this would have filled a defender’s to-do list for a whole month. In the age of AI, all of this was reported within a single “Cybersecurity Black Week,” an exceptionally eventful seven-day period amid an already turbulent Black October. AI-assisted research helped uncover at least two of these flaws: PHP2Shell and the Brotli bug. On top of the breakneck patching pace, security teams faced mounting pressure to deliver status reports to other departments, management, customers, and the media.

Beyond their severity, the issues stood out for the variety of responses they demanded. Some required emergency runtime patches and upgrades; others called for containment, credential rotation, or the replacement of outdated certificate trust bundles. In several cases, installing the latest version was only the beginning of a long remediation process.

With so many problems landing at once, the main challenge was separating real risk from hype and prioritizing accordingly. Here is our assessment.

PHP2Shell: The loudest headline, with real-world limits

PHP2Shell generated the biggest media frenzy of the lot and, with it, a major headache for security teams, prompting many organizations to take their websites offline and look for emergency fixes. The name refers to two memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP core, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affecting PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11. Both vulnerabilities received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable PHP servers. In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection.

With PHP powering an estimated 69% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, government agencies in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere urged organizations to patch immediately, with some advising that affected internet-facing systems be isolated or taken offline if they could not be patched promptly. Government websites in the Netherlands, Germany, France, and other countries were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. The PHP project released fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, along with source-only backports for the end-of-life 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 branches. The rollout was complicated by a premature public leak, which forced the coordinated disclosure timeline forward.

While the flaws clearly belonged near the top of the patching list, early evidence suggested they were considerably harder to weaponize than initially feared. Successful exploitation requires specific conditions and knowledge of the target, and public proof-of-concept exploits did not work against a default PHP installation, according to Sansec.

On October 22, ESET was among nine security companies that told NBC News they had not seen any successful attacks, even though more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits were circulating. The remediation challenge extends beyond obvious web servers: PHP can also be embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces, and third-party products, while end-of-life PHP branches do not receive normal upstream binary releases.

Linux kernel: Reports went public before fixes were ready

As if the PHP issues weren’t severe enough, on October 21, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent several reports on unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the kernel’s private security address while also copying public mailing lists. As a result, technical details of vulnerabilities for which fixes were not yet generally available became public, prompting stable kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman to question why the reports had been sent to public lists without patches.

The two most severe issues, both rated CVSS 9.0 by ZDI, affect KSMBD, the Linux kernel’s built-in SMB server. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct path that could lead to RCE, while ZDI-CAN-33774 is a race condition that could also lead to RCE. Exploiting ZDI-CAN-33549 requires an RDMA-capable interface, a writable KSMBD share, and SMB Direct negotiation, significantly narrowing the number of systems exposed to that particular attack. Other reports concerned local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the networking stack and the VMware graphics driver, as well as an information disclosure issue in the NVMe target code (NVMET).

To remediate, security teams had to track each report independently, consult distribution advisories, and restrict exposed services where practical while awaiting verified fixes. Kernel updates also required rebooting into the patched kernel and checking the running version, not merely confirming that a new package had been installed.

LiteLLM: Compromised, not merely vulnerable

On October 21, attackers published a malicious version of LiteLLM, 1.107.0, to PyPI and pushed compromised images to the project’s official container registries. According to the project’s incident report, its release pipeline was breached using GitHub CLI credentials associated with three developers. One of the stolen tokens belonged to an owner of the project’s GitHub organization, allowing attackers to disable branch protections and modify the release workflow to point to a lookalike repository. LiteLLM, a Python proxy for LLM providers, has about 23 million weekly downloads, and the malicious version remained available on PyPI for roughly two hours before it was quarantined. It was the project’s second supply-chain compromise of 2026, after malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 appeared in March.

The payload combined a credential stealer with a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT). By abusing Python’s startup mechanisms, including a .pth file, it ran every time Python started, even if an application never imported LiteLLM. Execution therefore did not depend on exploiting an application flaw: simply running Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Affected environments had to be treated as potentially compromised, not merely vulnerable. According to LiteLLM, these included environments that ran litellm==1.107.0 and containers that executed affected images distributed under the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags during the compromised intervals. Removing or replacing the package was insufficient: teams needed to determine whether the malicious code had run, contain affected systems, rebuild from clean sources, and rotate exposed secrets from a clean environment. Cloud, source-control, and CI/CD logs also had to be reviewed for unauthorized activity.

Node2Shell: From Node.js to HTTP2Shell

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder, which Node.js bundles. Malformed compressed input can cause crashes, memory disclosure, or potentially RCE when an application decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. This can happen through explicit decompression, compressed request bodies, or automatically decompressed responses. Node.js rates the flaw as high severity, while the broader Brotli vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. According to Aikido, researchers demonstrated code execution against the official, unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux ARM64. Although the exploit did not work on every attempt, the demonstration showed that exploitation was practical, if not universally reliable.

Node.js shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, and Bun followed with version 1.4.4 or later. Node.js 25.x, 23.x, 20.x, and earlier releases are end-of-life and will not receive the fix. Within days, the story outgrew Node.js. The same decoder is compiled into the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages as well as into other HTTP software, which led researchers to rename the issue HTTP2Shell. The operational challenge was therefore not simply upgrading a single runtime but identifying every container, serverless deployment, and library that bundles the vulnerable decoder. The issue was fixed upstream in Brotli 1.2.1. Notably, OpenAI’s Codex Security had reported the underlying bug, and the fix had been present in the Brotli source since February without being recognized as a security issue.

GitLab: Credential leaks and authorization failures

On October 21, GitLab shipped a critical out-of-band patch release (versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) addressing 12 security vulnerabilities. The headline flaw, CVE-2026-110264, rated 10.0 under CVSS v3.1, is an integer overflow triggered when GitLab compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The affected versions date back to GitLab 7.0.

The other fixes addressed credential exposure, cache poisoning, authorization bypasses, and failures to enforce membership or merge-request approval policies. Reported unauthenticated attack paths included exposure of sensitive credentials through internal response headers and manipulation of a shared OAuth/OIDC discovery cache, while other issues required authenticated access. GitLab did not publish individual severity scores or exploitability details for these issues.

GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were already patched, so the work fell on administrators of self-managed instances. GitLab strongly recommended upgrading immediately, but with a catch: the older backport releases (19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) included only the critical fix, while the remaining 11 issues were fixed only in 19.3.6 and later. Administrators also had to verify that all deployment components had been updated and assess the potential exposure of credentials and private project data due to the fact that patching would not invalidate stolen credentials or reverse unauthorized changes.

eMudhra/emSign: Compromised certificate trust

The high-priority eMudhra/emSign incident involved no software vulnerability at all. Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) had insecure private keys, meaning attackers could potentially create certificates that would be trusted through the affected emSign certificate chain. While browsers had updated their trust stores and revocation lists, some Python tooling continued to trust the compromised intermediate CAs through its own certificate bundles. This created a risk of man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks against TLS connections, including those to python.org and pypi.org.

The Python Software Foundation urged users to upgrade immediately to at least certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, and uv 0.13.4, and the Python core team shipped expedited releases 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16, and 3.11.18 to update the bundled pip. The updates had to reach every host, application, and existing virtual environment. Container images had to be rebuilt with layer caching disabled to fetch the latest system certificates. The decisive check was whether deployed clients rejected the compromised trust paths; simply upgrading Python was not enough.

Cybersecurity Black Week showed that a severity score rarely tells the whole story. A 9.2-rated PHP flaw that attackers struggled to exploit, a 10.0-rated GitLab bug, exposed kernel reports with no patches, and a poisoned package that ran at Python startup each called for a different response. What they all had in common was a window of exposure: the time between disclosure and when the last affected system is patched. For the leaked kernel flaws, that window opened before any fix existed, and for end-of-life PHP versions, it may never fully close. This is where ESET’s multilayered protection comes in, using behavioural detection and other security mechanisms to help block exploitation attempts and keep systems protected until patches are applied.

At the same time, the signals defenders rely on were buried in noise, from scanning that was largely benign to a single behavioural rule firing hundreds of thousands of times in a week. What mattered most was quickly understanding which incidents actually affected an organization's environment and what each incident required. That is the problem ESET’s correlation engine, ESET LiveCortex, and its specialized cybersecurity model, ESET NeoCortex, are designed to solve: turning an overwhelming volume of raw data into understandable incidents so that defenders can act before attackers achieve their goals. To learn how they work, read Beyond the alert: How ESET is teaching AI to understand security incidents.

Background

Network-connected surveillance cameras are now widespread in both home and enterprise environments, so securing them is essential to safeguarding physical spaces and sensitive assets. As these devices continue to gain new features and network connectivity capabilities, vulnerabilities in their implementation can have significant security implications.

During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems. The flaw resides in a firmware update endpoint that is accessible without authentication and allows anyone with access to the local Wi-Fi network to knock cameras offline. A single request disrupts the camera for only about a minute, but sending periodic requests keeps the device offline indefinitely. We reported the issue to Intelbras, monitored the remediation process, validated the fix in the new firmware, and will now demonstrate the exploitation procedure step-by-step.

Following our notification, Intelbras patched the vulnerability and released updated firmware (R.260804) along with update instructions. A candidate ID of CAN-2026-2035970 has been assigned by MITRE following submission, pending the final CVE assignment. Additionally, the Intelbras team recently informed us that MITRE has classified the vulnerability as Medium, assigning it a score of 5.1 under the CVSS 4.0 framework. The issue discussed in this article is no longer present in the latest firmware version.

Firmware

Intelbras provides firmware files on its official website. While users can manually install these updates via an SD card, the cameras also natively support firmware upgrades over the local network via their web interface and mobile app. We obtained the firmware version v240927 for the iM3B-C (IM3 C) camera, which was the latest available version at the time of our research. According to Intelbras, the same firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Below, we can view the firmware version and the camera model used as an example.

To provide context, we will explain how the camera’s authentication mechanism works and why it is relevant to accessing the camera’s endpoints. The main firmware component is an ARM binary named sonia, responsible for controlling the kernel drivers used by the camera hardware, authentication, and livestream recording, among other things.

How authentication works

The global.login RPC method handles authentication at the /RPC2_Login endpoint. First, the client, such as the mobile app or a custom script, sends the username and an empty password. The camera responds with an authentication challenge (a set of values to verify the password without transmitting it). This response returns a temporary session, the encryption type in the encryption field, a random value, and a realm (authentication scope). At this stage, a false response is normal and does not indicate a failed login, as the authentication process is not yet complete.

Next, the client calculates the response password from the authentication challenge. It first generates an MD5 (username:realm:original_password) hash as the base. It then calculates a second MD5 (username:random:first_md5) hash, where first_md5 is the result of the previous step. To complete the authentication, the client sends this final result back to /RPC2_Login in a second global.login call, passing the username, calculated password, and temporary session ID.

If the login is accepted, the camera returns true and a new, authenticated session. This session must be used for all subsequent RPC calls, including the camera’s other endpoints, for example, the one that reboots the device or those that expose sensitive information.

Affected endpoint

The affected endpoint is the firmware upgrade route http://<ip_address>/firmwareUpgrade_service/Demo, which lacks authentication checks; furthermore, it fails to verify whether the firmware is actually valid before initiating the upgrade process. This creates a serious issue because the upgrade requires the camera to reboot, and that is precisely when the problem occurs: the camera enters reboot mode and eventually shuts down, appearing offline to the user and anyone who has the camera registered on their device.

PoC: vulnerability exploitation

Now that we have outlined how the vulnerability works, we will use a Python script on an iM3B-C camera to exploit it for demonstration purposes. The exploit contacts the camera’s endpoint to upload firmware. Below, we can see sonia creating the endpoint responsible for the firmware upgrade.

Next, the exploit will hit the endpoint and cause the camera to reboot. Consequently, mobile phones running the Intelbras app will lose connection with the registered device. Below, we can see the camera operating normally: the green light is on and the app is showing it is available for viewing.

The camera is online

After the exploit executes, we can see the effects: the camera goes offline and loses connection to the registered devices.

The camera is offline

The exploit is quite simple: it sends an HTTP POST request with the firmware, which causes the camera to accept the request and initiate the reboot process. It does not matter whether the firmware is original; the reboot process will start regardless.

New firmware version

After we notified Intelbras about this flaw in the endpoint implementation, the company contacted the OEM vendor. As a result, a new firmware version was released that requires authentication to initiate an update through this endpoint.

Below, we can compare the new firmware, which validates cookies and session data, with the old firmware, which performed no authentication checks and proceeded directly to the update routine.

Real risk

An attacker can remotely trigger the camera firmware upgrade and reboot process without authenticating or supplying a valid firmware image. This may cause the device to go offline, which results in a denial-of-service condition preventing legitimate users from accessing live monitoring or managing the camera.

The potential impact is significant due to the number of affected users. The Intelbras Mibo Smart app, which the company provides to connect and manage the devices mentioned in this report, has over 4,000,000 downloads. Brazil represents the largest user base, followed by Paraguay, Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Venezuela. As a result, exploitation of this issue affects a large number of users.

Takeaways

This is a medium-severity vulnerability that Intelbras is already aware of. The issue has been addressed in a newer firmware release (R.260804 along with update instructions), which mitigates this attack vector. Because the vulnerability directly affects the availability and normal operation of the affected cameras, it is highly recommended that users verify the firmware version currently installed on their devices and update to the latest available version as soon as possible. Keeping the firmware up to date is an essential security practice, especially for internet-connected surveillance devices, as outdated versions may remain exposed to known vulnerabilities.

Title: ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History
Context: Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people...
Full Text:
Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.

The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.

Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.

Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7.

Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration's policies and espouse "anti-Christian" ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown.

Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s.

Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025.

Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area.

Around 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order.

The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them.

Their defense attorneys say the heavy charges filed against the Minnesota 15 don’t align with their alleged conduct. “This is the first time I’ve had a client who’s accused of a conspiracy and went on a speaking tour,” says Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant.

Peeking Through the Keyhole

An internal ICE document laying out the scope of Operation Puppet Master—which led to the indictment of the Minneapolis 15—ends by noting, “This case has also been accepted under CUC Op Keyhole.” According to prosecutors, Operation Keyhole is a long-standing program created by HSI’s Saint Paul office to fund “undercover activity”—primarily equipment purchases and personnel costs—in a region covering Minnesota, North and South Dakota, Iowa, and Nebraska. The program has funded at least 77 investigations into “narcotics trafficking, child sexual abuse, financial investigations, and counter-proliferation” since it started in December 2008.

The CUC prefix, per an internal 2008 DHS handbook unearthed by the independent media outlet Unicorn Riot, refers to Certified Undercover Operations, a formal designation with clearly defined oversight mechanisms, procedures, and reporting requirements. Operation Keyhole’s parameters are reviewed every six months by a committee comprising senior DOJ and DHS officials. As of June 2026, when it was last renewed, Keyhole funded six active investigations, including Project Whipple Shield, which was initiated in February to probe claims of assault, stalking, and doxing of DHS agents and other federal employees, and underpins the Minnesota 15 indictment.

At least 11 undercover agents working under Operation Keyhole infiltrated Twin Cities anti-ICE activists, participating in martial arts and know-your-rights trainings, marches, general strikes, and community meetings. They also infiltrated activists’ communications network for identifying possible undercover ICE vehicles and dispatching activists to tail them through the Twin Cities, and penetrated several activist group chats on Signal, transmitting their contents back to other HSI colleagues for analysis and eventual inclusion in the indictment.

Activist conferences as far away as Seattle, Michigan, Chicago, and New York City were placed under surveillance as part of the investigation, and HSI teams photographed and ran the license plates of every car parked in the lot of a meeting location or seen transporting activists. There is also drone footage from unarmed Customs and Border Protection Reaper drones of the activists moving around the Twin Cities area.

The undercovers were part of a much broader group of more than 50 HSI agents, including at least two dozen from HSI’s little-known Special Operations Group, that took part in the investigation and surveillance of the defendants, both digital and in-person. Feds with decades of experience on complex financial crimes, drug cartel investigations, human trafficking, and organized crime were pulled into the Minnesota 15 investigation.

Several of the Minnesota 15 case agents are from out of state and appear in court records for the prosecutions of anti-ICE activists in other cities. This includes Los Angeles–based HSI agents Robert Kurtz III, who specializes in financial fraud, and Ryan Ribner, who allegedly assaulted SEIU California president David Huerta at a June 2025 protest of an ICE enforcement operation, arrested him, and then claimed the then 58-year-old Huerta attacked federal law enforcement. (Huerta’s charges were dropped in July after videos contradicting Ribner’s account surfaced.) HSI records show Ribner was also involved in at least two prosecutions of Southern California residents who physically confronted ICE and Border Patrol agents last year.

Other agents from the conspiracy investigation have also been involved in recent high-profile incidents. Tim Gerber, the “team leader” of an HSI Special Operations Group squad, led the investigation of former CNN host Don Lemon for reporting on a protest at a Minneapolis Church where an ICE agent was a pastor. Fellow SOG agent Yue Her was present at the scene of a 2025 incident when Renee Good’s killer, ICE Special Response Team agent Johnathan Ross, was dragged by the car of a man he tried to apprehend.

“This operation does not seem in any way limited to Minnesota,” says Spencer Reynolds, a former DHS attorney and counterterrorism lawyer who now works at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. “As we saw with the boots on the ground in the streets, with Greg Bovino leading CBP and Border Patrol special forces units on sweeping raids across the country, this is the intelligence and undercover investigative apparatus that is running in parallel to the door-kicking.”

Follow the Money

Mike German, a retired FBI agent who worked undercover domestic terrorism cases for years before becoming a sharp critic of post-9/11 federal law enforcement, likens the Minnesota 15 case to federal law enforcement’s long history of suppressing left-wing social movements, including the CIA’s Operation MH/Chaos, which surveilled the anti-war movement during the Vietnam War for evidence of foreign influence. One difference is the sheer scale—this time, it’s bigger.

According to a 2011 book by former CIA officer Frank Rafalko, the CIA secret investigation into suspected foreign influence on the New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement had 42 officers working the case at its peak. Court records show 119 HSI agents worked on the Minnesota 15 case alone.

“Broad monitoring of social media, communications, and financial transactions are used to link an ever increasing number of people as potential subjects of investigation and prosecution,” German says. “These are exactly the kind of intelligence activities J. Edgar Hoover adopted to suppress the Civil Rights and anti-war movements in the 1960s.”

The key difference today, German says, is the vast pool of data available to the feds.

HSI used highly invasive measures—including scrutiny of wire transfers, PayPal reimbursements, and other financial transactions; forensic digital analysis of website traffic; 15 terabytes worth of infiltrated Signal chats; and information from a commercial data broker—to identify individuals under investigation.

After a local activist uploaded a license-plate search tool on Fly.io, a developer-focused public cloud platform, to an infiltrated Signal chat, HSI agents reviewed website DNS queries and Stripe data along with data purchased from a commercial broker. This gave HSI access to SSH session logs, outbound connection records, the Fly.io account’s signup IP, and a Stripe card fingerprint on an account that had never completed a payment. Agents fused that with Minnesota DVS records and commercial data from the Thomson-Reuters CLEAR platform to produce a driver's license number, Social Security number summary, years of address history, phone numbers, property records, and jointly registered vehicles.

Documents concerning financial records requested through the Treasury Department’s 314(a) suspicious activity reporting program—created by the Patriot Act to enable speedy tracking of finances for terrorism and money-laundering investigations—show that the feds targeted records of 29 “subjects” during queries conducted on March 31, 2026. Emails viewed by WIRED between several HSI agents based in Los Angeles and Arizona show that batches of records were turned over pursuant to those inquiries, including some dealing with SEIU that a senior Minnesota HSI agent sent to a LA-based colleague to be filed “wherever these records are stored.”

HSI investigators used similar workarounds to warrants and grand jury subpoenas to obtain phone records for several journalists who covered Operation Metro Surge, as first reported by The Guardian. Court records show the feds used an administrative summons request reserved for violations of customs and taxation requirements, which does not fit the activity that made up the criminal charges filed by the Minnesota US attorney against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others.

The Minnesota 15 case is the clearest example yet of DHS pursuing the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on what have long been upheld as First Amendment–protected activities. But it’s unlikely alone.

Riach, the defense attorney, says the HSI reports show the agency is complicit in what he called “the new COINTELPRO.”

“What we saw during the immigration surges last year was that ICE is the administration’s paramilitary force, the projector of strength,” Riach says. “Here, we see that HSI are taking the FBI’s place as the investigative secret police—it’s the classic one-two punch of authoritarian regimes around the world.”
