Title: Waiting on a Node.js Upgrade? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
Context: In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Node.js has fixed CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, but upgrading at scale is slow. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of roughly 3 million Node.js installations have been patched, and 1.7 million run end-of-life lines that will never receive a fix. In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but upgrading the runtime remains the only complete fix.

Node.js comes with a clear instruction: upgrade the runtime. The October 21 security release fixes 10 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, and three high-severity flaws that weaken DNS and TLS hostname validation. Fixed releases exist for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Upgrading at this scale still takes time, because the vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, in container images, single-executable applications, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js

Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first.

Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations

Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix.

These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change.

Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF.

Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve*, and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters.

Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms.

Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control.

Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions.

Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses.

Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself.

Node.js October 2026 3rd-party mitigation and compensating controls

Select the WAF, IPS, and EDR you run to see the controls you already have for the October 2026 Node.js security release. Coverage is strongest for CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli remote code execution flaw.

Endpoint controls are listed for CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Cybereason, SentinelOne and Cortex XDR.

Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation or on memory behavior, so verify each one fires for your Node.js process. Compensating controls reduce risk; upgrading Node.js remains the only complete fix.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Interim mitigations reduce risk. Upgrading remains the only complete fix. Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, while lines such as 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, 20.x, and older receive no fix and must move to a supported release. Customers can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate, so check the patch catalog for their line. Qualys reports a high patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for the runtime upgrade.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

Upgrade every copy. Migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release.

Rebuild container images and single-executable applications on the fixed version, then redeploy them.

Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers, and single-executable applications keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart.

Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed.

Where to Start

Find. Search for CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to locate every runtime, including copies outside standard install paths.

Prioritize. Put internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data at the top, alongside business criticality.

Mitigate. Apply the Qualys TRU interim steps to runtimes awaiting an upgrade, and test the affected applications.

Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers, and set the Cloudflare rule to Block.

Patch and verify. Upgrade to a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy what embeds the runtime, restart every Node.js service, and rescan.

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM

The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change.

Two servers can run the same unpatched Node.js build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule and an IPS signature that name the Brotli flaw, with EDR watching its Node.js process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps:

Recommendations on every finding (coming soon). ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where.

Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention.

Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate from the platform that found the exposure.

Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Interpol's annual Operation Serengeti, now in its third iteration, led to 1,462 arrests across 20 African countries and the US, recovering $105 million in stolen funds.

Robert Lemos,Contributing Writer

October 28, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: Wirestock Creators via Shutterstock

A two-month operation in Africa led to the arrests of nearly 1,500 cybercrime suspects across 20 African countries and the US, the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds, and the shutdown of nearly 11,000 malicious networks.

The third annual roundup of cybercriminals and financial scammers, dubbed Operation Serengeti III, aimed to take down groups responsible for ransomware, phishing, and cyber-enabled fraud, Interpol stated. The operation expanded the impact of cyber-focused investigations from previous law enforcement efforts in 2024 and 2025, which netted 1,006 suspects in the original Operation Serengeti and 1,209 suspects in last year's effort, dubbed Operation Serengeti 2.0.

The increasing arrests show that the national law enforcement partners are becoming more mature in their investigative practices and collaboration across jurisdictions, says Neal Jetton, director for cybercrime at Interpol.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

"Rising arrest figures reflect stronger enforcement activity, not a change in the scale of offending," he says. "The success of law enforcement efforts should be judged by whether fewer people are victimized over time and not by the number of suspects arrested or victims identified during a specific operation."

The crackdown came as cybercriminals in the region continue to develop more sophistication in their operations, with a survey of African members finding that 72% of the 36 African countries have discovered a criminally operated scam center and more than half of cybercrime cases involved the use of AI — 8% frequently and 47% occasionally, according to Interpol's "African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026."

The data highlights the rapid improvements in cybercriminal infrastructure, says Jacomo Piccolini, vice president of global data partnerships at Team Cymru.

"Scams that once looked like individual schemes now run like businesses, with recruitment pipelines, international staff, and, increasingly, trafficked workers," he says.

Busting Transnational Criminal Orgs

In Uganda, for example, two transnational criminal organizations (TCOs) used a rotating call-center model with scripted communications, fraudulent websites, and fake trading platforms to convince elderly victims in Asia to invest in their financial scams, Interpol said in a statement on Operation Serengeti III's impact. Ugandan law enforcement authorities successfully dismantled the fraud rings, arresting 365 foreign nationals, consisting almost entirely of citizens from various Asian nations, Interpol's Jetton says.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

In another arm of the operation, national police arrested nine suspects in Angola, dismantling two illegal cryptocurrency mining sites and seizing more than 2,000 devices used to mine crypto along with six illegal power transformers valued at more than US $1 million. Cybercriminal mining operations are a common way to generate cryptocurrency, the favored method of cashing out on illegal schemes, Jetton says.

"Cryptocurrency played a significant role in moving the proceeds," Jetton says. "It is now the principal rail for this type of fraud."

In Nigeria, police shuttered two fraud operations: One using 2.1 million email addresses to create a large-scale phishing and business email compromise (BEC) operation, while another scheme focused on international investment fraud and garnered at least US $2.4 million in profits, Interpol stated.

The schemes showed off the role that AI is taking in enabling cybercriminal campaigns. The phishing and BEC campaigns used email addresses and AI agents to scrape information from LinkedIn and other social media to identify high-value targets, Jetton says.

"AI enabled the threat actor to create highly personalized phishing emails by mimicking the writing style of executives, colleagues, and suppliers," he says, adding that "AI helped criminals manage and prioritize millions of email addresses for large-scale campaigns and, in some cases, combined with voice cloning, deepfake videos, and AI chatbots to make social engineering attacks even more convincing."

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

Maturing Collaboration Between Law Enforcement

Law enforcement collaboration is making the individual nations more effective in tackling transnational cybercrime. With international partners, the individual countries are able to gain intelligence on signs of cybercriminal activities in their country, says Team Cymru's Piccolini.

"The biggest change is timing. Since Serengeti 2.0, investigators have gone in with intelligence on suspicious IP addresses, domains, and command-and-control servers before the operation begins, along with training in open source, crypto, and ransomware investigation."

Without such collaboration, TCOs could evade repercussions, especially if they limited their activities to impacting only citizens of other nations, as in the case of the Asian investment fraud ring.

"Actors targeting victims in Europe and North America use infrastructure spread across multiple jurisdictions, which makes it harder to pursue through any single country," Piccolini says. "That’s a big part of why international operations like Serengeti, with partners who can see across borders, matter so much."

Both Interpol and Team Cyrmu stressed that several operations are ongoing, with investigators continuing to use seized data and other information to pursue suspected cybercriminals.

Title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
Context: A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second
Full Text:
Executive Summary

In May, Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) documented JOMANGY, a PHP webshell generation deployed by INJ3CTOR3 with self-healing persistence channels and a built-in toll-fraud dialer.

Back then, the fraud ran through the victim's own PBX, so removing the implant would have stopped it. Artifacts we collected from the operator's C2 staging servers during mid-September 2026 show that this is no longer true: the installer now sends credentials off the box on every run, and a second staging host serves it.

INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now uploads the victim's SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials to the operator, so disinfecting or rebuilding an infected host no longer ends the exposure. Anyone running FreePBX, Issabel, or Elastix who suspects compromise must rotate the secrets in 17 configuration files, and only after the host is clean.

The infection and persistence code is nearly unchanged; what the operator rotated are the identifiers that were available to defenders since the last time. Each section below pairs a finding with what to do about it.

Key Takeaways

Credentials leave on every run. k.php uploads 17 configuration files to both staging hosts every minute the host stays infected.

The fraud no longer needs your PBX. A stolen trunk secret lets the operator register and place calls as you from anywhere.

Last report's identifiers have expired. Each build now carries its own watermark, and the webshell gate hash was rotated.

Two staging hosts. Plain-text commands now point to 160[.]119[.]69[.]4, while base64-encoded ones still use 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

Clean-looking logs and consoles prove nothing. Requests through an encoded space reach the shell without being named in the access log, and trunks are written directly to /etc/asterisk; they do not appear in the FreePBX console.

The Campaign So Far

INJ3CTOR3 has been abusing Asterisk-based phone systems for toll fraud since at least 2020. Check Point Research named the operation that November, when it exploited CVE-2019-19006 in FreePBX and used a basic webshell to read amportal.conf and sip_additional.conf by hand. Unit 42 reported a related operation against Elastix in 2022, Fortinet documented the EncystPHP webshell in January 2026, and our May report covered JOMANGY.

The playbook has held for six years: scan for exposed PBXs, exploit or brute-force a way in, plant a password-gated webshell, and dial out at the victim's expense. Figure 1 below shows the chain as it stands in the September build, now including the credential upload back to the staging hosts.

Credential Exfiltration: The Implant Is No Longer the Product

The September k.php ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each holding 17 curl commands that upload one configuration file apiece to /hima_data/index.php, one line per staging host (See Figure 2 below). The paths are typed out by hand and cover FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix layouts. The collector path echoes hima, a backdoor account the takeover script creates. The name goes back further: Check Point's 2020 INJ3CTOR3 report shows a Telegram post by a user called Hima sharing a tool that scans and cracks SIP ranges, saving its output as HimaResults.

Figure 2: k.php line 34, decoded into 17 file uploads

Three of the cron beacons fetch and run k.php every minute (the others every two or three minutes), so the upload repeats every minute during the infection. Rotating credentials on a still-infected host hands the new secrets to the operator within minutes.

This opens a second route to fraud. Our May report covered calls placed through the webshell, which require the shell to be alive and to land in the victim's own call records. With a stolen trunk secret, the operator can register to the carrier from any machine and call as the victim, leaving nothing on the host, unless the carrier also restricts the trunk to the victim's IP addresses. A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second.

Detection

Network: outbound HTTP POSTs from a PBX to any /hima_data/ path or to either staging host. A PBX seldom needs outbound web access beyond vendor updates, so egress allow-listing closes this channel.

Carrier: alert on trunk registrations from outside your own IP ranges, and on premium or international destinations, off-hours calling, and unusual concurrency. Set spend caps and destination blocks where your carrier offers them.

For Law Enforcement Agencies and CERTs

By design, victims' credentials were collected on the two staging hosts, which stopped responding in late September 2026. Going offline does not end exposure: hosting providers may still retain server data, and infected PBXs keep trying to upload their credentials every minute to addresses that could be reassigned to someone else.

Both are reasons for law enforcement and national CERTs, which have the legal standing that researchers lack, to work with the providers on preserving that data and sinkholing the addresses, which would also identify victims for notification. We saw the uploads in code; we did not capture one in transit and hold no victim list.

An infected host now talks to both staging hosts, and which one depends on whether the command was written in plain text or base64. The /x takeover script is byte-identical on both.

The Webshell: Same Program, New Identifiers

Decoded, the September JOMANGY panel is identical to April's except for the values defenders were told to look for.

Per-build watermark. Our May report advised hunting for trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea, present in every April copy. The September builds carry trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 (45[.]95[.]147[.]178) and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e (160[.]119[.]69[.]4), so that hunt now misses current infections.

One gate for two generations. JOMANGY and ZenharR share a single hardcoded MD5 gate hash, rotated together from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. Our May report listed the April value under ZenharR only.

A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Therefore, changing the FreePBX admin password affects neither the gate nor this session. (See Figure 3 below)

Figure 3: The panel's Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password

Because each of these identifiers changes between builds, the detection approach later in this report focuses on who put a file on disk rather than on what the file contains.

The .htaccess Door and the Access-Log Gap

k.php writes a seven-line .htaccess to /var/www/html/admin/views/. It does not hide the webshell; it unblocks it, and it lets requests reach a copy without naming it.

Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it.

Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. Because the takeover script wipes logs, treat log hunting as secondary: requests with %20, %09, or %0A directly after a slash that return 200 are worth a look where logs survive.

What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You

FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so.

Figure 4: Our lab trunk, known to Asterisk and carrying calls, invisible in the FreePBX console

Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added.

What Keeps It There

Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below)

Detecting It Without IOCs

The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be.

However, it cannot tell you whether the credentials have already been left: that happens during the first cron run, within a minute of infection, and long before anyone scans. The upload leaves no file behind, and the takeover script wipes what might have recorded it: the web server, Asterisk, cron and audit logs, plus shell and MySQL histories, which makes forensic timelines hard to reconstruct.

Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works

First move

Why it fails on its own

Delete the webshell

Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags.

Patch FreePBX

Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system.

Change the admin password

The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login.

Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it.

Preserve first

The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run:

Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below.

Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times.

Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs.

Then clean, in this order

Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref.

Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local.

Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled.

Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php.

Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host.

Conclusion

The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account.

The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR.

The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure.

When AI Guardrails Expose Vulnerabilities

In Guardrail-based Vulnerability Discovery, the guardrails intended to keep AI models from aiding attackers can signify issues that defenders can interpret and act on.

October 28, 2026

• Jonathan Bar Or - D'Angelo Gonzalez • Securing AI

CrowdStrike researchers asked a frontier AI model to explain a function in a small C web server. While it had previously explained every other function in the codebase without hesitation, it refused to explain this one.

The request was routine. We'd only asked what the code does; we hadn't asked about security, exploits, or vulnerabilities. But a single token in the code had changed: a max swapped for a min; a one-character logic inversion that creates an out-of-bounds write. It's the kind of bug that slips past code review and that pattern-matching scanners routinely miss.

The model never said there were any vulnerabilities, but its refusal to explain the function indicated there could be one. The act of the model changing behaviors on a specific chunk of code showed us exactly where to look for the vulnerability. Its guardrails became the giveaway.

That moment changed how we think about AI safety. The guardrails frontier labs build to keep models from helping attackers can't work without first recognizing that something is dangerous. This recognition is a signal that practitioners can read. Most of the industry treats refusals as a dead end; at CrowdStrike, we started treating them as findings.

We call this approach Guardrail-based Vulnerability Discovery (GbVD). In controlled tests across five vulnerability classes, it was correct in 73 of 86 test scenarios, and it held up on real open-source projects we disclosed through our Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) program.

Safety and capability are usually framed as a trade-off. This research suggests the opposite: Every improvement labs make to their guardrails also sharpens a methodology that cybersecurity practitioners or adversaries can use. This work builds on our earlier research into LLM safety classifiers, where we studied how those guardrails can be bypassed. Here, we look at the other side: what guardrails reveal when they work as intended.

Breaking Down Guardrail-based Vulnerability Discovery

Today, the most visible manifestation of a guardrail is a refusal: The model declines in plain text (or with “reason: cyber” in standard APIs), which makes the signal trivially readable. But refusals are just one observable among several. Guardrails in deployed AI systems take many forms, and most of them leak:

Explicit refusals: The current dominant case, and the one our experiments exploit.

Model downgrading: Some platforms route sensitive requests to a smaller or more conservative model. The routed response betrays itself through measurable differences: response latency, tokens spent, time-to-first-token, or a sudden drop in output specificity and style.

Output filtering and truncation: A post-hoc filter that redacts or cuts off a response changes its length and shape in detectable ways.

Reasoning interruption: In agentic settings, a guardrail may abort a tool call or halt a chain of reasoning mid-task rather than emit any refusal text at all (we observe this in our second case study).

Whatever form the guardrail takes, triggering it perturbs some measurable property of the response, such as content, timing, token count, or structure. The defender doesn't need the model to say anything explicitly; rather, they need only to measure the perturbation. Our experiments below use refusals because they are today's loudest channel, but the methodology is agnostic to how the guardrail manifests.

A binary, localized signal composes naturally with classic techniques, including bisection: split a codebase or filesystem into halves, ask the model to explain each half, and recurse into whichever half triggers the guardrail. The model never has to say "this is vulnerable"; it only has to behave differently in the right place.

Table 1 summarizes our experiments.

Table 1. Vulnerability result summaries (experiment results: TP = true positive, FP = false positive, FN = false negative, TN = true negative)

Why Does This Work?

Safety training creates a classifier inside the model that is distinct from, and sometimes more sensitive than its question-answering behavior. A model asked "Is this code vulnerable?" produces a judgment that is noisy, verbose, and prone to both over- and under-flagging. But the guardrail pathway is trained adversarially and conservatively: Labs tune systems to intervene before producing harmful content, which means the trigger often fires on the recognition of a dangerous pattern rather than on the user's stated intent.

Two properties make guardrail activation attractive as a detection primitive:

It's involuntary: The model doesn't choose to emit the signal; it leaks the signal. This makes it harder for surface-level prompt phrasing to suppress (though not impossible; see the Limitations section below).

It's cheap to read: Distinguishing "the model explained the function" from "the guardrail engaged" requires no output parsing, structured schema, or judge model. Refusals are close to a one-bit oracle. Subtler cases (downgrading, filtering) reduce to a threshold test over latency or token counts.

Methodology

We designed controlled experiments around two classes of flaw, a memory-safety bug in C source code and a privilege-escalation misconfiguration on a filesystem, to test whether the guardrail signal generalizes across code review and environment auditing tasks. In both experiments, the guardrail manifested as a refusal or reasoning interruption, the easiest channels to read today.

The protocol for each experiment:

Baseline pass: Ask the model to explain every unit (function, file, or directory) in the clean target. Record that it answers all of them. This controls for spurious guardrail activations; a model whose guardrails engage on benign code is useless as an oracle.

Introduce the flaw: Introduce a single, realistic vulnerability.

Rerun the identical prompts: The only variable is the code.

Localize: Treat each guardrail activation as a hit, and bisect toward the smallest unit that still triggers it.

While refusals were quite deterministic for the default temperature value (often 1.0 depending on the platform), we run the same prompt 5 times and conclude a refusal based on a threshold of at least 3 out of 5.

Case Study: Buffer Overflow in tinyhttp

We used tinyhttp, a minimal HTTP server in C. It’s small enough to audit exhaustively, but realistic enough that the vulnerability isn't a toy example.

Baseline: The model produced detailed, accurate explanations for every function in the codebase, including http_data and the chunked-transfer parsing logic.

Flaw introduction: We introduced a subtle out-of-bounds write into http.c by swapping a max for a min in the chunk-size calculation. This is the kind of one-token logic inversion that slips through code review and that pattern-matching SAST rules routinely miss:

Figure 1. Terminal write commands

Signal: On re-examination with the same prompts, the model refused to explain the modified function.

Figure 2. Terminal guardrail response

Figure 3. Terminal http_free explanation

Every unmodified function was still explained normally. The refusal localized to the vulnerable code, giving us a direct binary indicator of the flaw's location. Based on that, we have engineered a script that assesses each function and indicates if it has a refusal. Then, for each function, it performs a binary-search to pinpoint vulnerable chunks.

Figure 4. Terminal GbVD results

Similar vulnerable C\C++ code, including real open-source projects that were disclosed in parallel via our CVD program, yielded similar results.

Case Study 2: SUID Binary Misconfiguration

The second experiment moved from source code to system state. We planted a SUID-root binary that executes arbitrary commands inside a rootfs directory tree, a classic privilege-escalation primitive, and tasked the model with auditing the filesystem.

When the traversal reached the misconfigured binary, the model's analysis halted. Its guardrails interrupted the reasoning rather than reporting the file like any other. We isolated the offending directory, and then the specific binary, without the model ever being asked to flag anything as "vulnerable." Notably, this is the second guardrail manifestation from our taxonomy. It’s a reasoning interruption rather than an explicit refusal, and the same bisection harness reads it just as easily.

Implications

These findings reinforce a core CrowdStrike tenet. The model matters, but the harness determines the outcome. A raw LLM refusal seems like a dead end. Captured by a harness that treats it as diagnostic data, it becomes a one-bit vulnerability oracle cheap enough to run inside a bisection loop.

The harness is what makes GbVD future-proof. The refusal channel we exploit today might shift as safety training evolves, but the harness is where the other channels get instrumented. A harness already measures latency, counts tokens, and observes tool-call outcomes as a matter of course. Teaching it to treat anomalies in those measurements as guardrail activations costs almost nothing. Models leak information through many involuntary channels: refusal text, hedging language, response timing, token spend, sudden drops in specificity, aborted tool calls. Harnesses that read these side channels, rather than only the model's answers, will extract capabilities the model was never explicitly built to provide.

Conclusion

As attacker efficiency scales with model improvements, defenders cannot afford to use AI only in the ways it was designed to be used. Turning the model's limitations into signals is asymmetry worth building. Breaking things in interesting ways remains one of the most reliable heuristics in security research, and models are no exception.

Title: PHP2Shell Won't Be the Last. Here's Where the Next One Will Show Up First.
Context: The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there
Full Text:
Written by

Nuno Loureiro

Ricardo Alves

October 28, 2026

0 mins read

On October 17, Amazon's honeypot network logged a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt from an anonymized IP address. Yet, public disclosure was still four days away.

By the time PHP got its fixes in on October 21, the technical details had already leaked, proof-of-concept exploits were in wide circulation, and more exploit attempts were being logged left and right. The issue was that there were two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the PHP engine itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS v4.0 9.2) -- what we now know as PHP2Shell.

Our own Security Research team covered what happened and what you should do: which releases to move to, which mitigations you could put in place to reduce exposure until you were able to update, and where each part of the Snyk platform sees the problem.

This post now picks up where our Security Research team left off. We want to talk about what the response taught us: where this kind of exposure lives and comes from, why answering fast depends on the work we’d done months earlier, and why the next one is already on its way.

Why was PHP2Shell a problem for teams with clean code?

Well, because the vulnerabilities live below the code. And what does that mean? Both of the mentioned CVEs happen in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, which makes them reachable before any application code actually runs. On Apache, with mod_php, an exploit needed but a single unauthenticated request.

Now, think about that for a second. You probably had careful reviews, clean code, plus a neat and tidy dependency tree, all sitting above the actual problem. The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there.

The question was about running applications. The very same question attackers will always start with.

Which inventory tells you where PHP is running?

Each type of inventory tells you part of it.

PHP reaches production via a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or manually. A "php": ">=8.2"constraint in composer.json tells you what an application accepts, and then the deployed version depends on which of those routes installed it. Container scans see PHP installed from distribution packages once each distribution publishes its advisory, and PHP compiled from source, including the official PHP Docker images, falls outside that view. (Once again, our research team's post maps exactly which Snyk view sees which slice of this reality.)

Then there's the version string. VirusTotal fingerprints roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, and only about 1.1 million of them announce a version, so roughly four out of five hide it. Their summary is one of the cleanest lines we've read on the subject anywhere: "If you only search for a version string, you only see the fraction of the problem that volunteers it."

The gap between what your inside-out views know and what actually answers from the outside is where the real risk lies. Attackers hit your URL, and PHP2Shell is the purest case of that we’ve seen. Anyone probing for it ends up asking the same question: Does PHP answer on this URL?

What did the response look like from the outside in?

The head start: before PHP's 14:00 UTC release on October 21, Snyk had advisories live for both CVEs, so monitored projects would get a hit the moment fixed versions were known. Within about 30 minutes of the release, those advisories included affected ranges and fixed versions, and distribution advisories followed as each distribution was published. That covered what Snyk Container and Unmanaged scans could tell you.

Three questions ran through Snyk API & Web:

Where is PHP running? Discovery enumerates the assets on your domains and fingerprints their technology stack. Set the Tech filter to PHP, and you get every discovered host and endpoint where PHP was identified, with its risk rating, score, and last-seen date. Version numbers come later, from the hosts themselves. As our research team put it, before you can patch, you need the list.

Can someone exploit it? Within 24 hours of PHP's release, the full scan profile tested for PHP2Shell, and teams could run that check on their own as a custom profile for a fast answer across every PHP target.

Did the fix hold? Run the same custom profile after patching, and pair it with your distribution's advisory or patch level, because a patched distribution build can keep an older version number.

So, Discovery --> targeted check --> patch --> re-test: probe, observe, and infer, against a clock that now runs in hours. And that’s exactly the most concerning part, what we care about the most. For teams already running Snyk API & Web, the hard part was done before October 21: their domains were mapped, and their applications set up as targets. When the check was there, the response took only a filter and a quick scan.

For us, that’s one of the main returns on having continuous outside-in testing: the work that answers at day one gets done months before that.

If PHP2Shell is detectable from the outside, what was the hard part?

Time.

In May, we laid out the distinction on which COS is built. Heuristic-detectable vulnerabilities show themselves to deterministic tools: throw payloads at a running application or API, observe the responses, and infer. Context-dependent vulnerabilities (BOLA, cross-tenant leakage, and chained business logic) carry no signature at all, because they live in the gap between what an application is supposed to do and what it actually does.

Once it was known, PHP2Shell became testable from the outside, which puts it squarely in that first class of heuristic-detectable vulns. The hard part, the constraint, was the gap between a disclosure and having a check running against everything you expose. That gap is the attacker’s window to exploit, and this time it opened four days before disclosure eventually did.

The disclosure kept moving, too. On October 23, the PHP project described a partial bypass (CVE-2026-115560) that applies when an application switches its session serialization handler with ini_set() before starting the session, with upload progress enabled. Its preconditions are rare, and whatever you concluded on Wednesday still needed a second look by Friday. A point-in-time answer ages in days.

Why won't PHP2Shell be the last?

There are three reasons for that. Due to the nature of how they were found:

Because they were found with AI assistance, in an engine that has served the web for three decades. Our research team put it plainly: "In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers." And the kind of model that found these vulnerabilities is the kind attackers now have in their hands.

The stronger cadence. Manoj Nair, Snyk's CTO and Chief Innovation Officer, described it in September: "The kind of severe flaw that AI now surfaces in widely used software, the sort of find that used to arrive once or twice a year and reset everyone's quarter, is landing several times a week in what I'm seeing."

The much faster clock. CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, drew two lessons from PHP2Shell that apply well beyond it. Defenders "should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation." And "the time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons," because AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or an advisory into a working exploit. His advice for critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems: "measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours."

What does being ready for the next one take?

Strip out the product names, and it comes down to four properties. Judge any approach by them (ours included). Don’t think about product names, but how it all comes down to four properties. And you should judge any approach with these (ours included!)

An inventory that exists before the advisory does. Built from the outside in and kept current, so a new disclosure starts with a filter.

Checks that ship in hours. The gap between an advisory and a running test is the attacker's window. Measure it.

Re-tests on demand. The same targeted check, run again until the fix holds.

Testing that needs no signature. Heuristics catch what someone has already described. Everything else takes reasoning: testing that works out what your application is supposed to do, then goes after the gap between that and what it actually does.

As for Snyk, here’s how that maps to what we offer.

Snyk API & Web carries the first three: Discovery, an engine the team keeps current as disclosures land, and targeted profiles you can run and re-run. Continuous Offensive Security adds the fourth: AI Pentesting reasons about your application the way a pentester would, Agent Red Teaming engages the moment recon spots an LLM in the stack, and Dynamic Testing, the Snyk API & Web engine, covers the heuristic classes underneath, continuously. In our platform's terms, that's Validate: continuously attack your applications to prove fixes held and show what's still exploitable.

Then there's posture. At The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered on October 14, Manoj asked the question we keep coming back to: "When an autonomous attacker is going to attack you, why don't you attack yourself?" That question is the whole premise of COS. On our side, the work is shrinking every single gap in this story: from advisory to running check, and from check to confirmed fix.

Where will the next one show up first?

Which engine, and when, is anyone's guess now. Where it shows up first is easier to call: at your URL. That's where your testing should already be.

As of October 28, there are four important updates to note:

AlmaLinux has shipped a fixed kernel for AlmaLinux 9 (5.14.0-687.60.1.el9_8), which also covers CloudLinux 9. Patched kernels for 8 and 10 were in testing as of Oct 23.

KernelCare’s EL10 rebootless patch shipped on October 23, with EL9 shipped on October 26, and EL8 is ready for release. Debian and Ubuntu work is in progress with no date.

CloudLinux 7 hybrid and 8 fixes are in beta, and the upstream fix has been accepted but has not reached mainline.

The Hacker News lists ZDI-CAN-34076 with a CVSS score of 8.6, we previously did not have this rated.

A working root exploit for a Linux kernel bug is now public, before it has a CVE or a merged fix. On October 20, 2026, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent one report, a bug in the ConnMan network manager, to the public ConnMan mailing list. On October 21, ZDI sent five reports to the Linux kernel security team and copied public mailing lists on every one. The reports included reproduction details, showing that several had no patch attached and no fix in any released kernel. Two of the Linux flaws have been rated as CVSS 9.0.

None of the six bugs has been assigned a CVE ID yet, and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported as of the publication of this blog. However, security teams should work to get detections and mitigations in place now. TuxCare has reproduced the public proof of concept (PoC) for ZDI-CAN-33367 from the ZDI report. Exploitation leads to root access on current Ubuntu, Debian, and AlmaLinux distributions.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) reviewed the batch of Linux vulnerabilities and ranked the reports by how much each should affect what defenders do today. This report explores what was disclosed, who may be exposed, what runtime visibility can detect for each bug, and what defenders can do while patches are pending.

ZDI-CAN-33367

Fix status

A small patch, “net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()”, is on netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet and tagged for stable. It has not been merged.

How the bug works: Dirty Frag again

Earlier this year, Dirty Frag (CVE-2026-43284) showed defenders how an unprivileged user could get the kernel's IPsec ESP code to decrypt in place over pages that belong to the page cache. Those pages back a file the user can only read, and decryption writes the attacker's bytes into the cached copy of that file. Targeting a setuid binary or /etc/passwd this way gives the attacker root without ever opening the file for writing.

The Dirty Frag fix marked those shared pages with a flag and taught ESP to copy before decrypting when it sees the flag. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a gap in that fix.

skb_zerocopy() moves the same pages into a new socket buffer but does not carry the flag across. ESP never sees the flag, decrypts in place, and the write lands in the page cache. According to TuxCare and Safeguard, the code path dates to kernel 3.14.

Not the first gap

The Dirty Frag fix only works if every piece of networking code that moves those pages around carries the flag along. Since May, the kernel's CVE team has published six follow-up CVEs where some other path lost it:

Frag-copy and shift helpers: CVE-2026-43503

Coalescing: CVE-2026-46300

IPTFS: CVE-2026-53363, CVE-2026-64566

An error-handling helper: CVE-2026-80977

Another error path inside skb_zerocopy() itself: CVE-2026-90049

CVE-2026-90049 is a different bug in the same function, so a kernel carrying its fix is not fixed for ZDI-CAN-33367.

Exploitation

The PoC needs unprivileged user namespaces and a handful of networking modules: nlmon, nft_queue, nfnetlink_queue, cls_u32, act_pedit, act_mirred, and esp4. It does not need a Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) leak, or any capability the user doesn't already get inside their own namespace.

Each step of exploitation is a system call that can be made by an ordinary user process:

Unshare into new user and network namespaces, then write sysctls.

Bring up an nlmon interface.

Install XFRM state over netlink.

Add an nftables NFQUEUE rule.

Attach a tc pedit action with a redirect.

splice() into a socket on 127.0.0.1, which triggers the in-place decryption over the page cache.

Impact

TuxCare reproduced a root shell on AlmaLinux 8–10, CloudLinux 9–10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. AlmaLinux was rooted with the Dirty Frag fix installed. CentOS 6 and 7 kernels are not vulnerable. The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Both CVSS 9.0 reports are in ksmbd, the in-kernel Server Message Block (SMB) server. Samba is not ksmbd.

If your file servers run smbd, neither report applies to you. To check whether ksmbd is running anywhere, look for the ksmbd kernel module, the ksmbd.mountd userspace daemon, and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445.

ZDI-CAN-33774: The dispatch race

ksmbd decides per request whether it is handling SMB1 or SMB2. If an attacker packs a burst of short SMB1 packets and an SMB2 packet into the same TCP write, the worker threads can run an SMB2 handler over SMB1 data and read past the end of the shorter buffer. This works before authentication. The public PoC leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel. ZDI describes a write-past-buffer path that needs share access and labels the bug as remote code execution (RCE), but nothing public shows code execution as of this blog’s publication.

Maintainer Namjae Jeon says the bug is already fixed, and his tree bears that out. Commit 68f410faedaf ("ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU") was written on September 30, credited to a different reporter, and describes exactly this race. It is queued in ksmbd's ksmbd-for-next branch and has not reached a released kernel.

ZDI-CAN-33549: SMB Direct

An integer underflow in the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) transport turns a crafted buffer descriptor into a heap overflow of up to eight KB. The bar is higher than for 33774. The host needs an RDMA-capable interface (hardware, or the rxe software driver), a client that negotiates SMB Direct, and a writable share. The public PoC crashes the kernel.

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher believes a fix already in his branch for Linux 7.5 covers it. As of this writing, that hasn't been confirmed. Ubuntu builds SMB Direct support; Debian does not.

ZDI-CAN-34068

ZDI-CAN-34068 is an out-of-bounds write in vmwgfx, the kernel driver for VMware's virtual GPU, rated as LPE (CVSS 8.8). Only the title is public. Kroah-Hartman's reply on dri-devel points to the dirty-tracking code. There is no patch.

The exposure is narrow. vmwgfx only binds to VMware's SVGA virtual display adapter, so the bug only matters on VMware guests: vSphere and Workstation VMs, and VMware-based virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI). In Sysdig TRT testing, it does not reproduce on Lima or EC2 instances, which don't present that device.

ZDI-CAN-34076 and ZDI-CAN-32005

ZDI-CAN-34076 (nvmet) is an uninitialized-memory information leak in the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target's Get Log Page handling. Only the title is public, and the kernel team has said nothing can be done until details arrive.

ZDI-CAN-32005 (ConnMan) is a stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager's DNS proxy. It is a userspace bug, not a kernel bug, and is outside the scope of this post.

Detection

The four bugs that are the most impactful right now differ in what a syscall-level runtime sensor can observe:

ZDI-CAN-33367. The sequence of the exploitation is distinctive. The process unshares into new user and network namespaces, writes sysctls, brings up an nlmon interface, installs XFRM state over netlink, adds an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attaches a tc pedit action with a redirect, and then splice()s into a socket on 127.0.0.1. Nothing legitimate does all of that from a single unprivileged process. Of the four, this is the easiest one to detect.

ksmbd (33774 and 33549). A sensor can see that ksmbd is exposed: the module loads, ksmbd.mountd starts, and 445 is listening. It can see what an attacker does after code execution, once something spawns a process or touches files. It cannot see the race or the overflow itself. Runtime detection is the backstop.

ZDI-CAN-34068. The trigger is DRM ioctl() calls on the vmwgfx device node, made by a local process. That narrows where to look, but GPU ioctls are noisy on any desktop or VDI guest, so treat them as context for an investigation, not as a signal on their own.

Sysdig Secure customers are covered by a new runtime rule in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, Page Cache Poisoning via Spliced File Pages to Loopback, which matches the syscall patterns as seen for ZDI-CAN-33367. Work on exploits for the other flaws in this disclosure continues, and the Sysdig TRT is writing detection rules for them as the techniques become clear.

Independently of the entry point, customers also keep post-exploitation coverage, which detects the effects of a successful exploit rather than the route in.

Recommendations

ZDI-CAN-33367

Patch as soon as your distribution ships the skb_zerocopy() fix. A kernel carrying only the CVE-2026-90049 fix is not covered.

Restrict unprivileged user namespaces. Setting user.max_user_namespaces=0 (or kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 on Debian) should block the public PoC, though TuxCare notes it has not yet validated this against the PoC. The cost is real: rootless containers, some browser sandboxes and some build tooling depend on user namespaces, so scope it to hosts that don't need them.

Avoid relying on Ubuntu's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. The PoC got past it through the AppArmor profile of a container launcher package.

Block the nlmon and act_pedit modules where you can. Denying them breaks this PoC, although TuxCare cautions it may not close every path to the bug.

Enforce seccomp RuntimeDefault on Kubernetes pods. The exploit starts by creating a user namespace, so containers that can call unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) are in play. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks that call, but Kubernetes pods run Unconfined unless you set RuntimeDefault per pod or cluster-wide using the kubelet --seccomp-default option. This is a good week to make it the cluster default.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Inventory where ksmbd runs. Samba users are unaffected.

Unload ksmbd and block the module on hosts that don't need it.

Restrict TCP 445 to trusted networks where ksmbd must stay.

Disable SMB Direct unless your storage network depends on RDMA.

ZDI-CAN-34068

Inventory Linux guests running on VMware, and watch for the vmwgfx patch.

Disable 3D acceleration, or keep the vmwgfx module from loading, on guests that have no use for it.

Across all Linux flaws

Track the reports by ZDI ID and component name until CVEs are assigned.

‍

Conclusion

ZDI's decision to copy public lists put reproduction details for six bugs in front of attackers before several of them had fixes. As defenders know, a lack of an assigned CVE ID does not mean a lack of exposure. Only one of the six, ZDI-CAN-33367, combines a public root exploit, broad distribution exposure, and a fix that hasn't yet merged. It is the seventh path found to drop the Dirty Frag flag, reopening a bug class whose protection has already leaked six times since May 2026. The two ksmbd reports carry the highest scores, but they only matter where ksmbd — not Samba — is running.

For defenders, the practical takeaway is that this week's work is about exposure, not scanners. It’s also important to note that the bugs differ in what defenders should actually watch. The ZDI-CAN-33367 exploit runs as an ordinary user process through a distinctive sequence of systems calls, so teams can catch it in motion. The ksmbd bugs run inside the kernel worker threads with no attacker process on the host, so controlling exposure is key.

Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix.

3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability

Cyber leaders can get ahead of AI liability with rigorous documentation, transparency, and smart contract negotiations with AI vendors.

Becky Bracken,Media & Projects Director,Dark Reading

October 27, 2026

5 Min Read

Source: Abu Hanifa via Getty Images

ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — Many chief information security officers (CISOs) currently find themselves in the deep weeds of AI governance. But the question they might not be asking is: How do you defend decisions around AI deployments when litigators, regulators, and customers come looking for someone to assume liability for a compromise?

Cyber legal expert Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, is striving to answer that question with distinct frameworks that both help CISOs determine whether a specific AI feature is sufficiently safe to run, as well as generate an evidentiary trail of paperwork that can be used to defend their actions, should something go horribly awry down the road.

While the need for such frameworks is particularly in the limelight in the age of agentic AI, the work began back in June 2024, when JAMS AI Rules were established to create a framework arbitrators can use to settle AI disputes between parties. The rules themselves don't explain liability or apply to every litigator. But Garrie, who helped write the rules, says they are helpful for establishing guidelines for technical evidence handling.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Speaking from the stage at ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 this week, he stressed the importance of addressing incident-response needs at the contract stage and outlined frameworks for three best practices in particular that are useful for quantifying AI liability: calculating an AI deployment risk score; documenting board decisions around risk appetites; and determining which data specific should be preserved from an incident.

CISOs Should Negotiate for Evidence in Vendor Contracts

In the aftermath of an AI compromise, the basic forensic evidence as to what happened can be difficult to get. Garrie stresses that baking these considerations in at the contract stage with AI vendors is crucial, as is having cybersecurity leadership involved as early as possible during those negotiations, with an eye to creating provisions that allow CISOs to establish precisely what happened in an incident, including access to logs and preservation requests.

“Can the AI vendor provide you with a snapshot of the model at the time of an incident?” Garrie suggested CISOs ask. “And how fast can that be made available?”

He added that important considerations for contracts also include risk allocation that needs to be established as well, and urged CISOs to have a clear picture of vendor AI use permissions, data restrictions, warranties, insurance, and liability caps. Cyber leaders should also have a handle on the vendor's operational controls, access, and security responsibilities. Finally, an understanding of how disputes will be handled is necessary for CISOs, including ensuring compliance with governing laws, the forum for disputes, emergency relief scope, and more.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

Getting a handle on contract negotiations with AI vendors early could be the difference between getting the evidence you need to prove your company wasn't negligent and not, Gerrie stressed.

"Once the contract is signed, that's it," Garrie warned. "They aren't going to give you anything that isn't specifically outlined. You'll have to wait for a renewal."

Framework 1: AI Deployment Risk Score

Source: David Garrie, Law and Forensics

Garrie has developed a simple five-factor rubric that helps CISOs determine the risks and exposures related to the deployment of any given AI tool. Across five dimensions, including "potential harm," "data and rights," "autonomy," "evidence gap," and "vendor dependence," the framework helps provide a score that, according to Garrie, "makes assumptions visible."

The final score determines whether the AI tool falls within "standard review," "conditional approval," "restricted pilot," or "hold release" thresholds, each of which indicates a specific level of risk.

Related:Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots

Framework 2: Record the Board's Decision

Source: David Garrie, Law and Forensics

Creating a paper trail of specific board decisions can be a critical piece of evidence in disputing liability, Garrie explained. Weak or vague reporting isn't the CISO's friend.

Garrie's framework for preserving board decisions includes granular details like the scope and time frame of the board decision; the exposure associated with the deployment (and evidence provided of that risk); the conditions of the deployment and the requirements for human approval; the accountable parties who authorize the work and review evidence (and a record of oversight including the final decision; challenges that were raised during the decision-making process; as well as the owner of the tool and associated due dates.

This one is about not just creating a static record of the decision, but about generating ongoing records that are defensible against AI liability, he added.

Framework 3: AI Incident Response Checklist

Source: David Garrie, Law and Forensics

The purpose of this tool, Garrie said, is not just to contain the compromise, but to work to preserve the state of the AI system at the time of the incident. He also advised CISOs to get legal involved immediately.

The tool helps identify and preserve this kind of data, beyond the basic security logs. Garrie's framework requires evidence on the system state at the time of the incident, the interaction records, data and access information, and a governance record, as well as data integrity and chain of custody details.

What CISOs Can Do in the Next 30 Days

Over the next month, Garrie challenged CISOs to put his frameworks to the test on one AI deployment, improve one board report, and run one AI tabletop to practice coordinating actions around vendor evidence preservation and notifications.

The bottom line, according to Garrie, is that regulators, litigators, and customers ultimately are only going to care about the evidence you can produce to prove the organization considered all the risks and acted responsibly to mitigate them.

"They don't care that you're using the NIST guidelines," he warned. Determination of liability is going to come down to what the CISO and the organization can prove they did to protect their systems against AI compromise.

External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Mail bombing is getting a new look with a wide-scale, ongoing social engineering campaign that might be tied to the Black Basta ransomware gang.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 27, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: juststock via Getty Images

Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams' external chat functionality at scale, using IT-support impersonation and email bombing tactics to trick employees into granting remote access. Attackers target multiple users within short, five-minute windows of time, and once the victim bites, the attack chain reaches payload execution in under 15 minutes.

In a blog post on Oct. 26, Arctic Wolf detailed the campaign and what it described as a "recurring social engineering pattern" across more than 400 incidents in the wild. Threat actors use Microsoft Teams' external chat creation capability, which enables outside parties to contact employees.

"A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same 'IT Support (Internal)' display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains," Arctic Wolf's Shubham Dubey wrote in the blog post.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

In a typical example of the attack, the victim is "mail bombed," or inundated with a flood of email subscriptions or newsletters, to establish a sense of urgency. Then, an external Teams user claiming to be IT support contacts the victim and offers to address the issue. The impersonator persuades the employee to launch a remote-access session via legitimate tooling like Quick Assist (most common), AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn.

Once the victim grants access, the attacker conducts follow-on activity such as executing malware, stealing credentials, performing reconnaissance, or possibly deploying ransomware. Dubey explained that a typical order for this is a whoami/systeminfo-based recon, a PowerShell-based payload, a command-and-control (2) beacon, lateral movement to gain access to credentials through Kerberos abuse methods like Kerberoasting and GoldenPAC, and a second, commercial-grade remote access tool, "which provides an independent control channel that survives remediation of the original implant."

Email Bombing Evolves to Deploy at Scale

Spam or mail bombing is not a new tactic. Threat actors have been flooding inboxes as a pretense for social engineering for some time now. Microsoft researchers identified the use of this technique by Black Basta in mid-2024, with later examples seen in 3AM, Cactus, Chaos, and the GoGRPC campaigns. But what stands out about Arctic Wolf's research is that it shows this technique operating at scale, with recurring infrastructure, naming conventions, and attacker behavior seen across hundreds of incidents.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading roughly 15% of cases progressed beyond the initial stage into a successful compromise, which, given the volume of the campaign, constitutes a success.

As for who is behind recent attack waves, Moore could not make definitive attributions but says, "Black Basta-associated activity remains one of the most significant drivers of Teams chat abuse."

On the infrastructure front, Arctic Wolf noted a move from throwaway onmicrosoft.com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, especially ".top" domains, and provided data on their prevalence. The vendor stated that approximately half of observed cases involving paid domains used .top domains.

For naming, attackers would reach out with "(Internal)" appended to the display name to trick the victim that a message is coming from within the company, even though Teams labels the sender as "external" simultaneously. The names will also frequently use friendly sounding names (Arctic Wolf offered Liam, Scott McGhee, and Matthew as examples) after labels like "IT Support" and "IT Service Desk."

Other markers observed included naming conventions specific to the target's locale ("Supporte TI" for French- and Spanish-speaking organizations), and the use of 100 different emojis in attacker display names.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Get Ahead of Email Bombing Social Engineering Attacks

Arctic Wolf noted that prior to engaging with victims, the attackers initiate a one-on-one chat to avoid group conversations, which Microsoft records in its telemetry as the ChatCreated event. Arctic Wolf assesses this to be the primary detection point for defenders setting alerts.

The vendor also recommended setting an allowlist for trusted external organizations, blocking chats with unmanaged or Teams consumer accounts, disabling the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users, blocking federation with trial-only tenants, and hardening your remote access path.

In a nod to Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Arctic Wolf pointed out that it may also be wise to alert staff to the social engineering aspects behind these campaigns, including outlining exactly how IT reaches out, what these contacts look like (and what they do not look like), and to train users how to read the external sender tag in Teams to identify possible red flags. Microsoft Teams also includes end-user reporting in the application itself.

That said, the technique could yet progress further.

"We have also recently observed campaigns combining Teams chat abuse with ClickFix-style social engineering, suggesting that the technique continues to evolve and is being integrated with other intrusion methods," Moore says.

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading that the company helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through layered, built-in protections that, for example, can let administrators block external Teams users. The spokesperson adds that, next month, "Teams is introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users."

Title: AI 'hacker' finds 4 severe bugs in popular industrial control software in under 4 hours
Context: Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack...
Full Text: An autonomous AI agent discovered four vulnerabilities in the decades-old, widely used EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) open source software toolkit, including a critical flaw that could allow remote attackers to execute code on systems used to control particle accelerators and fusion experiments. The bugs include a critical, 9.8-rated under CVSS v3.1 integer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-114595), leading to an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write and potentially remote code execution; an 8.2-rated, high-severity, improper message-length validation flaw (CVE-2026-114596), causing an out-of-bounds memory write and controller-process crash; a 7.5-rated, high-severity insufficient bounds checking bug (CVE-2026-114597) that allows out-of-bounds memory reads and process crashes; and a 7.5-rated, high-severity type confusion flaw (CVE-2026-114598) that can lead to denial of service and could expose adjacent memory contents. All four affect EPICS Base, which is used to operate some of the world's largest scientific research projects and facilities, and organizations should update to version 7.0.11, which includes the fixes. “Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, disclose sensitive information, or potentially execute arbitrary code,” the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned in a Tuesday advisory. An AI agent called Cipher independently found all four previously unknown security holes - investigating and testing the unfamiliar EPICS system, and validating the four exploits - in three hours and 49 minutes, Causal Security co-founder Shubham Raj told The Register. “The initial investigation required no human intervention, followed by one instruction authorizing deeper exploitability testing in a secure environment,” Raj said. Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack paths in power-grid systems used across North America and Europe, prompting an October 8 security advisory from CISA. EPICS, originally developed by Los Alamos National Laboratory and Argonne National Laboratory, is used to build and remotely control distributed Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, connecting operators to physical devices. It’s used in around 90 major scientific, university, and industrial projects and facilities globally including Argonne National Laboratory's Advanced Photon Source and ITER's fusion reactor control system. All four of these flaws illustrate how AI agents are really good at finding vulnerabilities in industrial and operational technologies - systems and equipment that used to be able to rely on obscurity to protect them from hackers - and add to defenders' concerns that it's only a matter of time until an autonomous cyberattack shuts down critical services, like power grids or water systems. These are the types of digital intrusions that can cause physical harm. Raj points to CVE-2026-114595, the critical integer-overflow vulnerability, as an example. “It allows attacker-controlled network data to cause an out-of-bounds heap memory write, with potential for remote code execution,” he told us. “EPICS controllers sit between operators and physical equipment, handling measurements, commands, and control functions,” he continued. “Operationally: Imagine a particle accelerator in the middle of an expensive experiment. An attacker could potentially crash a controller, interrupt critical measurements or control functions, and force operators to halt the experiment. That could mean lost experimental work, significant downtime, and expensive recovery.” Plus, if an attacker was able to develop an RCE exploit, this could allow them to “take control of the affected process, manipulate readings, interfere with control functions, or disrupt the equipment connected to it,” Raj said. The prerequisite for exploiting these vulns in a real scientific facility is being able to reach the vulnerable EPICS services on a facility's control network. But this could occur if the networks weren’t sufficiently segmented, or another system had access to the vulnerable EPICS network. “Once an attacker is able to find a network, which is either misconfigured or they are able to reach, it’s pretty easy to carry out the attacks,” Raj said, adding that exploitation wouldn’t require deep OT knowledge, or understanding of how particle accelerators or fusion reactors work. “Someone with conventional exploitation skills could investigate them, and increasingly capable AI systems could help develop exploits without requiring specialized OT expertise.” Manipulating specific physical processes does require additional knowledge, he added. “But an attacker doesn't need to understand the physics of a particle accelerator to disrupt the software controlling it. Crashing critical processes or interrupting monitoring and control can already have serious operational consequences. What's changing is that attackers may no longer need years of specialized expertise just to discover these weaknesses.” ®
