Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills

Nathan Hamiel outlines potential SecOps horror in the AI midst, as core technical capabilities go the way of reading an atlas or remembering phone numbers.

Elizabeth Montalbano,Contributing Writer

October 27, 2026

6 Min Read

Source: Jesse Grant via Getty Images

Black Hat India — Bengaluru — The use of AI as a tool to enhance cybersecurity operations is emerging as a double-edged knife for security professionals. While it can make them more capable, it could also spell the demise of the very skills they need to use it effectively.

That's the concern of Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, who has made a case for how evolving technology can erode technical skills since well before the generative AI boom. Now, that concern is getting much louder.

Speaking to Dark Reading recently, he says he began noticing the problem around 2005 and 2006, when he encountered cybersecurity professionals who lacked a firm grasp of the fundamentals of their work. At that time, he warned about the dangers of relying too heavily on various types of technical tools, declaring to cybersecurity professionals that "your tools are killing you," and warning that practitioners are moving away from being "hands-on" operators who investigate problems directly, and toward "hands-off" monitors who oversee results presented through tools, interfaces, and dashboards.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

It's a shift that's being exacerbated now by AI-driven automation, he says, and organizations need to move quickly to optimize the use of AI without the expense of cybersecurity skill-building.

AI Tools Can Simplify Things Too Much

While automation can simplify complex tasks and allow professionals to accomplish more, it can also distance them from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a solid understanding of the fundamentals, practitioners may struggle to recognize when a tool produces an incorrect result or when its findings require further investigation, Hamiel says.

"We need to keep these skills and not let them degrade because those skills are important to making the tools work in the best way possible," he tells Dark Reading from this week's Black Hat India conference, where he's giving a keynote entitled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems."

"What AI adds to somebody with knowledge and experience is some additional capabilities," Hamiel elaborates. "A domain expert wielding AI is going to be able to gain benefits from using that tool that a novice with no domain experience isn't going to be able to get."

This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into cybersecurity workflows. It also raises questions about how the industry will develop its next generation of experts if automation removes some of the hands-on tasks that junior professionals traditionally learn.

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

AI Hype vs. Cybersecurity Reality

The current discussion around AI often falls into extremes, Hamiel says. Some predict that the technology can go a long way toward solving major problems facing not only cybersecurity but also humanity, while others warn that it will bring the industry — and some even the world — to an end.

"You have the doomers," he says, "and you have people who say this is a big nothingburger. The truth is somewhere in the middle."

For Hamiel, understanding AI's impact requires separating what the technology can demonstrate in a controlled environment from what it can reliably accomplish in the real world. Impressive capabilities do not necessarily translate into the wholesale replacement of jobs or the disappearance of entire industries, he says.

The same distinction applies to cybersecurity, Hamiel says. Although AI can help identify vulnerabilities, generate code and support security investigations, those capabilities do not mean that the complex problems facing security teams have suddenly become easy to solve.

In fact, some recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity — such as OpenAI models autonomously hacking the Hugging Face framework, among others — may reveal a more familiar and persistent cybersecurity problem: organizations failing to address basic security weaknesses.

Related:AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost

"If you read some of the incident reports, these are organizations that weren't exercising basic security hygiene," Hamiel says.

In these cases, he argues, the weaknesses were already there, waiting to be discovered. "This wasn't just low-hanging fruit; this was fruit lying on the ground where anybody who looked for it would have found it," he says.

Rather than signaling an impending cybersecurity apocalypse, such incidents could prompt what Hamiel calls a "cybersecurity correction."

"It's not that there is this huge apocalypse happening; it's that many people weren't doing the right thing for a very long time," he explains.

In other words, AI may make it easier to discover and exploit existing weaknesses, exposing the consequences of inadequate security practices. The challenge for organizations is not simply to adopt new tools but to address the underlying problems those tools bring to light.

The Shift From Operators to Monitors

Indeed, the potential erosion of technical skills is not a problem that began with generative AI. Hamiel sees it as part of a longer trend in which technology increasingly mediates the relationship between professionals and the problems they are responsible for solving.

Hamiel's concern reflects what is often called the irony of automation: As systems take on more responsibility, the humans overseeing them can lose opportunities to practice the skills needed when those systems fail.

The consequences could extend beyond the skills of today's practitioners to the way the cybersecurity industry develops future experts, he says, especially in how lower-level work that AI can eliminate helps helping junior professionals learn.

Tasks that might appear repetitive or straightforward can provide essential experience, allowing new practitioners to understand how systems work before progressing to more complex investigations. "If you automate that, there isn't room for them to learn," Hamiel warns.

This creates a potential long-term problem for employers. AI may allow teams to complete certain tasks more efficiently today, but organizations still need experienced professionals who can investigate unfamiliar problems, evaluate automated findings, and respond when systems behave unexpectedly.

Using AI Without Losing Expertise

For cybersecurity pros to use generative AI effectively, then, it's simply a matter of applying it to tasks where it offers meaningful benefits while remaining aware of the skills that might be weakened if pros rely too much on these tools to do their jobs effectively.

"The goal here is to maximize the benefits and minimize the drawbacks," Hamiel says, something that is true for the use of any technology. "That's the framing that should be placed around this," he says.

Thus, the only way that organizations can adopt AI without losing essential cybersecurity expertise is to "apply them to the right types of activities," he says.

For cybersecurity pros, this means using generative AI for tasks such as threat hunting and threat intelligence, where preliminary analysis can help professionals work through information more efficiently, Hamiel notes. AI-powered penetration-testing tools are another area of promising development, extending beyond traditional vulnerability scanning to perform more complex tasks, he says.

Ultimately, the question is not whether AI will change cybersecurity, Hamiel says. That genie is most certainly already out of that bottle. Ultimately, the real challenge is ensuring that the industry does not become so dependent on increasingly capable tools that it loses the human expertise required to use them effectively, he says.

"Skills and expertise make your AI use more effective," Hamiel concludes. "If you have two professionals, and both use AI, the one with more knowledge of the task is going to make better use of the AI."

'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

The malware's focus on AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook to expose a forest of AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint.

Elizabeth Montalbano,Contributing Writer

October 27, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: Carl Court via Getty Images

A novel infostealer that specifically targets AI applications and development tools is changing the narrative on illicit data monetization, opening up fresh revenue streams through extortion and other abuses of the stolen data.

Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things, they said in a recent report. It targets Windows-based machines and the browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications running on them — among other apps and services — with data theft.

However, Aokigahara is notable in that it has a particular focus on emerging AI-driven assets, collecting authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools, according to Check Point. This sets it apart from many of the infostealers currently active in the wild.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

"This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software," according to Check Point.

Different Targets for Cybercrime, Different Financial Opportunities

The AI data offers unique opportunities for threat actors to benefit financially from the stealer's activities by using credentials or session tokens to "enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts," according to the report.

The malicious activity can also extend to developer and cloud environments, and thus threaten enterprises. Indeed, threat actors have already demonstrated how they use stolen credentials for GitHub accounts, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files to infiltrate cloud environments of enterprise targets.

This may also pave the way for extortion of organizations by holding stolen data for ransom, according to Check Point.

"Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services," according to the post. "If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment."

Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of security firm Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that "stolen AI credentials can yield a heavy harvest for an attacker. A paid AI subscription is a resellable asset, and the conversation history behind it is often full of proprietary code, which means these stolen sessions now carry extortion value alongside their resale value."

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

Aokigahara Infostealer Malware In Action

Once an Aokigahara infection begins, it scans a computer for sensitive data, including browser passwords, session cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, and credentials stored by AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. It also searches local application files for authentication tokens, API keys, and other potentially valuable information.

Other targeted data the malware looks for are developer and cloud credentials, including Git access data, SSH keys, and configuration files for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This data is valuable to give attackers access to private code repositories or cloud resources if the stolen credentials remain valid and have sufficient permissions, according to Check Point.

Indeed, "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring," Calderone observes, and some of those keys ultimately could give attackers access to the kingdom.

"The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run," he says.

Related:BragJack Attack Can Turn a Browser's Agentic AI Against It

Aokigahara also has built-in anti-detection mechanisms. It checks for analysis environments such as virtual machines and sandboxes, and packages stolen data into zip archives and then encrypts it before sending it to attacker-controlled servers.

Modern Defense as Attackers Expand Objectives

Aokigahara's targeting of AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook, potentially exposing AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint. The theft of this data then opens new pathways for financial gain for attackers and thus may provide an incentive for others to do the same, according to Check Point.

This means that defenders should start treating AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, with protections comparable to those applied to cloud credentials and developer keys. To that end, security teams should hunt for AI-session theft by investigating suspicious access to local application storage and authentication-related files belonging to AI assistants, coding agents, and developer IDEs.

Organizations also should more closely protect developer and cloud credentials by reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets on endpoints, using managed identity and short-lived credentials where feasible, and restricting access to cloud resources and source-code repositories.

Further, organizations can protect assets across exposed apps and tools by revoking exposed sessions and rotating secrets. If an endpoint is suspected of compromise, according to Check Point, they should assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens, not just browser passwords.

Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Scanner-Evading Code

Attackers have infected 953 online stores, mostly running Magento, with a JavaScript loader that has evolved to tell security scanners apart from real shoppers.

The campaign has been active since July 2025 and has cycled through five loader domains, according to research from Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec. Its latest domain, registered October 6, was found in the content management system (CMS) blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which had carried an earlier version of the loader.

The loader is stored in Magento's cms_block database table and has visitors' browsers fetch instructions from the attackers. Sansec said the server first works out whether a request comes from a genuine customer or a security scanner, and gives scanners nothing.

Latest Loader Filters Security Scanners

Before October, the operator relied on the Keitaro traffic distribution system to choose, for each visitor, between delivering a payload, redirecting the browser and returning nothing.

The loader Sansec first found on October 7 instead called the new domain directly and replayed code saved in the browser, so anyone served the payload would rerun it on later page loads, even with the domain down or blocked.

An October 23 rewrite added browser fingerprinting, checking for signs of browser automation and collecting hardware details, screen size, time zone and language before the server chose its response.

When scanning service urlscan.io loaded an infected store in an automated browser, Sansec found no injected content. The company has yet to obtain the final payload, so the campaign's ultimate purpose remains unclear.

Read more on malicious JavaScript in online stores: Global Magecart Campaign Targets Six Card Networks

Patches Did Not Always Stop Reinfection

Sansec said a March wave planted the loader on 471 stores within an hour, using webshells placed through PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356). Among 169 infected Magento 2 installations lacking at least one core patch, 102 showed evidence of file uploads via PolyShell or SessionReaper (CVE-2025-54236).

Patching alone did not prevent reinfection. A fully patched store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 picked up the newest loader on October 23, an hour after passing a clean scan. Sansec had spotted a rogue admin account and a GSocket backdoor on the store in September.

Sansec advised merchants to look for the loader in CMS content, review admin accounts and hunt for backdoors, rotate database, admin and integration credentials once the store is clean and apply the latest Magento and Adobe Commerce security updates.

It warned that removing the script leaves an attacker's write access to the database intact, so a compromised store can be reinfected while the original way in remains.

OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers - Infosecurity Magazine

Infosecurity Magazine Home » News » OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers

OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers

Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.

Title: UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court
Context: Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent
Full Text:
Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.

Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.

For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?

At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

ROSIE SWASH: Jess, I just want to have a couple of warm-up questions before we get into it. Tell us a bit about your background, how did you end up becoming MP for Lowestoft?

JESS ASATO: Sure. So, I grew up in East Anglia in Norfolk and Suffolk, and in a not very political family. I got the politics bug in 1997 when Tony Blair was talking about education, education, education. Having experienced it, I felt that we could be doing a lot better in our education system. So I joined the Labour Party and got involved with my local groups.

Before Parliament, I worked for the largest children's charity in the UK for three years on their policy and public affairs, trying to change legislation on behalf of the most vulnerable children in the country. Six years prior to that I worked for a domestic abuse charity called SafeLives where we did huge amounts of work to try and improve the situation for survivors of domestic abuse, particularly through the Domestic Abuse Act.

Those twin issues of women and children have become my focus in Parliament, and I’ve been very clear that my reason for being here, my mission really, is to be a voice for women and children.

Well, that’s a good entry point for us to start talking about this year. So in early 2026, there was widespread reporting on Grok, xAI’s chatbot, being used to create sexualized images of children and women, and those images being circulated on X. How aware were you at this point of the phenomenon of deepfakes being used in this way?

Very aware, and actually had been working with survivors who had experienced deepfakes for quite a number of years. Ever since the advent of AI this has been happening to women, and there’s also been developing risks of children both being put into child sexual abuse material and also children using nudification tools on other children, thereby criminalizing themselves because these tools are so easy to access and often free.

So I was already very alive to the huge harms being created by AI deepfakes of both women and children before Grok ever happened. It was a known harm, which is why many of the tools from other companies had already taken steps to stop them from being used to create this kind of content.

There are a number of tools where, if you type in “nudify,” or “take the clothes off this person,” the tool will refuse to do that. So into that environment came Grok.

Was there a particularly egregious example or incident prior to Grok when you became aware of deepfakes that really stuck with you?

There is a brilliant campaigner who goes by the name of Jodie. I think it was probably listening to the experiences of Jodie, who was deepfaked, and it was such an affront to her that somebody would do this, and then she found out it was actually a friend. Such a betrayal of trust.

These things destroy not just the individual involved, but often families and everyone around them too.

For people who don’t know, who exactly was Jodie? Is this a constituent of yours or someone who came forward to you specifically?

No, no, no. She's a very well-known campaigner on this issue. That’s not her real name.

I know it sounds obvious, but what exactly is nudification?

It is where you ask an AI tool to take the image or video of a real person and use generative AI to make that person either nude, partially nude, or engaging in pornographic acts. This is something that, because of the photorealistic nature of AI images, it has become increasingly hard to see what is a fake image.

It can often look incredibly, incredibly real.

So what was it particularly about the Grok scandal earlier this year that made you want to raise this in the House of Commons?

It was the fact that we already knew that you could stop this from happening by designing the AI tool to reject the ability to do this.

This was completely avoidable. That’s why I spoke out, but also because I’d just spent a year and a half campaigning to get a ban on nudification apps, and here was an all-purpose AI tool becoming a nudification app.

It just felt to me as though we were making strides in the UK, and then the world’s richest man and his product decided to turn the clock back.

So what exactly did you stand up and say?

What I did was I talked about the need for the government to accelerate its ban on nudification apps, which it did. So the then secretary of state for science, innovation and technology, Liz Kendall, said that she was going to bring that ban into law through the Crime and Policing Act, which she did.

But I also said that it was very important that we went further than that, because, of course, Grok itself is not a sole-purpose nudification tool. It has a general use, and therefore we needed to bring all AI chatbots under the auspices of the Online Safety Act. That is also what eventually happened in the Crime and Policing Act, and we’re now waiting until that legislation comes into effect. There’s got to be a consultation, I understand, before it does.

So technically another Grok could happen in this period, but in the future there would be much stronger measures that we could take against tools like Grok creating nudification content.

So that’s a really positive outcome of your interjection in Parliament, but what else happened as a result of you standing up?

Well, one of the things that happened was that I posted on social media saying that Elon Musk should stop Grok from being able to do this.

And then, of course, I became a victim of the same trend. So Grok put this woman in a bikini. And most of the images were sort of pornified, I would say. They weren’t nude images, but they were me with inflated boobs in a bikini.

Then people tried to make it funny, I guess, by putting a swastika on me or hammer and sickles. Or making me pregnant with quintuplets and putting me in a kitchen. Because of course that’s the only use for women—birthing and making dinner. But the really disturbing one was a video of me being surrounded by a group of men, chloroformed over my mouth, and then I fall backwards onto a chair. Then my skirts are lifted up. So no nudity, but clearly the next frame is meant to be a sexual assault. So it was really distressing and disturbing.

That was the point at which a friend said, “You probably need to reach out to a lawyer.” Because each of these things we reported to X, and none of them contravened their terms and conditions. We just kept getting those sort of repeat emails coming back. “We’ve looked into this, and there’s nothing to see here.” So I did engage a lawyer, who sent a letter to X to ask for these to be removed, and they were.

But it was at that point that he said, “I think you might actually have a case. We think that xAI have broken the law.”

It’s impressive how you handled it, but it must have been really awful.

It was; it was awful. This is done to demean, to degrade, and to push women out of online spaces. From my perspective, I tend to use bad or difficult things that happen as a way of thinking about how we change this for the future.

My old boss was an amazing woman called Tessa Jowell. She used to say to me, “How do we change this negative energy into something positive?” “How do we work our way out of this into a place where we actually feel that we’ve learnt from it?”

So I guess she instilled in me that sense that when something bad happens you’ve got a choice. You can wallow in it, you can try and forget about it, or you can use it as a catalyst for change.

So I was quite trepidatious about the idea of taking on a legal action. Not least because of the person who is at the top of xAI, now SpaceXAI. [Eds. note: The company recently rebranded itself as SpaceXSI.] He’s the world’s richest man. But also because I didn’t want myself to necessarily be the story. Many, many women had things that were created of them through both Grok and other nudification tools that are much, much worse.

Having said that, I knew that if there was the opportunity to say that actually they’d broken the law, there was an important point of principle on behalf of all of the women and the children whose images were manipulated and misused by Grok, who would never, ever be able to bring a legal case. So I decided that I wanted to do this, because I wanted to be able to show that no one is bigger than the law.

Doesn’t matter how rich you are or how powerful you are or how big a reach you have in terms of your social media presence or who your friends might be at the top of various governments. If you break the law in our country, you need to feel the force of that. As an ex-lawyer and now as a legislator, it is important that we uphold our law where it has been broken.

So it’s also about giving control back, I think, to us as individuals, but also as a society. So many of these digital changes have been done without our consent or say, and I think there’s a feeling that there’s a sort of runaway train that we’re all on, whether we want to be or not, because we all need to use online spaces for our work, for connection.

And so my view is that we should be expecting companies to respect our law or at least make new laws to bring them more into line with what society really needs.

You said that you gave it some thought. In that moment of trying to decide how to respond, what are you weighing up? Who are you talking to? Are you going back and talking to your team or your family to work out how you should respond, knowing that it may invite further speculation and further attention?

My family mostly, my husband in particular. It’s one thing being a politician and arguing your case to change the law on behalf of women and children; it’s another having your own legal case.

So I was worried about the impact that that might have on my family, my children. I also know that this can bring danger to politicians. So I worried about the fact that I am obviously engaging and making the defendant somebody who has got this very wide reach on social media. However, I don’t like bullies. I very strongly believe that it’s important to fight on the field that you’ve got, and this was an opportunity I felt to make a difference.

So I weighed that up and thought that it was worth having that kind of attention and potential danger, because there is a bigger issue here that we need to get right.

When you say you don’t like bullies, are you talking about, let’s face it, men who used Grok in this way in the first place, or are you talking about Elon Musk?

I’m talking about the men who use this as a form of trying to push women out of the online space. Actually it was quite clear in quite a lot of the comments that they were saying, “Well, if you don’t like this, then get off the platform.”

Either that or, “If this is too hot for you, get out the kitchen,” which I always find quite funny because they put me in a kitchen. I think it’s really interesting when you look at X in terms of its demographics in the UK, it’s highly weighted toward men. I think some of that’s down to the fact that there is just so much misogyny and abuse on it. So I’m assuming, and correct me if I’m wrong, that the other side of the response to going public is that other women have come forward to you.

Absolutely. Actually, one of the heartening things has been people coming forward and saying, “Thank you, because this has now given me the license to actually accept that what happened to me wasn’t my fault. It’s not my shame.” So, in a way, what I’m hoping is that this has helped some victims to process what has happened to them and understand that this was not right.

I’ve also had emails from parents where they’ve said that this has happened to their daughter. It’s been done by boys at school. I’ve had teachers saying that boys have made pornographic AI imagery of them. And it’s something where we’ve just sort of let it happen and wash over us and accept that somehow this is now a part of the society we live in.

So yes quite a number of people have come forward. Obviously not all of their experiences have been through Grok, and I think one of the things is that often, when you see these films or images, you don’t know what platform they’ve been created on. I mean, the only reason why I knew it was Grok was because it was integrated with X, and you could see the commands that had been given by the users.

But much of the time, when this content is created, most victims don’t know by whom or on what platform. And so there’s really very little they can do about it. And I think it’s that sort of sense of helplessness that you have been violated, and that is the word that comes up so frequently from victims of this particular issue.

It’s not just that it’s nudified. Of course, much of my content wasn’t. It’s the lack of consent. And lots of people say, “Oh, but it’s fake. It’s just a laugh.” But what people don’t understand is that it is hyperrealistic, and it’s your face.

It’s a piece of your soul. It’s not just pixels on the internet. It is a person. And because obviously I’ve worked for a long time in violence against women and girls and spoken to many victims of sexual assault and to children who’ve been victims of child sexual abuse, it is the lack of consent that is so disturbing.

It can leave people with PTSD and quite deep trauma. And there have been a number of people I’ve met who have said that the world seems less safe to them because this has happened to them.

I think you’ve already touched on it, but what is the biggest myth around deepfakes that you would wish to dispel?

That it comes without any harm.

That it’s just a laugh.

There is clear harm, even when it’s not done to demean or degrade. So even if it’s done sometimes by friends, the fact is that you haven’t consented to that. There is something about the human psyche which is that when you see yourself so realistically created in a different situation or scenario, something that’s not something you would have done, I think it’s quite discombobulating.

I think your brain can’t quite process it because your brain knows it’s not true, but it looks very true. And I think psychologically we still don’t really understand how this content is going to change the way we think about our world, how we know what is true and what isn’t true.

Right.

Now, of course, you can do fantastic things with generative AI. All I’m calling for is that we respect people’s consent, and that’s why one of the things I’ve been working on since this happened is to look at whether we could create a system of consent to be manipulated by AI.

Could we create a greater right over our likeness online so that there’s a new social norm, which is that no, you can’t copy and paste that picture into an AI chatbot and do whatever you want with it. That’s not yours. It’s not your data. It’s their data, and you’re breaching the law if you do that.

I think if we were to do that, we could have a wide range of applications. It wouldn’t just be in this space of the sexualization of women and children. But also with political disinformation. We are so close to a moment where somebody produces a hyperrealistic video of a politician saying something that they didn’t, and then that leads to real-world harm. And so we’ve got to find a new social norm that says unless for public figures it’s parody or satire—and absolutely you’ve got to protect that—but in all other instances your picture, your voice, and your moving image is your personal data, and it’s not for anyone else to use.

So that’s interesting because you’re touching on new social norms and the possibility of new laws to keep up with this technology. But your lawsuit is specifically under a data law. Talk to me about that versus a law around consensual imagery or deepfakes specifically.

So, my case is brought under existing law, the GDPR, the data protection law, and it contends that Grok misused my data without my consent. It didn’t have consent to process my data, the data being my face and my likeness. But also under privacy laws that I had a reasonable expectation of privacy and that particularly the video of me being prepared for sexual assault reaches a criminal threshold and that nobody should be expected to be on the receiving end of.

Let’s remember, this is actually a product that has been designed by software engineers and developers, and that actually products should not lead to an invasion of privacy and the harm that I then experienced as a result of that, including distress and a sense that I was being harassed by this particular creation of this particular video.

So, it rests on good solid legal grounds, and we await the defense from SpaceX AI.

I don’t know how much you can say, legally, but what part of the process are you in? What happens next? What’s the timeline for a resolution to this case?

So like with a lot of legal cases, it’s very, very hard to pin down a timeline. But my understanding is that we should be receiving the response and the defense from SpaceXAI in the near future. But we don’t have a deadline or a particular time that I can put on it.

After that, my understanding is that the case will then be looked at, and if there is a case to answer, then it will go to a court hearing. But once again, no idea when that might be. And I think there’s lots of legal things that I don’t understand that need to be worked out in the meantime as well between my lawyers and their lawyers.

Have you ever had any acknowledgment on X itself from Elon Musk or anyone at xAI about this case? Has he ever spoken publicly about it?

No.

Would you expect him to?

I don’t think so. They clearly want to challenge this case, and so the best place to do that, I think, is in the courts and to leave it to see whether the merits of the case come through.

You were in New York recently to address the city council about your case. You didn’t get to speak to anyone directly at the company, is that right?

No. I mean, despite being subpoenaed, they didn’t turn up. Four of the other frontier AI companies did attend under subpoena. SpaceXAI didn’t, but they eventually did get their hearing with SpaceX in the city council. So, they have now had their opportunity to put questions and indeed did raise my case with them, I understand.

Was it a little enraging to attend a hearing like that where a company that you’re suing doesn't bother turning up?

I think it’s quite rude to the elected members of the New York City Council when you are a business that operates in New York. Indeed, I was told that they were just a few subway stops from City Hall. So I had traveled quite a long way from England to be there. And they couldn’t be bothered to turn up, which yeah, it felt arrogant and a bit of a snub, but they’ve now got there, so that’s a good thing.

Since you made the decision to take this to the courts, there have been a number of proposals in Parliament, notably there was a proposal for a kill switch bill at one point. Now I believe it’s dead or it’s not going very well. Is that right?

So, yes, there have been proposals put forward for a kill switch. And my understanding is the government rejected that. There continues to be strong calls for regulation of particularly superintelligent AI. We’ve heard various theories, whether it’s 2 percent, 10 percent, 20 percent risk of human extinction from this sort of race to superintelligence, a recursive AI, and we wouldn’t allow those margins of risk in any other sphere.

We would not allow it in bridge building or airplane making. They didn’t even allow it when they were testing the nuclear bomb and the Trinity test. It feels to me as though so much of this decision-taking is outside of democratic structures. It’s not with the public. It is being done by some incredibly, exceptionally wealthy companies and organizations who say they have the interests of the planet at heart.

But each time, actually, they’re asked about whether that is the future of humanity or whether they think that these risks could kill humanity, there’s a sort of shrugging of the shoulders and, “We’ll just keep going because we want to make money,” I guess.

It has been reported in the British press that there are members of Parliament, some of whom are working on committees to do with technology, who still don’t really understand what AI is. And clearly you’re not one of them because you’re aware of the dangers of this issue. But do you feel working across parties that you’re still having to explain technology and its dangers and possibilities to people who are making laws, or should be making laws, to protect the public from AI?

Well, look, I don’t think that’s only the case about AI. We are humans after all, and we have to deal with every single subject that exists under the sun. We have to get our heads around things that we’ve never heard of before.

A bit like being a journalist actually.

That’s true. But you have to then make laws and decisions. So, I don’t want to be unfair to my colleagues.

You may be a specialist in housing policy and you then need to get your head around AI. But I would say that this is the most important issue in front of anybody in parliament or politics at the moment, and therefore, everyone needs to get their head around AI.

My background is in social policy for women and children. But because we did quite a lot of work on the Online Safety Act when I was working for a children’s charity, we campaigned to get the age verification ban for children in pornography into the OSA. And indeed, created quite a strong piece of legislation in respect of that.

We had to get our heads around online safety on the online space. The problem was, of course, that act didn’t include AI chatbots. There were a number of amendments that tried to get it in and we would’ve been in a much better place had we actually succeeded.

But you know, I’m still not a tech expert even though I had quite a while to try to understand these things. But my view is that this is definitely the new front line of where harms are occurring. We can see that hugely in the increase in AI-generated child sexual abuse material, which is absolutely exploding.

In the end it comes down to the people who create the products. And that’s why we should be seeing digital product regulation in the same way as we would any other product regulation.

I’m very, very hopeful that the government is going to look at it really, really closely because there are always design choices that you can make and that can help to prevent these harms, these harms that are completely knowable. We can predict these harms, and so it should be easy to design them out from the start.

Companies can put in more safeguards. Why don’t they?

Profit. But also, let’s be honest, these are global tools and companies. So unless you have international agreement it is a bit like playing whack-a-mole, isn’t it?

The person who made that horrible video of me being chloroformed lives in the US, so the police aren’t gonna follow it up because they’re out of the country.

Do you know who did it?

I don’t know who they are, but the police did find who they were because it’s a criminal offense what they did. They just weren’t able to bring the charge.

We’ve spoken in the last 40 minutes about the full spectrum of human awfulness. I don’t think there’s any area of it that we haven’t …

Oh, sorry. Welcome to my life.

I’m really struck by how cheerful you are despite this. How do you remain so upbeat and hopeful while dealing with all of this?

Because you’ve always got to have hope for the future. I do have a really strong conviction that with the right group of people pushing toward a goal, you can achieve that. You don’t have to accept that things will always be like this. When people come together, when communities come together, you can act for change.

We’re just about to introduce our ban on strangulation in pornography, which is another thing that I’ve been campaigning for and introduced an amendment last year, which the government accepted.

There are always things that we can do to change. You just need to keep going. And also I would say that when you work with these terribly dark areas, yes, it can be quite vicariously traumatizing. But actually the people who work within the sectors are some of the most hopeful people, partly because if you lose hope, then it’s really bad. And we can’t because we’re talking about protecting vulnerable children, and we are fighting for women and our rights to be free of this harm.

HTTP2Shell Vulnerability: How Should Security Teams Assess and Reduce Exposure?

Aqua Team

October 27, 2026

Updated: October 29th, 2026

TL;DR: The HTTP2Shell vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) is a critical flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression decoder that could allow attackers to corrupt memory and potentially execute malicious code. With a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, the vulnerability affects software beyond Node.js, creating potential exposure across cloud native applications and their dependencies. Security teams should identify affected components, determine whether vulnerable decoding paths are reachable and apply available updates. Aquasec has also confirmed that while the affected library was present in certain Enforcer images, its analysis found no exploitable decoding path and updated Enforcer releases are now available for both Update 47 and Update 45 LTS deployments.

What is the HTTP2Shell vulnerability?

HTTP2Shell, initially called Node2Shell, is a critical memory corruption vulnerability affecting Google’s Brotli decompression library. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw occurs when the decoder processes specially crafted compressed data, potentially allowing an attacker to crash an application, disclose sensitive information or execute arbitrary code.

Despite its name, HTTP2Shell is not a vulnerability in the HTTP/2 protocol itself. The flaw exists in Brotli, a widely used compression library embedded in applications and software dependencies.

This distinction matters because the potential impact extends beyond Node.js. Any application that incorporates an affected Brotli decoder and processes attacker controlled compressed data could be exposed, making it important for organizations to examine more than their Node.js environments.

Why does HTTP2Shell matter to cloud native environments?

HTTP2Shell highlights a challenge that security teams regularly encounter when managing vulnerabilities across cloud native environments. A single vulnerable library can be present in multiple applications, container images and third party components, making it difficult to understand where exposure actually exists.

In containerized environments, dependencies are frequently bundled directly into images or application binaries. Updating a library on the underlying host does not necessarily update the same library embedded in a running container.

The vulnerability also creates different levels of risk depending on how an application uses Brotli. An application that actively decompresses attacker controlled content may be exposed, while another application containing the same vulnerable library may never execute the affected code.

For security teams, this means that identifying vulnerable software is an important first step, but assessing actual exposure requires understanding how that software operates in production.

Why doesn’t finding a vulnerable Brotli library confirm exploitability?

Traditional vulnerability scanning is essential for identifying affected software, but a scanner finding alone cannot establish whether HTTP2Shell can be exploited in a particular environment.

Exploitation requires the vulnerable decoder to process Brotli compressed content that an attacker can influence. Simply having the library installed does not establish that this condition exists.

For example, two applications may contain the same vulnerable Brotli version, but only one may be configured to decompress untrusted content. Both applications could generate vulnerability findings even though their exposure differs significantly.

This is where runtime context becomes valuable. Understanding which components are active, how applications behave and whether vulnerable functionality can be reached helps security teams distinguish findings that represent immediate exposure from those that require further investigation.

That context does not eliminate the need for remediation. It helps teams make more informed decisions about where to act first.

What does an effective HTTP2Shell response look like?

An effective response combines comprehensive vulnerability identification with an assessment of the conditions required for exploitation.

Security teams should begin by locating affected Brotli libraries across their environments, including dependencies embedded in application images and third party software. Once identified, the next step is to determine which applications decompress content that an attacker could control.

Applications with an exposed decoding path should receive priority for remediation, particularly when they are running in production and accessible to untrusted sources.

Where corrected versions are available, organizations should update the affected software and verify that the corrected components are actually running. This is especially important in containerized environments where an application may continue using an older image even after a dependency has been updated elsewhere.

Runtime security adds another layer to this strategy by providing insight into workload activity and enforcing supported security policies inside running workloads. These controls complement vulnerability remediation, helping organizations manage production risk while software updates are applied.

How is Aquasec addressing HTTP2Shell?

Aquasec has reviewed the impact of HTTP2Shell on its own components and confirmed that the affected Brotli library was present in certain Aquasec Enforcer images.

However, our security analysis determined that the vulnerable decoding functionality is not used by Enforcer components. The Enforcer does not decompress Brotli data, meaning the conditions required to exploit HTTP2Shell through the affected decoder are not present in the assessed Enforcer execution paths.

Our assessment included examination of both source code and released binaries to verify that the vulnerable decoder is not invoked during Enforcer operation.

Although the vulnerable library was not reachable through Enforcer functionality, we have released an updated Enforcer versions for both Update 47 and Update 45 LTS containing the corrected Brotli package.

Aquasec Enforcer 2022.4 U47 SP2 (2022.4.951.5) and 2022.4 U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 (2022.4.880.50) are now available. We recommend that customers upgrade to this release to remove the vulnerable dependency and address associated scanner findings.

Customers looking for additional information about affected versions, our technical assessment and upgrade guidance can refer to the Aquasec Support Knowledge Base and the U47 SP2 release documentation or the U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 release documentation

What does HTTP2Shell tell us about vulnerability management?

HTTP2Shell reinforces an important distinction between identifying vulnerabilities and understanding their actual impact in production.

A vulnerability scanner can identify a component associated with a known CVE, but it cannot always determine whether the vulnerable functionality is being used or whether an attacker can reach it.

This creates a challenge for security teams managing large volumes of findings. Treating every finding as equally exploitable can divert attention from exposures that represent a more immediate threat.

Aquasec’s runtime security approach focuses on understanding what is happening inside running workloads and using that context to inform security decisions. Instead of relying solely on static vulnerability information, teams can combine scanning with runtime intelligence to focus remediation on the risks that matter most.

The objective is to reduce real exposure while maintaining protection for workloads that continue running during the remediation process.

What should organizations do now to address HTTP2Shell?

Organizations should review their application environments for affected Brotli dependencies and prioritize workloads that process compressed content from untrusted sources.

Corrected upstream Brotli releases include versions 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1. Node.js has also released security updates in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1. Organizations running unsupported Node.js versions should migrate to a supported release.

Security teams should also review vendor advisories for affected third party software, apply available updates and rescan their environments to verify remediation. Updating the underlying operating system alone may not resolve vulnerabilities in libraries bundled with applications or container images.

Aquasec customers should upgrade affected Enforcer deployments to either 2022.4 U47 SP2 (2022.4.951.5) or 2022.4 U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 (2022.4.880.50), depending on their deployment, and follow the documented upgrade and verification procedures.

FAQs

What is CVE-2026-111497?

CVE-2026-111497, also known as HTTP2Shell or Node2Shell, is a critical vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decompression decoder. It can cause memory corruption when an affected application processes specially crafted compressed data, potentially resulting in application crashes, information disclosure or arbitrary code execution.

Does HTTP2Shell only affect Node.js applications?

No. Although the vulnerability was initially associated with Node.js, the flaw exists in the underlying Brotli decoder. Other applications and software components that incorporate affected Brotli versions may also be exposed if they decompress attacker controlled content.

Does detecting HTTP2Shell mean an application is exploitable?

Not necessarily. A vulnerability finding confirms the presence of an affected component, but exploitability depends on whether the vulnerable decoder processes attacker controlled data. Security teams should assess the application’s behavior and exposure alongside the scanner finding.

Is Aquasec Enforcer affected by HTTP2Shell?

Aquasec identified the affected Brotli library in certain Enforcer images, but its security assessment found that Enforcer does not execute the vulnerable decoder. Aquasec has released updated Enforcer versions 2022.4.951.5 (U47 SP2) and 2022.4.880.50 (U45 Enforcer LTS SP9) with corrections for the affected Brotli package and recommends that customers upgrade to the appropriate release.

Can runtime security replace patching for HTTP2Shell?

No. Applying corrected software remains the recommended remediation. Runtime security provides additional context about workload behavior and can enforce supported security controls in production, helping organizations manage risk while remediation proceeds. Aquasec runtime controls are not the basis of its assessment that the vulnerable decoding path is unreachable in Enforcer.

Aquasec is a leader in runtime security, helping organizations protect cloud native applications and AI workloads where attacks actually happen. Built on a full agent architecture, the Aquasec Platform combines deep runtime visibility with real time enforcement inside running workloads to detect and stop threats as they execute. By focusing on exploitable risk and enabling immediate containment, Aquasec helps security teams reduce exposure and protect production environments without waiting for traditional remediation workflows.
