Title: Microsoft says ConnectWise breach let Chinese spies loose on 2,250 cloud tenants
Context: ARTEX is an open source penetration-testing framework written in Go that uses AI agents to automate everything from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to credential...
Full Text: China-aligned attackers used AI agents and compromised ConnectWise application credentials to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft says. The Windows giant revealed this week that the attackers, tracked as Storm-0940, used an open source AI penetration-testing tool called ARTEX to automate attacks against Microsoft 365 environments. In some cases, they went from picking a target to gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours. The findings shed more light on the ConnectWise security incident, which saw the IT management vendor pull the plug on its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services after discovering unauthorized access to application identities. ConnectWise didn't initially identify who was responsible, but Microsoft has now pointed the finger at Storm-0940, a China-linked espionage crew that's been operating since at least 2021. The group has traditionally relied on the usual tricks, including password spraying and exploiting internet-facing applications, but this time it used AI to do some of the heavy lifting. ARTEX is an open source penetration-testing framework written in Go that uses AI agents to automate everything from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to credential attacks and data theft. Microsoft says Storm-0940 began using it as early as September to target organizations worldwide, including government agencies, defense contractors, banks, manufacturers, and tech firms. Between October 10 and 14, the hackers made more than 151,000 failed sign-in attempts against 327 accounts at eight organizations. Microsoft observed no successful logins from that password-spraying campaign, but then the attackers shifted to compromised ConnectWise application identities. The compromised application credentials let the attackers exploit permissions customers had already granted to ConnectWise services, without needing an interactive user login. Armed with ARTEX, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, at times reaching 2,900 attempts a minute. Microsoft also observed AI-accelerated activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges, potentially allowing the attackers to stick around even after the original credentials were revoked. Most attempts failed, though Microsoft says the hackers still managed to establish persistent privileged access at numerous organizations. It hasn't disclosed how many customers were compromised or whether any data was stolen, cautioning that a successful login doesn't necessarily mean information was accessed. ConnectWise CEO Manny Rivelo said the company had contained the affected application connections and was gradually restoring services, although shutting down those connections wouldn't necessarily boot out attackers who had already established a foothold in customer environments. ConnectWise has been here before. In May 2025, it admitted that a "sophisticated nation-state actor" had broken into its systems and compromised a small number of customers using its ScreenConnect remote access software. There's nothing to suggest the two attacks are linked. Nor is Storm-0940 alone in making use of ARTEX. Microsoft says it has spotted attackers from several geographic regions using the framework, which is freely available for penetration testing. The underlying techniques are nothing new – stolen credentials, password spraying, and application abuse – but Microsoft says AI helped Storm-0940 execute them faster, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. ®

Title: IT department and auditors at major pharmacy chain got into a rip-roaring fight about using 'password' on Cisco firewall
Context: The conflict was so severe that the client continued to follow up and ask him to explain what he found again for the next three years – long after he had moved on to other projects
Full Text: Welcome back to PWNED, the column where we talk about companies and organizations that leave the doors wide open to attackers. This week’s sad story involves a major American pharmacy chain that couldn’t fill a prescription for password security. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request. Our tale comes courtesy of red team and pen testing specialist Dahvid Schloss, who currently serves as COO of Suzu Labs, a cybersecurity company that boasts “we break your systems before adversaries do.” Over a career spanning more than 15 years, Schloss has assessed the security of numerous businesses, including a large US pharmacy retailer that he asked us not to name. He wasn’t asked to break in, just to do an audit on all of the org’s corporate switches, routers, and firewalls. “So, I come across this firewall,” Schloss said. “That is an edge firewall, meaning this is what touches the internet. This part will add its enable password, which is the term Cisco uses for administrator. It had the enable password as 'password.' Just p-a-s-s-w-o-r-d.” As Schloss noted, the enable command on Cisco devices allows the user to gain administrative rights to the firewall, controlling network traffic. If someone connected to that firewall, either via SSH or through an exploit, and got normal user privileges, they could then elevate those privileges to admin and do something like shut off all traffic from the intranet to the outside world. Schloss actually didn’t guess that the password was “password,” but instead was able to decrypt the file holding the passwords by breaking Cisco’s own protection, something he said is easy to do. “That enable password was stored as Cisco IOS type 7, which isn’t really a hash,” he said. “It’s more of a reversible encoding with a publicly known key. Even back then, it was best practice not to use it.” But even if the password were stored in a secure place, it would be very easy for a threat actor to guess. So he marked the password failure down as a “high find,” a bad type of vuln that needs to be fixed right away. When he brought the password to the company’s auditing department, they put him on a phone call with the auditing team, the entire IT team, his own manager, and others. On the packed call, the auditing team, who had commissioned Schloss’s work, was very concerned about the firewall password, but the IT team didn’t think it was a very serious problem. The two sides screamed at each other for more than an hour while Schloss and his colleagues sat there quietly, staring at their cameras. “The audit team is like ‘yeah, we gotta fix this.’ And the directors were really harping on ‘this needs to be done’ and the IT team starts firing back,” Schloss explained. “It’s like ‘Why? Who’s gonna? What does it matter? No, this isn’t a high-priority find. This is maybe a medium. Yeah, it’s bad, but it’s not that bad.’” The call dragged on so long that Schloss was unable to finish presenting his findings and recommendations. The conflict was so severe that the client continued to follow up and ask him to explain what he found again for the next three years – long after he had moved on to other projects. He later learned that the auditing department controlled the bonuses for the IT team and there was a stipulation that any “high finding” would eliminate those bonuses. So they weren’t just arguing about “password” - they were really talking about the compensation for an entire division. The lesson here is more than “don’t use the word ‘password’ as a password.” It's also about misaligned incentives. Tying security posture to compensation seems like a good way to incentivize workers to follow best practices, but it also leads them to deny responsibility and minimize mistakes when they're found. ®

Title: MythicRatatoskr: An Yggdrasil-enabled backdoor deployed in a UAC-0099-Sandworm collaboration
Context: In the past, Gamaredon collaborated with a threat actor that we discovered and named InvisiMole
Full Text:
MythicRatatoskr: An Yggdrasil-enabled backdoor deployed in a UAC‑0099-Sandworm collaboration

MythicRatatoskr: An Yggdrasil-enabled backdoor deployed in a UAC-0099-Sandworm collaboration

ESET researchers uncover MythicRatatoskr – a previously unknown Go-based backdoor hiding its C&C server inside the Yggdrasil mesh network – that paved the way for a destructive attack against a Ukrainian grain firm

This report analyzes activity during which UAC‑0099 gained initial access on July 16th, 2025 and handed it off to Sandworm, which then conducted a data-wiping attack on September 17th, 2025. It particularly focuses on the MythicRatatoskr backdoor, which is unique in its use of the Yggdrasil mesh network to communicate with a C&C server hosted within it.

We presented our findings about MythicRatatoskr at LABScon on September 18th, 2026, and at the Virus Bulletin conference on October 16th, 2026.

On July 16th, 2025, UAC-0099 gained initial access to a grain logistics company in Ukraine via a spearphishing email with a malicious attachment, leading to the execution chain of the MATCHWOK backdoor.

One day later, the attackers deployed MythicRatatoskr, a previously undocumented backdoor that communicates with a C&C server hosted inside the Yggdrasil mesh network. We have not seen the backdoor used anywhere else, and we found indications that a Linux variant may also exist.

Yggdrasil is a decentralized mesh network that implements an experimental routing scheme in which the IPv6 communication between the nodes is end-to-end protected.

Ultimately, UAC-0099 handed off access to Sandworm, which then carried out a data-wiping attack.

Cooperation among Russia-aligned actors

The handover documented in this report is not an isolated phenomenon. As noted above, Sandworm is attributed to GRU Unit 74455, and UAC-0099’s targeting leads us to assess that it is aligned with Russian interests.

Earlier in 2025, we uncovered that Russia-aligned Gamaredon collaborated with Turla, another Russia-aligned threat actor; we documented our findings in our blogpost Gamaredon X Turla collab. Both groups are linked to the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation (FSB). This kind of cooperation underscores the potential for coordinated cyberespionage campaigns among Russia-aligned groups, likely intended to amplify their operational impact. In the past, Gamaredon collaborated with a threat actor that we discovered and named InvisiMole. Against that backdrop, a UAC‑0099-to-Sandworm handoff is unusual in the specific actors involved, but no longer surprising as a pattern.

According to ESET telemetry, the events unfolded as follows: at 06:59 on July 16th, 2025, a scheduled task named pdfopentask was executed on one machine in the target organization. It executed a PowerShell payload from %temp%\temporarydoc.txt.

A minute later, MATCHBOIL was deployed. MATCHBOIL is a downloader that deployed, in this case, the MATCHWOK backdoor (C&C: https://uztickets[.]com) from https://egyptanimals[.]com/animals/photoalbum. The following day, at 09:28, a new binary was delivered to the machine: the MythicRatatoskr backdoor. Due to the close proximity of time, we believe with high confidence that the MATCHWOK execution chain led to the deployment of MythicRatatoskr. Our telemetry further shows that additional MythicRatatoskr samples were subsequently deployed to other machines within the organization, this time using an OpenSSH SFTP server.

Later, ESET telemetry detected a SOCKS5 server on some of the machines, with one sample having been extracted from an unknown archive using WinRAR. We believe that the SOCKS5 server was deployed using MythicRatatoskr.

Approximately two months later, on September 17th, 2025, we detected data-wiping activity at the compromised grain logistics company. The data-wiping attack was executed by deploying the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy – standard Sandworm tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that we have observed numerous times in ESET telemetry.

Therefore, we assess that UAC‑0099 can act as an initial access group for Sandworm.

This blogpost focuses primarily on the analysis of the MythicRatatoskr backdoor, the Yggdrasil network that hosts its C&C server, and the accompanying SOCKS5 server. The first versions of MATCHBOIL and MATCHWOK have already been analyzed by CERT‑UA in its advisory, with MATCHBOIL and its evolution further covered in our blogpost MATCHBOIL: New tricks, same old evil intentions. These tools are therefore omitted here.

The word Yggdrasil originates in Norse mythology, where it refers to a sacred tree connecting the various realms of the cosmos. Within that tree lives a squirrel named Ratatoskr that carries messages between its top and its roots. Given the backdoor’s role as a messenger scurrying through the Yggdrasil network, we decided to name the backdoor MythicRatatoskr.

More technically, Yggdrasil is a decentralized mesh network that connects devices directly to each other without a central hub, building an encrypted IPv6 overlay on top of the internet so that participating nodes can exchange end-to-end-protected traffic. Legitimate users adopt such meshes for resilient connectivity, research, and hobby networking. Because no single server runs the mesh, the network is robust and hard to disrupt – properties that also make it attractive to adversaries. Importantly, Yggdrasil is not designed to provide anonymity.

The post-compromise execution chain relied on known malware already attributed to UAC‑0099 – namely the MATCHBOIL downloader and the MATCHWOK backdoor – which leads us to attribute this stage of the attack to UAC‑0099 with high confidence. We attribute the data-wiping activity observed two months later to Sandworm, also with high confidence, based on the TTPs involved.

Moreover, we assess with high confidence that UAC‑0099 handed off access to Sandworm at some point during the intrusion, although we have not yet been able to determine whether the MythicRatatoskr backdoor was operated primarily by UAC‑0099 or by Sandworm.

UAC‑0099 is a cyberespionage group targeting governmental organizations, financial institutions, and media, all in Ukraine. Based on the targeting, we believe with medium confidence that the group is aligned with Russian interests. UAC‑0099 can act as an initial access broker for Sandworm, a Russia-aligned group best known for its destructive attacks in Ukraine.

The group has been active since at least 2022 and was first reported by CERT‑UA in June 2023. Apart from MATCHBOIL, the group also typically deploys LONEPAGE, a PowerShell downloader named after the presence of the word page in its C&C URLs.

Sandworm is a Russia-aligned threat group that performs destructive attacks. It is mostly known for attacks against Ukrainian energy companies in December 2015 and December 2016, which resulted in power outages. In June 2017 Sandworm launched the NotPetya data-wiping attack that used a supply-chain vector by compromising the Ukrainian accounting software M.E.Doc. In February 2018, Sandworm launched the Olympic Destroyer data-wiping attack against organizers of the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang.

The Sandworm group uses such advanced malware as Industroyer, which is able to communicate with equipment at energy companies via industrial control protocols. In April 2022, CERT‑UA thwarted an attack against an energy company in Ukraine where the Sandworm group tried to deploy a new variant of this malware, Industroyer2.

Since February 2022, Sandworm has been very active in Ukraine, by deploying data wipers against strategic organizations.

In October 2020, the US Department of Justice published an indictment against six Russian computer hackers that it alleges prepared and conducted various Sandworm attacks. As we already mentioned, the group is commonly attributed to GRU’s Unit 74455.

According to ESET telemetry, initial access was gained via a spearphishing email with a malicious attachment – a finding that matches CERT‑UA blogpost. We assess that the MATCHWOK backdoor execution chain (already documented in the CERT‑UA blogpost) then led to the execution of MythicRatatoskr, a backdoor that communicates with its C&C server over the Yggdrasil network. Subsequently, the attackers probably used MythicRatatoskr to deliver a SOCKS5 server.

MATCHBOIL persists MATCHWOK by adding the registry value UpdateMonitor to the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\, with data pointing to the dropped MATCHWOK path.

MythicRatatoskr is started as a Windows service with the name ieupdate.

During check-in, MythicRatatoskr sends information about the current user, hostname, and local network settings to the C&C server. In addition, the operators can use MythicRatatoskr to exfiltrate files and screenshots to the C&C server by using HTTPS routed through the Yggdrasil mesh network. The data is not staged prior to exfiltration.

MythicRatatoskr is a backdoor written in Go that uses the Yggdrasil network (described in the Network protocol section) to reach its C&C server. As noted earlier, we named the backdoor after Ratatoskr, the squirrel from Norse mythology that scurries through Yggdrasil – the sacred tree connecting the realms of the cosmos – carrying messages between its top and its roots. We felt this was a fitting parallel for a backdoor that ferries data across the Yggdrasil network. There are signs in the binaries suggesting that the development started sometime between December 2024 and February 2025.

Function names left in the binaries – following a mix of mixed caps (CheckInAgent) and snake case (agent_run) – suggest either code merged from another project or inconsistent naming by the authors. Key functions handle service registration and Yggdrasil network initialization (main, runService), check-in and beaconing (agent_run, init_agent, CheckInAgent), configuration handling (saveConfig, Encrypt, Decrypt), command polling and dispatch (getTasks, doTask), and the backdoor commands themselves (upload, download, screencat, shell, manageProxy, etc.).

Some samples also include a 10-minute startup delay, likely to avoid immediately connecting to the Yggdrasil network on execution, helping to evade detection.

Table 1 presents MythicRatatoskr host-based artifacts that we observed during our analysis. Note the filename collision for krbtman.exe: it is MythicRatatoskr on some machines, and the SOCKS5 server on others.

Table 1. Host-based artifacts associated with MythicRatatoskr

C:\windows\system32\updater.exe

C:\Windows\system32\krbtman.exe

C:\windows\system32\windowsdefendersvc.exe

%localappdata%\Microsoft\OneDrive\OneDriveLiveUpdater.exe

c:\program files (x86)\microsoft.net\adomd.net\110\applicationasphost.exe

C:\OFFICE2010\Utilities\Act64.exe

%userprofile%\Downloads\WindowsDefenderSvc.exe

%userprofile%\Downloads\ieupdate.exe

%userprofile%\Downloads\ie.exe

%userprofile%\AppData\Local\Internet Explorer\ieupdate.exe

%userprofile%\AppData\Local\ieupdate.exe

C:\Windows\system32\.updatecache

%LocalAppData%/Temp/.crond(Analyst note: forward slashes are attackers’ typo)

According to Windows event logs obtained from the compromised machines, updater.exe and WindowsDefenderSvc.exe were started, and thus likely persisted, as Windows services.

To communicate with the C&C server, MythicRatatoskr relies on the Yggdrasil network – a decentralized mesh network in an alpha state that implements an experimental routing scheme. Each node in the network generates its own Ed25519 key pair, which allows protected end-to-end IPv6 communication between the peers. The IPv6 address is derived from the public key in the 200::/7 subnet range, which was deprecated by IETF in 2004. Anonymity is not among the goals of the project. We explore this topic more in the Network infrastructure section.

The yggdrasil-go repository already provides the necessary types and methods to join the Yggdrasil network. There’s also another project, called yggstack, that enables the Yggdrasil network to communicate via a network stack in the user space. This has the benefit of not needing to create a tunnel interface, which might be an issue if the user does not have the required privileges to create one, or if such an interface is not supported on the system. The MythicRatatoskr code is based on yggstack, making the malware portable.

There’s a publicly available network that one can join by adding at least one public peer into the Yggdrasil configuration. MythicRatatoskr specifically contains an embedded base64-encoded blob that contains a list of public peers in the URI format. Most peers on the list are still operational. MythicRatatoskr randomly picks three peers from the hardcoded list, which is the recommended number, and connects to them in order to join this public Yggdrasil network.

Once MythicRatatoskr is part of the Yggdrasil network, it communicates with its C&C server, which is also part of the network, via HTTPS on port 443.

Communication uses JSON-encoded HTTP POST requests containing a uuid (explained in Table 4, in the MythicRatatoskr main configuration section), a message type, and optional data. Four message types exist:

checkin – register the backdoor and send victim metadata such as username, hostname, and local IPs; the server responds with a fresh uuid and psk),

tasking – poll for new commands,

result – return command output, base64-encoded when present,

and getfile – retrieve file content for the upload command.

Although the C&C server is hosted in the Yggdrasil network – which may prevent network security tools from detecting outbound connections to it – blocking the public peer addresses is a viable mitigation.

We distinguish between two types of configuration:

a backdoor-specific configuration used by the malware itself; and

an Yggdrasil configuration used to join the mesh network.

MythicRatatoskr main configuration

The MythicRatatoskr configuration is stored in a file at a hardcoded path. The path can differ in each sample; we identified the following paths:

C:\Windows\Temp\.updatecache (in krbtman.exe, Act64.exe, ie.exe, ieupdate.exe, and windowsdefendersvc.exe)

C:\Windows\system32\.updatecache (in updater.exe, and windowsdefendersvc.exe)

%LocalAppData%/Temp/.crond (only in OneDriveLiveUpdater.exe)

The %LocalAppData%/Temp/.crond path is notable, since such a filename (.crond) along with forward slashes is expected for Unix-like systems. This indicates that a Linux variant (or macOS, FreeBSD, etc., though less likely) of MythicRatatoskr may also exist. Moreover, OneDriveLiveUpdater.exe contains an unused configuration path /tmp/.test_config; the filename suggests that this configuration path may have been used during testing and accidentally left in a Windows deployment.

All of the configuration filenames start with a dot. On Unix-like systems, programs used for listing files, such as ls, typically exclude these entries by default, effectively hiding them. This is not the case on Windows, where these files are not hidden. This further suggests the existence of a Linux variant.

The backdoor-specific configuration stored on disk is a JSON file encrypted via AES‑256‑CFB using a hardcoded key embedded in the binary, US3pM9KFxrZBSgc1pGl2wO4Kir1XjZP5Z9kBXBMYd2s=, which is decoded using base64 before being used. The first 16 bytes of the file represent the IV.

The configuration file is not required for the malware to start. MythicRatatoskr contains an embedded default configuration, which it encrypts and writes to disk during initialization. This allows operators to deploy the malware without a separate configuration file and update the configuration later via C&C commands. Backdoor commands are described later in the Capabilities section.

Table 2 presents the embedded MythicRatatoskr configuration common for all samples.

Table 2. Embedded MythicRatatoskr configuration

The value 123 is just an unused placeholder value that is replaced with the UUID returned by the C&C server during the check-in. A hardcoded UUID d71f1722-cf0b-4e27-9f8e-c95ec9b24a23 is used in the check-in message.

Although not part of the above configuration, MythicRatatoskr contains the following hardcoded C&C address for the proxy command: 201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838:8080. It is not possible to modify the value during runtime.

Initially, when MythicRatatoskr starts, it generates a new Yggdrasil configuration, including a new Ed25519 private key. Because the Yggdrasil IPv6 address is derived from the public key, the victim machine’s Yggdrasil IPv6 address changes each time the malware runs.

MythicRatatoskr then uses empty NodeInfo data and sets the NodeInfoPrivacy flag. As a result, other nodes in the Yggdrasil network won’t be able to get more information about the node, such as the Yggdrasil version or the operating system on which the node is running.

The backdoor uses a publicly available Yggdrasil network to reach the C&C server. To join the network, it needs to connect to at least one of the publicly available peers. All MythicRatatoskr samples contain the same embedded list of 32 peers from which three are randomly picked. The peer list is base64 encoded in the binary and was likely compiled by the backdoor authors from publicly available sources. We provide the full peer list at the end of the blogpost.

MythicRatatoskr supports standard backdoor functionality, including command execution, file system navigation, file transfer, screenshot capture, and proxying. Table 3 contains all of the backdoor commands; the command IDs are strings that are hardcoded in the code.

This command supports two subcommands: start and stop. As the naming implies, it is used to start or stop the proxy connection. It connects to the following hardcoded proxy server:201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838:8080

It is the same address as the C&C server, but a different port.

Once connected, MythicRatatoskr sends the string test.

Most of the code was copied from existing open-source projects, such as revsocks, as implied by the presence of debug strings like Accepting stream and Passing off to socks5, and the function name connectForSocks.

Unlike the standalone SOCKS5 server described below, MythicRatatoskr’s proxy command is used to create a reverse SOCKS5 proxy connection. The standalone tool creates a local SOCKS5 server instead.

The SOCKS5 server exclusively used by UAC‑0099 or Sandworm during the August 2025 activity is a simple tool written in Go that uses go-socks5 for managing proxy connections. The tool is internally named bindProxy.

Because MythicRatatoskr already includes SOCKS5 proxy functionality (see Table 3), it is unclear why the attackers deployed a separate SOCKS5 server. It is possible that MythicRatatoskr’s proxy command did not work as expected, so the operators installed this additional tool. Nevertheless, together they support both forward and reverse proxying.

Table 4 presents SOCKS5 server host-based artifacts that we observed during our analysis. Again, note the filename collision for krbtman.exe: it is MythicRatatoskr on some machines, and the SOCKS5 server on others.

Table 4. Host-based artifacts associated with the SOCKS5 server

C:\Windows\system32\krbtman.exe

%userprofile%\Downloads\krbtman.exe

%localappdata%\SMBCache\nbtresolver.exe

The tool uses go-socks5 to create a SOCKS5 proxy server that listens on 127.0.0.1, port 33690. The address is specifically used to allow only the local machine to access the service. To make the proxy server reachable from outside the victim’s network, the attackers could have used MythicRatatoskr’s expose command to expose it through the Yggdrasil network. Alternatively, they may have used another existing tunnel to access the machine.

As stated in its FAQ, Yggdrasil is not anonymous, so it is possible to locate nodes in the Yggdrasil network. First, we tried to find the C&C server 201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838, which we extracted from the MythicRatatoskr configuration, in the publicly available map of the Yggdrasil network at http://51.15.204.214/ to no avail because the map was last updated on August 8th, 2024, nearly a year before the intrusion took place.

We therefore generated our own map of the network’s spanning tree, which does include the C&C server, as shown in Figure 1. The C&C server is situated near the center of the tree, making it easily reachable from other peers. The colors of each node indicate how far the node is from the C&C server. For example, as indicated by the red color, the connection from/to the nodes at the edge can be unreliable. The coordinates (Coords) for the C&C are rather simple: the server is reachable via the node with ID 4, which is the root of the spanning tree.

Using Yggdrasil’s command line utility yggdrasilctl, we identified that the C&C server is configured with three public peers, shown in Figure 2.

The C&C server’s port 443 uses TLS certificates that are rotated regularly. This pattern is characteristic of certificates generated by revsocks, on which the server code is probably based.

In this campaign, we observed cooperation, or at least operational handoff, between two Russia-aligned threat groups with different roles. UAC‑0099 appears to have gained initial access to a Ukrainian logistics company using its known tooling. That access was later used in activity culminating in a destructive Sandworm operation.

In addition, we identified a new backdoor, MythicRatatoskr, which is attributed to either UAC‑0099 or Sandworm. The C&C server for this backdoor is hosted within the Yggdrasil mesh network, and the use of such infrastructure made determining the server’s physical location particularly challenging. The backdoor was probably used to deploy the SOCKS5 server to route connections through the compromised network.

To our knowledge, this is the first documented case of Yggdrasil being abused in this way by a state-aligned threat actor, and it may signal a broader trend of adversaries adopting experimental peer-to-peer networks to increase the resilience and stealth of their infrastructure.

Ultimately, Sandworm carried out a data-wiping attack by deploying the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy, a technique consistent with previous Sandworm destructive operations.

Title: The Keys Are in the Browser: Secret Exposure Across AI-Built Websites
Context: Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit
Full Text:
Cyble scanned 1.3M+ newly registered domains and found AI-built sites leaking live secrets to the browser: OpenAI keys, Stripe keys, and database tokens.

Spinning up a website no longer takes a developer. A prompt to an AI app-builder returns a working, styled, deployable site in minutes, and when one template works, the same operator clones it across a dozen domains before launch. That is also how secrets end up in plain sight.

Over a month, Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) scanned more than 1.3 million newly registered domains, identified the ones built by AI app-builders, and read their public front-end code for exposed credentials. We built our own classifiers to spot AI-generated websites as they are registered, paired with a scanner that pulls exposed keys and credentials straight from their public code. On 35 of the 22,306 AI-built sites we identified, a genuinely private secret was sitting in the browser: live OpenAI keys, Stripe secret keys, backend database tokens, and, in several cases, a single credential cloned across a whole fleet of domains.

Thirty-five is a small number, since counting every key-shaped string on an AI-built site is easy and misleading, as most are meant to be in the browser; a single reCAPTCHA key appeared on thousands of sites. We kept only the credentials that are never supposed to leave a server. Those are the findings below.

This report walks through the two leak patterns we observed, what appears exposed, what an attacker can do with these keys, and how to shut down the exposure.

AI-built Websites are leaking the keys that power them

An AI-built site generates its content with a Large Language Model (LLM), and the key to that model often ships in the page the visitor downloads. That is the plainest pattern we found, and the most on-the-nose.

Five AI-built sites carried live OpenAI API keys in their client-side code, sixteen distinct keys across them, and four of the five are confirmed AI-generated. One AI-writing site stands out on its own: it shipped twelve different OpenAI keys, one per content category, as plain values in its bundle. Figure 1 shows a single entry, with the key masked.

Figure 1 – Live OpenAI keys embedded as plain values in an AI-writing site’s JavaScript (key masked by CRIL).

A handful of sites, but each key is sensitive to exposure. An OpenAI secret key is a billing credential: anyone who reads the page can spend the owner’s balance, exhaust the rate limit, or run the bill up until someone notices and revokes it. Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit.

Clone-and-leak: one secret across a whole fleet

An AI builder makes the hundredth site as cheap as the first, so an operator clones a working template across many domains, and whatever secret sat in the template now sits on every copy. We saw this in two shapes.

A Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet. Thirteen near-identical domains, each a short word (ask, call, chat, get, hello, hey, hi, its, join, let, meet, my, see), glued to one brand, all served the same client bundle, and all embedded the same live Slack incoming-webhook URL. Figure 2 shows the URL in the shipped bundle, masked.

Figure 2 – One Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet, in each site’s shipped bundle (secret and workspace IDs masked).

Anyone who can read the page can post messages to the operator’s Slack workspace via that webhook. That works for spam, for phishing aimed at the operator’s own staff, or for flooding a channel.

One Stripe secret key across four domains and two brands. A single Stripe secret key appeared on four domains under two separate brand names. The same sk_live_ value across all four points to one operator, or one shared Stripe account, behind every site. Figure 3 shows the assignment.

Figure 3 – The same live Stripe secret key reused across four domains under two brands.

A Stripe secret key provides full API access to the account, including the ability to create charges, issue refunds, and read customer and payout records. That one key exposes the operator’s whole payment account on every domain in the fleet.

The 13-domain Slack fleet runs on Bubble, a no-code and AI app builder, as confirmed by Bubble’s x-bubble-perf response header and client markers. Bubble serves each app from a dynamic.js bundle, and any value a developer places in a client-accessible field ships inside that bundle in plain text. The Stripe cluster runs on a Next.js build instead, which shows that the pattern spans builders rather than tracing to a single platform.

What else is exposed

Four AI-built sites exposed a Supabase service role JSON Web Token (JWT) on their front ends. A service-role token bypasses row-level security and grants full read and write to the project database. In terms of impact, it sits at the top of the set because it opens the entire backend rather than a single service.

Most of the remaining secret-looking strings on AI-built sites carry no/minimal exposure.

3,824 sites shipped browser-safe values: reCAPTCHA site keys, Stripe publishable keys, Supabase anon keys, builder telemetry tokens.

2,172 sites carried Google API keys, which matter only if they are unrestricted.

1,461 sites exposed a Supabase or Firebase backend address, which is a real exposure only when that backend’s rules are open.

Filtering those out is why the confirmed count is 35, not several thousand. Table 1 breaks the 35 down by type. The values stay withheld, and a few sites appear under more than one row.

What an attacker can do with these

Every credential in Table 1 is a working key to a live account. An attacker reads a public web page, copies a value, and calls an API. Here is what that buys them, key by key.

OpenAI and other LLM keys: Run inference on the victim’s account until the bill or rate limit stops them. On a metered account, that is direct financial loss; on a funded one, it is a free, anonymous model endpoint that the attacker can point at anything, billed to the victim and running under their quota and identity.

Stripe secret key; Drive the victim’s payment account through Stripe’s own API: create and refund charges, push the account toward fraud, and pull the customer list, email addresses, and payout history. One key is a money problem and a data-breach problem at once.

Supabase service-role token: Read and write the entire production database, past whatever row-level security the app configured. That means stealing every user record, altering or deleting data, and planting content the app will serve back to its own visitors.

Slack incoming webhook: Post into the operator’s own Slack as if from inside. Flooding a channel is a nuisance case; the real risk is internal phishing.

AWS access key: With the paired secret and enough permission, reach into the owner’s cloud: spin up resources (crypto-mining is the usual first move), read storage buckets, or pivot further in.

GitHub token or OAuth secret: Read or push to the owner’s source repositories or misuse their identity integration.

One exposure counts many times over. When the key sits on a cloned fleet, it is live on every domain in that fleet, so an attacker who finds it on one site has compromised all of them.

Conclusion

AI app-builders made it almost free to publish a website, and just as free to clone one, and most of what they produce is worth nothing to steal.

The exceptions are what we went looking for. A small, steady set of these sites hand over the key that runs them, and when an operator copies one site across a fleet, the leak rides along to every domain.

Against the millions of domains registered each month, the number is tiny, but every hit is a live account an attacker can reach and exploit just by opening the page.

If you build on these tools, read your own shipped code before you publish it. If you defend an organization, assume your keys may surface on sites you never built and look for them.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

Our Recommendations

For developers and AI-builder users:

Keep every secret key (OpenAI sk-, Stripe sk_live_, a Supabase service-role token) in a server-side function or backend workflow, never in a client-accessible field.

Use only the browser-safe variants on the front end, publishable and anon keys, and enforce access with Supabase row-level security, Firebase rules, and API key restrictions.

Rotate any key that has ever sat on the client side, and treat it as already compromised.

Read your own page source before you ship, and search it for sk-, sk_live_, service_role, and hooks.slack.com. If you find them, so can anyone.

For SOCs and defenders:

Monitor public code and newly registered domains for your own keys and webhooks; don’t just paste sites.

Treat a secret found on one domain of a template fleet as exposed on all of them, and scope the response to the fleet, not the domain.

Cloud Security Maturity Lags Despite Widespread Adoption, SANS Warns

Nearly all organizations now run production workloads in the cloud, yet only 40% consider their cloud security strategy advanced or optimized, highlighting a significant maturity gap, according to SANS.

This is according to the 2026 SANS Cloud Security Survey Insights report which surveyed 400 IT and security professionals.

SANS found that 51% of respondents were running enterprise-scale (2501 to 10,000 workloads, containers, or instances) or hyperscale (more than 10,000) environments and 73% already having a dedicated cloud security team or role.

The report also noted that 93% of organizations already run production workloads in the cloud and 65% run more than one provider.

SANS noted that because so many respondents have a dedicated team for cloud security, it indicates that a maturity gap persists despite organizations being well-resourced.

Overall, 45% of respondents described their cloud security strategy as “intermediated” with partial implementation of a defined strategy.

This partial implementation is an issue, according to the report, and leads to security incidents.

Misconfiguration Make Up Nearly Half of Critical Cloud Incidents

The report found that misconfiguration is the leading cause of critical cloud incidents (45%), close to double that of the next highest factor, credential theft, which made up 22% of incidents.

What’s more, misconfigurations often remain in place for significant periods, with around half of organizations (49%) found to need more than 24 hours to close a known critical gap.

"Misconfiguration is not an exotic attack class. It is a known gap sitting in an account somebody already owns," said Serge Borso, SANS Principal Instructor. "What makes it persist is not the attacker. It is the distance between finding the gap and fixing it, across too many consoles with nobody clearly owning the result. That is why consolidation and enforcement matter more right now than implementing yet another detection tool. The industry has finished deciding to move to the cloud and is now paying for how fast it did.”

Despite the security maturity gap, cloud security budgets were found to be increasing for most, with 28% of respondents reporting significant investment to modernize or adopt new technology such as AI or Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), and another 42% reporting incremental growth.

Overall, 70% of organizations are spending more on cloud security than a year ago. Only 7% reported budget cuts.

Just 21% of respondents said their organization runs a single consolidated CNAPP platform. Meanwhile, 31% still maintain separate point solutions across Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM). Of those surveyed, 23% are actively evaluating a move to consolidate.

The SANS data points towards three priorities for security teams in the year ahead:

Strengthen cloud security by enforcing automated policy checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines, preventing misconfigurations before deployment

Reduce security tool sprawl by consolidating posture management, workload protection and identity security tools into unified platforms

Extend zero trust beyond authentication by adopting continuous, context-based controls that limit what users and workloads can access after login

Full Text: Indian certification authority eMudhra has defended the laughably weak private keys it used to sign some digital certificates it issued, and suggested others should share the blame for the incident. In case you’re coming to this one late, news broke yesterday that private keys the company used to sign certs were beyond weak: one was literally just the number “4,” and several others were short strings of easily guessed two-or-three-digit numbers. It’s easy to deduce the value of those keys, which makes it possible to forge certs and impersonate websites or other resources. That’s gold for scammers, phishers, and other miscreants. The entire infosec industry has pointed that out, urged swift adoption of better certs, and lamented the fact that implementing replacements will be a long and thankless task. eMudhra’s statement about the incident says it generated keys during “a Key Generation Ceremony (KGC) held on April 30, 2025, using FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Hardware Security Modules (HSMs).” Such hardware is the standard kit for the job and should in theory produce nicely complex keys and store them securely. But something went wrong. “A flaw in the KGC caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the statement claims. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores. eMudhra is working to establish the root cause.” The company then gets a tad defensive. “These roots and issuing CAs have gone through independent audits for two years in a row and have been in browser trust lists since mid-2025,” the statement adds, seemingly shifting some blame to auditors and other stakeholders. The announcement then points out that eMudhra’s TLS business generates just one percent of its revenue, meaning this mess won’t impact its bottom line too much. That’s nice to know for the company’s investors but rather misses the point that whoever relies on the company now has an urgent, unwanted, and costly job to do replacing certs. “eMudhra is working directly with customers who may be affected to give them replacement certificates, so that critical services are not disrupted. The company is also working with the root programs and continues its root-cause investigation,” the statement adds. The company allows that the incident “may have some reputational risks on eMudhra which cannot be quantified.” Ya think? ®

Title: How APT41 revived the BlackLotus bootkit to attack diplomatic organizations in Central Asia
Context: For instance, the Exploit Prevention component available in Kaspersky products prevents exploits from running if the patch is not applied, or if it is a zero-day vulnerability...
Full Text:
Introduction

Back in October 2022, Kaspersky GReAT was looking into a peculiar advertisement on a hacking forum. A cybercriminal had been advertising a UEFI bootkit, dubbed BlackLotus, that could bypass Secure Boot, for $5,000. Given the low price for such powerful capabilities, the cybersecurity community initially took this advertisement with a grain of salt. As no BlackLotus samples were found in the wild, no one could at the time verify the claims made in the forum post.

BlackLotus advertisement

However, about half a year later, in March 2023, ESET confirmed that the BlackLotus advertisement was genuine. The researchers tracked down samples of this bootkit and confirmed that it can indeed bypass Secure Boot through a vulnerability called Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894). As this vulnerability was still exploitable in 2023, Microsoft had to release multiple security updates to address it.

Since the release of these updates, the BlackLotus bootkit has gone quiet — no publicly known attacks have used it. Yet in early 2026, we discovered a malware sample similar to BlackLotus that was used in an APT campaign in Central Asia. In this report, we share our findings, including new payloads and possible attribution of this campaign.

The return of the infamous bootkit

In early 2026 we identified a complex APT attack targeting diplomatic agencies in Central Asian countries — namely Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This attack involved a UEFI bootkit that we dubbed BlackX. Having examined it, we found it to be similar to BlackLotus.

Attackers have been deploying BlackX after compromising the victim machine networks and obtaining administrator privileges. To install the bootkit, we observed them dropping the following files:

inst.exe, an installer executable

PVMDIJGKAX2, an RC4-encrypted extensionless file containing files and strings required for the installation

The installer was launched with the command line C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1. The last argument here is the RC4 key used for decryption.

Curiously, the file inst.exe does not contain any malicious strings or embedded blobs. All the files needed to install the malicious payload are inside PVMDIJGKAX2, which makes it harder for incident responders to retrieve the bootkit components.

The installer package drops a set of files to both system and UEFI partitions, designed to exploit the Baton Drop vulnerability. We noted that the implementation of the exploit is remarkably similar to the one used in the BlackLotus malware. As with BlackLotus, the goal of the exploit is to install custom Machine Owner Keys (MOK), which allows loading arbitrary EFI files on the target machines to manipulate Secure Boot.

While the vulnerability exploitation chain was implemented very similarly to BlackLotus, we spotted differences between the exploits in BlackLotus and BlackX. That said, the source code of the BlackLotus bootkit has never been published online. This could mean that the attackers behind BlackX either reverse-engineered the BlackLotus bootkit or purchased its source code from cybercriminals. Either way, this is an interesting observation, as we rarely see APT actors borrow ideas or code from cybercrime actors.

Payload launched by the bootkit

The UEFI payload delivered during the Baton Drop exploitation has a classic bootkit goal — to inject a malicious driver into the Windows kernel. This driver differs from the one deployed by BlackLotus and is signed with a certificate belonging to an organization named 温江区明宇网络技术服务工作室 (English: Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio). At the time of writing, this certificate (serial number: 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072) has been revoked by its issuer.

The driver aims to tamper with security solutions installed on the machine. For example, it disables process, thread, and registry callbacks related to security solutions. It also tampers with ETW providers so that security solutions cannot access their output. Curiously, some of the tampering procedures are designed to run only if Kaspersky or Avast solutions are installed on the infected machine. However, during dynamic analysis of this driver, we found that these procedures are useless — they fail to interfere with Kaspersky products in any way.

The driver also protects the bootkit’s files from tampering. It intercepts kernel requests to open these files and returns a handle to calc.exe instead of a malicious file handle.

User-mode second-stage payloads

Apart from tampering with security solutions, the driver also deploys a user-mode payload. We observed two such payloads, used for cyberespionage, in the wild. One of them is a RAT that can load further-stage .NET payloads. This RAT uses cloud storage for C2 server communications — we observed its versions using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk. Having connected to a cloud storage service, this RAT iterates over files available there and interprets them depending on the file suffix. Below is a list of supported suffixes:

File suffix

Description

Type

0X01

A .NET file. The task is to parse it and run the method TEST.Class1.RunCMD(argument_array) from the module

Input

0X02

Result of the call TEST.Class1.RunCMD(argument_array)

Output

0X03

Task to upload a file to the drive

Input

0X04

Uploaded file

Output

0X05

Task to download a file to an infected machine

Input

0X06

File download status

Output

SSSR

Contains initial system info

Output

We also observed another payload delivered through the bootkit, which we dubbed OxiDLLRunner. It is a malicious DLL obfuscated with OLLVM. It is loaded by the legitimate file googleupdate.exe (original filename: jcef_helper.exe, MD5: AF8A983B9ADA07EAE1259BF2953ABD40), which is also delivered by the bootkit. The DLL decrypts the contents of the file v8_context_snapshot.bin, which resides in the same folder, and then jumps to the beginning of the decrypted content. The decrypted data starts with shellcode followed by a PE file, which is a Rust payload designed to communicate with the www[.]archivetj[.]com C2 server. During communication, this payload is supposed to receive DLL files exporting a function named create_plugin, which are then executed in separate threads.

Attribution

Based on the following facts, we have attributed this attack to the APT41 threat actor with medium confidence:

In June 2026, ESET published a blog post on attacks by the FishMonger threat actor, which the community assumes to be related to APT41. This post describes a kernel implant with a PDB path starting with C:\Users\xdd\Desktop. While describing the campaign, the post also suggests the possible use of an unspecified UEFI bootkit component, which might exploit CVE‑2023‑24932. We observed the identifier “xdd” used multiple times in the BlackX bootkit payloads, so we assess that BlackX is the UEFI bootkit referenced in the ESET blog post;

The payloads deployed by BlackX are loaded using a legitimate executable abused via DLL sideloading, and an encrypted file — this pattern is common among Chinese-speaking threat actors;

The OxiDLLRunner file has been obfuscated with OLLVM, an obfuscator commonly used by Chinese-speaking actors.

Why did the target organizations get infected?

During our initial analysis of BlackX, we thought that attackers succeeded in deploying it due to the negligence of the target organizations. Baton Drop, the vulnerability used to deploy BlackX, was disclosed back in 2023 and was patched, so we first thought that the infected machines lacked the relevant updates. However, our investigation proved this wrong — the targeted machines were fully patched.

Instead, we found out that the problem was with the patch itself. As it turned out, the patch for the Baton Drop vulnerability is designed to revoke the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components. However, this revocation does not happen automatically upon patch installation — the user has to trigger it manually. This is done with the following steps:

A registry flag is set inside HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Secureboot;

A scheduled task named Secure-Boot-Update is created.

This patch is designed to be applied manually — for instance, applying it automatically could break dual-boot systems relying on the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate to load. At the same time, this patch deployment practice creates a problem — as it is extremely unusual for a system administrator to take extra steps after installing an update. Usually, when applying patches, system administrators take no further action unless an installation failure occurs. These instructions for activating the patch are buried deep on the Microsoft website, and we assess that they are quite hard for an average IT administrator to notice.

Curiously, Microsoft’s plan for deploying the Baton Drop patches mentions an “Enforcement Phase” that involves revoking the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate automatically, without user interaction. At the time of publishing this post, this stage has not been implemented. On October 19, 2026, this certificate expired, but this does not prevent the vulnerable binaries from loading unless the certificate is blocklisted.

It is likely that the threat actor behind this campaign took into account that few organizations realized the importance of manually activating the Baton Drop patch. As such, we believe they decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit.

Conclusion

Patch management is important for every organization, as updates from vendors help protect software and hardware against known vulnerabilities. However, sometimes installed patches fail to protect against the flaws they address. The BlackLotus story we described is not the only such example — for instance, in 2025 Microsoft released an update against the ToolShell vulnerability that also had to be applied manually.

However, modern security solutions are designed to account for such cases when installed patches fail to protect against security flaws for one reason or another. For instance, the Exploit Prevention component available in Kaspersky products prevents exploits from running if the patch is not applied, or if it is a zero-day vulnerability with no available patch. It is thus crucial to equip all machines in an organization with security solutions and constantly monitor the alerts they raise.

UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

The United Arab Emirates says it's creating a foundation of security and safety as it transforms its public service footprint.

Robert Lemos,Contributing Writer

October 22, 2026

5 Min Read

Source: Zarko Prusac via Shutterstock

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) plans to move half of its government operations, services, and sectors to autonomous AI agents over the next two years, prompting a conversation around how it intends to secure and monitor those AI agents.

To that end, the UAE has implemented a "control tower agent," conducts audits using agents and humans, and considers monitoring and establishing trust as critical to its efforts, Omar Sultan Al Olama, minister of state for artificial intelligence, told attendees on Oct. 14 at the World Economic Forum's (WEF) Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai. Security and trust are critical to achieving the nation's goal of autonomous government systems that improve quality of life and to not risk harm to citizens, he said.

"There is an oversight that ensures that we understand what agents are doing, how they're taking certain actions — there's a continuous audit that is being done," Al Olama told attendees. "There's an audit that's done by agents, and there's an audit that's done by humans to ensure that this doesn't go haywire in any way, shape, or form."

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

In April, the UAE Cabinet unveiled a framework to transition 50% of the federal government's sectors, services, and operations to agentic AI within two years. The effort aims to redesign government policies and processes to embrace AI capabilities, creating "smart systems" that take proactive actions to reduce operational costs, provide more efficient services to citizens, and make government more efficient, according to public notes from the meeting.

The UAE's plans for agentic AI should not be surprising. While global AI diffusion — a measure of the number of adults who used a generative AI product in a specific period — hit 19% in the second quarter of 2026, the United Arab Emirates has taken the lead globally with more than 73% of the population using AI during the quarter, according to Microsoft's "Global AI Diffusion: Q2 2026 Trends and Insights" report.

Yet at the same time, the risk landscape is changing, often because of AI use. The UAE has already faced significant increases in attacks over the past two years, many powered by AI agents, as political tensions and military conflicts continue to build in the region.

UAE Says It's Focused on Secure & Safe AI Deployments

The government's Agentic AI Project will roll out in several phases across ministries and federal entities, it said. On Oct. 9, the Ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and Development reviewed the first phase of the project, focused on "building government capabilities, surveying and assessing government services, operations and tasks, and setting priorities," according to a statement announcing the review. The second phase will establish a national technical ecosystem for agentic AI, under the name "FedAI," that will enable government agencies to develop and operate agentic services and conduct internal competitions, such as hackathons, to develop applications.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

The UAE leads other nations with 73% of its population using generative AI at least once in the quarter. Source: Microsoft

The coming phase includes training for government employees in agentic AI development and generative AI technology to provide a foundation for the future, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahya, one of the UAE's two vice presidents and deputy prime minister, said in the statement.

"We are building a government system that is smarter, more flexible, and more proactive; a system that leverages agentic AI to develop services, operations, and tasks, and to shape policies and decisions," he said. "This should be achieved in a secure and reliable digital infrastructure, in a way that strengthens the readiness of the UAE Government for the future and reinforces its leadership in developing government work models."

Security and trust are critical for operations conducted by agentic AI systems, and that means monitoring and auditing agentic activity, says Evin McMullen, co-founder and CEO of AmanTrue, an Abu Dhabi-based startup creating a governance control layer for agentic AI.

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

"Any institution, certainly a government that's adopting AI agents at scale, [and] especially related to internal operations or citizen services, should be able to show who acted in the event of an agent action," she says. "Which agent, who authorized it — which human being and associated institution — and what the limits or definition of the task was."

AI Governance Lagging for Organizations

Governance is a key problem facing deployments of AI agents. Because of their often transitory nature, their ability to obscure on whose behalf they are acting, and their occasional penchant for going rogue, agents and their actions need to be tracked closely. However, 29% of security teams have discovered unknown AI agents running in production that were never registered, and nine in 10 organizations had a security incident in the past year attributable to agentic AI, according to an Oct. 20 report released by cloud-computing and AI-infrastructure platform ServiceNow.

As more organizations adopt agentic services, governance becomes more important, especially when multiple organizations work through agents on the same data and services, says AmanTrue's McMullen.

"When many services intend to act through the coordination of agents, an institution has to be able to show which agents specifically accessed a given data record on whose authority, within what defined limits, with what output," she says.

Gaining trust in autonomous systems will require that the AI agents are closely monitored, tracked, and controlled, the UAE's Al Olama said at the World Economic Forum event.

"The government's only currency is trust," he said, adding that "if the government makes one wrong decision, you lose a lot of that currency. ... The same would be true with AI. Once we have one breakthrough event, where AI exits the sandbox and goes and harms people, I think it's going to take a long time for us to regain that trust."

Title: Turn Your Vulnerability Backlog Into Pull Requests With Agentic Remediation
Context: For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization
Full Text:
Written by

Brendan Hann

Ryan McMorrow

October 22, 2026

0 mins read

The Evo Remediation Agent is now in Open Preview, bringing automated dependency resolution to Evo Agentic AppSec. AppSec teams can now run ongoing remediation campaigns across repositories and deliver proposed fixes to developers through validated pull requests.

Fixing a dependency vulnerability can mean choosing an upgrade, resolving dependency conflicts, adapting the application, and/or checking the result. That work competes with everything developers are already building. As teams introduce code and new vulnerabilities at increasingly exponential rates, AppSec needs a way to accelerate remediation across the applications they protect.

With the help of agentic remediation, AppSec teams can start by leveraging campaigns targeting a defined set of repositories and vulnerabilities. Snyk supplies the model and hosted sandbox environment, and developers receive proposed changes through their existing source code management (SCM) workflow. The developers continue to retain control over final review and merging.

Give AppSec a way to drive fixes

A remediation campaign defines which vulnerabilities the agent works on, in which repositories, and on what schedule. AppSec teams set the scope, and Evo Remediation Agent works through eligible vulnerabilities and opens pull requests for developers to review.

For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization. Recurring campaigns repeat that work on a schedule as repositories and vulnerability findings change.

That gives AppSec teams a way to initiate remediation without asking each developer to install and run an agent. Teams can follow repository outcomes across a campaign, review where the agent produced fixes, and investigate where remediation efforts still need attention.

Snyk first brought automated dependency updates into developer workflows with automatic Fix PRs across SCA and Container. Agent Fix extended remediation to source-code vulnerabilities detected by Snyk Code, our first AI-native solution generating and checking proposed fixes. The initial Evo Remediation Agent then brought a broader workflow into the CLI and ADE: plan the fix, apply changes, and validate the result in the developer’s environment. Now, fully validated, the next iteration of the Evo Remediation Agent brings campaigns that automate agentic remediation to AppSec teams.

Starting once again with Open Source vulnerabilities, teams can put the agent to work across repositories and make remediation an ongoing part of their security program.

Security context guides the work

A dependency update can require changes throughout an application. The agent uses Snyk findings to plan updates, applies changes in a hosted sandbox, and checks its work with builds, available tests, and rescans. This feedback helps the agent work through the changes an upgrade requires.

When the agent produces a fix, it opens a pull request and records each action attached to the change. Teams can restrict campaigns to fixes assessed as non-breaking, and the agent does not merge changes. Developers review the proposed changes and decide whether to merge them.

Evidence behind the remediation engine

Generating a fix only helps reduce risk if a developer can merge it. A pull request that breaks the build, fails existing tests, or leaves the vulnerability in place adds review work and doesn’t shrink the backlog. A high mergeable fix rate is what turns agent fix suggestions into backlog reduction because more of the fix pull requests actually get merged with less developer rework.

The VulnBump benchmark tests the mergeable fix rate of the engine that powers Evo Remediation Agent. Across 307 dependency-upgrade tasks, the CLI-based Remediation Agent passed all four verification checks on 90.2% of tasks. Claude Code with Snyk findings passed 77.5%, and Claude Code alone passed 59.6%. All three used the same model.

Those checks cover the outcomes that matter to a dependency fix: dependencies resolve, the targeted vulnerabilities disappear on rescan, the application builds, and previously passing tests still pass. The results show the value of combining security context with a purpose-built remediation workflow.

Fix first. Prioritize the rest.

Remediation programs usually start by deciding what to fix. Evo Remediation Agent reverses that order, giving AppSec teams another way to act on the backlog. Recurring campaigns work through eligible vulnerabilities in scope, so what reaches your team is then the work that needs human judgment.

Repository outcomes and journals help teams understand where the agent made progress and where further work remains. AppSec teams get a running view not only of the backlog, but also the pull requests opened, while developers get a record of why each change was made. Remediation consequently becomes an ongoing part of the security program, with your team setting the standard for what ships.

Bring remediation to your team

Workspaces

SCM integration

Preview access for your Tenant.

Title: Behind Japan’s Warnings of a Cyber Crisis
Context: The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved...
Full Text:
Reporting on cyberattacks against Japanese entities rose 48% between Q2 and Q3 2026, encompassing ransomware, exploitation of vulnerabilities, credential leaks, and service disruptions. Significant incidents exposed millions of customer records and disrupted operations across multiple sectors, with attacks on shared service providers extending the impact to downstream organizations. Further incidents in October 2026 indicate that these trends have persisted into Q4. This report examines potential contributing factors, including demand for Japanese personal information, legacy systems, software vulnerabilities, weak API controls, and AI’s likely role in lowering technical and language barriers. New incident-reporting requirements under Japan’s Active Cyber Defense (ACD) law, effective October 1, may further increase the number of disclosures of incidents affecting Japanese organizations.

A Significant Increase in Cyberattacks

Throughout Q3 2026, Insikt Group observed a significant increase in reported cyberattacks targeting organizations in Japan. Between Q2 and Q3, reports of such incidents rose 48%, from 621 to 918, according to the Recorded Future Intelligence Platform. Our observations were subsequently validated by statements from Masaaki Taira, head of Japan’s National Cybersecurity Strategy Headquarters (NCSH), declaring a “state of emergency in cyberspace” in Japan following a number of high-profile breaches.

Trend Micro similarly noted an increase in cyberattacks against Japanese organizations, reporting that the number of cyberattacks affecting the country between January and September 2026 exceeded the total for the entirety of 2025, with 86 attacks reported in September alone.

Q3 2026 breach disclosures from Japanese organizations highlight several risks, including operational disruption, exposure of sensitive data, and phishing-enabled account compromise.

The figure below highlights some of the most significant breaches in Japan observed throughout Q3 2026.

Figure 1: Selection of significant breaches in Japan during Q3 2026; the figure is not comprehensive (Source: Recorded Future)

At least two features set the Q3 Japan breaches apart from other such breaches. The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved ransomware, stolen cloud credentials, and exploited web-facing systems. The second is the scale of the attacks: single incidents now routinely affect millions of user records or organizations downstream that rely on the targeted services, such as roughly 33 million records leaked from the EPARK PeakManager reservation platform in July and 6.6 million accounts from Times Car in September.

This trend has continued into Q4. On October 7, a ransomware incident affected IDCFrontier, a Japanese cloud provider, disrupting 495 companies and local governments. Almost a week later, on October 13, 2026, a data breach affected the Japanese software company Sourcenext. In this incident, an unidentified third party misused the company’s member information retrieval API to compromise 22,519,960 customer records containing personally identifiable information, including email addresses, passwords, names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, employment information, and more.

Our observations complement October 2026 warnings issued by several Japanese agencies, including the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center (JPCERT/CC), the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), and the Innovation Platform Agency (IPA), regarding a series of cyberattacks targeting Japan-based organizations. JPCERT/CC’s notice warned of at least four consistent tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) linked to recent incidents:

Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in unpatched systems or misconfigurations;

Attacking internal and external APIs, sometimes using stolen API credentials;

Exploitation of CVE-2026-72898 (CVSS score 10), a SQL injection vulnerability, in the Metabase application;

The deployment of web shells contained within .war and .jsp files on internet-accessible web servers.

Later reports attributed the cyberattacks targeting Japanese company websites to artificial intelligence (AI) agents linked to activity ranging from basic website scanning to extended attack sequences that involved multiple tools and techniques.

Japan-based Macnica Security also reported a surge in cyberattacks since July 2026 involving personal information leaks from web systems. The company noted that this increase is unique to Japan compared with other countries. According to Macnica, of the 119 cases disclosed in 2026, approximately 68% were announced since July. This accounts for about 31% of the total 265 cases over a 34-month period. The company similarly observed unauthorized access through weak authentication, stolen credentials, or exploited software vulnerabilities and site-specific flaws in application design, APIs, or access controls. Macnica could not confirm the use of AI in these attacks.

Explaining the Increase in Incidents

Multiple factors are likely responsible for the recent increase in attacks affecting Japanese organizations.

High Demand in the Criminal Ecosystem for Japanese User Data: Criminals on the dark web place a premium on data from Japanese organizations due to Japan’s financial and identification requirements and its status as a wealthy, developed economy.

Widespread Use of Legacy Systems and Software: According to an April 2026 article by Money Forward, more than 60% of Japanese firms still use legacy systems, end-of-life software, and older operating systems. Such systems no longer receive security updates and official patches from vendors, leaving known flaws exposed to increasingly automated attempts to exploit them.

Operationalization of AI Tooling: While the specific models abused are not yet confirmed, commercial AI products are widely believed to have been leveraged in the recent spate of attacks against Japanese organizations, both for automating the attack sequence (such as automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation), and for reducing the barrier-to-entry historically attributed to the complexity of the Japanese language (such as through the easier drafting of convincing phishing emails in proper business Japanese). Notably, financial institutions in neighboring South Korea were recently the target of an intrusion campaign leveraging ARTEX, a Chinese open-source AI penetration-testing tool attributed to a group Recorded Future refers to as TAG-217. On October 19, the Japanese cybersecurity company GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae reportedly concluded that ARTEX was used in attacks against roughly 80 Japanese companies, with 8 of those attacks occurring in the 30 days prior to its report.

New Incident Reporting Requirements: Effective October 1, 2026, Japan’s new Active Cyber Defense (ACD) Law imposes mandatory reporting requirements on designated critical infrastructure operators. This is unlikely to account for the surge in reported incidents due to the law’s implementation date in Q4 2026, but it does imply that we will very likely continue to observe a higher volume of incident disclosures from Japanese organizations going forward, and the impending implementation of the law may have induced some organizations to disclose incidents in Q3 that would otherwise have gone unreported.

Recommendations

Insikt Group recommends that Japanese organizations consider the following:

Migrate away from and/or update legacy systems. Outdated and unpatched devices or software (including operating systems) provide an attractive, easy vector for threat actors to compromise organizations via previously disclosed vulnerabilities and exploits. AI-enabled scanning and automated exploitation have further increased the risk to these systems. Where possible, replace end-of-life hardware and software.

Harden internet-facing systems. Secure internet-exposed hardware and services such as virtual private network (VPN) servers, web application firewalls, load balancers, small office/home office routers, IP cameras, and DVRs by patching known vulnerabilities, restricting administrative access, enabling additional logging, and disabling unnecessary services. These devices have been increasingly exploited by cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors alike over the last several years for initial access.

Strengthen API controls. Verify authorization for every API request, test whether users can access other customers’ records, restrict API key privileges, and limit bulk data retrieval.

Protect accounts against phishing. Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and train staff to be vigilant against increasingly well-crafted Japanese-language phishing messages.

Limit data exposure and prepare for disruption. Delete unnecessary personal information, restrict data export permissions, test restoration from protected backups, and establish manual alternatives for critical services such as reservations and dispatch.

Adopt privileged access management (PAM). Limit administrative and super-user accounts, providing elevated rights only on a temporary, just-in-time basis.
