Title: A patched PHP server can still be a compromised one by Lucie Cardiet
Context: Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad...
Full Text:
On October 20, details of two critical flaws in PHP leaked online before the fixes were ready. PHP, the scripting language behind a large share of the web, moved its patch release up a day and shipped it on October 21. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed php2shell), let an attacker run commands on a web server through PHP itself, with no login needed.

Patch now. CISA added both flaws to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on October 26. That advice is right, and it leaves a gap. This post is about the gap.

Attackers were testing the flaw before the fix existed

Fixes are out for PHP 8.2 to 8.5,and PHP says PHP 8.1 and older will not get updates. One estimate counts about 884,000 such servers still online, a rough figure from a single source.

Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw early attacks, and the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned organizations to update immediately or take systems offline. How many real servers were taken over is still unclear. Amazon says it does not know whether the attempts it saw would have worked outside a honeypot.

On October 23, CrowdStrike and Flare still reported only probing and failed attempts, many of which crash PHP rather than give an attacker control. The next day, Perplexity's Adel Karimi recorded successful remote code execution on a honeypot, and on October 26 CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, with a federal patch deadline of October 29. Karimi's test used a deliberately favorable setup, so it shows the flaw works, not how often attacks like it succeed.

Every flaw has been out there for a while before anyone announces it

A flaw becomes news on the day it is announced, not the day it appears. PHP's own maintainers first spotted signs of this problem in a 2024 audit, and attackers reached it before the public did.

We have seen this pattern before. When Log4j hit in December 2021, Vectra wrote that the first sign of an attack was hard to spot and that the safest assumption was that at least one server in an estate was already compromised. Other flaws in the software your business runs are very likely in the same position today: known to someone, announced to no one. Patching deals with the ones you hear about. It cannot help with the rest.

The PHP servers you miss matter most

PHP runs WordPress,Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, hosting control panels, and a lot of software that never mentions PHP. The servers you know about will get patched. The ones you do not know about are the ones attackers find first, because nobody is watching them.

Appliances and management interfaces that ship PHP are the likeliest place an attempt becomes a compromise, and they are rarely monitored like web servers. Flare, relaying one researcher's report, says some ship PHP without address randomization, which removes the main obstacle for an attacker. Ask your vendors which of their products include PHP.

No team patches everything on the day a fix ships. Knowing which servers face the internet, and which hold the most valuable data, turns a backlog into a short list of decisions, including which services to switch off until they are fixed. On any server you suspect was hit, save logs and a snapshot of memory before restarting, because a restart erases traces.

‍

What happens after a PHP server falls

An attacker who gets code running through PHP usually does not need malware. The web server already has a shell, a network connection and access to files, so they can use the tools already installed on the machine to look around, find credentials and move from one system to the next. Nothing looks wrong, because the web server is doing web server things with slightly different commands. That is the first of the three detection gaps I write about: nothing looks wrong.

What changes is where the server talks to. A web server that has served the same pages for years suddenly reaches places it never did before, calls out to unfamiliar addresses, or starts talking to internal systems. That behavior shows up in network traffic, not in patch status. A view of the network is how you see what a server is actually connecting to, whether or not anyone is watching the server itself.

What Vectra AI can and cannot see

Vectra AI is not really concerned about what the initial attack vector is. What we see is what happens afterward.

PHP is the story today. Next week it will be something else: another flaw, a phone call to a help desk, someone on the inside. What we look at does not depend on which door was used. We watch what a system does once an attacker is inside, so we do not need the way in to be known or the flaw to be published. That matters most when the entry point is unknown or the vulnerability has not been announced yet.

Uncovering Potential PHP Servers and Shadow IT

One of the challenges in securing PHP infrastructure is knowing where it exists in the first place. Forgotten applications, unmanaged servers, and shadow IT can create security blind spots, even after known vulnerabilities have been patched.

Vectra AI's PHP Server Visibility dashboard provides an additional investigative tool to help security teams identify potentially overlooked PHP servers using indicators observed in unencrypted HTTP traffic, such as .php endpoints and PHPSESSID cookies. Analysts can then investigate whether these hosts are also receiving externally originated encrypted traffic, helping prioritize potentially exposed systems for further investigation.

The dashboard is not intended to provide a complete inventory of PHP servers. It can only identify systems exhibiting observable PHP-related indicators, and encrypted traffic or limited network visibility may leave some servers undiscovered. Instead, it acts as an assistant to existing asset discovery and threat-hunting workflows, helping analysts uncover potential shadow IT, investigate exposure, and identify systems that warrant closer examination, even after patching.

Detection rules for known php2shell exploit attempts

Vectra Match now contains rules to detect the PHP2Shell attacker behaviors when proper visibility is provided to the attacker traffic. They flag known exploit attempts in network traffic when that traffic is visible to us, so they catch attempts at the door, while the detections above catch what follows. An attempt is not a compromise. A match is a reason to look at that server, not proof that it was taken over. This is available for all Vectra Match customers.

The rules, by ET rule number:

2072548: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Handler-mismatch Session Injection (CVE-2026-109619)

2072549: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Header Amplification OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072550: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Nested Empty File Control OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072551: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Chunked Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072552: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Binary URL-Encoded POST for $_POST Corruption (CVE-2026-109618), commented out in the rule set, so off by default

2072553: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072554: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Code Injection in Filename (CVE-2026-109619)

2072555: ET HUNTING PHP Generic Upload Progress Session Manipulation, a hunting rule, not an exploit rule, so treat a match as a lead

2072556: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Multipart Part Count (CVE-2026-109618)

2072557: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Empty Multipart File Controls (CVE-2026-109618)

What a compromised PHP server reveals about your resilience

The old measure of success was whether attackers get in. The better one is how far they get. Patching, a sound network design, splitting the network into zones, least privilege and knowing which systems carry your most important business processes all limit that distance. The network record can show whether anyone came through the door before it closed, and where they went next.

The three gaps are walked end to end in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks white paper.

Title: PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk
Context: “It's coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild
Full Text: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure. On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed. They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure. The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked. The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday. “Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told. “Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus: “On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call' Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak." “These things are messy,” Lorenc said. Chainguard learned “something was coming in PHP” on Friday from one of the researchers that found the bugs, Lorenc told us. Later that night, using his company’s AI harness and a frontier model, the CEO and the Chainguard team independently found the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. All it took was a “basic prompt of ‘find bad vulnerabilities in PHP,’” Lorenc wrote in a subsequent LinkedIn post. On Saturday, Chainguard began working with the PHP maintainers, confirmed that some of its findings matched the bug reports, and helped test the patches. “The patches are crazy - this is not a simple vulnerability,” Lorenc told The Register. “It really did take them months to build a real, working patch for it. And then on Monday, the rumors started, and yesterday it just spiraled.” Some people published POCs on social media, other security vendors reported seeing real-world exploitation, and late Tuesday night Lorenc told us he decided to ship the fixes, and notified the PHP coordinated disclosure channel about his plans. “People were getting hit in advance” of the official PHP disclosure, “so we made the call to ship the fixes under that,” Lorenc said. “It's coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild.” Also on Tuesday night, Chainguard published built artifacts and made them accessible to anyone, not just customers. “And then I woke up this morning and saw that this was all our fault,” Lorenc said. When asked if he would do anything differently, given the fallout from Chainguard’s early disclosure, Lorenc said no. “This process and policy is based on trying to coordinate as much as possible until shit hits the fan and people start weaponizing things,” he said. “It sucks, because we really are all on one team, and there's bad guys over there doing stuff.” Chainguard’s honeypots trapped IPs from China and Russia targeting the vulnerabilities on Wednesday, Lorenc added. “Just being told there's a vulnerability in a piece of software - even something as big as PHP - is enough to find it,” he told us. “I did that myself without any other knowledge on Friday." "I think this is kind of the new normal. People are able to build an exploit in hours without even knowing what the vulnerability is." What we know about the CVEs and how to exploit them While we still don’t know the scope of exploitation - or what will happen to vulnerable legacy systems that don’t have security fixes - threat hunters predict it’s going to be a doozy. “Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them,” Wiz researchers Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld, and Tomer Schwartz warned on Wednesday, adding the oft-quoted stat that PHP powers 70 percent of all websites in the world. “Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4,” the Wiz kids wrote. “Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.” Both bugs are related to how PHP handles memory management and error handling, and both lead to remote code execution (RCE). They can cause a corrupted internal PHP state when a request ends unexpectedly, and then a later request can reuse that state, leading to memory disclosure or RCE. “Both are memory corruption vulnerabilities,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity explained. “If an attacker can shape the memory PHP trusts, they can potentially hijack what it does next, and in these cases that means remote code execution.” CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w) leads to RCE via out-of-memory corruption. “If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory,” the project maintainer wrote. “On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs.” CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp) allows RCE via stale state. “A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request,” according to the PGP Foundation. “A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.”®

Title: TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions
Inside a Global AI-Assisted Hacking Campaign
Context: However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea
Full Text: IntroductionIn October 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz investigated AI-assisted cyberattacks that combined the ARTEX penetration testing framework with AI coding assistants and custom automation scripts. Initial reporting of the incident identified the targeting of South Korean financial institutions. However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea. The AI-assisted attacks were widespread and targeted organizations around the globe and in multiple industry sectors.In this blog post, ThreatLabz examines the operator’s working environment, explains the roles assigned to AI models and tools, and analyzes the targeting and objectives reflected in the operator’s prompts. Key TakeawaysIn October 2026, ThreatLabz discovered information about an AI-assisted attack combining a customized ARTEX deployment with Claude Code, Codex, and Grok workspaces. Custom scripts shared instructions and supported handoffs between AI sessions.ARTEX was configured to use a DeepSeek model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, but other configurations also specified DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok.Prompts directed AI models to divide investigation tasks and review one another’s findings, including instructions for GLM to review work performed by DeepSeek and its subagents.Saved project records and synchronization scripts were designed to preserve investigation context and progress across accounts, servers, and AI sessions. Prompt histories revealed targeting across multiple industries and geographic regions. Requests for bulk personal and transaction data, alongside questions about selling stolen data, suggest the attacks were financially motivated. BackgroundThreatLabz identified an ARTEX deployment that included AI assistant configurations, synchronization scripts, network routing tools, and a Claude Code prompt history. The recorded prompts spanned August 4 through October 4, 2026 (UTC). CrowdStrike separately reported on related ARTEX infrastructure and the targeting of South Korean financial organizations on October 7, 2026. This blog examines the broader working environment of the attacks and targets. Operator InfrastructureThe figure below illustrates the threat actor’s environment based on saved configurations and instructions.Figure 1: Architectural diagram of AI-assisted attack environment using ARTEX. Technical AnalysisThe following sections examine the operator’s infrastructure, customized tooling, AI environment configuration, and targeting objectives, offering a closer look at the workflow behind the campaign.Work server and jump serverAs Recorded Future detailed in their recent blog post, the operator's work server stored project files, scripts, AI settings, and a local ARTEX deployment. The jump server, 38.244.50.120, served as the default route for connections to targets.The jump server also ran additional AI sessions. The operator delegated research tasks to Grok on that server and instructed a separate AI session to review Grok’s findings. This setup divided work between the two servers, with the operator providing oversight and direction. Three custom scripts synchronized shared AI instructions and supporting files across accounts, which are described in the table below.Script namePurposetools/sync-all.shUses SSH and rsync to copy AI instructions, reusable task guides, saved notes, and tools to the jump server's root, claude, grok, and gemini accounts.sync-memory.shCopies saved AI notes, known as memory files, to locations on the jump server.tools/sync-cc-users.shCopies shared Claude Code instructions and supporting files to the gemini and glm accounts on the work server.Table 1: Custom synchronization scripts and their purposes for AI-assisted attacks.Each account maintained its own AI service settings. The synchronization scripts were designed to update model references within specialist agent instructions to match the destination account, allowing the workspaces to use shared instructions with different model configurations.The scripts also incorporated backups and validation checks designed to avoid overwriting modified destination files. These mechanisms indicate that the operator intended to keep configurations consistent across environments.Customized ARTEX deploymentARTEX is an AI-assisted penetration-testing framework. Its planner-and-worker architecture lets an operator define a goal, which AI agents break down into tasks, execute using tools, and document by retaining assets and findings for review. The recovered deployment extends the framework with additional tools for web, network, and Android analysis.The saved Docker Compose file defines an ARTEX container and a PostgreSQL 16 database. It configured the ARTEX interface to use host port 8890 and mapped PostgreSQL to 127.0.0.1:5435. The ARTEX container uses a custom image tagged artex-local:perf2-20261003. The corresponding Dockerfile adds tools including nmap, sqlmap, nuclei, httpx, jadx, apktool, and frida-tools. It also adds Python libraries for web processing and spreadsheet output and replaces the original ARTEX program with the operator’s local version.AI model setupThe operator changed model routing over time and used account names that did not always match the configured model. To understand this setup, it is important to distinguish the client application, such as Claude Code, from the model service receiving its requests.For example, the saved ARTEX environment configuration specifies:ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER=openai ARTEX_LLM_MODEL=deepseek-v4.1-flash ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL=https://xcai.pro/v1Here, openai specifies an OpenAI-compatible API format. The model field requests deepseek-v4.1-flash, while the base URL routes requests to xcai.pro. These settings identify the requested model and gateway endpoint, but do not confirm which underlying model the gateway actually served.The table below summarizes the model assignments recorded in the collected configurations. Model names are reproduced as requested IDs and were not independently verified.Workspace or componentRequested model IDsRoleARTEX local deploymentdeepseek-v4.1-flashModel backend for ARTEX's task workflow, configured through https://xcai.pro/v1.Codex (.codex/config.toml)deepseek-v4-proAlternative coding-agent interface configured to send requests to https://api.deepseek.com/v1.Local account named gemini, running Claude Codedeepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace using shared instructions and specialist agents.Local account named glm, running Claude Codeglm-5.3Workspace configured to request GLM and use the shared workflow.Jump-host accounts named root and claudeglm-5.3, glm-5.3-flashAssigned analyzer and collector roles in the jump-host synchronization script.Jump-host account named grokgrok-4.7-xhigh, grok-4.7-build-fastAssigned analyzer and collector roles; operator also requested remote research and continued auditing.Jump-host account named gemini xcai/deepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace the operator explicitly requested to reconfigure to use DeepSeek.Table 2: AI model configuration and assigned roles used in the AI-assisted attacks.In some instances, the threat actor assigned distinct roles to individual AI models. The prompt history includes instructions for DeepSeek to conduct the initial investigation, followed by GLM reviewing the findings for potential gaps. One translated prompt states: "When DeepSeek says it has exhausted all attack surfaces and I say to start a GLM review, GLM should review DeepSeek's previous work and its subagents' work."Later prompts assigned GLM additional investigation tasks, extending its intended role beyond reviewing DeepSeek’s findings.The operator requested both Grok’s native terminal application and a Claude Code setup configured to use Grok as its underlying AI model. For the Claude Code integration, the operator installed a bridge service called grok2api on the jump server. Prompts assigned extensive research tasks to Grok on that server and other AI sessions to review its output. The prompt history shows repeated requests to modify this configuration, but the specific setup used for each task could not be confirmed.The records establish the use of the Claude Code application, with configurations specifying DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok. However, since the underlying model responding to each session could not be independently verified, it's possible that some sessions used Anthropic’s Claude models.Persistent project stateThe operator organized each investigation into a separate folder. A script created files to record targets, testing progress, notes, vulnerability reports, and supporting evidence. These records provided context that an AI assistant could read to resume an investigation in a later session.File or folderWhat it recordsscope.mdWebsites, servers, or applications selected for investigation.surface.mdDiscovered pages, APIs, and other entry points, including their testing status.notes.mdCompleted work, decisions, and next steps.findings/Reports on potential or confirmed vulnerabilities.evidence/Supporting files, such as captured responses and tool output.Table 3: AI-assisted attack investigation files and folders and their purposes.The operator also configured a mechanism to help AI sessions retain context, track progress, divide tasks, and resume work started in other sessions:Provide project context with each prompt: An automated hook script (tools/project_context_hook.py) was configured to execute when a new prompt was received, read the current project files, and attach a brief summary of testing status, recent notes, and paths to relevant memory files. This provided context to help the AI continue previous work.Distribute tasks among specialized AI agents: The operator created tailored instructions for agents assigned to discover APIs, review source code, or analyze Android applications. The primary AI session was directed to validate their outputs before recording them as confirmed findings.Reduce operator approval requirements: The instructions directed the AI to assume that all supplied targets were preauthorized. Some application settings also permitted autonomous actions without requiring explicit operator approval for each step.Facilitate cross-session handoffs: The operator configured Codex to ingest saved instructions and notes, allowing other accounts to access prior conversation histories. A task guide also instructed the AI running under the jump server's gemini account on how to take over an ARTEX task and review its results.Proxy exits, tunnels, and cloud backupThe operator instructed the AI tools to connect to targets through the jump server. Additional proxy configurations provided separate outbound IP addresses for individual projects, helping limit direct connections between the primary work server and target environments.SSH tunnels were configured to support bidirectional communication between the two servers for AI and file services. Background monitoring tasks were configured to restart supporting services and tunnels if they were interrupted.Investigation assets were archived to Backblaze B2, with reports, supporting evidence, source code, data exports, and backups organized into separate directories. This structure followed the operator's directive to separate each target's operational data from its final analysis report for easier retrieval.Target profile and objectivesThe prompt history showed targeting beyond South Korean financial institutions, including dating applications, SMS providers, cryptocurrency and payment platforms, gift-card portals, gambling sites, retail platforms, educational services, logistics companies, and legal settlement systems. The targets also spanned multiple geographic regions, suggesting an opportunistic approach. The recorded prompts included requests to scan or investigate organizations in Canada, China, Cuba, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Malaysia, Nigeria, South Africa, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United Kingdom, the United States, and Vietnam. The figure below shows the geographic distribution of targets referenced in the operator’s prompt history.Figure 2: Geographic distribution of targets referenced in the AI-assisted attacks prompt history.The table below summarizes representative target categories and the desired outcomes requested in the threat actor's prompts:Target or sectorRequested outcome in the prompt historySocial and dating servicesCollect frontend files and subdomains; gain access to user records.SMS providersGain administrative access, obtain SMS-channel credentials, or identify ways to send unlimited messages at no cost.RetailObtain customer order data.EducationObtain course-purchase records or user data.Investment servicesReview prior investigation records and obtain current data.Cryptocurrency and digital assetsFind a vulnerability that would allow NFT gifts to be obtained for free.Legal claims administrationReview investigation records, analyze claim workflows, and assess opportunities for additional access.Table 4: Representative target sector categories and requested outcomes in AI-assisted attacks prompt history.Prompt histories indicate an explicit focus on obtaining structured personally identifiable information (PII) and mobile phone numbers. In one instance, the operator stated that database dumps lacking phone number fields were of no value and requested alternative injection methods. In another prompt, the operator questioned why a specific SQL query targeting demographic data for female users over 30 returned only approximately 300 records.The threat actor instructed AI models to decrypt encrypted fields, parse transaction histories, translate database schemas into Chinese, and remove irrelevant metadata. These requests suggest an intent to prepare datasets for monetization.Prompts about underground data marketplaces further support this assessment. In one example, the operator asked: "If hackers compromise Korean data, where do they usually sell it?"Additional prompts focused on extracting payment gateway API keys, exploiting NFT minting workflows, and gaining unauthorized administrative privileges.To reduce the risk of detection, the threat actor explicitly warned AI models not to initiate direct account withdrawals, noting that unauthorized financial transactions could trigger security alerts or create traceable records. Threat AttributionThe recovered records point to a Chinese-speaking operator. The operator wrote predominantly in Chinese, requested Chinese as the default response language, specified China Standard Time, and instructed the AI to translate exported data fields into Chinese. In discussions about SMS services and app downloads, the operator referred to Chinese services and applications as “domestic.” The operator also supplied the same mobile number in mainland China format for accounts with a Chinese proxy provider and a cloud-phone service. ConclusionThis investigation shows how a threat actor combined open source security tools, AI assistants, and custom automation scripts to launch attacks globally. Shared project records, specialized agents, and instructions for reviewing other models’ findings created a workflow designed to continue investigations across AI sessions under the operator’s direction. The prompt history also revealed broad targeting and an emphasis on obtaining personal and financial data, indicating the attacks were likely financially motivated.To defend against AI-assisted attacks, organizations should adopt a Zero Trust architecture that minimizes internet exposure and enforces least-privilege access. Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

The effort is aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure.

October 21, 2026

3 Min Read

PRESS RELEASE

SANTA CLARA, Calif. — October 13, 2026 — Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), Microsoft Corporation and Oracle today announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure.

To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads.

Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

“An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security,” said Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell. “By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry.”

“As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important,” said Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure. “Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security.”

“An open specification for integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM) capabilities is an important step toward enabling cryptographic operations where data is processed, protecting keys within a hardware security boundary and supporting cryptographic verification of workload integrity,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure at Oracle. “This effort aims to establish a common foundation for adoption across the industry.”

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

About OCP and the New Security Working Group

The Open Compute Project (OCP) is a collaborative community focused on redesigning hardware technology to efficiently support the growing demands of compute infrastructure.

As founding members of the new OCP working group, Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle will collaborate with the broader OCP community to publish a joint technical specification, with an initial draft targeted for release around the 2026 OCP Global Summit and version 1.0 to follow. The companies plan to demonstrate the new technology in their exhibit booths and during Security Track presentations at the OCP Global Summit (October 12-15) at the San Jose Convention Center in San Jose, California.

Organizations interested in participating in the security working group are encouraged to join through the Open Compute Project.

Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we’re ultimately changing the way tomorrow’s enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better.

Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Research finds that, among respondents experiencing data loss, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incidents before data left the organization.

October 21, 2026

4 Min Read

PRESS RELEASE

SEATTLE — (BUSINESS WIRE) — Data loss prevention (DLP) tools are often functioning as after-the-fact forensic systems rather than prevention controls, according to DLP in the AI Era, a new survey from the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA), the world's leading not-for-profit organization committed to AI, cloud, and Zero Trust cybersecurity education. The study, conducted in collaboration with Jazz, found that 73% of organizations said they experienced at least one confirmed data loss incident in the past 24 months. Among the respondents, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incident before data left the organization.

“Enterprise DLP has moved beyond the question of whether it should be deployed to whether it’s doing what it is intended to do. Enforcement is being softened, analyst capacity is consumed by noise, and new data-exit channels created through GenAI are exposing gaps legacy DLP was never meant to handle,” said Hillary Baron, AVP/Research, Cloud Security Alliance. “In the AI era, where employees and applications can move sensitive data through more channels than ever, organizations can’t afford to discover gaps after the fact.”

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Among the report’s findings:

Perceived visibility exceeds demonstrated capability. While close to half (48%) of security teams ranked GenAI as their top exfiltration risk, less than a third (29%) are able to produce a routine 30-day report showing sensitive data sent to GenAI tools.

Modern risks lack modern enforcement. Paradoxically, the highest-ranked risks are among the least strictly enforced, and the lowest-ranked are among the most strictly enforced. Both GenAI (48%) and cloud storage uploads (41%) were cited as top exfiltration risks, but only 22% of organizations strictly block on GenAI and 19% on cloud storage uploads. Conversely, removable media, which ranked last (10%) as an exfiltration risk, is strictly blocked by 31% of respondents, the highest strict-block of any channel measured.

DLP alert overload fuels fatigue. Fifty-four percent of teams are triaging DLP alerts where the majority turn out to be false positives, and 90% report at least one measurable impact from alert fatigue in the past year, including 21% who report voluntary staff departures directly attributable to DLP alert burden.

Business friction determines enforcement posture. Seventy-one percent of respondents reported that their security teams received pushback on DLP enforcement during the past two years. Among those teams, 66% reduced enforcement for specific teams/use cases; 8% reduced enforcement broadly across the organization; and 3% reduced or paused the program entirely. Across the full respondent base, 54% softened enforcement in some form.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

“Security teams know GenAI is creating new ways for sensitive data to leave the business, but many still cannot see the full impact,” said Ido Livneh, Co-Founder & CEO, Jazz. “Across the customer environments we observe, the average organization uses nearly 170 AI tools and fewer than 10 are sanctioned. Teams need to understand how data is actually moving so they can focus on real risk without blocking legitimate work.”

The survey was conducted online by CSA in June and July 2026 and received 433 responses from IT and security professionals. Respondents represented organizations ranging from fewer than 1,000 to more than 50,000 employees and were primarily located in the United States and Canada. Jazz funded the research and co-developed the questionnaire with CSA research analysts, while CSA independently performed the data analysis and interpretation.

Title: PHP2Shell: How to Protect Vulnerable PHP Workloads While Patching
Context: Aquasec provides vulnerability detection and runtime controls to help identify exposure and restrict supported unauthorized activities while customers apply security updates

PHP2Shell: How to Protect Vulnerable PHP Workloads While Patching

Aqua Team

October 21, 2026

TL;DR: PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected PHP installations. Security researchers have reported exploitation attempts, and the vulnerabilities may also expose sensitive information from PHP worker memory. Aquasec’s platform and services are not affected by PHP2Shell, but customers running PHP applications may have vulnerable workloads in their environments. Aquasec provides vulnerability detection and runtime controls to help identify exposure and restrict supported unauthorized activities while customers apply security updates.

What are the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities?

PHP2Shell refers to two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affecting the PHP runtime. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 severity score of 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected installations.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP itself rather than individual application code, meaning applications can be exposed even when their own code is secure. Affected web serving environments include PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, PHP-CGI, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. Researchers identified Apache mod_php as a particularly high risk configuration because a demonstrated exploit can execute before application code runs.

The PHP project released the following fixed versions on October 21, 2026.

PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported by the PHP project, although distribution vendors may provide security fixes through backported packages. Organizations should verify remediation with their relevant vendor rather than relying exclusively on the version string.

Why do the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities require immediate action?

Security researchers have reported attempts to exploit both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. On October 21, watchTowr reported exploitation attempts targeting both CVEs, while Cloudflare reported attack traffic and attempts to adapt payloads to evade deployed firewall protections. At the time of those reports, no successful compromise of a specific server had been publicly confirmed.

The vulnerabilities also present a potential information disclosure risk. Researchers demonstrated that attackers may be able to read sensitive information from PHP worker memory without first achieving remote code execution. This information could include passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and other sensitive data associated with application activity.

The combination of potential code execution and memory disclosure makes rapid remediation important. Security teams need to identify affected PHP installations, apply security updates and verify that the corrected runtime is active.

AI assisted vulnerability research adds another consideration. Researchers reported using AI tools to help develop working exploits for longstanding PHP vulnerabilities, illustrating how quickly previously overlooked weaknesses can become actionable. Security teams need to reduce production exposure while remediation proceeds rather than depend entirely on patching timelines.

Is Aquasec affected by PHP2Shell?

Aquasec’s platform and services are not affected by CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. The concern for customers is whether PHP based applications running in their own environments contain vulnerable PHP installations.

Customers should review container images and running workloads to identify affected PHP versions, particularly in internet facing applications. The fact that Aquasec itself is not affected does not mean that applications protected by Aquasec are automatically free from the vulnerabilities.

Aquasec provides vulnerability detection to help customers identify affected images and runtime security controls that can reduce exposure to supported unauthorized activities while remediation is underway.

Why is vulnerability scanning alone insufficient?

Vulnerability scanning identifies affected software, but a finding does not mean the risk has been eliminated. Organizations must locate vulnerable images, update the PHP runtime, test application compatibility and redeploy corrected workloads.

Remediation can be more involved for applications that depend on older PHP releases or legacy components. During this process, vulnerable workloads may remain in production even when security teams know which systems require attention.

Runtime security provides an additional layer of control by restricting supported unauthorized actions inside running workloads. Aquasec vulnerability detection helps identify affected images, while runtime context helps teams prioritize those that are actively deployed.

Neither scanning nor runtime enforcement removes the underlying vulnerability. The objective is to identify exposure, restrict behaviors that runtime policies can control and complete remediation as quickly as possible.

How can runtime security reduce exposure to PHP2Shell?

Runtime enforcement can restrict behaviors attackers may attempt after gaining code execution, including launching unauthorized shells, executing newly introduced binaries or establishing prohibited outbound connections. These controls can limit an attacker’s actions even while the underlying PHP vulnerability remains present.

However, PHP2Shell demonstrates the boundaries of these protections. Memory disclosure may occur within an existing PHP worker without launching another process or introducing a new executable. Controls designed to restrict those activities do not necessarily prevent an attacker from reading sensitive process memory.

Runtime protection should therefore complement security updates. Organizations need to patch the vulnerable runtime while using enforcement to reduce exposure to supported attack behaviors during remediation.

How does Aquasec protect PHP workloads?

Aquasec enforces security policies inside running workloads, allowing security teams to restrict supported unauthorized actions without depending exclusively on vulnerability specific signatures.

Four runtime control areas are particularly relevant to PHP workloads.

Restrict unauthorized process execution. Runtime policies can restrict PHP workloads from launching unnecessary shells and download utilities such as `sh`, `bash`, `curl` and `wget`. This can interrupt certain attempts to execute additional commands or retrieve malicious payloads.

Prevent unauthorized executable changes. Aquasec Drift Prevention can block execution of executable files that were not present in the original container image. This helps restrict newly introduced malicious binaries, although it does not independently prevent a PHP script from running through the existing interpreter.

Restrict unauthorized network activity. Appropriate runtime network controls can restrict unnecessary outbound connections and help limit certain reverse shell activities or communication with attacker controlled infrastructure.

Protect application files. File integrity monitoring can detect unauthorized modifications to sensitive application directories. File modification restrictions can prevent changes when properly configured, including changes to PHP web roots where malicious scripts might be introduced.

The effectiveness of these controls depends on workload coverage, policy configuration and the attack technique. In enforcement mode, validated policies can block supported unauthorized actions. They should not be represented as complete protection against either PHP2Shell vulnerability, particularly the reported memory disclosure path.

How can Aquasec customers identify vulnerable workloads?

Aquasec provides vulnerability detection for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 across supported PHP workloads, including container images using standard Linux distribution packages and official PHP images.

Customers should do a full scan of container images and review the associated running workloads to identify affected PHP installations. Combining vulnerability findings with workload context helps teams prioritize vulnerable images that are actively deployed, especially those supporting internet facing applications.

After patching, teams should rebuild affected images, redeploy them and rescan to verify remediation. Distribution specific security backports should also be considered when reviewing results.

For detailed guidance on identifying vulnerable workloads, configuring runtime controls and applying security updates, see the Aquasec Knowledge Base article.

What should organizations do now?

Organizations should prioritize five actions.

Identify affected PHP installations. Inventory container images and running workloads, including legacy PHP releases and internet facing applications.

Apply official security updates. Update the PHP runtime rather than only the application. Restart Apache, PHP-FPM and other long running PHP workers so the corrected runtime is active.

Review runtime policies. Validate applicable controls in Audit mode where supported, review legitimate application behavior and move appropriate policies into Enforce mode.

Full scan and verify remediation. Rebuild and redeploy corrected images, complete a full scan of workloads and confirm that fixed packages or runtimes are active. Consult distribution vendors about backported fixes where relevant.

Use temporary mitigations only as a bridge. Review PHP’s official mitigation guidance if immediate updating is not possible. These measures reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not replace patching.

Aquasec customers who need assistance reviewing their environment can contact their account team or open a support ticket through Aquasec Support Portal. For additional information, see the Knowledge Base article.

PHP2Shell reinforces the need to combine vulnerability detection, timely remediation and runtime control. Aquasec’s platform and services are not affected by these vulnerabilities, but customers running PHP applications should identify their exposure and apply the available fixes. Runtime enforcement provides an additional layer of protection while remediation proceeds, helping restrict supported unauthorized activity without suggesting that every exploitation path can be blocked.

FAQ

Is Aquasec affected by PHP2Shell?

No. Aquasec’s platform and services are not affected by CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. However, customers running PHP based applications may have vulnerable workloads within their environments.

Is PHP2Shell being actively exploited?

Security researchers have reported exploitation attempts against both vulnerabilities. The reporting available on October 21, 2026, did not confirm a successful compromise of a specific server. Organizations should treat the vulnerabilities as urgent and apply official security updates.

Can Aquasec prevent PHP2Shell exploitation?

Aquasec runtime enforcement can restrict supported unauthorized actions, including certain process execution, executable changes and network activity. These controls do not guarantee protection against every exploitation path or the reported memory disclosure risk.

Does Aquasec runtime protection replace patching?

No. Runtime enforcement can reduce exposure to certain attack behaviors while remediation is underway, but updating PHP remains necessary to fix the underlying vulnerabilities.

How can customers verify that remediation is complete?

Aquasec customers should complete a full scan of updated container images and review workloads to confirm that fixed PHP packages or runtimes are deployed. They should also ensure that long running PHP workers have restarted and that no affected workloads remain in production.

Built on a full agent architecture, the Aquasec Platform combines deep runtime visibility with real time enforcement inside running workloads to detect and stop threats as they execute. By focusing on exploitable risk and enabling immediate containment, Aquasec helps security teams reduce exposure and protect production environments without waiting for traditional remediation workflows.

Title: 'PHP2Shell' Bugs Signal Red Alert for Security Industry
Signal bug could keep your mic - and camera - on after hangup
Context: The vulnerability, CVE-2026-113380, was published by MITRE on Tuesday and given a CVSS score of 9
Full Text: Make sure you don’t say anything mean or secret after hanging up a call on Signal, as a bug in the encrypted messaging app’s calling library could prevent a call from ending properly, potentially leaving audio and possibly video active. The vulnerability, CVE-2026-113380, was published by MITRE on Tuesday and given a CVSS score of 9.3, marking it as a critical issue in Signal’s open-source RingRTC library in every single version before 2.72.0. That update was pushed out last month, but the vulnerability wasn’t made public until now. RingRTC is Signal’s own calling library built on top of WebRTC, a technology introduced in 2011 that has since become widely used for voice and video communication over the internet. RingRTC provides Signal-specific calling functionality using WebRTC, which already encrypts media traffic, but that isn't stopping RingRTC from failing to hang up calls in certain conditions, according to the CVE report. What’s happening is, in essence, a denial-of-service attack on RingRTC’s finite state machine (FSM) event queue, which handles events involved in managing calls. If one of the people on the call saturates the FSM queue with requests, it can become overwhelmed and fail to process a hangup request, preventing the call from terminating properly. The vulnerability is classified as CWE-754, or improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions, according to a report posted to GitHub. A conceptual proof of concept is available in the GitHub report linked above, using a Python script to simulate how flooding an event queue can prevent a hangup request from being processed. Were a malicious actor to exploit this, the person on the other end may think the call has been terminated, but either or both of their video and audio channels could still be open. The attack complexity is considered low according to the CVE, and while CISA’s known exploited vulnerabilities catalog doesn’t indicate this has been spotted in the wild, Signal users ought to ensure they’ve updated their apps - mobile and desktop - to the latest versions to ensure they don’t end up being caught on a hot mic without any notice. Comparing RingRTC 2.72.0 to the previous version indicates that Signal's fix allows the call's finite state machine (FSM) to detect termination requests independently of the event queue, while adding a timeout to prevent stalled processing from indefinitely blocking a hangup. It's not entirely clear from Signal's release notes when the fixed version of RingRTC reached the Android, iOS, and desktop versions of its apps. Signal Desktop's release history indicates that RingRTC 2.72.0 was incorporated in September, but the precise rollout dates across all platforms remain unclear. We’ve reached out to Signal to learn more, but haven’t heard back. In the meantime, best to update your installation to be sure you’re not still vulnerable. That, and watch what you say after hanging up a call. ®

Title: Survey Finds High-Profile Executives Feel Untouchable as Digital Exposure Turns Into Physical Risk
Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
Context: Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server
Full Text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

New PhaaS Platform Uses AI to Craft Phishing Lures and Mask Malicious Activity

A new phishing phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform, dubbed Athena StealthRoute, has been found to use AI tools to both deliver and conceal phishing attacks.

Researchers at cybersecurity firm Abnormal AI first identified Athena StealthRoute-linked infrastructure during an August 2026 phishing campaign.

In the six months to October 9, the firm identified approximately 89,700 attack-related messages containing the platform's distinctive link pattern across around 2,280 organizations in the US and Europe.

Read more: Phishing Dominates as Initial Entry Method for Cyber-Attacks

Of note is the platform’s AI Studio, which offers six specialized workflows for requesting customized phishing lures, supporting materials and benign-looking decoy content.

The broader Athena StealthRoute platform includes a marketplace and link-cloaking capabilities designed to divert security scanners away from malicious destinations.

The researchers noted that Athena StealthRoute illustrates how much of a phishing operation can be packaged and sold as a service without performing credential or token theft itself.

Abnormal AI noted that the AI Studio gives threat actors another way to prepare phishing content without writing every lure from scratch or relying exclusively on ready-made materials. They can instead request content tailored to different pretexts and audiences.

AI Studio is integrated into Athena StealthRoute's broader offering, which also combines domain and link management, a marketplace for campaign materials, visitor monitoring and cloaking controls.

Athena StealthRoute still relies on external infrastructure for credential and token harvesting, but much of the preparation and delivery workflow can be managed through a single console, the researchers noted.

Five of the six offerings in the AI Studio focus on the creation of phishing lures and related materials. However, the sixth option extends to decoy content intended to conceal the phishing attempts. The White Page option produces structured, benign-looking content that could be used as a cover when Athena StealthRoute's cloaking layer directs scanners and other unwanted visitors away from malicious destinations.

How to Detect and Defend Against Athena StealthRoute

Abnormal AI said that for defenders, the platform’s combination of cloaking and customizable content reinforces the limitations of relying on individual messages or link inspections to detect phishing attempts.

“Security scanners may encounter benign content where intended victims would reach malicious destinations, while variations in lure copy can make exact wording less useful for linking-related attacks,” the researchers said in their analysis.

Shared backend infrastructure, matching operator-console code and recognizable link structures offer additional signals for identifying Athena StealthRoute-associated activity even as individual domains and lures change.

Finally, because credential and token harvesting occur through separate downstream services, investigations must also account for the particular theft mechanism involved.

Title: ‘This Is Not a Drill’: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Are Setting the Internet on Fire
Context: On Wednesday, the developers behind the much-used PHP programming language released emergency security updates designed to fix critical flaws that could be exploited to allow...
Full Text:
Internet security and web administration teams around the world are scrambling to prevent widespread disaster. On Wednesday, the developers behind the much-used PHP programming language released emergency security updates designed to fix critical flaws that could be exploited to allow attackers to gain dangerous remote control of victim systems.

The PHP Foundation detailed the two critical vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—which impact “all PHP installations serving web requests” going back to PHP version 5, released in July 2004. However, only PHP 8.2 and newer are still supported and will receive patches, according to the alert. The PHP Foundation noted, though, that some PHP distributions and third-party vendors still produce legacy fixes. The caveat is significant because ubiquitous and foundational web layers like PHP can persist forgotten and un-updated in historic internet infrastructure.

“There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice,” the PHP Foundation wrote in its advisories. Security experts warn of the potential dire consequences of overlooking unpatched systems.

“This is not a drill,” says Lukasz Olejnik, an independent security consultant and visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London. Since its development in the 1990s, PHP has evolved into an essential scripting language for web development and is used across vast swaths of the internet in websites and software. Everything from publishing systems like WordPress and Drupal to e-commerce platforms like Adobe’s Magento are built on PHP.

Olejnik likens the widespread use of the programming language to critical infrastructure.

“The impact is enormous,” he says of PHP’s security flaws, adding that millions of systems could be impacted. “Especially if attackers would turn to exploiting these vulnerabilities fast. Worst case is wormable malware affecting big chunks of the internet.”

The overriding fear for security teams and developers is that malicious hackers could quickly jump upon the vulnerabilities and begin exploiting deployments before they are fixed. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported it was “seeing early attacks emerging” before the PHP Foundation had detailed the vulnerabilities and released fixes. “We expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release,” security firm Sansec wrote ahead of the fixes, which were released just before 10 am ET on Wednesday.

“Most of the web runs on PHP and this bug is in a file upload interface that’s like a front door with no lock,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “An attacker does not need to know which site they are hitting or even the actual software it runs. They send one crafted upload to any server they can find, and that is the entire attack.”

Ahead of the updated versions of PHP becoming available, some organizations took their websites offline as a precautionary measure. Multiple sites belonging to the Finnish government, including the National Land Survey, were inaccessible, according to reports. French government websites and the Port of Rotterdam’s website were also offline, according to Reuters.

“Everybody should patch immediately, exploitation may happen very fast and at a scale,” says Olejnik. “AI makes exploiting such vulnerabilities of immediate importance. Like, indeed, a minute or so.”

Security company Wiz, which is owned by Google, claimed its researchers discovered the vulnerabilities in PHP partially using AI tools, while OpenAI and security firm Calif also say they independently discovered the issues and worked together. Dubbing an exploitation demonstration php2shell , the Wiz researchers write that in some cases the vulnerabilities can be exploited “fairly easily.”

“The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory,” Wiz writes in its research. “That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.”

Details of the upcoming vulnerabilities first appeared from the maintainers behind PHP on October 20. In a short post on the PHP website, the PHP Foundation wrote it was giving “advance notice” of the security flaws and upcoming release of the fixes. While omitting specific details about the vulnerabilities or the versions impacted, it said both flaws are considered to have a “critical” 9.2 score out of 10 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).

“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild,” the security warning on the PHP site said ahead of Wednesday’s release. According to reports from Bleeping Computer and Ars Technica, some details about the vulnerabilities may have leaked before they were due to officially be published.

The early warning from the PHP Foundation may have given some developers, security teams, and companies enough of a heads up to start preparing to update systems using PHP. Ahead of the details being published, warnings from the EU’s Computer Emergency Response Team (EU-CERT) and Australia's cybersecurity agency said IT teams should be prepared to update their systems as soon as possible, with the potential for websites to be taken offline while fixes are applied.

Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) published an alert saying organizations should “prepare for immediate updating of systems” using PHP. “Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organizations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated,” the agency wrote online.

The NCSC advises that organizations and businesses should identify systems running PHP across their tech infrastructure. There should be a particular focus on systems using PHP that are connected to the internet, including monitoring them for any potential exploitation. The next step is applying PHP updates as they are available and monitoring for updates from software companies as they may use PHP within their apps or services.

“If you find signs of compromise, isolate the system, preserve your web server and PHP logs, and report it to your local FBI field office,” Brett Leatherman, the FBI’s cyber assistant director posted online. “Those reports help us identify the actors involved and warn other organizations before they become victims.”

Title: AI Guardrails Aren’t Stopping Criminal Hackers
Context: Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported...
Full Text:
As AI adoption spreads among both malicious hackers and defenders, even relatively unsophisticated cybercriminals are incorporating agentic AI into their campaigns and getting around model safeguards, according to new details published on Wednesday about recent successful attacks by four different threat groups.

Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported groups—one that operates in Chinese, one in Spanish and English, one in Indonesian, and one in Russian. The former two exhibited sophisticated AI “harnesses,” the software that supports and guides a model to carry out tasks. The latter two showed less technical prowess, researchers found, but were still able to compromise multiple targets. All had left their AI infrastructure openly accessible on web servers, allowing the researchers to analyze their activity and which models they used—largely versions of Anthropic’s Claude as well as versions of the open-weight Deepseek models. All the actors devised ways to allow their campaigns to run autonomously over relatively long periods of time.

“You can leverage different models for different aspects in the operation. Model routing and selection is very important because it’s expensive and a lot of times would be overkill to use newer models,” says Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work. The researchers observed the attackers using both open- and closed-weight models; in almost all cases, they were using older versions rather than working with frontier models. Meyers notes that doing as much as possible with older models is common in legitimate AI usage, too, as costs mount.

The attackers also used multiple models to take advantage of differences in the guardrails meant to prevent people from using AI to carry out digital attacks.

“The models don't all have equivalent guardrails and protections, even from one company,” Meyers says. He adds about the sophistication of the hacking campaigns overall that “these attacks are not using new exploits or novel vulnerabilities. They’re really just taking advantage of the speed and the volume that you can use AI for in conducting these operations targeting the bulk of security hygiene issues in a lot of these environments—things that were preventable but weren’t prevented.”

The researchers found that all four threat actors circumvented AI safeguards, often by convincing a model that the activity was all legitimate and authorized, often for penetration testing or other security evaluation. One method used by many of the groups involves adding files to an agent’s working directory to try to show that tasks are approved and authorized. The attackers also used traditional jailbreaking methods, crafting prompts and narratives framing their hacking as authorized and benign, and proactively addressing potential questions or concerns the models might raise. The more sophisticated actors were typically more strategic in their world-building, while the less sophisticated actors sometimes resorted to more crude and aggressive prompts that tried to bully the models into accepting that the activity was legitimate.

The Chinese-speaking actor also used what's known as a “run time patch,” in this case a tool known as ClawGod, to add functionality on top of Claude Code and attempt to remove the “CYBER_RISK_INSTRUCTION” from the Claude Code system prompt, an instruction directing Claude Code to only participate in authorized security testing, not abusive or destructive hacking.

The actor that worked in Spanish and English targeted Argentine health care entities and successfully compromised at least 15 organizations. CrowdStrike researchers see evidence that the actor stole credentials and medical records from at least one of these victims. The actor special built a penetration testing harness, the kind an organization would use to test its own infrastructure, to find and fix vulnerabilities. Using models including Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Deepseek V4 Pro, the group set up a full infrastructure for autonomous attacks involving a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent to direct the steps of an attack and an “Executor” agent to carry them out.

The attacker working in Chinese also built penetration testing harnesses to guide Claude Code in reconnaissance and then autonomously attack once a human had selected a course of action. The researchers found that the actor successfully compromised government targets in both Brazil and Colombia and also targeted private organizations in Brazil and the United States in a range of sectors that include biotech, healthcare, food and beverage, retail, technology, and travel.

According to the researchers, the Chinese-speaking actor primarily relied on Claude Opus 4.8, but also used other models including Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Deepseek Chat. The actor accessed Claude through an AI proxy service based in China but set up multiple fallbacks to other AI tools if Claude was not available through the proxy.

Anthropic did not provide comment ahead of publication, and Deepseek did not immediately respond to WIRED's requests for comment.

The researchers say that both the Russian-speaking actor, which seems to have been focused on financially motivated “e-crime,” and the Indonesian-speaking actor (the least sophisticated of the four) used more basic, publicly available skills and harnesses to carry out their attacks. But both were still successful at compromising targets. This included multiple Indonesian government domains, a Bangladeshi government domain, and some private-sector targets, in the case of the Indonesian-speaking actor.

“What we are seeing is humans are doing some of the initial probing in these situations and then they’re engaging the AI for the hacking at scale,” CrowdStrike’s Meyers says. “I find it interesting that even with agentic attacks with all of these capabilities, we could still see that there’s a human behind it and what they’re up to.”

Full Text:
Five years ago, AI security was a forward-looking line item. Today it’s an operational reality, and the data shows most security programs haven’t caught up.

In the 2026 State of AI Security report, the Orca Research Pod found that 51.5% of organizations are building custom AI apps. 56% are running agent frameworks in production. This isn’t a pilot phase anymore. Agents have real cloud permissions. RAG pipelines are wired into sensitive data. Models are fine-tuned on proprietary datasets. It’s production infrastructure now, and nobody’s wrapped the usual production controls around any of it.

The gap is everywhere in the report:

81% of organizations with AI packages carry at least one known vulnerability, up from 62% two years ago. Half of those alerts have public exploits.

57.1% of Bedrock-using organizations run agents with no safety guardrails configured.

Between 87% and 98% of AI workloads across AWS, Azure, and GCP have never had customer-managed encryption turned on.

33% of organizations have GitHub Copilot deployed, and Stanford research found developers using AI coding assistants write measurably less secure code while rating it as more secure than it is.

This isn’t one misconfiguration. It’s AI shipping faster than the governance meant to secure it, and that now includes the applications AI itself is generating.

Regulation is closing that gap on its own timeline. The EU AI Act’s high-risk obligations take effect August 2, 2026, with fines up to €35M or 7% of global turnover. Colorado’s amended AI law takes effect January 1, 2027. If you deploy AI in the EU or in high-risk use cases like hiring, credit, or healthcare, the misconfigurations in this report are compliance liabilities today.

Your organization has AI risk. The adoption numbers guarantee it. What matters is whether you can show where you stand, to a regulator, a board, or your own team, before someone else asks first.

Benchmark Where You Actually Stand, Then Get Your Next Step

Industry-wide numbers tell you what the space looks like. Where your organization falls against them tells you what to do Monday morning.

Orca’s AI Security Readiness Assessment gives you that read in five questions and under a minute. No email required to see your score. It covers the five domains where AI risk lands first for security leaders:

AI visibility — sanctioned and shadow AI across your cloud and SaaS footprint. The layer most CISOs say they can’t fully see.

AI in your SOC — whether AI is doing real security work for your team, or just adding another surface to defend

Governance — what you could put in front of a regulator today, not what your policy says you’d eventually produce

Wherever you land, your result comes with a next step matched to it, not a generic thank-you page.
