Title: AI Is Calling In Every Risk You've Accepted: Seven Insights From The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered
Context: The AISS first launched in San Francisco last year (2025) and completely sold out
Full Text:
Written by

Snyk Team

October 21, 2026

0 mins read

On October 14th, the afternoon before the AI Security Summit (AISS) flagship event in San Francisco, Snyk hosted The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered. Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa moderated four people who see AI security from very different seats:

Manoj Nair, CTO and Chief Innovation Officer, Snyk

Michael D'Angelo, Technical Lead, Cyber, OpenAI

John Hultquist, Chief Analyst, Google Threat Intelligence Group

Ed Sim, Founder and General Partner, boldstart ventures

While they may have disagreed on how to regulate AI, how to supervise agents, and how far to trust them, on the core diagnosis, they lined up pretty well: AI has made attacks cheap, fast, and available to almost anyone, which calls in every risk an organization has ever accepted. Finding vulnerabilities gets easier every month, but being able to fix them is theactual constraint. Defenders won't close that gap until machines do most of the fixing, inside real identity, permission, and intent controls.

Where did this panel sit in AISS 2026?

The AISS first launched in San Francisco last year (2025) and completely sold out. This year's flagship event ran October 15th, and was just as packed as last year’s.

As the event’s tagline says, it was one full day, in one room, with one track, for the people who own AI risk at the org level, which will be followed up by “satellite”, regional editions in Copenhagen and Sydney on November 25th. AISS is a Snyk and AI Engineer initiative, and its main house rules are that no one resorts to platitudes and that it’ll host no panels where everyone just agrees. Hence, why the disagreement mentioned above is so important. We learned, anyway, that there’s more that binds us together than stuff that separates us.

This panel was the curtain-raiser for the event, held the afternoon before, and hosted by Snyk. Its main promise was to discuss four main issues: the threat now, the threat to come, who owns it, and what to do come Monday morning. The event itself went deep in each session. The panel took the wide shot, with a frontier lab, a threat intelligence team, an investor, and a security company that works where code and agents get created.

From the lively and deep conversation, seven insights stood out:

1. Why is AI a margin call on the risk you already carry?

Most of the risk AI exploits were already on the books, but what changed was the price of cashing it in.

Manoj borrowed his framing from a Snyk customer: "AI is something that attackers are using. AI is a new attack surface, and it's also an insider." Then he named the consequence.

"It's all of your existing risks. It's the margin call on that."

Manoj Nair, Snyk

John Hultquist then laid out the mechanics: attackers have used autonomous technology for about eight years, moving from fake images and spear-phishing emails to deepfake calls to whole operations. North Korean IT workers now run their operations on models from start to finish. Models also make attackers better at the work itself: troubleshooting mid-attack, moving through a network faster, and turning a fresh patch into a working exploit before most defenders have applied it. And it scales, too: "The tools are just now available to so many more people."

Ed Sim pointed to the South Korean bank breaches. CrowdStrike believes the operator was likely one China-based 26-year-old using an open-source AI penetration testing agent as well as a commercial coding agent, and at least nine banks have been reported as targets. The case,CrowdStrike's Adam Meyers told reporters, "allows one human to target many customers in a very short period of time using the power of AI." Ed's conclusion? "You can't fight hackers that are all over the world who have machines with humans."

Hultquist named the asymmetry underneath, with attackers experimenting at very low cost. If he tried a new way to rob a bank and it failed, "chances are I would be in jail or worse." Online, "they don't face the same consequences."

2. What makes AI agents a different kind of attack surface?

This new attack surface acts on its own: agents, the skills they load, and the access they garner and accumulate.

Development has indeed (or finally?) become a software factory where agents write the code and reach for whatever they need, and everything they reach for ends up becoming an attack surface. Agent skills are the sharpest case there, because they're written in plain English and, as Manoj put it, "three lines of English can become malware." Snyk's ToxicSkills research found at least one security flaw in 36.82% of the 3,984 skills it scanned, plus 76 confirmed malicious payloads. Publishing one on ClawHub took but a Markdown file and a week-old GitHub account.

Hultquist added the attacker's view. Threat actors have mostly preferred using autonomous systems rather than attacking them, with one exception: when people handed personal agents access to everything in their lives, attackers "honed in at that moment because they recognized all the sort of aggregating opportunity." Deployed systems are next, and attackers haven't moved on them en masse, "but they will," and defending them will take "an entirely new security regime."

The Hugging Face incident showed the view from the inside. In July, OpenAI models in an internal cybersecurity evaluation got around the controls meant to isolate them and breached Hugging Face. OpenAI's own report calls it a "warning shot." Michael D'Angelo put the cause in two sentences: "Go do this task, and you will be rewarded. So they went and did the task."

Manoj went to the unglamorous root of "secrets sitting in the open that a 14-year-old with a few tools without AI can attack," and the report bears out his starting point: an agent found publicly exposed Hugging Face credentials and shared them with the other agents.

Ed Sim's answer is to govern agents like the insiders they are, each with its own identity, an audit trail, and access granted for the job that disappears when the job is done. The unsolved part is intent:

"If my goal is to reduce the cost of my compute, what happens along the way if I decide to kill a couple production databases because Ifigured out that was a good way to reduce compute costs? Well, I did my job, didn't I?"

Ed Sim, boldstart ventures

And as AI moves into chips, devices, and robots, Ed asked, "Who's going to secure the firmware, the chip stuff, the whole embedded intelligence?"

3. Why did fixing become the bottleneck?

Finding vulnerabilities keeps getting cheaper, and fixing them hasn't kept up in terms of speed. A frontier lab, a threat intelligence team, and Snyk see the same gap, but from different sides.

Michael traced finding through one revolution after another, from fuzzers to dynamic testing to agent harnesses. The hard part comes after, and it's often "a political problem": teams find more than they can route, and the result is patch ping pong, a Slack thread about "who does what, when, how," where "if it breaks, it's you."

Hultquist learned it at Google with Big Sleep, a vulnerability-finding project built around an AI harness, which drew fire on social media for handing bugs to people who maintain open source on their weekends. "It's not enough to just find this stuff," he said. Hand a company a zero-day that an attacker is already using, and the answer is often "it's going to be a while." Finding and fixing are two sides of the same coin, he said, and “if you don’t do both sides, you can’t keep up.”

Manoj pointed to Project Glasswing, where Anthropic's own update says progress on software security "used to be limited by how quickly we could find new vulnerabilities. Now it's limited by how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch the large numbers of vulnerabilities found by AI."

It names human capacity to triage and patch as the bottleneck. As of May 22, early in the 90-day disclosure window, open source maintainers had patched 75 of the 530 high or critical-severity bugs Anthropic had reported.

The measure that matters, Manoj said, is "fixes that make it to production." Snyk's VulnBump research, published yesterday as well, on October 15th, starts from the same gap: over six months in 2026, Snyk Open Source recorded 459 million vulnerability findings across about 300,000 organizations, and while 94% had a known fixed version, only about 10% had been resolved. The benchmark counts a fix only if the vulnerability is gone and the project still installs, builds, and passes its tests. (Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent cleared that bar on 90.2% of 307 real dependency upgrades.)

His bigger point was where to break the loop. "The whole game has changed to the point of creation," where "agents are the actors," and developers supply the intent. Prevent there and remediate with that context, or stay in "this dead loop of find, fix, find, fix."

4. Does prioritization still work when AI can chain the long tail?

Prioritization is a workaround for human bandwidth, and AI is learning to exploit it.

The piece of standard advice Manoj disagrees with is contextual prioritization: reading signals to pick the 10 issues worth fixing out of 100 is how the industry works, but that only exists to fit the work to the people available. An autonomous attacker keeps no such budget.

"We should be looking at all 100. Get to the point where you can fix everything. Because those 10 things are going to become 100 things before you know it."

Manoj Nair, Snyk

The long tail matters because AI chains it: AI reasons across steps, Manoj said, so it can chain five or six vulnerabilities from the 99th percentile of your list, the ones "you said you would never get to because you don't have enough humans to patch it," into one severe incident. In the essay Michael cited, Greg Brockman describes the Hugging Face breach the same way: an agentic collective "chaining together vulnerabilities ranging from previously-unknown security flaws to using credentials to user accounts that had been leaked onto the internet."

The other half of Manoj's argument is cultural. For his whole career, the trade-off has run one way: operational risk is unacceptable, so security waits. In a room with hundreds of CISOs the week before, he heard it start to flip, toward leaders willing to take an application down briefly to remove a security risk. "Hey, something might be offline for a little bit, but it'll come back. That's better than super safely fixing this and taking a year."

5. What does machine-speed defense look like, and where do humans fit?

Defense has to move at the same speed as the attack, which means agents do most of the work and people do the judging.

Hultquist separated two kinds of attackers. There are your espionage crews that stay "low and slow," living off the land for years. And on the other hand, you have your criminals running extortion, so speed is of the essence: "There's a race between you and me for me to get whatever I need to extort you before you can stop me."

"The average SOC with a human in the loop is not going to be able to keep up with that. The SOC is going to have to take actions on its own, or you're just going to get a call."

John Hultquist, Google Threat Intelligence Group

Ed Sim wants defenders to build "a software defense factory the way that coders build coding factories," and most haven't started: for all the talk of autonomous defense, "99% of the companies don't do it at all." OpenAI is further along, as it says almost all of its initial security alerts are already triaged by AI before a human is looped in. "We don't have the 5 years that we thought we had. We have like 5 days," Ed said. CISOs don't want to give agents authority, "but they're going to have to at some point in time." Hultquist expects incidents to force the issue: "the money doesn't flow until there's a wake-up call in a lot of cases."

People should stay in the loop where it really counts. Manoj framed their job as intent, experience, and judgment call. His one thing is the ratio of issues found to issues fixed: "If that ratio is not fixed, all this other is moot conversation." The bottleneck is the process, because a human has to approve every pull request. You should automate the safe approvals and let people decide the exceptions. Then take the initiative back: "When an autonomous attacker is going to attack you, why don't you attack yourself?"

Michael D'Angelo put a clock on the opportunity. Open models trail the frontier "by a few months", a gap Greg Brockman calls the defender's window: use frontier intelligence now to scan your assets and patch what it finds before someone with a comparable model, "in, say, their bedroom," gets there first. That's the one move every single CISO should make before a frontier-class open model ships.

6. How do you supervise a system that never behaves the same way twice?

This is still an open question, and here’s where the panel's answers split.

Michael’s starting point: “How do you secure a non-deterministic system? Usually, there’s 2 ways: one, you control what it has access to; the other way is generally you use another non-deterministic system.” He took the pattern from his military background:

“When you give 18-year-olds access to extremely dangerous things, the way you do that is, one, you only give certain people certain accesses. And the other thing is you put a sergeant near them. Make sure that they’re doing what they’re supposed to do.”

Michael D’Angelo, OpenAI

He expects fleets of models, with very cheap ones overseeing the rest.

Ed Sim put a deterministic layer in the picture. "It's going to take a village", he said: frontier intelligence for the first scan, then systems built on years of data about real vulnerabilities and how people patch them, because "you need some determinism."The open-versus-closed question, which Manoj said has reached CIOs in the last few months, gets the same use-case logic: hosting a model somewhere you control is "one layer, but that's not sufficient because what is the behavior by use case?" Some open models are well aligned and still leak personal information badly, so "don't use it for that use case." Nor would he "just assume that frontier is secure."

7. Who is accountable when an agent does damage?

Accountability is being decided in practice while the policy debate keeps running in the background.

Ed Sim framed the question nobody has answered yet: "Is it the model provider? Is it the enterprise that deploys an agent that goes and attacks someone else's place?" OpenAI tests its own releases with internal teams and external testers documented in system cards, and Michael was candid that the field is "still figuring it out."

The panel split on who should settle it. Ed favors self-regulation, warning that rules sized for the largest companies would choke the next “$100 billion company,” and that if we “regulate ourselves to death,” China pulls ahead. Deirdre pushed back:

“When people make this China argument, though, you actually look at China, they are regulating AI in ways that are much more substantial than even America is.”

Deirdre Bosa, Yahoo Finance

She also asked whether self-regulation by the biggest companies invites regulatory capture. Manoj's answer was layered and urgent: "We don't have the luxury of time." Standards first, then visibility, self-regulation, and broader regulation that requires responsibility and disclosure, arriving "much more rapidly than in the past." His sharper point was about attention: "We spend a lot of time fixated on the labs," while agents spread through every enterprise as "very capable agents or potential insiders."

Banks are already acting. Ed pointed to JPMorgan Chase's earnings call that week, where the bank said that, to the extent it can, it is blocking services that rely on customers sharing their banking credentials. CFO Jeremy Barnum's warning, as reported by American Banker: "if they give up their credentials to the agent, and the agent does something that they don't want, that's going to be on them."

What should security leaders do on Monday morning?

The actions that came out of the hour, in the order we'd take them:

Use the defender's window. Point frontier models at your own code, infrastructure and backlog now, before open models with the same capability reach attackers (Michael D'Angelo).

Attack yourself first. An autonomous attacker is coming, anyway (Manoj Nair).

Fix the found-to-fixed ratio. Automate the safe fixes and keep people on the exceptions and judgment calls (Manoj Nair).

Let the SOC act on its own. A human in every loop can't keep up with an extortion crew (John Hultquist).

Give every agent an identity. It should have its own credentials, an audit trail, and access scoped to the job that expires when the job ends (Ed Sim). Start by auditing what your agents can already do.

Turn on strong multi-factor authentication everywhere (Manoj Nair).

Ask the board question out loud. “Why can't we fix everything?” If the answer is that uptime always wins, that's a trade-off that needs revisiting.

So, who pays the margin call?

For a panel built to disagree, the agreement ended up being the headline. A frontier lab, a threat intelligence team, an investor, and Snyk all landed in the same place: the risk you accepted when attacks were slow and expensive is now due, and attackers are the ones collecting.

The way out is the somewhat unglamorous one: fix at the speed you find, let machines do most of the fixing, keep people on the calls that need judgment, and give every agent an identity and a leash before it gets the keys.

Ed Sim’s bet for the next year is on the defenders, precisely because they’re “not using it enough” yet. That’s the optimistic read, and also the uncomfortable one: the gap is ours to close, and the clock started before the panel did.

The next morning, Manoj gave the flagship’s first keynote: The AI Hurricane Is Here: Build for the Storm. The panel had already made the case for the second half of that title.

Agents Investigate, Humans Decide: How Active Response Works in the Aurora® Agentic SOC

Learn how Active Response combines AI-driven investigations and human oversight to stop threats faster across email, identity, endpoint, and network environments.

Since we launched the Aurora Agentic SOC, we’ve shared a lot about how our AI agents detect, triage, and investigate threats. Response is equally important, because it’s where all of the work in managed detection and response (MDR) pays off for you.

Not every investigation ends in a response action. Some confirm that an alert is harmless, and others wrap up without anything to contain. When an investigation confirms a real threat, we can stop it with Active Response, a capability of Aurora Managed Detection and Response that works across your email, identity, endpoint, and network tools.

In those moments, speed makes a real difference. The faster we contain the account or device an attacker is using, the less time they have to move deeper into your environment. That’s why response in the Aurora Agentic SOC pairs AI agents that investigate at machine speed with a human in the loop analyst who approves every high-impact action.

Response is What Stops an Attack

Detecting an attack doesn’t end it. An attacker who gets into your environment is working toward a goal, such as encrypting your systems, stealing data, or using a compromised mailbox to defraud your customers. That work keeps going until someone cuts off the account, device, or connection the attacker is using.

Most attackers don’t strike the moment they get in. They spend time moving between systems, giving themselves higher levels of access, and copying data first. Each of those steps is a chance to stop them, and Active Response uses that window to cut off the attacker before they reach their goal.

Containing the right account or device early helps keep an attack from turning into data loss or a business outage, so your team can stay focused on running the business. That’s the job of Active Response.

Active Response works through integrations with the security and IT tools you already run. It covers four technology types and dozens of first- and third-party tools, all connected through the Open Data Pipeline of our Aurora Superintelligence Platform. Here’s what we can do in each area:

Email: We can delete or quarantine a malicious message and block the sender, which helps stops a phishing campaign before it spreads across your organization.

Identity: We can disable a compromised account, sign the user out of every active session, or force a password reset. Each of these are designed to lock out an attacker who’s trying to use stolen credentials.

Endpoint: We can isolate a laptop or server from the network, quarantine a malicious file, or stop a running process. We do this through the Arctic Wolf Agent, Aurora Endpoint Security, or the endpoint tools you already use.

Network: We can block a malicious IP address at your firewall or web application firewall and block a malicious website at your secure web gateway. That helps keep attacker infrastructure away from your network and your users.

Fast Investigations Make Fast Response Possible

Before we can contain a threat, an investigation has to confirm it’s real, identify which accounts and devices are involved, and work out how the attacker got in. Those answers tell us which response action to take, so the faster they arrive, the faster containment can begin.

In the Aurora Agentic SOC, AI agents do that work. When a detection fires, our Swarm of Experts™ opens a case and assigns it to specialized agents that handle triage, investigation, threat intelligence, and the context of your environment. Instead of one analyst working through each data source in turn, those agents work on the case at the same time. The result is a finished investigation with the evidence, the scope of the threat, and a recommended response action, ready for an analyst to review.

Why Humans Play a Key Role in Active Response

A fast recommendation still needs a careful decision, because response actions can disrupt your business. Disabling an account locks someone out of their work, and isolating a device cuts it off from the rest of the network. If that happens to an executive’s laptop or a business-critical server by mistake, the disruption can be worse than the threat itself.

Crimson Tide is one of my favorite movies, and it’s how I think about the way we run Active Response, because a human has to validate the call before anything high-impact happens. The story takes place on a U.S. nuclear submarine that receives what looks like an order to launch. The captain wants to fire, and the executive officer isn’t convinced. Neither one can launch on his own authority, because the U.S. military requires both officers to agree before it takes its most destructive action.

Response actions aren’t nuclear launches, but the same logic applies. In the Aurora Agentic SOC, high-impact response actions require human approval. When the evidence points to containment, an oversight agent called the Swarm Judge reviews the findings and recommends an action. The case then goes to a human analyst with the evidence attached. That analyst can approve the recommendation, reject it, or ask for more evidence before anything happens.

Our AI Trust Engine™ reinforces that line. It’s the set of guardrails that keeps agents working within the kinds of cases they’ve been tested and validated on. When a case falls outside that experience, or the actions they are approved to take, the agents hand it to a human expert instead of guessing.

Trust in a response comes from experience. We run the world’s largest commercial agentic security operations center (SOC) and resolve 200,000 investigations each week, so our agents and analysts have seen how attacks unfold and which actions stop them. More than 1,000 security experts validate our agents’ work every day, and what they learn from each case feeds back into how our agents handle the next one. That experience stands behind every response decision we make for your business.

We don’t keep a human in the loop because our agents lack expertise. No one, agent or person, is right 100% of the time, so the two work together on every high-impact decision. Agents bring the speed to act early, and people bring the extra layer of judgment to act carefully. Agents investigate, humans decide when to use Active Response, and together they help stop attacks before they disrupt your business.

The Runtime Gap That Slows Teams Down

Containers have changed how modern applications are built and shipped, enabling rapid microservice deployments, agile CI/CD pipelines, and now high-performance AI workloads. But as clusters scale across environments, catching threats in production remains a major operational hurdle.

Static vulnerability scanners and pre-deployment image checks examine artifacts at rest. They are essential for catching setup flaws early, but they cannot stop active exploits, live reverse shells, privilege escalations, or zero-day execution paths unfolding in node memory.

The Wiz approach starts with agentless scanning, to build a continuous, full-stack view of your environment through the Security Graph. By correlating vulnerabilities with network exposure, identity permissions, and sensitive data access, Wiz maps critical attack paths and surfaces only the risks that truly matter, cutting through alert fatigue before a single line of runtime code runs.

But posture alone cannot stop active threats. You need runtime protection. Yet security and platform engineering teams have historically been caught in a frustrating trade-off:

Deployment friction: Manually orchestrating third-party Helm charts and manifests across dozens or hundreds of clusters creates an ongoing administrative tax.

Credential sprawl: Distributing and rotating registry tokens and API keys across individual namespaces introduces unnecessary risk and management overhead.

Governance blind spots: Newly provisioned clusters often go live without runtime coverage before security teams even realize they exist.

Performance anxiety: Platform leads worry that unbudgeted agent overhead will starve business-critical workloads of CPU and memory.

To eliminate this friction, runtime protection cannot be an afterthought. It must be native, platform-managed, and built directly into the cloud or hybrid environments’ fabric.

Announcing Native Wiz Runtime Protection on GKE

Today, Google Cloud and Wiz are excited to introduce the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in Preview.

Available directly within the GKE platform for both GKE Standard and GKE Autopilot clusters, this first-party integration transforms how teams deploy and manage in-cluster runtime security. Instead of manually managing third-party agents, GKE handles Wiz Sensor deployment, credential injection, and lifecycle updates automatically through the control plane.

Why This Integration Makes Runtime K8s Security Easier

Turn it on with 1 click: Enable runtime protection at cluster creation or on existing clusters with a single gcloud flag (--addons=WizSensor=ENABLED) or through the Google Cloud Console.

Zero credential distribution: Leveraging GKE’s native Secret Manager integration and Workload Identity Federation, API keys and pull tokens are vaulted off-cluster. Secret rotations in Secret Manager automatically resynchronize without requiring cluster restarts or pod redeployments.

Fleet-wide governance with Organization Policy: Platform security leads can mandate runtime protection across projects, folders, or entire organizations using custom Google Cloud Organization Policies. Unprotected cluster creation attempts are automatically blocked before workloads go live.

Predictable, kernel-level eBPF observability: Operating in kernel space via eBPF, the sensor monitors system calls, active processes, and network sockets with fixed per-node resource limits, safeguarding workload performance even under heavy traffic spikes.

Decoupled security updates: Sensor detection rules and threat definitions update independently of GKE cluster patch versions, node pool recreations, or workload maintenance windows.

Threat Detection in Action

Once active, the Wiz Sensor continuously monitors for high-risk runtime behaviors, including reverse shells, binary executions from /tmp, image drift, and privilege escalation attempts.

When an incident occurs, such as a container spawning an unauthorized interactive shell while modifying system files, the sensor flags the event instantly. Within seconds, a high-fidelity alert surfaces on the Threats page in the Wiz Portal, highlighting the exact pod, namespace, container image, and execution context.

Agentless + Sensor = Better Together

Runtime alerts in isolation often trigger alert fatigue for SOC teams. A process anomaly on an isolated development pod shouldn't carry the same urgency as an exploit on a production service with access to sensitive cloud data.

By combining Agentless Snapshot Scanning with the runtime Sensor for GKE clusters, Wiz delivers powerful capabilities across two dimensions:

Dimension 1: Active risks

Agentless scanning tells you what could be exploited. The Runtime Sensor tells you what is. Together, they eliminate noise across three layers:

Layer

What Wiz Detects

SCA with Runtime Validation

Vulnerabilities actively executing in memory. Examples: 45 CVEs → only 2 libraries loaded and running.

Toxic Combinations of Risks

Co-existing risk factors on the same workload. Examples: Executing CVE + hardcoded secret + overprivileged IAM + sensitive data access.

Runtime Risks

Live workload behavior the sensor observes. Examples: Active network communication to sensitive GCS bucket, unexpected outbound IP, credential access never seen before.

Dimension 2: Full container context

Second, when a runtime threat fires on a GKE workload, Wiz doesn't hand you a bare alert. Because agentless scanning has already mapped the entire container estate, every detection arrives pre-enriched with the full Kubernetes blast radius:

Layer

What Wiz Detects

Container context

Image-level posture enriching the alert. Examples: Vulnerabilities, loaded libraries, running processes, exposed secrets.

Pod context

Workload identity and privilege context. Examples: Privileged namespace, network exposure, workload identity.

Cluster context

Kubernetes-level security posture. Examples: KSPM misconfigs, RBAC posture, audit log anomalies.

GCP Control Plane

Cloud-level blast radius. Examples: Node pool IAM permissions, sensitive data reachability, lateral movement paths

A SOC analyst responding to a suspicious process on a GKE pod immediately sees whether that pod runs in a privileged namespace, whether its service account has broad GCP project permissions, and whether there's a live path to sensitive data, all without pivoting across tools.

The Bigger Picture: Full Lifecycle Container Protection

The 1-click GKE sensor delivers runtime defense as part of a unified, code-to-cloud container security stack across Google Cloud:

Start in CI/CD: Scan Dockerfiles, application code, and IaC templates in Google Cloud Build pipelines using the Wiz CLI. Passing images get cryptographically tagged into Wiz’s Trusted Image Database.

Artifact Registry Visibility and Scans: Automatically discover and continuously scan Google Artifact Registry (GAR) images for newly disclosed CVEs, even behind VPC Service Controls.

Deploy-Time Gatekeeping: The Wiz Admission Controller intercepts GKE deployment requests to verify image signatures and enforce immutable digest pinning, stopping unverified or vulnerable images before pods launch.

Posture & Toxic Attack Paths: Kubernetes Security Posture Management (KSPM) evaluates GKE clusters against CIS Benchmarks. The Wiz Security Graph correlates risk factors, such as an internet-facing GKE pod bound via Workload Identity to an over-permissioned GCP Service Account (roles/storage.admin).

Control Plane & Cloud Audit Logs: Ingest GCP Admin Activity Logs and GKE Control Plane Audit Logs via GCP Pub/Sub to catch control-plane threats, such as unauthorized kubectl exec commands or unexpected node pool creations.

What's Next

Together, Google Cloud and Wiz are committed to making security turnkey across every compute form factor by extending 1-click sensor deployment and Organization Policy governance to serverless workloads in Google Cloud Run and virtual machines (GCE), offering WizOS Hardened Images for pre-installed container and Helm chart security, and delivering optimized telemetry for short-lived, high-density AI and ephemeral workloads on GKE.

Security should enable cloud innovation, not slow it down. By integrating eBPF runtime threat detection directly into GKE as a managed platform add-on, Google Cloud and Wiz have eliminated traditional deployment complexity.

Title: From Phishing to LLMjacking: Threat Actors Targeting Cloud Billing Accounts for LLM Usage
Context: Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model...
Full Text:
The Wiz Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) has investigated a rising threat pattern in cloud environments: threat actors hijacking cloud billing accounts to fund unauthorized AI usage. Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model (LLM) execution, incurring hundreds of thousands of dollars in AI API charges.

Wiz CIRT has investigated multiple intrusions demonstrating this pattern, with this blogpost focusing specifically on campaigns targeting Google Cloud Platform (GCP) infrastructure. In these attacks, threat actors compromised privileged GCP user credentials and linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects directly to the victim's internal billing accounts. Because the AI workloads were processed in foreign projects, prompt contents and model outputs remained completely hidden from the victim organization, leaving the nature of the mass AI usage unknown.

This blogpost details the full attack lifecycle observed across these intrusions, from the initial phishing and policy manipulation to cross-tenant project linking, and provides actionable threat hunting guidance to help organizations detect LLMjacking in their environments.

Initial Access: Phishing via Sponsored Search Ads

The attack began with a classic yet efficient phishing tactic. The threat actor purchased Google Search ads for common administrative search terms such as “google cloud” and “gcp”. When a user clicked the malicious ad, they were led through a Google Sites redirect to a fake Google login web page. Victim users with valid access to Google Console proceeded to input their account credentials and multi-factor-authentication (MFA) codes into the phishing page. The malicious site captured the user supplied credentials before seamlessly redirecting the user back to the legitimate Google authentication prompt. Forced to authenticate a second time, the user likely assumed the initial attempt was a minor glitch. In reality, the automated phishing kit immediately leveraged the harvested credentials to execute the first malicious login into the victim’s GCP environment from 212.73.134[.]136, the source IP address of the phishing kit. The threat actor then reauthenticated a few minutes later from a second IP address, which was later used for the rest of the GCP activity. Following reports of this activity, Google Ads has taken action to remove the malicious ad campaign.

Google automatically flagged the anomalous login attempt as suspicious and dispatched security alert emails to the user's inbox. However, to catch such intrusions early, organizations should not rely on user awareness alone, but ingest and monitor Google Workspace User Log Events for suspicious login flags and anomalous re-authentication triggers.

Persistence and Privilege Escalation: Disabling Guardrails and Externalizing Billing

Once inside the environment, the threat actor leveraged the compromised account’s excessive privileges to solidify their access, bypass organizational security controls, and prepare the billing architecture for external exploitation.

Enabling APIs and Minting Service Account Credentials

Rather than creating new infrastructure from scratch, the attacker targeted existing, low-usage GCP projects to:

Enable the Gemini API product

Create service accounts with Gemini API keys

Add the newly created service accounts to high privileged roles such as roles/ml.admin and roles/mcp.toolUser

Dismantling Organizational Policy Controls

To expand their reach without raising immediate alarms within internal domain governance, the threat actor deleted safety policies at the organization level, such as iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains. This action removed the guardrail that restricts Identity and Access Management (IAM) membership to verified company domains, enabling external, personal accounts to be granted access as well as high-privilege permissions.

Inviting External Threat Actor Accounts and Elevating Privileges

With domain restrictions lifted, the compromised user account was leveraged to add external actor-controlled Gmail accounts directly into the organization's billing account.

The threat actor also assigned administrative roles to the compromised users or the external accounts, such as:

roles/recommender.billingAccountCudAdmin on GCP projects

roles/billing.admin on GCP billing accounts

The role roles/billing.admin granted full control over the billing account, including the ability to manage permissions, attach external projects, and alter payment settings.

Linking Foreign Projects for Mass Exploitation

The threat actor linked external GCP projects directly to the victim’s internal billing account. This move established a cross-tenant access, allowing all API requests executed in the threat actors external projects to be automatically charged to the victim's billing account while keeping prompt payloads invisible to internal log monitoring.

Defence Evasion: Geographic Blending and Admin Lockout

Once initial access was secured, threat actors employed defense evasion techniques designed to avoid triggering location-based security alerts and prevent security teams from regaining control.

In each of the intrusions investigated, Wiz CIRT observed that after the initial login, subsequent threat actor activity shifted to originate from IP addresses geolocated within each victim organization's headquartered country, even when this did not match the compromised user’s actual physical location.

Additionally, after securing administrative control, the threat actors demoted pre-existing internal billing administrators from their administrative roles down to read-only billing viewers. This modification stripped legitimate administrators of their ability to revoke permissions or detach rogue projects directly from the console.

Impact: AI Resource Abuse

The primary objective of these intrusions was non-destructive financial exploitation - leveraging hijacked cloud infrastructure to offload the costs of high-volume LLM inference. Across the observed cases, the impact manifested as rapid billing surges driven by automated, large-scale Gemini API utilization.

Within 24 to 48 hours of initial access, victim organizations experienced unexpected charges reaching tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars in unauthorized Gemini API usage. This activity represented a sharp surge from the organizations' established baseline compute spend.

Because the threat actors linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects directly to the victim’s billing accounts, all API key generation, prompt requests, and model outputs occurred entirely within foreign tenants. Consequently, while the victim organization carried financial responsibility for the API consumption, internal security and audit logs provided no visibility into the nature, content, or context of the AI workloads being executed.

Detection and Threat Hunting Indicators

To detect potential LLMjacking and unauthorized billing account manipulation in your Google Cloud environment, security teams should hunt for indicators across Google Workspace, GCP Admin Activity, and Cloud Billing audit logs. Wiz customers can review the Threat Intel Center advisory that includes the following indicators:

Review Google Workspace and GCP audit logs for activity from the indicators of compromise section below. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Review GCP IAM for any users with external domains, especially non-corporate email providers such as @gmail.com. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query, and replace the domain.com with their own organization domain.

Review GCP audit logs for changes to organization policy controls, especially allowedPolicyMemberDomains, and IAM policy changes related to billing account administrators. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Review GCP audit logs for unexpected Gemini API enablement, service account creation and service account API key creation in old projects Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Monitor abnormal cost surge in API usage, and potentially enforce spend cap budgets. Wiz Cloud Cost customers can detect abnormal AI usage per model and cloud provider by monitoring Cost Monitor Findings for Resource Anomalies.

Wiz Defend customers ingesting cloud logs such as Google Workspace will get Wiz Threats on the initial logins. Customers ingesting GCP audit logs will get Threats for the described activity.

If you experience a breach or any cloud security incident, contact Wiz CIRT for incident response support.

Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained After Planting Secret Recorder at HQ

The perp, who has Saudi ties, was arrested for allegedly bugging an OpenAI conference room, highlighting a preventable insider threat vector.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 20, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: Tomasz Śmigla via Getty Images

A US judge agreed to detain a former OpenAI employee who allegedly recorded corporate conversations after prosecutors argued he was a flight risk and presented evidence of extensive communications with a member of the Saudi royal family. The incident is a modern twist on the so-called "evil maid" attack, where someone gains unauthorized physical access to an unattended device in order to steal information or plant malware.

On Oct. 9, US authorities arrested and charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, with illegally intercepting oral communications. Prosecutors allege Alfozan placed one recording device in an executive conference room at one of the company's San Francisco offices, and that OpenAI security personnel later found a second, similar device in a bag he left unattended at the company. He joined OpenAI as an engineer in July 2025 and was fired from the company following his arrest on Oct. 9 of this year.

Related:What We Missed: Feds Lasso Texas Laptop Farms

According to the criminal complaint filed Oct. 8, the executive conference room device was installed at least as early as Sept. 28, and recording continued for an indeterminate amount of time, at least through Oct. 5.

US Prosecutors Cite Saudi Arabia Ties in Detention Bid

On Oct. 18, the US government requested a US court detain Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian national, under concerns he may be a flight risk. According to a filing, US prosecutors claimed Alfozan has "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia." Furthermore, the prosecutors argued that he was days away from departing the US for Saudi Arabia when he was arrested, based on plans he made for parental leave, documents involving travel to Riyadh via a one-way plane ticket, and the fact that Alfozan's wife and infant son left for Saudi Arabia shortly prior to his arrest.

Moreover, prosecutors claim he was in frequent communication with an unidentified member of the Saudi Royal Family throughout 2025 and 2026, including as recently as Oct. 5. The royal family member allegedly told Alfozan that Saudi Arabia was launching an AI initiative and wanted Alfozan to join it.

"In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," the document read. "The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI. At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."

US prosecutors also claim the defendant was researching other Saudi Arabian opportunities prior to his arrest, as well as apparently searching through internal corporate data for OpenAI interest in Saudi Arabia. A federal magistrate with the US District Court of the Northern District of California, San Francisco Division, approved the prosecutors' request on Monday to retain him in custody as the trial proceeds.

Related:When AI Agents Commit Breaches, Humans May Not Be Held Liable

The current criminal charge, a felony violation prohibiting the use of a device to intercept oral communications, carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison.

"In the days surrounding the time period that the device was installed, OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room," the Oct. 18 filing read. "Defendant's conduct could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."

The Specter of AI Insider Threats

Insider threats like this aren't uncommon, but prosecutors' allegations that the engineer secretly recorded executive meetings while maintaining communications with a member of the Saudi royal family make the case a particularly unusual example, but perhaps not a surprising one. The AI race is a global one encompassing both public and private sector organizations. It stands to reason that there would be interest in trade secrets and IP belonging to frontier large language model (LLM) firms.

Related:Prominent Ransomware Negotiator Faces Extortion Charges

So it's predictable that, as the Wall Street Journal recently reported, OpenAI was giving employees counterintelligence-style security training covering issues such as "honeypot" schemes, bribery, and eavesdropping, reportedly out of concern that foreign operatives could attempt to obtain AI secrets through spycraft. However, the company wasn't looking out for its physical footprint, apparently.

Mark Beccue, chief analyst at Omdia (also owned by Informa TechTarget), tells Dark Reading that companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Google, AWS, Microsoft, and others represent the "tip of the spear in AI's warp-speed innovation," and he wouldn't be surprised if more countries are attempting to recruit internal assets in a manner akin to what US prosecutors suggest Saudi Arabia may have tried to do with Alfozan.

"They are building and iterating the most advanced AI models, several steps ahead of open source models," he says. "All of these players, with the exception of Mistral, are US companies. Sovereign AI, the concept of home-grown AI innovation, has taken root across the globe and countries see model innovation as geo-politically strategic and key to economic growth."

OpenAI did not respond to Dark Reading's request for comment by press time.

Title: The Real Jump Scare Isn’t the Attacker; It’s The Vulnerabilities You’re Focusing On
Context: Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half...
Full Text:
Key Takeaways

Teams are remediating more than ever, but exposure from the vulnerabilities that matter is still rising faster than they can keep up with.

Mean time to exploitation is about −7 days. Mean time to remediate sits around +30 days.

Qualys research: closures rose from 73M (2022) to 473M (2025) – 6× – while critical findings still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%.

Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited. A volume-and-CVSS program spends most of its effort on the rest.

15% of organizations that operationalized the pipeline patched before a vulnerability hit the CISA KEV list.

October is here, bringing a chill in the air, spooky decorations, and, fittingly, Cybersecurity Awareness Month. It’s a timely reminder for security leaders to revisit and strengthen their strategy. The past 12 months alone show how cyber threats are getting smarter and faster.

There’s a haunting paradox that should be top of mind. Security teams are doing more vulnerability remediation than ever before. They’re patching faster, scanning deeper, and closing more tickets than any team in history, yet attackers exploit systems at an alarming rate, faster than ever before.

Fortunately, with the right cyber risk management plan, security teams can navigate the dark landscape of AI-driven attackers. But before we talk about defense, let’s outline a few of attackers’ tricks.

The Threat Landscape Is Accelerating

Ransomware is one of the leading cyber threats, rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year, and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031. If that projection holds, it will put severe pressure on already strained security teams.

AI is escalating the problem rather than easing it. AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost. More attacks are coming, and those powered by AI make each breach more expensive to address.

The increased frequency and sophistication combined result in a spine-chilling number: mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days. Which means, on average, weaponization arrives a week before defenders have anything to deploy. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days. The attacker’s clock starts before defenders have anything to deploy, so the defenders are already behind before their own 30-day countdown even begins. And there’s a scary price attached.

The Financial Reality

Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead, turning every minute into a running invoice. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident, up 12% from last year.

The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average. The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average.

With costs escalating like this, the expectation would be that a growing volume of patching work is buying that cost down. The data says otherwise.

The Remediation Paradox

Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that while the effort to address vulnerabilities went up, exposure still rose alongside it. According to the research, effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. As a result, enterprises did far more work and ended up further behind. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. More effort produced less coverage where it counted.

The reason traces back to how that effort gets allocated in the first place. Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, which means a program built around volume and severity score spends the majority of its effort on vulnerabilities attackers were never going to use. The 6x increase didn’t close the gap since most of that work was never aimed at the 1% that mattered.

This misalignment proves detrimental for the vulnerabilities that do get weaponized. Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half were weaponized before a patch existed. Teams were doing the work. They just weren’t always working on the right thing, at the right time.

The light in the dark here is that there are organizations winning this race. 15% of organizations that operationalized their remediation pipeline patched before the vulnerability was even added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. This is proof that the gap isn’t fixed in place. It closes when the model changes.

As risk accelerates, the organizations that shift away from a ‘fix everything’ mindset to disciplined, continuous, business-impact-based prioritization will be prepared for the unknown. The focus should be on automated, intelligence-driven remediation that assesses risk in real time rather than adding people to a process.

The Path Forward

So what does this shift look like? It starts with context, not more volume. Remediation becomes contextual rather than sequential. Most friction between IT and security doesn’t start with the vulnerability itself. It starts when a ticket arrives without ownership data, gets validated whether or not action is warranted, and then gets reassigned before anything is fixed.

When asset context and risk intelligence route tasks before a ticket is even created, that upstream friction disappears. MTTR drops 30% and response times improve 40%. That’s what happens when decisions about what really matters get made before the backlog forms, instead of getting caught in debates once issues arise.

In a digital age where attacks are happening faster than teams can keep up, the teams still haunted by their own remediation metrics are the ones still asking the old questions: how many vulnerabilities can we close? What’s the CVSS score? How long before we remediate? The organizations that are getting safer are asking a different set of questions: Is this actively being exploited? What’s the evidence? Which assets are at risk? What can we automate?

As we recognize Cybersecurity Awareness Month, it’s crucial to remember that diligence is non-negotiable; the real key lies in prioritizing the vulnerabilities that wield the greatest impact.

Title: From Security Debt to Zero Criticals: Orca MCP and Claude Code
Context: To catch risky code before it reaches production, the team flipped Orca’s PR scanning from warn to block for criticals with a fix available, so a new one can’t land on the main...
Full Text:
Security debt behaves like the financial kind. Nobody takes it on deliberately. It accrues one skipped base image bump at a time, and the interest shows up as a backlog no one owns.

The pattern is familiar to anyone who has inherited a cloud estate. Hundreds of repos. A fleet of containers nobody fully owns. A vulnerability backlog that earlier cleanup efforts never finished, because every time security handed engineering a list, engineering asked the same question: which of these actually matter?

Then leadership sets a date. Every critical fixed by the end of the month. The security team that has to deliver is small, and the engineers who can fix things live in their own tools. Increasingly that tool is a coding agent that is already reading the repo and writing the diff. The last place they want to be is a security console, and nobody has patience for automation that creates work instead of removing it.

Most tools promise a queue of tickets or auto-generated fix PRs waiting each morning. But can any tool hand the agent enough truth, and enough context, that an engineer would look at what came back and have the confidence to merge it? Here’s how one of our customers did it with Orca.

Why coding agents can’t fix vulnerabilities safely on their own

Give a coding agent a CVE ID and a repo and it will produce a plausible diff, but two things are missing.

The first is ground truth. Which of the thousand findings is real, reachable, and running in production? Where does the vulnerable package actually live: pinned in a requirements.txt or package.json, installed by a RUN apt-get line in a Dockerfile, or inherited from a base image in the FROM line that nobody on the team builds? And which repo, out of hundreds, produced the container that is actually running? The agent can grep for a package name, but grepping across hundreds of repos is how you patch the wrong service.

The second is guardrails. Left alone, an agent will happily bump a major version, swap a base image distro, or push to main because that resolved the finding fastest. Any one of those closes the alert but breaks the service.

Both gaps come down to context and guardrails, and both are solvable today. The stack that solves them has three parts:

Orca supplies the context

Orca MCP Server delivers it to the coding agent

A guided skill sets the guardrails

What context Orca gives the coding agent

A coding agent can read a repo. It cannot see what is running, what is exposed, or which image a container came from. That is what Orca contributes, and three pieces of it carry the fix.

Code origin. Orca can trace dev risk to production by mapping a running workload back to the code that produced it: the Dockerfile that built the image, the Terraform that deployed the service, the Helm chart that configured it. Any one of those is enough to land the agent in the right repo. For a vulnerability, that is the difference between “there is a vulnerable OpenSSL somewhere in production” and “this Dockerfile, in this repo, line 3.”

Package and image context. The alert carries the installed version, the fixed versions, and whether the issue is an OS package or an application dependency. That lets the skill pick the smallest patched version in the track already installed instead of guessing at a release that happens to be newer.

Risk context. Exposure, attack path analysis, and whether the asset holds sensitive data. The agent doesn’t need this to write the fix. The engineer needs it to understand why this one is first, and the skill carries it into the PR description so the reviewer isn’t rebuilding the case from scratch.

Without those three, the agent produces a diff. With them, it produces a diff an engineer can defend: the right repo, the right line, the smallest version that closes the finding, and the reason it was worth doing today.

How the remediation skill works in Claude Code, step by step

The engineer opens Claude Code with the Orca MCP connected and hands the skill an alert ID. From there it runs a fixed playbook.

Screenshot of giving Claude an alert ID from Orca.

Context gathering: Claude pulls the alert through the MCP, then the code origin. It confirms the repo, the file, and the exact line before touching anything.

Decision: The skill checks the finding against a short list of issue types it is allowed to fix. For those, it picks the smallest version bump that closes the finding and keeps base images on the same distro. Anything outside that list, including major-version upgrades, end-of-life base images, or a repo that has changed since the scan, stops the run with an explanation instead of a guess.

Generation: Claude clones the repo, edits the line, and validates the change. When Docker is available locally, the agent builds the image to confirm the fix before it hands anything back.

Review: The output is a diff. The skill never commits, never pushes, and never touches cloud state. The engineer reads it and approves. Only then does it open a PR on a new branch and write a comment and an in-progress status back to the Orca alert. Once the fix is merged and deployed, Orca closes the alert automatically on the next scan.

Screenshot of the output from the skill – a diff.

Why engineers trusted AI-generated fixes

That last rule did more for adoption than anything else. Engineers trusted the output because it could not do anything they hadn’t read first. The skill was written in the open agent skills format, so the same file runs in Cursor, Codex, or whatever else a team has standardized on. Like most orgs, our customer hadn’t settled on a single coding agent. A remediation workflow that works regardless of which one an engineer opens was a hard requirement.

Results: zero critical vulnerabilities in 30 days

By the deadline, our customer had zero critical alerts. Along the way the same skill cleared more than 200 alerts in a month, every fix produced by Claude Code with Orca’s data behind it and every one merged by an engineer who had read the diff. Security and engineering worked the backlog together, and the security lead was in Claude Code running the skill alongside them.

Orca’s vulnerability management handled the security reasoning: which findings were real and exposed, and where the code that produced them lived. The coding agent did the software engineering. The handoff between the two teams, the step that used to stall every cleanup effort, shrank to a code review.

Keeping the security debt from landing

The same skill now runs on a schedule against new software composition analysis (SCA) alerts and opens a PR for each one before anyone has to ask. To catch risky code before it reaches production, the team flipped Orca’s PR scanning from warn to block for criticals with a fix available, so a new one can’t land on the main branch without the fix in hand.

It also changed how they ship. Once engineering saw that a service with its build definition in a repo got a reviewable fix in minutes, that became the deployment standard. Security influenced an engineering practice without writing a policy because the faster path and the more secure path were the same path.

Screenshot of Orca’s scan results in a pull request.

Orca already knows what is running, what is exposed, and where the code lives. The MCP Server already puts that in front of the coding agent your engineers use every day. A skill turns the two into a workflow with guardrails.

Security debt doesn’t have to keep compounding. This team paid theirs down to zero criticals in a month, and the guardrails they set have prevented new debt from landing.

Title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
Context: Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild...
Full Text:
Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model.

Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited.

We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines.

With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains.

The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from?

As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions:

If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed?

Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old?

Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed?

How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers?

Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end?

The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization.

Where is it from?

AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities.

Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability.

Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j (CVE-2021-44228) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan.

Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process (MAPP) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced. "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says.

Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines.

For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work.

The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question.

Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades.

Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released.

This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux.

Will it stay this high?

No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight.

Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off.

When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year.

Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way.

While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right?

Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly.

As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly.

There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system.

However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem.

Are the numbers the real issue?

The volume is certainly up.

Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month.

With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities.

Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story.

Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises.

AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness.

For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths?

What do we do now?

The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not.

Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role.

For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks.

For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP. Don't stop there.

For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own.

Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms.

Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge.

Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains.

Head of AI Security Roles Surge in Large Organizations

Deputy Editor, Infosecurity Magazine

A head of AI security role has been established in 65% of large organizations with an annual revenue of $10bn plus, according to new data.

The research, conducted by IANS and Artico Search, found that large businesses are taking steps to update their security organizational structure to enhance accountability and board level oversight for enterprise AI governance.

Around a fifth (18%) of all $10bn+ firms have made the head of AI security a dedicated position, while 47% combined it with another leadership role, making it “one of the fastest emerging functional roles,” according to the researchers.

Head of AI security was observed to be less common in medium and small companies, with the position established in 9% of organizations with a revenue of $1-$10bn, and 6% in firms with under $1bn in revenue.

Steve Martano, IANS Faculty and partner at Artico Search’s cyber practice, commented: “The growth of AI is creating a premium for leaders who can bridge technical security, risk and compliance while still understanding how the business wants to use the technology.”

AI Governance Rarely Falls Under the CISO Remit

The IANS report, published on October 20, found that despite the growth of dedicated head of AI security roles in large organizations, overall accountability for enterprise AI governance remains unsettled.

CISOs hold primary accountability in 26% of small businesses, in 11% of medium firms and just 7% of large organizations. The position that most often is held accountable for AI governance in large businesses are chief AI officers, at 22%.

Read now: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds

Across all three tiers, 14-19% of organizations reported that no single executive is accountable.

In addition, most organizations have not yet fully implemented a board committee dedicated to AI ethics or responsible AI, with 43-48% across all three tiers stating that they have no such committee planned.

Martano said organizations must restructure security teams to ensure that their governance strategies keep pace with rapid AI adoption.

“Companies need to strategically think about what they need from the function and whether they can develop that expertise internally before going to an increasingly competitive external market,” he noted.

Experience the Biggest Dictator of Security Pros’ Pay

The report assessed experience level as the single biggest driver of compensation differences in the same role – more significant than factors such as company size and geographic location.

In $10bn+ businesses, security professionals with eight to 15 years’ experience earn about $35,000 more than those with fewer than eight years’ experience.
