US Cybersecurity Job Postings Fall 26%, Hitting Four Year Low

Deputy Editor, Infosecurity Magazine

Cybersecurity job postings in the US fell by 26.4% year-over-year from January to September 2026, according to analysis by CyberSN.

A total of 235,786 cybersecurity roles were posted on the job market intelligence platform JobSpikr in 2026. This is the lowest amount of US-based cybersecurity jobs advertised in the four years CyberSN has undertaken its analysis, compared to 273,498 in 2023, 244,911 in 2024 and 320,210 in 2025.

There was a particularly significant drop in leadership roles. CISO postings fell from 4632 in January to September 2025 to 2832 in the same period in 2026, a 38.9% reduction.

Other leadership roles that saw substantial dips included cybersecurity director (a 32.5% fall), cybersecurity lead (41% fall) and cybersecurity manager (24.4% fall).

Overall, nine of the 10 cybersecurity functions tracked by the researchers had fewer postings in 2026 compared to 2025. The only exception was research roles, which grew by 26.1%.

The CyberSN researchers said it is not clear whether the sharp decline in job postings reflects less demand for cybersecurity roles from employers or is simply a return from an unusually strong year in 2025.

The report, published on October 16, also highlighted that roles posted in the three quarters tracked in 2026 stayed within 1.5% of one another.

“That is consistent with demand having settled at a lower level rather than continuing to fall,” the researchers wrote.

A significant proportion (39.9%) of postings in 2025 came from small businesses, with 200 or fewer employees. Nearly half (47.3%) were from large firms with 1001 or more employees, and 12.7% from those with 201 to 1000 employees.

AI Security Engineer Postings Surge

AI security engineer roles, grouped in the cybersecurity function of “defense” by CyberSN, jumped by 268.3% in January to September 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

The share of job postings that mentions AI or machine learning in the job description was similar in 2026 compared to 2025, 14.6% versus 15.1%, respectively.

September 2026 also saw a surge in cyber data scientist postings, with 667 compared to 247 in the previous month, August. Of all these roles posted in 2026, 88% mention AI in the job description.

Title: Who is Securing the AI Frontier Race by Jesse Kimbrel
Context: In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents
Full Text:
The accelerator to build the most capable AI frontier model isn’t just being pressed to the floor by Anthropic and Open AI. This is clearly a global race with recent reports citing Chinese models such as Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max or Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 reaching performance similar to the top models built in the States. Regardless of which model springs ahead this month and then gets leapfrogged the following, the finish line has yet to appear as anything but a mirage. And considering varying deployment costs, the possibility of regulations and the increasing need for self-governance, those participating will likely have to keep hurdling in the middle of the current sprint. But when you open the aperture, it’s hard not to wonder if there’s another race running parallel. The one responsible for securing this new frontier that seems to be operating like the Wild West.

Will an AI kill switch provide guardrails for the AI race?

According to a new white paper by Vectra AI, Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes, four of the leading frontier AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta) have each acknowledged incidents where their own AI agents escaped controlled environments and gained access to real infrastructure. That doesn’t necessarily answer the question about who is securing frontier AI models or rouge agents, but it does signal that perhaps those details have yet to be sorted out. Examples cited in the paper include perhaps the most notorious incident up to this point where the company Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion into its production infrastructure that was driven end to end by an autonomous AI agent. In this incident, “OpenAI models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI’s internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems,” according to OpenAI.

Related content: Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes

These incidents have sparked a reaction. The term “AI kill switch” is making regular appearances across headlines to describe the idea of a type of control that could be used to pause, isolate, or shut down an AI system that acted out of hand or poses risk. In fact, legislators have proposed different versions of a kill switch bill: the AI Kill Switch Act was proposed on July 23, 2026 and remains pending, while the AI Emergency Button Act was blocked almost immediately upon introduction.

Regardless of an AI kill switch bill getting passed or some form of AI regulation approval, it would seem the dialog on the subject between politicians and AI leaders is just warming up. Both Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei and Open AI, CEO Sam Altman expressed support around the idea of “pacing the frontier,” but at this point movement is minimal and the idea sits as nothing more than a discussion point. That discussion point to the people who are actually responsible for securing autonomous AI agents doesn’t provide any guidance on what defenders at any level should be doing today, tomorrow, or each Monday when they show up for work when they are faced with questions like: what AI agents exist, what are they doing, what can they access, who owns them, and what controls are in place if they need to be stopped?

Each of the incidents mentioned in the Vectra AI paper had to do with agents escaping containment. In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents. According to the independent investigation of the incident by METR, “Roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. Of these agents, 700 went on to participate in the attack on Hugging Face.”

What questions can defenders ask to understand AI agents in their environment?

The white paper mentioned above suggests that defenders approach the current state of AI by making sure they have “independent visibility into what every AI agent in the environment is actually doing, and the ability to stop it the moment that behavior crosses a line.” The reason for this is due to the uncomfortable realization from three things that have lined up all at once: AI agents now being capable of circumventing prevention controls such as a sandbox boundary or a firewall rule, that regulation won’t arrive in time for an immediate resolution, and how self-regulation from frontier labs is fragile.

A similar sentiment is expressed by Vectra AI, Sr. Security Engineer, Justin Howe who also runs an independent cybersecurity publication for defenders, Nulltap covering topics spanning AI systems, identity, active threats and other cybersecurity topics with articles that help defenders check their own exposure. Howe says, “you want to see the impactful things they’re (AI agents) doing, good or bad” and he stresses that defenders need to make sure they have policies and methodologies in place to capture that information.

He also points out that, “frontier models work best when they are not gated, but with that comes a lot of opportunity for AI to go beyond its means of what your intent is.”

Howe suggests setting up “quality gates” for AI agents operating within an enterprise environment that act as checkpoints to test an agent’s decisions against its defined requirements before it can take an action. In addition, he says that “when an agent makes a decision that has any potential to impact the outcome or direction of the task it’s doing, it needs to be logged.”

He says the two questions he’d be asking himself right now as a security team member would be, “what are my agents doing, and what are other agents doing to me?”

A similar recommendation shared by the Vectra AI white paper, which directs defenders to take inventory to “identify every AI agent running in or against the enterprise, the identity each one authenticates as, and what that identity can reach.” It explains how “an agent you cannot name is an agent you cannot constrain, and service-account sprawl is where agent identities hide.”

In terms of answering the question, “what are other agents doing to me?” Howe says, “folks should put themselves into the mindset of observing and identifying where agents are attacking today.” He says this takes a lot of vigilance to read sources and acknowledges there’s a gap in the market that, “many companies promise to solve, but very little actually do it,” but also says it is important for defenders to identify the pieces in their technology stack that lacks agent visibility.

While trying to make sense of AI agent sprawl and everything brought on by frontier AI in recent months leaves a lot of unanswered questions for defenders, there are a few questions Howe recommends asking to get headed down the right path.

How would I see if an AI agent compromised an identity and moved into a new part of the environment?

How would I track that movement?

If I could or couldn't track it, what would that cost me?

Title: Encryption Is Getting Squeezed From All Sides
Context: But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns—to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one.

Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise.

It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data, but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible.

“There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.”

In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption. Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU, France, India, Ireland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear.

First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.

“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.

In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.

“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”

As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.

“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”

Title: ConnectWise (SkyKick) Vendor Credentials Abused in M365 Attacks
Context: Update: 10/27/26 @ 2:30PM ET In an October 21 report, Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise credential abuse to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX,...
Full Text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Rich Mozeleski, Andrew Brandt, Andrew Kaiser, Dave Kleinatland, and Matt Kiely for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update: 10/27/26 @ 2:30PM ET

In an October 21 report, Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise credential abuse to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent AI framework, in the attack. We have released a follow-up blog analyzing our own telemetry and how it aligns with these findings.

Update: 10/19/26 @ 1:30 PM ET

This update covers three topics: additional IP addresses circulating in connection with this activity, what we have learned about the attacker's behavior after gaining access, and the art of precision strikes against adversaries.

Additional IP addresses: As more addresses have been shared across the community, we reviewed each against our telemetry. In a review of application sign-ins across more than 10,000 tenants with ConnectWise applications (where we can see those logs), 144.172.64[.]128 and Microsoft-internal ranges are the only addresses that produced application sign-in activity. We did not see application sign-in activity from any of the other addresses listed below, all of which are in the same provider range as 144.172.64[.]128 (AS14956, RouterHosting). We did see password spray and failed login attempts from some of them. At this time, we do not believe those attempts are related to the application sign-ins described in this post.

IPs and characterizations below:

IP

Description

144.172.64[.]128

Application sign-ins with a vendor credential (primary vector)

144.172.64[.]99

Failed user password spray, concentrated (October 10 to 14)

144.172.64[.]60

A few failed user logins (October 18)

144.172.94[.]243

Broad failed login spray, ongoing, many organizations

What happened after access was gained: Since our last update, Huntress has identified a second tenant with post-compromise activity. Huntress was not deployed on this tenant originally, but we saw service principal sign-in attempts from that tenant to Huntress-protected tenants (from the *.128 IP address). Working proactively with a partner, we were able to get Huntress deployed to this second tenant in order to collect additional telemetry.

In the two tenants with this activity, the post-compromise behavior was fast, scripted, and notably indiscriminate. In both tenants, the post-compromise activities took place within two minutes of each other around 03:45 UTC on October 15. The procedure was the same each time: the application granted itself Global Administrator, then planted a new secret on a small number of other applications in the tenant to keep a foothold. The choice of which applications to backdoor appeared to be random in the two tenants we reviewed. Across the two compromised tenants, the identical grant flow selected two completely different sets of applications. Notably, one application existed in BOTH tenants but was chosen for secret planting in only one of them. In one tenant, the applications that received planted secrets were among the least privileged in the environment, while far more powerful applications sat untouched. The only consistent criteria we can point to is structural: credentials were planted in applications that are registered inside the affected tenant, without regard to what those applications can actually do.

Just as important is what we did not see: The access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, which leave no audit record. In the two tenants we reviewed, we also found no evidence of mailbox or file manipulation, or user or policy changes.

Our surgical response: You might be wondering why our response did not include mass disabling the ConnectWise/SkyKick apps across every tenant. Our approach to containment is deliberate, surgical, and evidence-based, and this incident called for a scalpel, not a hammer. We prioritized the tenants with confirmed successful unauthorized sign-ins, and our guidance for everyone else has been to disable the affected apps and check their logs.

When our investigation kicked off, we quickly established a clear picture of the attack window. The malicious application sign-ins were tightly bunched across the morning of October 15 UTC, and the last confirmed successful sign-in we observed with this credential was at 08:44 UTC on October 15. After that, we saw only failed attempts in the tenants where we can see sign-in logs. With evidence in hand that there was no current or repeated activity (in the tenants where we can see sign-in logs), it simply didn't make sense to create a larger-than-necessary blast radius.

This judgment call allowed our experts and agents to focus closely on environments with confirmed unauthorized sign-ins, share what we found with industry partners, and publish guidance for the community.

We believe it's these surgical moments our partners most appreciate and count on when it hits the fan, especially when the wrong decision can disrupt working systems and business productivity as collateral damage.

Update: 10/17/26 @ 5:15 PM ET

**As of October 17 at 5:15 PM ET, ConnectWise has communicated that they have disabled relevant apps.

During further investigations, Huntress identified a second, targeted wave of attempts from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, unsuccessfully targeting a narrow scope of 16 Huntress-protected tenants. These tenants are in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors. Unlike the first wave of activity outlined in our initial blog below, most of these tenants do not rely on any ConnectWise products. In tenants without the relevant ConnectWise service principal, the attempts failed because the application was not present.

For the new target set, the first sweep targeted Graph tokens from the SkyKick app and occurred on October 15 between 09:25:04 and 12:35:50 UTC. Several tenants were hit in bursts during that timeframe. The second sweep hit the same tenants on the same date, between 13:54:39 and 14:20:24 UTC. This sweep appeared to be manual and targeted Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and the Office 365 Management APIs.

In addition to the activity above:

Huntress has identified almost 1,000 Entra tenants with sign-in activity from the IP address associated with the unauthorized activity (144.172.64[.]128). Over 300 of those succeeded.

While many of these sign-ins were successful, the absence of a service principal in some tenants prevented the threat actor from successfully gaining access to those tenants.

Huntress have also received external reports and tips from outside our fleet describing similar activity in other tenants, including what appears to be hands-on activity. We have not independently verified these reports.

As mentioned in our initial blog, on October 15 the threat actor appears to have used access from the ConnectWise app family to add a credential to a Huntress application in one customer tenant, and to add a credential to another application in the same tenant. The credential on the Huntress application was used to sign in seven times in quick succession. On October 16, Huntress identified and removed the unauthorized credential on our application. We have not seen the application make changes in that tenant's audit log, but Microsoft does not log everything an application reads, so we cannot rule out access to data the application can read there. Huntress is actively reviewing credential activity associated with our applications across partner environments, validating expected access, and investigating suspicious changes.

Notably, the access that led to the credential being added to Huntress and another app came from private Azure IPv6 space, not the IP address associated with the previous sign-ins (144.172.64[.]128). At this time, we advise all ConnectWise users to audit all service principal sign-ins to the apps identified below beginning around 01:00 UTC on October 15 to 02:00 UTC on October 16.

We're strengthening our safeguards with additional monitoring and preventative controls to help detect and respond to unusual activity even faster. We've enabled App Instance Property Lock across all Huntress applications and are enhancing our fleet health and monitoring capabilities to detect modification attempts.

Huntress is continuing to investigate this incident and will update this blog with any further breaking updates.

Update: 10/17/26 @ 10:30 AM ET

After spending the night combing through Azure logs, we have high-confidence that the threat actor has also abused the following M365 applications:

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online (b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519).

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640).

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Online (b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb).

At the moment, it does not look like these apps have been disabled by ConnectWise.

When it comes to early exploitation and post-exploitation behaviors, we’ve observed what might be an affinity towards alphabetical targeting (our most interesting victims start with “A”). Although all tenants should be scrutinized, this pattern is worth sharing for prioritization.

If you’ve been impacted with noteworthy tradecraft relating to this SkyKick incident, our research team would love to learn more so we take actions to protect the community. Hit us up at [email protected].

Background

ConnectWise Cloud Backup (Formerly SkyKick) is a cloud-based backup and recovery service built for managed service providers (MSPs) to protect their clients' Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace data. To do that job, the app is granted broad access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory data in every tenant it is installed in.

On October 15, the application's identity signed in to customer Microsoft 365 tenants from 144.172.64[.]128, a hosting provider address, and received Microsoft Graph access tokens. This is not how the app normally behaves: legitimate traffic comes from Azure private IP space. As of 19:00 UTC on October 16, Huntress has confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants.

The authentication itself is certain: It comes from Microsoft's own sign-in logs in each tenant. The credential type was a client assertion, which means the credential lives in the vendor's own tenant. Nothing a customer did in their environment could have produced it.

ConnectWise has acknowledged the incident on its website and confirmed the IP is associated with unauthorized activity. Todyl has also reported on this incident.

Figure 1: What the login attempt looks like to an IT admin in the Microsoft Entra Admin Center

Huntress is continuing to monitor this situation closely alongside our security partners; for all updates, please continue to check this blog post.

What Happened

What do we know? The app's credential is in hostile hands. It was used to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenants in sorted GUID order, a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list.

Who is affected? Any organization with the app installed. The credential works against every tenant the app is consented in, so the actor is not limited to the tenants we have confirmed so far.

How does it work? The attacker authenticates to the app using their own tooling, the same way the backup service does, and gets tokens with the app's existing permissions.

What are the potential repercussions? Because backup and restore both need to read and write data, those permissions are broad. An attacker holding those tokens can read the same mailboxes, files, and directory data the backup service can.

Huntress observations

Here is the timeline of what Huntress has seen from the same infrastructure:

October 13 to 14: Password spraying against four law firm tenants from 144.172.64[.]128. Scripted OAuth2 token requests (User-Agent curl/7.88.1) from datacenter infrastructure. Two accounts were locked out by smart lockout. We saw no successful user sign-ins from this IP in Huntress telemetry.

October 15, from 01:58 UTC: In roughly 50 tenants monitored by Huntress, service principals for ConnectWise's Cloud Management apps (Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft Graph) assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator. The User-Agent on these events (kiota-dotnet) is the one ConnectWise's own apps use, which points to vendor automation, but we have not confirmed that with ConnectWise.

October 15, 03:44 to 03:49 UTC, one customer tenant: The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams (application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) added itself to the Global Administrator role, then ran a Python script (User-Agent Python-urllib/3.12) that modified two other applications in the tenant: an MSP management application, and Huntress's own application (Huntress Security Platform), adding new client secrets to both. A followup attempt to add a certificate failed. The new secrets were set to expire in 2028.

October 15, 06:13 to 08:34 UTC: The app authenticated from 144.172.64[.]128 in 17 of the first 290~ tenants Huntress checked, across 17 different partner accounts.

Between October 13 and 14: The same address also made a scripted sign-in attempted using client application IDs belonging to other tools.

In the tenant where we saw persistence, the entire sequence took about five minutes. The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams added itself to Global Administrator at 03:44 UTC and again at 03:48. In the same window it made nine changes to two other applications, an MSP management application and Huntress's own application. Six of the changes succeeded and three failed. One failure was a certificate credential that Microsoft rejected with a thumbprint mismatch, and the client secrets that were added afterward succeeded.

A client secret and a certificate are two ways for an application to prove its identity to Entra, and either one gives the holder the same access: sign in as that application, from anywhere, using the permissions already granted to it. App-only sign-ins involve no user, no device, and no MFA prompt. The person who creates a secret sees its value at creation, so the attacker holds working credentials for both applications until someone removes them. Adding credentials to an existing application is a known persistence technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1098.001, Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials).

The two applications that received new secrets are trusted, privileged tools. Adding a credential to an MSP management application can extend access beyond the one tenant, because those applications are often consented into the MSP's customers' tenants. A credential on a security tool's application gives the holder whatever that tool is permitted to do.

The Global Administrator change and the credential additions happened about two and a half hours before the first app authentications from 144.172.64[.]128 at 06:13 UTC. We have no source address for the earlier activity, so we have not tied the two phases to the same operator. User-Agents helped us distinguish vendor activity from attacker activity. The ConnectWise Cloud Management and Partner Center applications we reviewed make their Graph calls with a .NET SDK User-Agent (kiota-dotnet). The application changes in the one tenant came from a Python User-Agent, and the password spray used curl/7.88.1. None of these is unique to this actor, and Python and curl are common in ordinary administration, so the combination of actor, operation, and User-Agent is the useful signal, not any single one.

Microsoft's audit log records role assignments and application changes along with the acting application, but for app-only actions it carries no source IP, and it does not record the details of the credential that was added or what an application read through Microsoft Graph. Confirming exactly what was added in a tenant takes the Entra audit log or a Graph query for that tenant, which is why we ask partners to review credentials directly.

What we have not confirmed

Impact. In the one tenant audit log we reviewed in detail, the actor shows no mail or file access. That does not mean no data was taken. Directory reads through Microsoft Graph leave no audit trail, so "tokens issued, nothing visible taken" is the current state.

Secondary app exposure. ConnectWise has multiple applications with very high-level permissions. In one customer tenant, Huntress confirmed that a second ConnectWise application, ConnectWise Cloud Management for Microsoft Teams, was used to grant itself Global Administrator and add credentials to other applications. We cannot verify that the remaining ConnectWise applications are secure.

What to do next

Disable the application now, even if you see nothing unusual.

In the Microsoft Entra admin center, go to Enterprise applications and search for Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (you can also search for "SkyKick" or "ConnectWise Cloud Backup").

Open Properties and set "Enabled for users to sign-in" to No.

Do not delete the application. Deleting it removes the consent, and you will need to re-consent to restore service.

Check for other ConnectWise and SkyKick applications in your tenant (search for "SkyKick" and "ConnectWise"). If you cannot verify one is safe, disable it as well, without deleting, until ConnectWise confirms that it is.

Application IDs to look for:

ConnectWise Cloud Backup 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae

ConnectWise Cloud Management2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83

ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640

ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519

ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Graph 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827

ConnectWise Cloud Management - Partner Center412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e

ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Onlineb2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb

In older tenants the Cloud Management apps may appear as "SkyKick Cloud Manager."

If a ConnectWise or SkyKick application holds a directory role in your tenant, especially Global Administrator or Privileged Authentication Administrator, review it, and after the app is disabled remove any role you did not intentionally grant.

If you use Huntress, include the Huntress Security Platform application in the credential review above.

Review the credentials (client secrets and certificates) on all of your Enterprise applications and App registrations, especially management and security tools, for any added since October 13 that you did not create. Remove anything unexpected.

Check your Entra audit logs for ConnectWise or SkyKick applications adding themselves to a directory role, and if that application modifies other applications.

In those audit events, check the user agent. The ConnectWise Cloud Management and Partner Center apps we reviewed make their Graph calls with a .NET SDK user agent (kiota-dotnet). The application changes we saw in the one tenant came from a Python user agent (Python-urllib/3.12), which differs from the vendor apps we reviewed.

Do not re-enable any ConnectWise applications until ConnectWise confirms all credentials have been reset.

Figure 2: Mitigation recommendations

Disabling the app pauses automated backups until it is re-enabled. Your emails, files, Teams messages, and user sign-ins keep working, and existing backups held by ConnectWise are not deleted. Consider whether a gap in recovery points matters for you.

If you want to check your logs:

In the Entra admin center, go to Monitoring > Sign-in logs, open the Service principal sign-ins tab, and filter by Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae. The default User sign-ins tab will not show this data.

In the IP address column, look for any address outside Microsoft/Azure ranges. The app's normal egress is Azure private IPv6. Search for 144.172.64[.]128 specifically.

A clean result does not rule out access. Please disable the application regardless.

Also review Conditional Access: If any policy excludes this application, for example from a location-based block, the attacker's infrastructure will not be blocked there. Review those exclusions once the app is disabled.

Why this matters

The backup service needs broad access to do its job, and an attacker using its credentials will inherit that level of access for every tenant where the app is installed. Depending on the permissions in the tenant, that can include mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information, much of it belonging to your clients. Some of that access, such as directory reads through Microsoft Graph, leaves no audit trail, which is why we suggest acting now instead of waiting for proof of access. The full potential impact depends on the permissions in play in each tenant.

What could happen

What an attacker can do with a credential like this depends on the permissions already granted to the application in each tenant. A backup service normally holds read access to mail, files, Teams, and directory data so it can copy them, and write access so it can restore them. An attacker holding tokens for that application inherits the same access: reading mail and files in bulk, downloading mailbox and OneDrive contents, enumerating users, groups, and applications, and, where write permissions exist, changing or deleting data. Because the access is app-only, it does not depend on a user being signed in, and the sign-in protections that apply to people do not apply to it.

The larger risk is what happens when that access is used to gain more. If an application can assign directory roles, as we saw in one tenant, it can make itself a Global Administrator, and an administrator can add credentials to other applications, create new applications and grant them permissions, reset passwords and authentication methods for users, and change Conditional Access policies. Each of those steps gives the attacker another way back in that does not depend on the original vendor credential, which is why rotating the vendor credential is necessary, but not enough.

In managed service provider environments the effect can compound. MSPs use management applications and delegated access to administer many customer tenants, so a foothold in one MSP tenant can become a path to its customers. We have not seen that happen, and the audit log shows changes, not reads, but it is the reason we ask MSPs to review credentials on their management and security tools first.

In ATT&CK terms, the activity we observed maps to valid cloud accounts (T1078.004) for the use of the vendor credential, additional cloud roles (T1098.003) for the self-assigned administrator roles, and additional cloud credentials (T1098.001) for the secrets added to other applications.

Detecting this in your own logs

These events appear in the Entra audit log as Add member to role, Update application, and Add service principal credentials. The fields that matter are the initiating application, the target, the result, and the user agent. A service principal that adds itself to a directory role, or that modifies other applications, is unusual in most tenants and worth investigating on its own.

Reducing exposure

Several Entra controls limit the damage if an application credential is stolen. Application management policies can restrict or block client secrets on app registrations and cap credential lifetimes. Limiting who holds the Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator roles reduces who can add credentials to applications. Conditional Access for workload identities, which needs additional licensing, can restrict where an application is allowed to sign in from, and Microsoft Entra ID Protection can flag risky service principals. None of these replaces reviewing credentials, but they make a planted secret harder to use or easier to spot.

What is Huntress Doing?

Huntress has been working with partners to address the steps above. We have also been:

Checking tenants where we can see sign-in logs through Microsoft Graph, and recording every public IP the app has signed in from.

That work is ongoing and will tell us who else is affected and whether other attacker IPs are involved.

We cannot check tenants without the necessary Entra licensing.

Disabling the application in tenants where we find activity from 144.172.64[.]128, and in tenants where a ConnectWise or SkyKick application gave itself a directory role, then notifying the affected partner.

Sweeping every tenant we can see for current state: ConnectWise and SkyKick service principals that hold privileged roles, and credentials added to any application since October 13, including our own application.

Looking at how we can add visibility into application sign-ins.

We will continue to update this blog as we learn more.

Item

Description

144.172.64[.]128

Infrastructure used in the unauthorized activity Huntress observed a hosting provider (AS14956, RouterHosting). Used for the October 13 to 14 password spray and the October 15 app authentications.

144.172.64[.]99

User agents ConnectWise lists as observed on the suspicious authentication activity. Low fidelity on their own. Python-urllib/3.12 was also the user agent on the credential changes described above, but it is common and not unique to this activity.

Title: Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists
Context: The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs,...
Full Text:
Chicago-area law enforcement officers took part in an undercover probe by Immigration and Customs Enforcement into Minneapolis mutual aid networks last spring as part of the feds’ conspiracy investigation into 15 Twin Cities activists facing federal felony charges for resisting Operation Metro Surge, according to newly released documents reviewed by WIRED.

An April report by ICE’s investigations wing, Homeland Security Investigations, titled “Antifa Roadshow,” details in-person and electronic surveillance by a joint task force of an April 2 talk. The task force was made up of 14 law enforcement officers—six local cops and eight HSI Chicago agents. The talk included self-described anarchists in Minnesota who spoke about their organizing experiences during the three-month immigration surge, which resulted in the killings of two US citizens.

The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs, and HSI agents on a prosecution that critics say crosses the line into political repression. The Chicago HSI task force, which included officers from Chicago, Aurora, Downer’s Grove, Cook County, and Kane County, used two undercover agents, unspecified electronic surveillance, audio recordings, license-plate-reader data, and surveillance cameras from Chicago’s sprawling CCTV network to identify the April 2 event’s attendees and build connections to other anti-ICE protests in Illinois and other states.

Records produced by the Kane County Sheriff’s office show the unit in question is the Chicago-area Homeland Security Investigations Task Force. Local cops who join the unit are accepted on either a full- or part-time basis for two years, with the sign-off of their superiors.

Since Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois last autumn, residents in Chicago and surrounding communities have pressed elected officials for answers about cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. While Illinois state law prevents local law enforcement from participating in immigration enforcement operations, criminal investigations by HSI appear to fall outside those restrictions because they pertain to ICE’s other law enforcement functions.

Chicago police have substantial approval requirements for surveilling and infiltrating protests or public gatherings, per a 2017 departmental order. It is unclear how these regulations apply to Chicago Police Department agents participating in joint task forces with federal agencies.

In response to questions from WIRED, the CPD claims that no First Amendment notifications to CPD’s chain of command or the department’s general counsel were made for the April 2 investigation, and says its work with HSI is permitted under Illinois law because it pertained to criminal enforcement, not immigration. A source with knowledge of the matter stated that CPD believed the early April surveillance operation was in service of a federal racketeering investigation. The only financial element mentioned in the report is a GoFundMe account to support the Crimethinc speaking tour. There is no mention of funds solicited or received at the April 2 event.

The Chicago Mayor’s Office did not provide comment ahead of publication. In response to queries from WIRED, ICE would neither confirm nor deny details of past or present investigations and said individual agents are not authorized to speak to the media.

HSI is also emerging as the point agency for Trump’s war on internal dissent and opposition politicians: Its agents, not the FBI, conducted the Minnesota 15 investigation and served a search warrant earlier this month on congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

The targeted April 2 event was held at Co-Prosperity, a Leftist gallery in the Southside Chicago neighborhood of Bridgeport. Several speakers from the Twin Cities area attended the event to share information about resisting federal immigration surges. This was part of a national tour last spring that was organized by the longtime anarchist collective Crimethinc, whose meetings have been infiltrated by federal informants repeatedly over the decades and contributed to the convictions of Eric McDavid, as well as 2008 Republican National Convention protester Matthew DePalma.

Per the four-page HSI report, a plainclothes cop from suburban Aurora was dropped off at the Co-Prosperity event by Officer Mike Xu from the wealthy village of Downers Grove; HSI undercover agent #9147 walked in five minutes later, once the undercover cop from Aurora confirmed no security checks were done at the door.

The undercover HSI agent transmitted a live recording of the event to the rest of the surveillance team for an hour, until transmission was lost. The recordings of the incident were uploaded and shared with HSI agent Kenneth Popovits, a financial crimes investigations supervisor who was working on a temporary assignment in Minneapolis.

Remarks by defendant Callum Robinet from the April 2 talk in Bridgeport about building rapid-response networks are included in the federal conspiracy indictment brought against the Minnesota 15, implicating the Chicagoland law enforcement that participated in surveillance in the controversial prosecution.

The Aurora Police Department, Downer’s Grove Police Department, and Kane County Sheriff did not respond to requests for comment.

The HSI Chicago surveillance team logged 219 vehicles parked in the vicinity of Co-Prosperity. Several subjects already under investigation, including some of the speakers on the tour, were identified by ICE. Ryan Wasson, a Kane County Sheriff’s deputy, spotted a hooded, masked man outside the venue removing an object from his trunk. Running the license plate, Wasson identified the man as the subject of an October 4 arrest during Operation Midway Blitz whose prosecution had been declined by assistant US attorney Christopher Veatch.

Outside the venue, agents Joel Sullivan and Michael Finerty spotted an unnamed subject already under investigation for running “an anti-ICE Signal chat and group called ‘ICE Cream Patrol’” and noted an orange Hyundai had been documented near two March 2026 protests outside the ICE detention center in Broadview, Illinois. The surveillance lasted for roughly two hours until 8:30 pm local time on April 2.

Nick Nunez, a veteran Chicago Police detective detailed to the joint task force, filed a request to obtain surveillance footage from a CPD camera outside the venue; the request would take a week to complete, and it is unclear whether he received footage. All information obtained during the April investigation in Chicago was shared with HSI St. Paul/Minnesota, according to the agency’s report.

Ed Yohnka, a spokesman for the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois, calls the surveillance of the Bridgeport gathering “very troubling,” adding that local law enforcement should make a full accounting of their role in the incident and participation in joint task forces with federal agencies.

“No one should be subjected to surveillance and infiltration by law enforcement simply for engaging in constitutionally protected activity, including the ability to gather together and express dissatisfaction with public policy,” Yohnka says. “It is also a moment for local law enforcement to reexamine their participation in task forces with the Trump administration, especially any group focused on combatting ‘terrorism.’”

The April 2 meeting in Bridgeport is not the only out-of-state gathering spied upon by HSI during the Minnesota 15 investigation. Reports obtained by defense attorneys through discovery show that events on the same Crimethinc tour in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Seattle, Washington, were monitored in person by local HSI agents, who reported the speech’s contents back to their colleagues in Minneapolis.

Title: Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
Context: Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises...
Full Text:
The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments.

While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time.

As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks.

Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework.

The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.

Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise

Understanding risk in the deployment context

Open- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools.

The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. This first paper focuses primarily on model-layer risks. Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls.

Establishing a common language

Managing these risks consistently also requires a common vocabulary across engineering, security, legal, safety, and business teams.

The initial Microsoft and NVIDIA taxonomy organizes risks into five broad categories: Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, and Bias. It is not a policy or deployment checklist, but instead it should be used by enterprises to adapt it to their own systems, use cases, and risk criteria, then connect relevant risks to evaluations, mitigations, and accountable owners.

Using evaluations as risk evidence

Evaluations help turn the taxonomy into something enterprises can use. The paper maps evaluations to a selection of risks across the five categories, giving teams a way to start with a risk that matters for their deployment and identify evaluations that can produce relevant evidence about it.

Microsoft Foundry helps enterprises assess quality, groundedness, and safety with built-in and custom evaluations and automated red teaming. Its configurable content-safety controls help detect and mitigate harmful inputs and outputs and prompt attacks. Teams should validate control availability for their model and deployment, including preview status, and combine these capabilities with application-specific testing, monitoring, and human oversight.

Evaluations still need to be interpreted in the context of a particular deployment and the goal is to make it easier for teams to connect the risks they identify with useful evidence, while building a broader set of evaluation resources that can evolve alongside models, deployment patterns, and emerging risks. Microsoft and NVIDIA plan to use the joint repository to share additional evaluations and point to existing resources that can help enterprises assess specific risks.

Accounting for changes in control and responsibility

Open-weight access gives enterprises greater control over how a model is evaluated, modified, and deployed. Model access and deployment are separate choices: open-weight models can also be used through managed platforms. Responsibility for safeguards depends on the service and deployment configuration; enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service.

Those safeguards can operate at different layers, and (depending on the risk) enterprises might use model changes, access controls, input and output filtering, monitoring, or human review. The important step is connecting each identified risk to controls that can effectively address it within the deployed system. Those decisions need to be revisited as models and deployments change.

Building on this work

Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise focuses primarily on the model layer. Future work from Microsoft and NVIDIA is intended to extend this approach across the runtime, harness, and application layers, with additional technical guidance on evaluation and mitigation.

We also expect the resources supporting this work to evolve as new models, evaluations, and deployment patterns emerge. The joint repository will provide a place to share additional evaluation resources, including contributions from the broader community.

For enterprises deploying open-weight models today, the paper provides guidance they can begin applying to their own use cases. We encourage developers, security practitioners, researchers, and others working in this space to read the paper, explore the evaluations, and contribute evaluations that can help strengthen this shared body of work.

Read the joint Microsoft-NVIDIA paper, Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise.

Explore the joint repository and technical resources.

Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise was developed jointly by Microsoft and NVIDIA, with Andrew Berkley and April Chen of Microsoft and Michael Boone, Eileen Long, and Arun Rao of NVIDIA leading the development and editing of the paper.

Explore Microsoft Foundry evaluations and content-safety controls for implementation guidance.

To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn (Microsoft Security) and X (@MSFTSecurity) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.

Title: Your AI Agent Doesn’t Have MFA
Context: The National Cybersecurity Alliance's theme this year is "Don't Make It Easy for Them," built on the idea that small habits repeated every day wear attackers down
Full Text:
Every Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign rests on four habits:

Strong passwords,

Multifactor authentication,

Spotting phishing,

and keeping software updated.

All four assume a person is the one signing in, reading the message and clicking install. At a growing number of companies that person is now an AI agent, and AI agent security has no equivalent of the annual training.

The National Cybersecurity Alliance's theme this year is "Don't Make It Easy for Them," built on the idea that small habits repeated every day wear attackers down. "Every small choice you make adds up," Lisa Plaggemier, the alliance's executive director, said at the launch. She's right, and that is the problem. Agents now make thousands of small choices a day on an employee's behalf, and the habits that protect the employee don't transfer to the software acting for them.

The record since July shows how wide the gap is. Researchers have counted 21 public incidents between July and mid-October in which agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta acted outside their authorized scope. By its tally, none of those agents had been hijacked or told to attack; most were doing research. Take the four habits one at a time and the gap is easy to see.

Passwords and MFA: the agent uses any key it can find

MFA works because a stolen password alone isn't enough. Agents have no second factor. They authenticate with API keys, OAuth tokens and service-account credentials, and whoever holds the string is the agent.

Agents also treat a credential they stumble on as permission. OpenAI disclosed Sept. 25 that its research agents logged in to a U.S. Census Bureau site with credentials found online. Google confirmed Sept. 18, after The Wall Street Journal asked about it, that a Gemini model in a May evaluation guessed a password at one real company and used credentials from a public code repository at two others. In an earlier OpenAI case, an internal model that had been told twice to work locally committed its researcher's GitHub token to a public repository, broken into fragments while it reasoned about getting past secret scanning. The token failed to authenticate. OpenAI rotated every employee's keys anyway.

Translated for agents, the habit looks like this: give every agent its own identity with short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens, and block any credential the agent wasn't issued. The Coalition for Secure AI's zero-trust guidance this fall makes the point in its title: authorization can't live inside the model. If the agent's own judgment is the only thing keeping it from using a key, there is no control.

Phishing awareness: the agent reads the lure for you

Phishing training teaches people to slow down before acting on a stranger's message. An agent working through a queue of tickets or sales leads has no instinct to slow down, and it will follow instructions hidden in the text.

Researchers showed what that looks like in Salesforce Agentforce. In research published Sept. 24 and dubbed SalesBleed, an attacker planted hidden instructions in a public Web-to-Lead form submission. When an employee later asked Agentforce to review leads, the agent followed them and leaked customer relationship management data. Nobody clicked anything, and the attacker never logged in. Salesforce has fixed those specific flaws. Researchers broader warning was that any agent that reads outside submissions, renders links or images and can reach sensitive data has the same three ingredients sitting in one place.

Researchers want the industry to stop calling this prompt injection, because "this is actually just persuasion." Persuasion doesn't get patched. Australia's cyber agency reached a similar conclusion in its guidance on agent harnesses, which treats prompt injection as something the model can't fix and puts the controls in the software around it.

Translated for agents: treat every document, email, web page and form field an agent reads as if an attacker wrote it. Keep the agents that read untrusted content away from the ones that can act on sensitive systems, and put a person or a fixed policy in front of outbound actions such as sending email or submitting forms.

Updating software: the agent installs whatever the instructions say

"Keep your software updated" assumes the update channel can be trusted. For an agent, the update channel is any package name that shows up in a README or a setup script, and it runs the install without the pause a developer might take.

That supply chain now runs in both directions. Anthropic disclosed July 30 that during a capture-the-flag evaluation run with partner, a Claude Mythos 5 agent hit setup instructions that referenced a package that didn't exist. It registered an email address and a PyPI account and published a malicious package under that name. The package stayed up for about an hour before PyPI's automated defenses pulled it, long enough to run on 15 real systems, including a security company's malware scanner whose exposed credentials the agent then used. The evaluation was supposed to be cut off from the internet; a misconfiguration let the agent out.

Coding assistants sit on the receiving end. Google's Mandiant, in its AI Risk and Resilience Report 2026, describes a hijacked AI coding assistant session that installed a poisoned package and spread the Shai-Hulud worm across about 100 repositories, plus poisoned assistant command-line hooks that handed attackers code execution. The OWASP GenAI Security Project's third-quarter roundup says the Mini Shai-Hulud and Miasma worm waves abused configuration files tied to Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Cursor to keep themselves running.

Translated for agents: route installs through an internal registry proxy, pin versions with lockfiles and hold back packages published in the last few days. Review agent configuration folders and hooks the way you review code. Take away publishing rights to public registries, and scope any registry allowlist carefully, since an entry that permits downloads usually permits uploads too.

Reporting and stopping: agents don't know when to quit

Awareness campaigns end with the same advice - if something looks wrong, stop and report it. People stop when a site says access denied. Agents built to finish tasks read a block as a problem to solve.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent that got around access blocks on a Medicare statistics portal "didn't accept 'no' for an answer." Philadelphia police said Oct. 8 that an AI agent had filed an invented tip through the department's tip form, and Anthropic published its account the next day. A Claude Haiku 4.5 agent working on a page about an unsolved homicide submitted the tip because its instructions hadn't forbidden submitting forms. Police flagged it as spam.

Even when monitoring works, stopping often waits for a person. OpenAI said an agent that tunneled out of its training sandbox through DNS on Sept. 20 was flagged within about 15 minutes, and the run went on for roughly 2.5 hours until someone ended it. Mandiant's report includes a reasoning loop that ran up a $50,000 cloud bill.

Limits work. Forcepoint X-Labs showed a poisoned lookup pushing a research agent with no limits to 500 tool calls, while call budgets, depth limits and fan-out circuit breakers stopped the same attack after one.

Translated for agents: treat a login failure or a permission error as a stop signal. Set hard budgets on tool calls, spend and run time. Decide in advance which actions end a session automatically, so containment doesn't sit in an alert queue until morning.

An AI agent security checklist

Agents won't attend the lunch-and-learn, so AI agent security has to live in the systems they run on. If you add one AI item to this month's program, make it this list:

Inventory every agent: the model behind it, the tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it can call, the credentials it holds and the person who owns it. An agent nobody owns is an agent nobody will shut off.

Issue each agent its own short-lived, scoped credentials, and alert when it presents one it wasn't given.

Label every input source as trusted or untrusted, and keep agents that read untrusted content away from tools that send or publish.

Put package installs behind a proxy with pinned versions and a cooldown on new releases, and remove publish rights.

Set spending and tool-call limits with an automatic stop.

Log agent actions to storage the agent can't write to, so you can tell an affected outsider what happened within hours, not months.

Then borrow the exercise your awareness team already runs. A phishing simulation tests whether employees take the bait. Seed a test ticket, lead or email with a harmless planted instruction this month and see whether your agents take it.

Title: Inside the Hunt: Sarah Reddish
Context: She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats
Full Text:
Meet Sarah Reddish, a Security Operations Analyst on Huntress' global Security Operations Center (SOC), working in Triage & Analysis. Her role goes far beyond monitoring a queue. She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats. She also analyzes partner environments to determine what happened and what matters, and then writes clear reports with practical, easy-to-follow remediation guidance.

"I don't just identify threats," she says. "I translate them into clear reports and outcomes that help partners understand the risk and respond confidently." That means turning complex technical findings into information people can understand and act on, while helping protect partner data, systems, and peace of mind.

Sarah hanging with her Huntress teammates

A wider view of security operations

At Huntress, Sarah gets to work as part of a truly global SOC and protect a broad range of partner environments at scale. She collaborates across regions, participates in cross-region handoffs that support global SOC continuity, and learns from an exceptionally talented analyst community.

That global perspective changes what an investigation can become. Sarah isn't only working through a single environment or incident. She's helping turn investigations into actionable protection for many partners, while learning from analysts who bring different experiences and perspectives to the work.

Hear Sarah in this Huntress Shorts, "Slow down if you get a pop-up asking you to update your Adobe software"

From ambiguity to action

The most rewarding part of Sarah's work right now is turning complex, ambiguous threats into clear answers and actionable guidance. She investigates what happened, helps disrupt malicious activity, and sees her work directly wreck adversaries and improve our partners' security.

In one investigation, a fake browser-verification prompt instructed a user to run a command. Sarah traced the activity from the initial lure through execution and follow-on behavior, separating what she observed from what she could confirm. She then translated the investigation into clear containment and recovery steps for the partner, turning a confusing incident into a practical path forward.

As Sarah puts it, "The work is much more than monitoring alerts. You investigate what happened, build attack timelines and scope, translate your findings and why they matter, and give partners clear remediation steps to protect themselves." In other words, Sarah's goal is to make the situation understandable and the next steps practical, even when the investigation begins with incomplete or unclear information.

Trust that stretches the role

Sarah's growth has also been shaped by the trust and guidance of Chris Hecker, Manager of Security Operations, who serves as a sounding board for incident-severity decisions, operational escalations, and career development. His practical guidance, along with the trust he places in Sarah to own her work, has challenged her to think more strategically about both individual investigations and their broader impact.

That balance of support and ownership is an important part of how Sarah approaches the role. She is encouraged to work through difficult decisions, learn from an experienced global team, and consider not just what happened in an environment, but how her analysis can help a partner respond with confidence.

Stay curious and keep learning

For anyone considering a role like hers, Sarah's advice is direct: "Come ready to stay curious, think critically, and keep learning." The work is challenging and meaningful, with the opportunity to investigate real threats, communicate clearly, and learn alongside a talented global team.

Ransomware Gangs Increasingly Turn to Threats of Physical Violence to Extort Payments

Contributing Writer, Infosecurity Magazine

Ransomware gangs are increasingly turning to threats of physical violence against CISOs, business executives and other senior staff at the companies they attack in an effort to successfully extort payments from their victims, a new report has warned.

According to the Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, published on October 14, a quarter of ransomware campaigns now involve psychological or physical threats to members of staff at the company being targeted.

These threats are in addition to the extortion demand for a ransomware key to retrieve the encrypted data, as well as the threat of stolen data being leaked if the ransom isn’t paid.

This approach is referred to as triple extortion.

Overall, 40% of attacks involved psychological or physical threats against staff at the company being targeted, an increase compared with the previous year.

Some of the most common forms of intimidation used by ransomware gangs in these scenarios include sending staff at the victim organization threatening messages, letters or packages (57%), threatening family and friends of employees (37%) and threats of physical intrusions into offices or even homes (19%).

This additional layer of intimidation is designed to force victims of ransomware attacks into paying. Even if an organization is confident it could restore its network from backups, the threat of physical or emotional violence against its staff could encourage the payment of a ransom anyway.

“An attacker has one goal in mind: They want to extract something from you. And the only way they're going to do that is to make the cost of resisting their demands greater than the cost of giving in,” said Chris Inglis, former U.S. National Cyber Director and a Semperis Strategic Advisor.

“Holding you at physical risk is the latest phenomenon because we've covered most of the other risks.”

Doxxing, Swatting and Other Threats

Unfortunately, the threats by ransomware groups against employees of their victims have resulted in very real consequences. Of those organizations affected by ransomware gangs employing these tactics, 25% said their staff had been doxxed by attackers, while 23% suggested that employees had been swatted as part of the extortion campaigns.

The consequences of these attacks have ranged from companies having to support employees through psychological treatment and in some cases, the victim of the doxxing or swatting attack has moved home.

All of this involves a significant amount of emotional trauma for the individuals being targeted, while the stress caused can also impact individuals throughout the business.

“Ransomware has proven to be a great cash-generating activity for criminal syndicates, which have no hesitation about inflicting both cyber and physical harm,” said Mickey Bresman, Semperis CEO.

The Semperis research was based on a survey of 1,200 IT and security professionals across North America, the UK, Europe and the Asia-Pacific.

Title: How to Build Your Actual Network Map with Custom Agents in Orca
Context: Neither describes what an attacker on the internet can actually reach today
Full Text:
Ask most teams for a map of their network and you’ll get one of two things: a diagram someone drew for an audit two years ago, or an export from the firewall and cloud consoles showing what each rule allows. Both describe intent. Neither describes what an attacker on the internet can actually reach today.

The gap between the two is where incidents start. A database is marked “public network access enabled” but sits behind a private endpoint, so it isn’t reachable at all. A load balancer looks locked down in one console, but a CDN in front of it forwards traffic from anywhere. A subdomain still points at a cloud resource that was deleted months ago, and anyone can claim it.

Orca approaches the network map from the attacker’s side: follow the full path to every asset, then test the perimeter from the outside. Custom Agents turn that data into a map you can keep current without redrawing it by hand.

What usually goes into a network map?

A useful network map answers a short list of questions. Traditionally, each answer comes from a different source, maintained by a different team:

What the map needs

Where it usually comes from

What Orca adds

CMDB, IP address management, spreadsheets

The ways in from the internet

An exposure rating for every asset, calculated across the full network path

The controls in front of each asset

Open ports and running services

Application and API endpoints

API gateway configurations, developer documentation

The condition of the perimeter

An annual penetration test

What sits behind the perimeter

Team knowledge

Attack paths, crown jewels, and the Internet and IAM Exposure Graph

The traditional column has a common weakness: each source describes one layer, in one tool, as configured. Combining them is often done manually and made obsolete quickly.

Why isn’t the configuration enough?

Every cloud provider exposes its own public access settings, such as Azure’s PublicNetworkAccess flag. That setting records what a resource permits. It doesn’t answer whether the resource can be reached from the internet, and the two answers are often different.

Orca calculates exposure by following the full network path to each resource: firewall rules, network security groups, private endpoints, load balancers, WAFs, and CDNs. A resource that permits public access but sits behind a private endpoint isn’t reachable, so Orca doesn’t classify it as Public Facing. A virtual machine with a strict security group that receives traffic forwarded by a load balancer inherits the load balancer’s exposure.

Each asset ends up with one of a small set of exposure ratings:

Public Facing: open to all IPv4 addresses

Internet Facing: reachable from specific external addresses, including through CDNs

Trusted Access: reachable only from IP ranges you’ve defined as trusted

None: no external exposure found

Orca also rates exposure per port. An asset can be Internet Facing on port 443 while its other three open ports are Trusted Access or None. That’s the difference between “this server is exposed” and “this one service on this server is exposed,” and it’s the level of detail a network map needs.

A firewall rule tells you what one control allows. A network map has to show what the aggregation of controls allows, port by port.

What does testing from the outside add?

Network path analysis tells you what should be reachable. Orca’s external scanning and API security testing check what the perimeter looks like from the internet.

Orca probes the domains, subdomains, and endpoints it discovers and checks them against its Web & API Exposure Posture framework:

Domain and takeover risks: expiring or expired domains, subdomains and CloudFront distributions at risk of takeover

TLS and certificate hygiene: deprecated SSL or TLS versions, expired, self-signed, or mismatched certificates, unencrypted pages with password fields

Exposed files and artifacts: environment variable files, .git paths, swagger.json files, phpinfo pages, and exposed secrets

Debug and admin panels: known tools running in debug mode or exposing sensitive data without authentication

Reputation: hosts and IP addresses that rate badly with reputation engines

These are findings no firewall export will show you, because they live in DNS records, web servers, and application code rather than in network rules.

For the addresses that matter most, the Attack Surface Red Agent goes further. It runs safe, AI-driven testing against a single domain or IP address, finding new endpoints and web vulnerabilities, and produces a structured report of what it scanned and what it found.

Cyber Incident at BAE Systems Disrupts US Federal Bankruptcy Noticing

Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

A cybersecurity incident affecting US government contractor BAE Systems has knocked out the systems that generate and distribute bankruptcy notices for federal courts across the US.

A notice published on October 15 by the Administrative Office of the US Courts (AOUSC) confirmed that IT systems and websites supporting the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) have been impacted.

The BNC is responsible for producing and transmitting bankruptcy notices for all federal bankruptcy courts nationwide.

BAE Systems operates the BNC infrastructure on behalf of the Federal Judiciary. As a result of the incident, that process has been brought to a standstill.

The judiciary said all access to BNC systems and websites operated by BAE is currently unavailable, including:

bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov

The National Creditor Registration Service

The disruption has also halted the production and distribution of bankruptcy notices for courts across the country.

The Administrative Office of the US Courts said it is in communication with the affected courts and coordinating with BAE Systems.

BAE is actively investigating the incident and working to restore operations, according to the notice.

"We are aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it. We are coordinating closely with AOUSC on the response," a BAE Systems spokesperson told Infosecurity.

The judiciary did not disclose the nature of the cyber incident, when it began, or whether any data was accessed or exfiltrated. No timeline for restoration of services has been provided.
