Patch automation has existed for years. Yet in most enterprises, automated remediation jobs still wait in line behind change approvals and maintenance windows while critical exposures stay open.

The reason is that risk cuts both ways. Leave a vulnerability unpatched, and you invite exploitation. Push a faulty update, and you risk failed installs, rollbacks, or outages. Without evidence of how a change will behave, Security and IT teams default to caution, and the backlog grows.

Patch automation was never the blocker. Confidence is.

Today, we’re closing this gap with TruRisk Eliminate 2.0, the Autonomous RemOps platform. Powered by TruConfidence, its AI-powered Remediation and Orchestration Intelligence engine, and Agent Sara, Qualys’ autonomous AI agent for risk remediation, TruRisk Eliminate determines the right remediation action and executes it across your entire attack surface while keeping operations resilient.

The Confidence Gap: Why the Remediation Backlog Keeps Growing

AI-powered discovery is finding vulnerabilities faster than ticket-driven remediation can close them. Patch Tuesday recently hit 974 CVEs in a single month, on a process built for about 100. Attackers are taking advantage. The Verizon 2026 DBIR found that 31% of breaches began with the exploitation of vulnerabilities, up from 20%, making it the top initial access vector.

Remediation has not kept pace. The same report shows the median time to remediate a known exploited vulnerability (KEV) rose from 32 to 43 days, and only 26% of KEVs are fully remediated. Qualys research shows the same widening gap between the speed of threats and the speed of remediation.

The ability to automate is not the constraint. Qualys customers already automate remediation at scale: automated patch deployments rose 81% between the first and second quarters of 2026. They can because Qualys gives them the evidence to trust each change, from which exposures matter to how reliably a patch will deploy. What stalls machine-speed remediation is the lack of evidence needed to confidently move beyond manual, human-led remediation workflows. Without that, automated or autonomous remediation stalls.

Before letting autonomous remediation run, Security and IT teams need answers to these questions:

What must be fixed? Only 1% of vulnerabilities are exploited in the wild. Teams need to fix the validated exposures first, then tackle the long tail.

Does it need a patch? Not every exposure needs one. A mitigation, an uninstall or an existing security control can close it faster, with less disruption.

If it needs a patch, will it work and can it be automated? Teams need to predict whether a patch is safe to deploy and will not cause any business disruption, then roll it out progressively.

How do we control the rollout? Teams need to deploy changes progressively: zero-touch automation for high-reliability patches on low-impact applications, and ring-based deployment for everything else.

Did the environment stay healthy? Teams need ensure that risk was eliminated to maintain operational resiliency.

Answer these four questions with evidence, and remediation can run at machine speed without putting business continuity at risk.

How it Fits in the Autonomous RemOps Cycle

Closing that gap takes more than a better patch tool. It takes a new operating model for remediation: Autonomous RemOps.

Traditional patch tools push what is in the catalog and stop at “deployed.” Autonomous RemOps replaces that ticket-driven process with a continuous, evidence-based Decide → Execute → Prove. It determines what to fix, executes the appropriate remediation path across the entire attack surface, and demonstrates that the business remained resilient.

TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 runs that cycle in five steps. First, Qualys ETM and Agent Val validate what must be fixed. Second, TruConfirm credits the controls already in place. TruConfidence powers the final three steps, where autonomy carries the most operational risk: choosing the remediation path, controlling the rollout, and proving that it held.

Meet TruConfidence: Remediation Intelligence You Can Trust

TruConfidence is the remediation and orchestration intelligence layer behind TruRisk Eliminate. For every exposure, it answers one question: what is the safest and most effective way to eliminate this risk? Agent Sara puts that answer to work through waves. Together, they cover the full remediation lifecycle before, during, and after every deployment.

TruConfidence Before the Deployment

Once Qualys ETM and Agent Val have validated which exposures are exploitable and TruConfirm has credited the controls already in place, TruConfidence determines the right remediation path for each exposure.

Then you can determine whether a patch is needed at all. Patchless Remediation closes exposures by mitigating, uninstalling unused software, running a custom script or isolating the host. Third-Party Mitigation Intelligence extends those options through the tools teams already run, such as Zscaler and CrowdStrike.

When a patch is the right remediation action, the AI-Powered Patch Reliability Scoring predicts whether the patch is safe to deploy before it runs, drawing on global telemetry and Qualys customer deployments.

TruConfidence During the Rollout

Agent Sara efficiently implements TruConfidence’s decisions, eliminating ticket queues. She prioritizes eliminating the exploited 1% first and then automatically addresses the remaining vulnerabilities.

She organizes the backlog into remediation waves; each matched to its level of risk. You define the waves to fit your environment, and Agent Sara runs them.

A typical setup might look like this:

Easy Fixes: High-reliability patches on low-impact assets deploy zero-touch.

Connectivity-Sensitive: Changes are sequenced carefully to protect systems with critical network dependencies.

Operational Risk: Changes are held for closer review before proceeding.

Beyond Patching: Exposures are routed to the patchless path TruConfidence selected.

Every change moves through progressive rings, from Pilot to broad deployment, and is observed before it reaches the next tier. A low-reliability signal automatically pauses progression, keeping the blast radius as small as possible.

Agent Sara works within your rules, not around them, enforcing maintenance windows, asset groupings, and rollback controls, and requires human approval wherever a critical service, identity infrastructure, or production databases are involved.

TruConfidence After the Rollout

A successful install is not the finish line. Operational Resiliency continues to correlate health signals after each change, monitoring for CPU spikes, memory issues, and service impact. Stable metrics confirm the change held, while anomalies pause the rollout and trigger rollback. When a remediation fails, AI-Powered Failure Analysis explains the root cause in plain language, such as a pending reboot or a missing prerequisite, and recommends the corrective action. Every change ends with evidence, which means faster recovery and fewer war rooms.

Remediation that reaches every corner of your attack surface

TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 goes past agent-based endpoints. It extends remediation to perimeter devices, cloud and applications, so teams can deal with an exposure wherever it lives. Each asset gets the response that fits it: patch it, mitigate the risk when no patch exists yet, uninstall the vulnerable software, isolate the asset or apply a custom fix.

For assets that can’t host an agent, Eliminate works through Qualys scanners and the security and IT integrations you already have. Every exposure gets a path to remediation, not just the ones on managed endpoints.

TruRisk Eliminate already runs remediation at scale:

Each pass through the cycle first closes validated exposures and moves the long tail into the next waves, so the backlog shrinks continuously rather than piling up between change windows. And because every change is backed by proof, TruRisk Eliminate becomes both the system of record and the system of action for cyber risk reduction.

Passkey Authentications Double but Adoption Remains Slow

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

Passkeys are an increasingly common feature on log-in screens but widespread adoption remains relatively low, according to new data from Dashlane.

The credential security specialist analyzed millions of aggregated, anonymized passkey authentications that it managed between July 2025 and June 2026 to compile its third annual Passkey Power 20 report.

It revealed that passkey authentications by Dashlane users have nearly doubled year on year, reaching 2.5 million per month in 2026.

Additionally, over half (57%) of its users now store at least one passkey, compared with 40% last year.

However, the phishing-resistant authentication technology still accounts for a minority of logins on major sites like Google (28%), PayPal (18%), Amazon (17%) and eBay (8%).

Read more on passkeys: Half of Cybersecurity Pros Still Rely on Passwords Despite Security Concerns.

Passkeys are much harder for scammers to crack as there’s no password to guess or steal: the user logs in via a device PIN or biometric such as a face scan.

They are cryptographically tied to legitimate websites, and even if the latter were breached, the hacker wouldn’t have access to the user’s private key, which stays on their device.

That’s why institutions like Report Fraud recommend passkeys as one of the most effective ways to mitigate account takeover attacks.

Closing the Gap to Passkey Adoption

For businesses, passkeys can keep sensitive corporate data and systems safe and reduce the password-reset workload for IT support.

In this space, Dashlane noted an expansion in the number of applications supporting the login mechanism.

HubSpot and Cisco Duo led the way in terms of volume of authentications, but there were also new entrants to the top 20 in the form of HR and payroll platforms like isolved HCM and BambooHR, as well as AWS and Dropbox.

The key will be closing the gap between passkey support and adoption, Dashlane argued.

It pointed to four approaches:

Making passkeys highly visible and easy to use within existing workflows

Promoting passkeys as a faster alternative to passwords, with higher completion rates

Starting to remove alternatives like one-time passcodes and passwords

Setting a deadline for mandatory passkey use

Application developers forcing users to adopt passkeys are few and far between, although Japanese internet company LY Corporation has announced a spring 2027 deadline for Yahoo Japan users, the report noted.

More should at least make the system their default method for user logins, argued Dashlane CPO, Christophe Frenet.

“Despite sustained growth, we’re not on the other side yet,” he said. “There’s still more work to be done to make passkeys easier to use, and more companies need to go from soft adoption to enforcing the change, so that passkeys become the main authentication method rather than a secondary one, as they still are today.”

French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

While many supermarkets in France are still grappling with food stock disruptions due to a cyber-attack that targeted refrigeration controllers on October 11, the scope of the incident could be larger than previously observed.

Recent developments suggest that the incident does not only impact Danfoss refrigeration controllers, but also temperature regulation devices from Dixell Electronics, an Italian brand owned by American heating and cooling equipment provider Copeland.

Notably, French local media France 3 reported that an E. Leclerc supermarket in the Tarn region, in the south-west of France, experienced disruptions to its refrigeration systems, despite using Dixell equipment instead of Danfoss.

French national newspaper Le Monde also reported a supermarket near Bordeaux, where attackers reportedly changed freezer settings from −22°C to 150°C. A technician observed several settings being altered per second, suggesting automation.

A security advisory published by the French national Computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) on October 12 specifically named Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series as well as Dixell xweb and Copeland xweb as “affected systems.”

Fears of Deliberate Industrial Sabotage

Speaking to Infosecurity, Amir Preminger, CTO of industrial security provider Claroty, said refrigeration controllers are a prime target, not just for supermarkets but also cold-storage facilities, warehouses, pharmaceuticals, chemical manufacturing and more, that often go overlooked by security teams.

“Industrial control systems such as refrigeration controllers are often assumed to be on safely isolated networks, however, our research found many of these devices are directly exposed to the public internet. While this convenience significantly reduces maintenance costs by allowing engineers to troubleshoot issues remotely, it also lowers the barrier to entry for attackers,” he said.

Preminger assessed that while the attack did not necessarily require sophisticated skills, the targeting was a clear deliberate attempt to cause damage.

“I don’t think it’s sophisticated,” he said. “However, you cannot cause a defrost by mistake by typing the wrong parameter. You need to initiate the defrost. Somebody needed to guide the exploit, the campaign to have that impact.”

He compared the apparent tactic with an incident at a food-processing facility in Israelin 2025. In that case, an attacker inside the facility’s network manipulated a refrigeration compressor and caused it to defrost. While the impact was similar, Preminger did not claim the incidents involved the same group.

He argued that the broader concern was that refrigeration controllers were exposed to the internet. Preminger said such exposed Danfoss devices could be found outside of France too, including in Israel and the US, but he did not know what software versions those devices were running or whether they were vulnerable.

He also cautioned that patching alone does not make internet exposure safe. His advice was to keep critical devices off the public internet and restrict access through measures such as corporate virtual private networks (VPNs) or even access point name (APN) gateways.

He also urged operators to segment their networks, inventory their equipment, and know who can access each device. “Gate your devices, segment your devices. That’s the first frontier,” he said.

Why Supermarket Fridges Are Connected to the Internet

Supermarket fridges are generally connected to the internet to comply with legislation, which, in Europe, requires them to maintain timestamped monitoring of temperatures to strengthen food safety and to install an alarm system in case of an abnormal rise in temperature.

This connection also allows for remote maintenance.

“This is an essential system for the proper preservation of food products,” emphasized Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Coopérative U, in a post on X.

Title: Medicare scam calls, texts and ads: What to watch for this Open Enrollment
Context: And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity
Full Text:
Medicare Open Enrollment season is here, and so are the scams

Medicare scam calls, texts and ads: What to watch for this Open Enrollment

Open Enrollment is peak season for Medicare fraud – here’s how to tell real outreach from fakes and keep your details safe

Scammers love a pretext. And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity. From October 15 to December 7 beneficiaries are able to review and amend various parts of their plan. There’ll be ads, emails, messages and calls from genuine insurers at this time. Some might even ask for personal and health details.

That provides great cover for fraudsters, and enough plausibility for even skeptical consumers to drop their guard. Here’s what to look out for.

How do these Medicare scams work?

There are various ways scammers could approach you. They could call, message, email, or send a note on social media. They might also place an ad on Google, mocking up a website with official-looking logos and language to appear as if it’s a legitimate insurer, a specialist agency, or even Medicare itself.

The pretext for getting in touch, or posting the ad, could vary. Common ones include:

You should compare/change your plan by the December 7 deadline

Your Medicare card needs updating or replacing

You could qualify for additional benefits or lower premiums

Your existing coverage (or specific prescription coverage) is changing

You could be eligible for a new plan

They need to verify your account details

Your account has been linked to fraudulent activity

All seem plausible. But the scammer will usually employ some tried-and-tested social engineering techniques to pull you into their deceit. Urgency is a common tactic. It fires our synapses in specific ways that make us stressed and less likely to think logically, while possibly also triggering a fear of missing out. The real deadline of December 7 adds an element of truth to the lie that makes it more plausible still.

If you were told by an official-sounding representative that you could lose your benefits if you don’t act, or that you have just days to claim a lower premium offer, would you stop and think?

If they’re successful, the scammer will move on to the next stage: harvesting your personal, financial and/or medical information. They might ask for your:

Health information such as doctors, prescriptions and medical records

Insurance information including provider, plan, member ID and policy details

Bank details and/or credit card information

Once you’ve handed some or all of the above over, you’re unlikely to ever hear from the scammers again. But in the background, they’ll be working hard to monetize your information for their own gain.

What do they want with your data?

There are various ways they might do this, depending on what data they’ve tricked you into handing over. They might want to commit various forms of identity fraud, using your personal and financial details to access your bank and personal accounts, or take out new credit lines in your name.

Alternatively, they may try to use your information to submit fraudulent Medicare claims in your name, for services, equipment or prescriptions that you never received. Or to actually obtain these goods and services. Scammers might even try to manipulate your Medicare enrollment in order to generate fraudulent commissions or compensation.

In September 2026, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) identified around $17.5 billion in suspicious financial activity that may be linked to healthcare fraud like this.

Depending on exactly what avenue the scammers explore, an incident could leave you out of pocket, impact your coverage, impair your medical records, and plunge you into a bureaucratic nightmare that leaves you in severe emotional and mental distress.

How to spot and avoid Medicare scams

All of which makes it more important than ever that you’re able to spot the tell-tale signs of a Medicare scam at this time of year. You should be extremely dubious of any unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true.

Yes, genuine insurers might get in touch seemingly out of the blue. But this will usually not be without your prior consent. And they should never try to strong-arm you into handing over details.

The best approach to steering clear of Medicare scams during Open Enrollment season is to:

Spot the warning signs listed above, and if in doubt, put down the phone or don’t reply to the message. You can always verify separately with the caller/sender to check if they are legitimate (using contact details sourced separately from the inbound contact).

Be very careful about online searches. Don’t click through on any Google ads, and if you’re looking for official Medicare sites be sure the address has a .gov ending.

Type the name of the site you want to visit directly into the search/address bar. Medicare is at Medicare.gov (800-633-4227), while HealthCare.gov (800-318-2596) is where to check if you qualify for savings. Help is also available from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), or local Senior Medicare Patrol.

Report any suspicious contact.

Some insurers and other third parties may pick up the phone to get in touch during the Open Enrollment period. But you should be able to tell them apart from fraudsters because they will clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straight off the bat.

They should be courteous and provide you with ways to verify who they say they are, even if it means hanging up. And they’ll often be calling because you initiated contact with their organization.

What to do if you’ve already been scammed

If you feel like you’ve fallen victim to a Medicare scammer, don’t panic. Work through the following steps:

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general

If you have handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card

If you’ve handed over other identity-related information, consider reporting the incident to IdentityTheft.gov

Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges

Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity

Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on

Don’t fall for recovery fraud. If anyone gets in touch after an incident promising to get your money back or sort everything out on your account for a fee, it’s another scam

Your health is important. But so is your personal information. So slow down this Open Enrollment season and verify every request for personal and medical details.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

When is Medicare Open Enrollment?

It runs from October 15 to December 7 each year, during which time you can make some changes to your coverage.

Would Medicare or my insurer ever call me during Open Enrollment?

A representative from Medicare, your insurer or a third party may call. But put the phone down if they start pressuring you into handing over your details, asking for financial information, or promising too-good-to-be-true benefits. Call them directly to double check, eg 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

What are the main red flags for a Medicare scam?

Watch out for unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true. Contact could come via email, phone, social media, or text. Scammers might also buy Google ads to lure you.

What do Medicare scammers want?

They want your medical, financial, personal and possibly your insurance details. They might want this to commit identity fraud, access your bank account, submit fraudulent Medicare claims or obtain goods and services in your name, or manipulate your enrollment.

Can a Medicare scam affect my healthcare?

Yes. Fraudulent claims or misuse of your medical identity could impact your insurance coverage, medical records, prescriptions and access to healthcare. It may also land you with plenty of distressing administrative work to clear your name.

How do I know if a phone call is a Medicare scam or not?

They should clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straightaway. They should allow you to hang up and verify their identity. Usually they’ll only call because you have requested it.

What should I do after falling for a Medicare scam?

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general. If you’ve handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card. Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges. Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity. Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on. Don’t fall for recovery fraud scammers who promise to get your money back.

The Sovereign Advantage: Why MSPs Who Move First Will Control the Board

In chess, the first player to move gains more than a step. They shape how the board develops from that point on. Digital sovereignty works the same way. MSPs that make their sovereign move now build an advantage that could decide who leads the market.

That is the idea behind our webinar, The Sovereign Advantage: Move First to Control the Board, where Alina Drăgănescu (Deputy GM of the Business Solutions Group and SVP of Business Operations, Bitdefender) and Nadine Pilote (Managing Director, Septeo IT Solutions) join Mia Thompson (Senior Product Marketing Manager, Bitdefender) to discuss what it takes to build a sovereign, compliance-ready security practice.

Key webinar takeaways to expect

Understand the difference between data residency and data sovereignty.

Explore why cybersecurity sovereignty requires three forms of control working together: data, technical, and operational.

See how Bitdefender takes a unified approach that is European-built, European-operated, and EU-governed.

Learn how MSPs can add a sovereign service tier for regulated customers without changing their operating model.

Gain clarity on the ways Bitdefender EU Sovereign MDR brings sovereignty into security operations, with monitoring, investigation, and response delivered within the EU.

Why Does a Cybersecurity Platform Hold More Than Security Data?

A modern cybersecurity platform collects signals from across the organization, so it holds one of a client's richest operational datasets, not just security events.

Twenty years ago, security tools had a narrow view. Today, a cybersecurity platform brings together signals from endpoints, servers, identities, email, cloud workloads, networks, SaaS applications, and increasingly AI-powered tools. It does not just see security events. It sees how an organization operates.

That changes the questions buyers ask. They no longer stop at "can this platform protect us?" They want to know where the information is stored, who governs access to it, which laws apply, and who ultimately controls it?

What Are the Three Dimensions of Cybersecurity Sovereignty?

Cybersecurity sovereignty requires three forms of control that work together: data sovereignty (control over security data), technical sovereignty (control over the technology), and operational sovereignty (control over operations). Sovereignty is achieved only when all three are in place.

1. Data sovereignty: control over security data

Security telemetry, logs, and incident data stay protected under European governance, with EU-based storage and processing, controlled access, and trusted, certified sovereign European cloud infrastructure.

2. Technical sovereignty: control over the technology

The cybersecurity platform itself is governed under European jurisdiction, built on European-designed technology and the EU legal framework, with reduced exposure to non-EU legal authority.

3. Operational sovereignty: control over operations

Security services are delivered from the EU, with monitoring, investigation, and response staying within it.

A provider can store data in Europe, but without technical and operational sovereignty, jurisdictional risk may remain.

How Does Bitdefender Approach Cybersecurity Sovereignty?

Bitdefender takes a unified approach that combines data, technical, and operational control, delivered as European-built, European-operated, and EU-governed cybersecurity.

The outcome is not simply European data residency. It combines data, technical, and operational control, backed by European infrastructure, governance, and cybersecurity technology.

Bitdefender is headquartered and governed in the EU, and it develops its technology under EU jurisdiction. GravityZone is available through sovereign cloud deployments with European partners, including OVHcloud in France, Secunet in Germany, and Aruba in Italy.

How Can MSPs Add a Sovereign Service Tier Without Changing Their Operating Model

MSPs can keep their scalable operating model and add a sovereign service tier for regulated or sensitive customers, all on the same unified GravityZone platform. Sovereignty does not have to be an all-or-nothing infrastructure decision.

A strong approach is to start by understanding your customers:

Identify which industries, clients, datasets, and workloads carry the highest jurisdictional risk.

Define the level of sovereignty each one needs.

Introduce a sovereign tier where it creates genuine customer and commercial value.

What Is Bitdefender EU Sovereign MDR?

EU Sovereign MDR is AI-enabled, human-led 24/7 Managed Detection and Response delivered entirely within the EU sovereign operating model. It brings sovereignty into security operations, which matters because customers increasingly ask who can access their data during an investigation, and where the team doing that work sits. This is where Bitdefender MDR becomes a leading solution for sovereign-ready service delivery.

24/7/365 MDR delivered by EU experts from an EU-based SOC

All monitoring, investigations, and incident response remain within the EU

No follow-the-sun handoffs or case escalations outside the EU

Threat research, malware analysis, and detection engineering remain within the EU

AI-assisted investigations use sovereign-hosted LLMs, so customer data is never processed by public AI services

People, processes, tooling, and service delivery stay under EU control, even during incident response. For MSPs, it also means growing a security service without building a full security operations center themselves.

What Does "Moving First" Mean for MSPs?

Moving first means making the sovereignty choice before you are forced to, and acting before sovereignty becomes a mandatory line in every customer tender.

Both speakers close on this idea. For Alina, moving first looks like this:

Focus on the customers for whom jurisdiction matters most.

Build a sovereign-ready service option.

Train your commercial and technical teams to explain it.

Put processes in place to deliver it consistently.

The advantage is not simply saying you offer sovereign cybersecurity. It is being able to demonstrate how it works, where the data is processed, who governs the technology, and how customers stay protected without sacrificing operational effectiveness.

Title: TAG-193’s Regional Espionage Operations
Context: Observed in April 2026 and likely used against Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, this chain exploited the WinRAR vulnerability CVE-2025-8088 to place malware in the Windows...
Full Text:
Joint research by Cisco Talos and Recorded Future’s Insikt Group examined sustained cyber-espionage activity by TAG-193 targeting government organizations across Central Asia and the wider Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Tracked by Cisco Talos as UAT-6275 and also known as Silent Lynx, TAG-193 combines diplomatic and economic targeting with an interest in environmental policy, water resources, and forestry. Exposed infrastructure provided new visibility into its malware, operational practices, and evolving delivery techniques. The findings point to possible links to Kazakhstan, but questions remain about the group’s origins. This post highlights how TAG-193’s operations reflect the intelligence value of regional diplomacy and resource management, and how its expanding toolkit supports that mission.

Government Targeting across the Region

TAG-193’s targeting extends across government institutions responsible for diplomacy, economic development, agriculture, and environmental management. These organizations hold information that can inform negotiations, economic planning, and regional security decisions. Across Central Asia, shared river systems and interconnected energy and transport infrastructure give such information particular strategic value.

Figure 1: Timeline of TAG-193 campaigns

Our research examined TAG-193 campaigns from early 2025 through May 2026, identifying activity involving government entities in Russia, Tajikistan, Belarus, Armenia, and Uzbekistan. Lure documents and impersonated services indicated additional targeting interests across the region. Together, these findings suggest a sustained intelligence-collection mission encompassing diplomatic priorities and the management of natural resources.

Figure 2: Overview of TAG-193 victimology

Diplomacy, Water Security, and Resource Management

Several TAG-193 intrusions identified through Recorded Future® Network Intelligence occurred around diplomatic developments involving Kazakhstan. Following Kazakhstan’s parliamentary consideration of a treaty on allied relations with Tajikistan, we noted communications between a Tajik government entity responsible for economic development and TAG-193 infrastructure. Additionally, activity involving a Belarusian agriculture-related government entity preceded a senior bilateral meeting in Astana. While these temporal associations do not establish that the TAG-193-related activity was connected to the described developments or reveal what information the operators sought, they do provide context indicating TAG-193’s targeting interests.

TAG-193’s recurring interest in environmental and resource-management institutions is also noteworthy. Observed activity involved an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and infrastructure associated with Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, which supports digital forestry management, environmental monitoring, and ecological restoration. Additional targeting involved Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, at the confluence of the Volga and Oka rivers within the Caspian Sea basin. Although its geographic location alone does not establish a water-related collection objective, earlier reporting linked TAG-193 to the targeting of water-resource organizations across Central Asia, providing further context for this apparent interest.

In Kazakhstan, water security is closely tied to economic stability and national security. Dependence on cross-border water supplies leaves the country exposed to upstream decisions about water use, storage, and diversion. Climate change, glacier loss, and inefficient irrigation place additional pressure on water availability, with implications for agriculture, industry, and domestic supplies. The Aral Sea disaster illustrates the lasting economic, environmental, and public-health consequences of water mismanagement, helping explain why water security remains a strategic priority.

Trusted Accounts and Services Support Access

TAG-193 frequently sends spearphishing emails from compromised government accounts, using official-looking documents to make its communications credible. Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery. While not independently establishing successful compromises of the organizations these documents reference, they do indicate targeting interests.

Figure 3: Example lure document used by TAG-193

The group also uses public services such as GitHub to host malicious scripts and payloads. Together, trusted sender accounts and familiar hosting services help malicious content blend into routine government workflows.

Exposed directories on TAG-193 infrastructure revealed additional malware and a previously undocumented GitHub staging account. These operational security lapses enabled researchers to connect campaigns and trace changes in the group’s tooling.

An Evolving Toolkit

TAG-193 relies heavily on lightweight, interactive reverse shells that allow operators to issue commands on compromised systems. Its tooling includes LAPLAS, multiple FoalShell variants, and PowerShell-based reverse shells. Analysis of recovered samples identified four infection-chain types, including a newly observed chain using exploit-assisted delivery.

Observed in April 2026 and likely used against Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, this chain exploited the WinRAR vulnerability CVE-2025-8088 to place malware in the Windows Startup folder, enabling execution when the user next signed in. The activity demonstrated the group’s adoption of vulnerability exploitation alongside its established social engineering techniques.

Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available FortiWeb exploit recovered from TAG-193 infrastructure suggest that TAG-193 is interested in expanding its operational capabilities. However, the research did not confirm that the group exploited the FortiWeb vulnerability in the wild.

Clues to TAG-193’s Origins

Russian-language artifacts, apparent malware-testing submissions from Kazakhstan, and activity patterns consistent with Kazakhstan’s working hours collectively support an assessment that TAG-193 likely operates from Kazakhstan. These indicators inform the geographic assessment but do not establish the group’s organizational affiliation or state sponsorship, both of which remain unresolved.

Figure 4: TAG-193 activity analysis

Looking Ahead

TAG-193 is likely to continue targeting government, diplomatic, and resource-management organizations across the region. Its sustained operations and adoption of additional delivery techniques suggest continued investment in gaining access to institutions holding information of strategic interest.

For defenders, the findings underscore the importance of protecting environmental agencies, forestry platforms, and economic ministries, as well as foreign affairs and national security institutions. Monitoring for compromised email accounts, malicious content hosted on trusted public services, and unexpected remote-access activity can help identify intrusions that begin with seemingly routine government communications.

For further details on this research and our accompanying presentation, see “Break the Silence: Tracking Silent Lynx Through Exposed Infrastructure” on Virus Bulletin’s website, as well as Cisco Talos’s related blog post, “Break The Silence: Kazakhstan-Nexus UAT-6275 Targets Government And Energy Organizations Across The CIS”.

About Insikt Group®

Recorded Future’s Insikt Group, the company’s threat research division, comprises analysts and security researchers with deep government, law enforcement, military, and intelligence agency experience. Its mission is to produce intelligence that reduces risk for customers, enables tangible outcomes, and prevents business disruption.

Title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
Context: At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an...
Full Text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

Title: An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
Context: OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office
Full Text:
An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, whom federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room.

He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing.

OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office.

Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US District Court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest.

FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but neither prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.”

OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep.

Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview, Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations.

The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment.

Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies.

Executives Only

According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.”

The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated.

OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted.

After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing.

According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found.

He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

Internal Reconnaissance: A High-Volume, Noisy Campaign

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.

The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.

Authentication Abuse and Documentation Browsing

The pattern continued with credential testing. Over a period of a few months, the threat actor launched multiple password-guessing campaigns. They hammered at internal systems with brute-force authentication attempts, focusing on administrator accounts.

While doing this, they systematically targeted internal documentation and data shares. Using automated web requests, they scraped individual pages and attachments from internal systems and enumerated various operational and network shares.

The activity observed did not match the behavior typically associated with a sophisticated threat actor. The noise behind the scanning and login attempts, along with using common system identifiers, pointed to an opportunistic attacker attempting to compromise multiple systems. Their actions showed little effort to remain hidden or avoid detection.

Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation

In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code execution vulnerability on the central configuration management server. This server handled software distribution across the bank, making it a prime target for privilege escalation and long-term persistence.

However, the attacker's luck ran out. The moment they attempted to execute unauthorized code, Cortex XDR identified the activity and contained the threat before it could escalate. The attacker was prevented from gaining a persistent foothold or moving laterally throughout the network.

When Unit 42 engaged, our team initiated a comprehensive threat-hunting effort. We performed a deep forensic review of endpoint telemetry across approximately thousands of systems, alongside logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. Ultimately, no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors were found. Bank leadership acted quickly to review the exposed documentation and rotate all compromised credentials, completely neutralizing the threat.

What This Investigation Revealed

This case serves as a critical reminder that not every cyber threat is advanced and multifaceted. Opportunistic actors will gladly take advantage of simple oversight, such as missing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a VPN or an unpatched edge device, to compromise and break into an environment. That being said, an attacker's lack of sophistication doesn't make them harmless.

Defending against this type of intrusion relies on foundational security hygiene and swift response. This includes:

Enforcing strict identity access controls

Ensuring timely patching

Using endpoint detection to stop lateral movement

By pairing timely containment with thorough threat hunting, the organization prevented the intrusion from turning into a catastrophic event.

Outcomes

Unit 42 independently validated the incident to confirm the root cause, restoring leadership confidence through strategic guidance and complete incident management. Beyond resolving the immediate threat, we delivered specific, prioritized recommendations to harden the bank's security posture. To ensure enhanced protection, the organization expanded its defensive coverage by deploying additional Cortex XSIAM and Cortex XDR licenses and broadening its incident response retainer service.

Title: Fake WatchGuard VPN Site Steals Credentials
Context: ]net As of October 8, detections for the domains linked to this attack were thin, which is not totally surprising given that the domains weren't actually deploying malware
Full Text: Acknowledgments: Thanks to Stephanie Fairless and Andrew Brandt for their help in analysing this attack. Background A simple search on Google or Bing for a VPN client download may seem like a run-of-the-mill task, but it can also expose users to convincing credential phishing sites. In January 2026, WatchGuard's Secplicity team published research into a credential-harvesting campaign targeting VPN providers, covering lookalike download sites for WatchGuard, F5, Fortinet, SonicWall, and Sophos clients. This campaign included two domains impersonating WatchGuard itself: watchguard-vpn[.]com and watchguard-vpn[.]net. The findings included a .NET executable posing as their Mobile VPN with SSL application, served from a GitHub repository, that sent entered credentials to a command-and-control (C2) server. Researchers said they also observed Bing's Copilot recommending watchguard-vpn[.]net when asked about "watchguard vpn," although at the time of their research that domain had "no backend logic to direct users to the spoofed downloads page." Two months later, Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported activity linked specifically to watchguard-vpn[.]com. Microsoft attributed this wider campaign iteration to Storm-2561, a financially motivated actor that has been active since May 2025. The attack chain highlighted by Microsoft involved pushing spoofed vendor sites up the search results, delivering a signed, fake MSI that sideloads malicious DLLs, harvesting credentials typed into a fake client, and then showing an installation error and pointing the victim to the real vendor download so nothing looks wrong afterwards. Fast forward to October: the Huntress SOC analyzed an incident that involved one of the initial domains that WatchGuard had reported back in January – watchguard-vpn[.]net – that was consistent with previous reports of this credential-theft campaign targeting WatchGuard VPN credentials. However, further investigation into the incident showed that this latest iteration of the attack chain is slightly different. Rather than downloading a fake client, the domain instead downloads a genuine, validly signed WatchGuard installer. As of October 13, the main domain linked to the activity Huntress observed (watchguard-vpn[.]net) was offline. Prior to publishing, Huntress notified WatchGuard about this active campaign and shared the relevant infrastructure details. Figure 1: End-to-end flow of the WatchGuard VPN credential phish. Technical Details Initial access: A typo and a search engine On October 7, Huntress Managed Defender flagged suspicious activity that stemmed back to activity from a user account at a managed service provider. Further investigation into the incident revealed that an administrator had searched Bing for "watchguard vpn sll download." Eight seconds later, they clicked through to www.watchguard-vpn[.]net, a page titled "WatchGuard Firebox VPN Client." The click went through Bing's standard bing.com/ck/a result redirect, with the destination encoded in the u= parameter (aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud2F0Y2hndWFyZC12cG4ubmV0Lw decodes to hxxps://www.watchguard-vpn[.]net/). This redirect is consistent with a standard Bing search-result click and, alongside the lookalike domain's apparent search-result placement, supports classifying the lure as SEO poisoning rather than malvertising. Secplicity and Microsoft have also described related activity in this campaign as SEO poisoning. Figure 2: The lookalike domain for a routine VPN download search. We took a closer look at watchguard-vpn[.]net as part of our investigation. The malicious domain Video: The attack chain When targets arrive at watchguard-vpn[.]net, they see a domain that pretends to be the legitimate WatchGuard website, and offers an option to "Download WatchGuard SSL VPN." The fake WatchGuard website also includes information about WatchGuard products and a "WatchGuard Mobile VPN Questions" section (likely meant to bolster SEO ranking). Ironically, at the bottom of the page, the website includes the disclaimer: "An independent English-language fan site about WatchGuard Mobile VPN. Not an official sales, download, or support channel." Figures 3 and 4: The malicious domain (left) versus the actual legitimate WatchGuard domain (right) When targets click through the site, they are sent to the download page at watchguard-vpn[.]net/index.php, which poses as a "WatchGuard Support Page" and gives several options for downloading the VPN for different OS configurations. Credential capture: Inside popup.js Clicking on any of the download options presents victims with a pop-up prompt that reads "To install WatchGuard SSL VPN, please enter your connection details" and asks for three things: Server, Login, and Password. The phishing logic lives in a single file, popup.js, about 150 lines of plain, unobfuscated JavaScript. Figures 5 and 6: Targets are taken to a download page (left) and when they click "Download" the credential prompt is shown (right) The legitimate Mobile VPN with SSL client also asks for these three values when users connect, so the prompt looks reasonable. Notably, the "Server" field is particularly useful for the attacker—it gives them the VPN server's address that they can authenticate to. The submission handler sends the form contents to the collection domain: Loading Gist... The user's typed input is wrapped in JSON and posted to watchguard-ssl[.]online, tagged to indicate whether this is the first or second attempt. The fetch is wrapped in a try/catch statement that only logs a console warning on failure, so even if the collector is down, the user sees nothing unusual. Interestingly, the attack chain purposefully rejects the first submission into this pop-up from the target. The script clears all three fields and replaces the header with red text: headerText.innerHTML = 'Incorrect data, please enter again to start installation'; attempt = 2; Anyone who mistyped their passwords will now type more carefully, and anyone unsure which of their passwords applies is likely to try the other one, so the attacker gets a second set of credentials to validate against, with the attempt tag marking which submission came last. Figures 7 and 8: The forced "Incorrect data" message after the first submission (left) and then the second prompt (right) The twist: The payload is the real thing After the second submission, the pop-up turns green ("VPN client installation has started"), and the script creates a hidden link and clicks it: const DOWNLOAD_FILE = 'https://cdn.watchguard.com/SoftwareCenter/Files/MUVPN_SSL/12_11_5/WG-MVPN-SSL_12_11_5.exe'; This is WatchGuard's official CDN. The file is a Inno Setup installer for "Mobile VPN with SSL client", version 12.11.5, copyright WatchGuard Technologies. It carries an Authenticode signature from WatchGuard Technologies, Inc., issued by Sectigo Public Code Signing CA R36, with a countersignature timestamp of 4 November 2025. We recomputed the Authenticode SHA256 digest of the file (fb3c39ba…0032ac1f) and it matches the digest in the signature, so the binary has not been modified since WatchGuard signed it. For attackers, the use of a real, signed VPN client makes the phishing attack far more convincing, and more difficult to detect. First of all, there's no trojanized installer or malicious DLL for security defenses to flag. Second of all, victims are still getting their expected outcome. Because they're still getting an actual installer, this alleviates any suspicions. This is a twist on the same idea in the attack chain that Microsoft highlighted, where attackers sent the victim to the real installer afterwards so nothing looks wrong—but now with the fake client removed from the middle. In the particular case that we investigated, the browser history actually recorded no download from cdn.watchguard.com for the timeframe in question. Because the script only triggers the download after the second submission, this suggests the user did not complete both rounds, although they may have entered their credentials in the first round. Huntress Managed Defender flagged the incident 21 seconds after the malicious domain loaded, and the SOC was able to provide the organization with remediation steps before the attack could escalate. Old domain, new backend The WHOIS record for watchguard-vpn[.]net shows a creation date of August 22, 2026, with Realtime Register B.V. as registrar. Secplicity recorded the same domain in January resolving to 74.208.236[.]39; as of October 9 it resolves to 80.249.132[.]140 on Site BV hosting (LeaseWeb Netherlands, AS60781). This indicates the domain was registered again after WatchGuard's January observation, but available evidence does not establish whether the same operators controlled both registrations. The current iteration hosted a working credential-harvesting flow. The credential collection endpoint, watchguard-ssl[.]online, was registered through Dynadot on September 14, 2026 and resolves to 158.94.209[.]19 (Omegatech LTD, AS202412, Amsterdam). The table below outlines an infrastructure timeline for the lure and collection domains. Date (UTC) Event Jan 13 2026 Secplicity reports watchguard-vpn[.]net (then 74.208.236[.]39) with no backend Aug 22 2026 watchguard-vpn[.]net (resolving to resolves to 80.249.132[.]140) registered (Realtime Register B.V.) Sep 14 2026 watchguard-ssl[.]online registered (Dynadot) Sep 17 and 22 2026 urlscan.io submissions of watchguard-vpn[.]net Oct 7 2026 Victim lands on www.watchguard-vpn[.]net As of October 8, detections for the domains linked to this attack were thin, which is not totally surprising given that the domains weren't actually deploying malware. Only seven VirusTotal vendors flagged the lure domain, and two flagged the collector, with no AbuseIPDB reports against either IP. Conclusion This attack chain raises the bar by removing the malware component and making it harder to detect. The operators give victims a convincing installation experience while bypassing many endpoint-focused security controls, through collecting VPN credentials in the browser and then delivering the legitimate, signed WatchGuard installer from WatchGuard's own CDN. If you think you entered credentials on this or a similar site, you should immediately reset the password for every affected account and treat the VPN endpoint associated with those credentials as known to the attacker. Defenders should also enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) on top of a username and password. Monitor for SSL VPN logins from hosting providers, unfamiliar ASNs, or countries where the account has never connected from. Defenders should also block watchguard-vpn[.]net and watchguard-ssl[.]online as well as the IPs outlined in the IOC section below. Finally, defenders should publish (and bookmark) official VPN-client download links, including software.watchguard.com, in client documentation. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) Item Description watchguard-vpn[.]net Lookalike WatchGuard VPN download page hosting the credential modal (registered 2026-08-22) 80.249.132[.]140 Lure hosting, Site BV / LeaseWeb Netherlands (AS60781) watchguard-ssl[.]online Credential collection endpoint receiving JSON POSTs (registered 2026-09-14) 158.94.209[.]19 Collector hosting, Omegatech LTD (AS202412), Amsterdam popup.js Credential capture modal script; fields server, login, password, attempt

New Proofpoint-Ponemon Institute report finds nearly three in four U.S. healthcare organizations experienced disruption to patient care due to cyberattacks

SUNNYVALE, Calif.– October 13, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, and Ponemon Institute, a top IT security research organization, today released findings from their fifth annual Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare report, revealing that cyberattacks are increasing in frequency, cost, and operational impact across U.S. healthcare organizations.

97% of organizations surveyed experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks climbed to 51, from 43 in 2025, and the average cost of the most expensive cyberattack rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million. AI adoption is also outpacing governance, with AI agents operating without guardrails emerging as a leading cause of data loss, cited by 24% of respondents.

“Cyber resilience has become essential to healthcare resilience,” said Ryan Kalember, chief strategy officer, Proofpoint. “When a cyberattack delays a procedure, extends a hospital stay, or forces patients to another facility, cyber risk becomes patient risk. AI is now adding another dimension as people and AI systems access the same sensitive data and clinical workflows. Healthcare organizations need security built around those interactions so they can adopt AI without compromising the trust patient care depends on.”

This year’s report, based on responses from 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare organizations, highlights several trends:

Operational disruption is becoming healthcare’s biggest cyber cost

More attacks are driving higher costs and greater disruption. The average cost of the most expensive cyberattack increased from $3.9 million in 2025 to $4.2 million in 2026.

Downtime and recovery carry the greatest financial impact. Disruption to normal healthcare operations averaged $1.39 million—the single largest cost category—followed by $1.05 million from idle time and lost productivity.

AI adoption is moving faster than governance

AI is becoming part of healthcare operations and security. 45% of organizations have embedded AI in cybersecurity or both cybersecurity and patient care, while another 30% plan to adopt it.

Security and governance have not kept pace. 60% lack controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems, only 42% use security measures specifically designed for AI systems, agents and generative AI, and just 32% have full visibility into employees’ use of unsanctioned AI tools.

AI is introducing new dependencies and data risks. Supply chain risk from AI vendors (40%), data leakage through prompts (36%) and AI-generated phishing and social engineering (34%) are organizations’ leading AI-specific concerns.

Cyber disruption is reaching the bedside

Cyberattacks are directly affecting patient care. Across the four attack types studied—cloud/account compromise, ransomware, supply chain attacks, and business email compromise (BEC) —an average of 53% of respondents reporting care disruption cited increased complications from medical procedures, 52% cited longer patient stays, and 52% cited delays in tests or procedures.

Supply chain attacks had the greatest impact on patient care. 90% of organizations experiencing these attacks reported care disruption, up from 87% in 2025. Ransomware was most associated with longer patient stays (70%), while BEC was most associated with delays in procedures and tests resulting in poor outcomes (68%).

Data loss is also a patient-care risk. Organizations experienced an average of 21 data loss or exfiltration incidents involving sensitive healthcare information over two years. 54% said these incidents disrupted patient care; among that group, 56% reported increased mortality rates. Employee negligence remained the leading reported cause of data loss, while AI agents without guardrails emerged as a cause for 24%.

Healthcare’s move to the cloud is raising the stakes of account compromise. 35% of organizations have moved clinical applications to the cloud, up from 30% in 2025, while another 44% plan to do so within the next two years. Yet cloud/account compromises — up to 20 per organization on average — disrupted patient care for 65% of respondents, a number climbing as adoption accelerates.

Ransomware payments decline, but disruption persists

Fewer organizations are paying ransoms, and payments are falling. 31% of organizations experiencing ransomware paid, down from 33% in 2025, while the average costliest ransom payment fell from $1.2 million to $1.1 million.

The clinical consequences remain significant. 72% of organizations experiencing ransomware reported patient-care disruption, up from 67% in 2025. Among those reporting disruption, 70% cited longer patient stays.

Healthcare Cyberattacks Hit Harder, Cost More

Study Warns of Rising Attacks, Care Disruptions, Added Costs and New AI Risks Marianne Kolbasuk McGee (HealthInfoSec) • October 13, 2026

Credit Eligible

The frequency of cyberattacks on healthcare organizations, the disruption of those incidents on patient care, workflow and hospital operations - and their associated financial costs - are climbing, according to new research.

See Also: Live Webinar | Hurtling Toward a Cybersecurity Crisis: The Hidden AI Risks Businesses Can’t See

A survey of 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare institutions conducted in May 2026 found that nearly all organizations had experienced at least one cyberattack within the last year, according to the new report by the research firm Ponemon Institute and security vendor Proofpoint released on Tuesday.

Operational disruption expenses related to the attacks now account for the single-largest cost of a cyberattack, averaging $1.39 million, the research found. That's up from $1.2 million in 2025, which includes expenses stemming from system unavailability.

"When critical systems go down, the consequences extend well beyond financial losses to delayed procedures, longer hospital stays and interruptions in essential patient services," said Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint.

We're seeing more attacks, higher costs and greater disruption to patient care," she told ISMG.

In fact, 97% of survey respondents said their organizations experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks organizations reported also rose - to 51, from 43 in 2025.

The average cost of the most expensive cyberattack also rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million, up from $3.9 million in 2025.

"What concerns me most is that cyberattacks are increasingly becoming healthcare operational crises, not just IT incidents," Biddle said.

But when it comes to the costs associated with the attacks, fewer healthcare organizations are paying extortion demands even as ransomware continues to disrupt patient care. "It's a reminder that avoiding a ransom payment doesn't necessarily mean avoiding the consequences of an attack," she said.

"Ultimately, the findings point to a broader shift in how we think about healthcare cybersecurity. Success can't be measured only by the attacks stopped or data protected. It also has to be measured by whether clinicians can continue doing their jobs and patients can continue receiving care."

At the same time, healthcare providers are embracing AI faster than they can secure and govern it, she said. The survey found that 45% of organizations have embedded AI in cybersecurity - or in both cybersecurity and patient care - while another 30% plan to adopt it.

Sixty percent of the respondents admitted their organizations lacked controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems, with only 42% saying they use security measures designed for AI.

Those Ponemon Institute/Proofpoint findings appear to sync with other recent findings by other researchers. For instance, recent research by privacy and security consulting firm Clearwater found similar gaps between AI adoption in healthcare and the lack of governance (see: Healthcare AI Governance Has Visibility Problem).

AI technologies hold enormous promise for improving care and efficiency, but many organizations still lack the visibility and governance needed to manage the risks, Biddle said. "That gap is particularly concerning in an industry where sensitive data and operational continuity are so closely tied to patient outcomes."

The AI-specific risk of greatest concern according to nearly 40% of the survey respondents was supply chain risk from AI vendors. That was followed by other AI risk concerns, including data leakage via prompts; AI-generated phishing and social engineering scams; inadequate privacy protections; and non-compliant tool usage.

"Healthcare organizations don't necessarily need to slow AI adoption, but security needs to evolve alongside it rather than follow it," Biddle told ISMG. That starts with understanding where AI is being used, what sensitive information it can access and what actions AI agents are permitted to take.

"Our research found that 60% of organizations lack controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems. That's a gap healthcare leaders need to prioritize as AI becomes more embedded in clinical and operational workflows."

But healthcare organizations can't neglect human risks that have long made the sector vulnerable, from phishing and compromised accounts to employee mistakes and data loss, she said. "As people and AI agents increasingly work alongside one another, the priority should be protecting those interactions while ensuring critical healthcare services remain available."

Resiliency in the face of disruptive healthcare cyberattacks was also top of mind of many experts who spoke at the ISMG HealthSec cybersecurity summit in New York City last week.

"Moving from cyber defense to cyber resilience is important for anybody in any sector, but I would argue that it's even more important for the healthcare sector," said Guru Gurushankar, senior vice president and general manager of healthcare and life sciences at security firm Color Tokens.

"In healthcare, I cannot turn away patients during the downtime. I cannot turn away ambulances. I cannot reschedule elective surgeries and even emergent surgeries," he said. Cyber resilience plays a critical role in delivering uninterrupted clinical care, he said. That requires certain key technical controls.

"Microsegmentation has to be core essential because that is the proactive way in which you prevent a simple breach incident from becoming a large-scale catastrophic incident," he said.

Proofpoint's Biddle said she expects the line between cybersecurity and healthcare resilience to become increasingly blurred.

"As clinical applications move to the cloud and AI becomes more embedded in everyday workflows, healthcare organizations will face growing pressure to secure not just their systems and data, but the processes that keep patient care moving," she said.

The question will increasingly shift from whether an organization can prevent every attack to how effectively it can maintain and restore critical services when something goes wrong, she added.

"AI will add another dimension to that challenge. As agents take on more responsibility, healthcare organizations will need to move beyond governing who can access sensitive information to understanding what AI systems can do with it," she said.

AI governance, data protection and third-party risk will ultimately become much more central to healthcare cybersecurity strategies moving forward, she predicted.

European Retail Firms Confirm Cyber Incidents

Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

Several retail firms across Europe have confirmed cyber incidents that are causing operational disruptions.

On October 12, Netherlands-based multinational retail company Ahold Delhaize confirmed it was experiencing “a security issue” within its networks and had to take “some systems offline” to protect them.

The disruption was reported to affect three of the group’s brands, including supermarket chain Albert Heijn, operating in the Netherlands and Belgium, Dutch drugstore chain Etos and Dutch liquor store chain Gall & Gall.

The next day, Reuters reported that South African retail group The Foschini Group (TFG), owner of high-street fashion brands Hobbs and Whistles, was investigating a “cyber incident.”

The press agency said TFG became aware of an incident on October 11 affecting its UK subsidiary TFG London, with “certain IT systems” impacted.

Specifically, it was reported that the affected brands include Phase Eight and Hobbs and Whistles brands.

The South African group added there is “no reason to believe that payment information is at risk” at this stage. Other TFG high street brands, including Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected. The group’s TFG Africa and TFG Australia subsidiaries are also not experiencing any operational disruption.

TFG said it had reported the incident to the relevant UK authorities.

Commenting on this TFG incident, Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, noted, “The fact that Inside Story and White Stuff within the same group were unaffected, and that TFG’s wider Africa and Australia operations were untouched, suggests some degree of system separation was in place. That separation, which limited the blast radius, is worth noting as a positive.”

Additionally, according to The Times, H&M is also examining information circulating online about a potential incident.

However, at the time of writing, the retailer said it had found no indication that its data environment had been compromised.

There is currently no indication that these incidents are in any way related to each other.

ASOS Confirms Scope of Cyber-Attack

The incidents come days after customers of UK fashion retailer ASOS received a strange push notification indicating the company was hacked.

While the firm confirmed the unauthorized intrusion into “third-party platforms” it uses to communicate with customers and that personal information including names and contact details and some non-personal account related information “have been accessed,” it reiterated, in its latest customer update, published on October 13, that no payment-card information or account passwords were impacted.

The latest alerts also come as many supermarket chains in France are still dealing with a large-scale cyber-attack where attackers tampered with refrigeration controlling systems in the night between October 11 and 12, leading to the loss of a large amount of food products and financial losses estimated in hundreds of thousands of euros.
